News.title: Son, 31, shoots dead University professor dad and stepmom before torching his car – as he smirks in chilling mugshot
News.content:
IN COLD BLOOD Son, 31, shoots dead University professor dad and stepmom before torching his car – as he smirks in chilling mugshot







Next

A UNIVERSITY professor and his wife have allegedly been gunned down by the educator’s son, who flashed a chilling smile in a mugshot.

Asia Nguyen-Duy also known as Daniel Jones, 31, was arrested after claiming “full responsibility” for the killings in a chilling video filmed after the alleged double murder.



Pipo Nguyen-Duy, 64, and his wife, Tran Thi Phong, 56, were found dead with multiple gunshot wounds at their Ohio home on Wednesday.

Shocking courtroom footage captured by NBC shows four officers dragging a completely limp Nguyen-Duy to the defence table during a hearing on Thursday.



Plastered across the suspect‘s forehead is the acronym “EBK”, slang for “everybody killa.”

Prosecutors claim Nguyen-Duy knocked on a stranger’s door after the bloody killings and asked a woman to record a video of so it could be posted online.

In the chilling clip Nguyen-Duy appeared to confess to the killings and claimed to be escaping a cult, according to the prosecutor.

Nguyen-Duy said: “Everything I did was on my own accord and I take full responsibility.”



The two bodies were discovered on the first and second floors of their Oberlin home, respectively, after police tracked down the son and conducted a welfare check on his family.

Officers later found Nguyen-Duy with scratches and injuries to the face and arms.

The suspect allegedly confessed to police and directed them to where the bodies could be found, prosecutors said.



The weapon used in the shooting has not been found.

Prior to the arrest, police had found a smoldering car earlier that morning which was later found to be the suspects.

Inside Nguyen-Duy’s charred Toyota hatchback, firefighters found personal items stuffed in a cardboard box, including a passport and keys.

Live ammunition rounds were also recovered from Nguyen-Duy’s car.

The suspect was hit with six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault, and one count of tampering with evidence, and is being held in the Lorain County Jail.



Nguyen-Duy is being held on a $3 million bond.

The case has been bound over to Lorain County Common Pleas Court, where it will next go before a grand jury.

The suspected killer reportedly had several run-ins with police dating back to 2016, according to court record obtained by The Post.

These include incidents of theft, invasion of personal privacy and reckless driving.

The slain father was a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College and Conservatory which has been rocked the tragedy.



Studio art classes were paused or modified in the wake of the professor’s death.

An exhibit of his internationally acclaimed photography was placed on display at the campus art museum to provide students, alumni and collaborators a place to gather.

Carmen Twillie Ambar, president of Oberlin College and Conservatory, called it a deeply challenging moment for our community.

She said: “I am simply overwhelmed with sadness, and I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community.”

Earlier this month, a grandfather killed eight people including his own pregnant daughter.



Angelina Stone, 24, was gunned down alongside her children, five-year-old Isiah, two-year-old Amari’anna and unborn baby Kyrie.

It is understood that eight of the nine victims were related with the ninth identified as a family friend.

The 45-year-old suspect was found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot in the family home in Pennsylvania.

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said:“It was horrific. It was the worst scene I have ever experienced,”

News.title: Fears grow for teen, 18, who vanished after night out in UK town as cops ‘extremely concerned’
News.content:
DESPERATE HUNT Fears grow for teen, 18, who vanished after night out in UK town as cops ‘extremely concerned’







Next

FEARS are growing for a teenager who vanished after a night out as cops say they are “extremely concerned” for the boy.

James, 18, failed to return to his home in Swadlincote, Derbyshire, after going out in nearby Ashby-de-la-Zouch.

The teenager has not been in touch with his friends or family since leaving home on Thursday evening.

He was reported missing with cops now launching an appeal for the public’s help locating James.





The 18-year-old is described as white, around 6ft 4ins, of stocky, muscular build and with brown hair.

He was last seen wearing jeans, a brown jumper and black trainers.

A spokesperson for Derbyshire police said: “We are appealing for urgent help finding James, who is missing after a night in Ashby-de-la-Zouch.

“It is completely out of character and we are extremely concerned for his welfare.

“Officers are searching for him but we are also want to hear from anyone who has seen James or knows where he might be now.

“Anyone who can help should contact us immediately quoting incident 690 of October 30.”

News.title: Can I report my neighbour for setting off fireworks? Full laws and rules explained
News.content:
Next

BONFIRE Night is fast approaching, but Brits could be breaking the law without even realising it, with strict rules on when and where fireworks can legally be set off.

Those caught flouting the rules risk hefty fines, an unlimited penalty or even up to six months behind bars.

While fireworks are allowed to be privately used, it is against the law for anyone to set off fireworks between 11pm and 7am.



On Bonfire Night (November 5), the 11pm to 7am rule is extended by one hour, so you can continue to use fireworks up until midnight.



If a neighbour continues to use fireworks beyond this time, they can be reported to the police.

The law also says you must not set off or throw fireworks (including sparklers) in the street or other public places.

Individuals doing so, at any time, can be reported to the police.



While fireworks are legal, they can only be bought during certain times of the year in the UK.

They can be bought between October 15 to November 10, December 26 to December 31 and 3 days before Diwali and Chinese New Year.

Individuals found breaking these rules can be fined an unlimited amount and imprisoned for up to 6 months for selling or using fireworks illegally.

Rule breakers could also get an on-the-spot fine of £90.

The PM expressed his personal “sorrow and regret” for the suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade.

He ruled out considering financial reparations however and added that he wanted to offer a “structured dialogue” with those affected.

Writing in The Guardian, Mr Burnham said: “Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do.





“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave.

News.title: Evacuated residents from Russian-occupied city finally arrive in Ukraine after ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump
News.content:
Next

EVACUEES from Russian-occupied Oleshky have finally arrived back in Ukraine after a rare truce brokered by Melania Trump.

Residents draped in Ukrainian flags were disembarking buses and tearfully embracing their loved-nes after arriving from the war-ravaged city.



Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location.

Volodymyr Zelensky thanked the United States and first lady Melania for their mediation in a post on Telegram.



The Ukrainian leader wrote: “When the world pays attention, people are rescued.

“Further steps toward de-escalation and real progress toward peace are also needed.”

After leaving Oleshky, the residents had travelled by bus to Crimea before flying to Belarus and then onward to Ukraine via a border crossing.

The operation was carried out under the most significant ceasefire since Russia‘s illegal invasion of Ukraine four years ago.



The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, which began at 3 am on Tuesday, is expected to continue through Sunday evening.

An estimated 2,000 remaining residents in Oleshky were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.



Volunteers from organisations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.

Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2 years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.

“We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed,” she said.

Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.

He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours, but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family’s home and animals fell through.



Daria said: “We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it that was the last time they saw him.”

She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Russia’s ombudswoman and lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia.

Civilians were seen on Saturday arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol, Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but Melania said on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.



Apart from Melania, Pope Leo XIV also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.

News.title: Letting off fireworks this weekend could land you with £5,000 fine, cops warn
News.content:
Next

POLICE have issued a warning to avoid being fined £5,000 when letting off fireworks over the Bonfire Night period.

Brits across the country will be attending firework displays, but if you’re letting off fireworks yourself, there are strict rules you need to follow in order to avoid a hefty fine.

The North Herefordshire Police recently reminded the public that it is illegal to let off fireworks in a public place, with offenders facing a fine of up to £5,000 or a £90 fixed penalty notice.



In addition to this, they also warned that selling fireworks to anyone under the age of 18 is against the law.



This can result in a maximum fine of £5,000 and/or six months in prison.

The police force also issued a reminder that all sold fireworks must comply with CE safety standards.

The sale of bangers, mini rockets, aerial shells, maroons and fireworks that fly erratically is also considered illegal.

The police also noted that they have the power to stop and search anyone they suspect of carrying fireworks.

A statement read: “Irresponsible use of fireworks can damage property, cause injury, scare people (particularly the elderly) and frighten animals.

“Please remember these rules to keep yourself and everyone else safe, and to reduce anti-social behaviour.

“We hope you have a safe and enjoyable time, but please be considerate to others.”



Also, fireworks cannot be set off between 11 pm and 7 am on most days, but this rule is extended by one hour to midnight on Bonfire Night.

Safer Neighbourhood Team officers will be carrying out patrols throughout the coming weeks and on Bonfire Night itself.

News.title: Ukraine hits Putin with kamikaze drones launched from weather balloons sparking chaos at Russian airports
News.content:
Next

UKRAINE has launched kamikaze drones from weather balloons in a blitz on Moscow’s busiest airport – sparking travel chaos across the country, reports say.

Incredible images appear to show a high-altitude balloon dangling a drone, as nearly 1,000 flights are grounded nationwide.



Thousands of passengers were left stranded across Russia on Saturday as Volodymyr Zelensky ramps up efforts to cripple the capital’s airspace.

Pro-Kremlin war channels have confirmed the use of a new tactic, noting: “This is the device the enemy is using to target the Russian capital in an attempt to disrupt the Moscow aviation hub.'”



The inflated objects are reportedly used to fly the drones to the target area at high altitude before they are launched to cause maximum damage.

Fuming passengers at airports across the country hit boiling point on Saturday.

Footage showed massive queues inside major international airport Sheremetyevo, where a suspected balloon drone strike took place.

Ukrainian national security commentator Andriy Kovalenko said: “Russians are posting videos from Sheremetyevo airport.



“The consequences of Putin’s geopolitics are manifesting in constant transportation disruptions.

“They chose this path, and they must bear the consequences.”

Another clip shows plumes of smoke rising near the major aviation hub amid suspicions a drone had crashed in the vicinity.



Vnukovo Airport – used by Russian officials and VIP guests – suffered 119 delays and ten cancellations.

Some passengers have reportedly been waiting days for their flights as planes are held at other airports, unable to fly to Moscow.

Novosibirsk – the largest airport in Siberia – suffered around 100 disrupted aircraft.

St Petersburg’s Pulkovo reported 138 delays or cancellations.

A proportion of the chaos is as a result of regular drones launched from Ukraine.



Many passengers in Moscow complained about a lack of information from the authorities.

A woman on a Pobeda Airline flight said: “There are children on board. There is no food, only water.”

It comes as the Russian Defence Ministry claims to have downed 2,690 Ukrainian drones in the past two-and-a-half days – among the highest figure of the entire war.

Ukraine says the blame lies with Putin – who refuses to halt his war – and Russians who support him.

Echoing this sentiment, Ed Miliband blasted Putin to the face of his Russian counterpart telling him: “We all know you are the aggressor.”



Confronting Russia‘s foreign minister at a heated G20 summit, he slammed the Kremlin’s relentless bloodshed in Ukraine and warned “you are not winning this war”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The fiery comments come just one day after Putin’s forces brutally bombed a railway station in Dnipro, Ukraine – killing 15.

Horrifying photos show multiple double decker buses and trucks engulfed in flames and shooting hellish black-orange plumes into the skies.

News.title: Man, 45, arrested for ‘attempted murder’ after two men ‘mowed down in Range Rover hit-and-run’ in car park
News.content:
SMASH TERROR Man, 45, arrested for ‘attempted murder’ after two men ‘mowed down in Range Rover hit-and-run’ in car park







Next

A MAN has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after two men were seriously injured in an alleged hit and run.

Officers were called to a disturbance on Marina Way outside Hollywood Bowl in Brighton at around 10.30pm on Friday.



The two injured men, aged 22 and 30, were struck by a vehicle, believed to be a black Range Rover, and the driver left the scene, according to Sussex Police.

A 45-year-old man was later arrested on suspicion of attempted murder, causing grievous bodily harm and possession of cocaine, the force confirmed.



He remains in custody.

Det Insp Jennifer Pietersen said: “We are aware that this incident may cause concern to those visiting the area.

“However, this is believed to be an isolated incident.”

Officers are asking witnesses or anyone with dashcam footage to get in touch.



Anyone with information is urged to contact Sussex Police online or by calling 101, quoting Operation Stargate, to assist with the ongoing investigation.

News.title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.

He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".

The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.

It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. As King Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.

During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities.

On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.

"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in a piece for the Guardian, external.

He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation".

He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference".

The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour.

Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.

He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."

In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."

Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing".

"Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footingâ¦ it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."

Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point.

"My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.

Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.

Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.

News.title: After 28 years and 36,000 miles, Karl Bushby is almost home
News.content:
With his journey almost complete, Karl Bushby reflects on adventures that have taken him across four continents, as well as strained relationships and how life as he knows it is about to change dramatically.

Back in 1998, the former paratrooper, then aged 29, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, to walk an unbroken path to his home city of Hull, without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return to the UK until he had completed his journey, and not to use transport to advance.

Now 57, he is embarking on his final few miles having hacked his way through the jungles of the DariÃ©n Gap, crossed the frozen Bering Strait and, just a few weeks ago, swum the English Channel.

At the end, he will be met by his 36-year-old son Adam, a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he has never met, his father and brothers. His mother will be waiting at his childhood home that he left 28 years ago.

News.title: Responsible or panicked? Meet the people around the world already preparing for crisis
News.content:
Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (Â£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement.

"It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.

A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.

Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.

His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.

Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.

In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.

Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".

News.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
News.content:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.

The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.

One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.

This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.

On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lÃ¨se majestÃ© law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.

This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.

"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

News.title: Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials
News.content:
Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has nearly three years to go before he has to call an election and he has repeatedly and categorically ruled out going to the country early.

But the discussion persists - and many think it is a real possibility.

After Wednesday's Budget, that talk has only increased.

As one former Labour minister puts it: "Why would you sprinkle round a few politically smart (albeit small) giveaways now but delay all the really tough and unpopular decisions on welfare and defence to an autumn spending review if you weren't creating a window for a spring election?"

Others have also suggested to the BBC that Chancellor John Healey's plans felt like a pre-election programme.

They argue the Budget contained voter-friendly measures on the cost of living, such as Â£100 help for many with energy bills and extending VAT cuts on electricity bills. Young voters are to be offered help on to the housing ladder, through the Your First Home scheme.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has questioned why some-voter friendly measures announced by Healey will only be in place until the summer.

Could it be, she suggests, that the prime minister plans to go to the country before these measures run out?

(The counter-argument to this is that household energy pressures are less severe in the summer.)

Some MPs also point out the prime minister is popular at the moment and Labour is leading in most polls.

Reform, who had led the polls for some time, have had a difficult few months.

Will things ever look better for Burnham, they ask.

News.title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.

She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care.

The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.

Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.

Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.

In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.

But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.

But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.

The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.

The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.

In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

News.title: UK could see 10 days without rain after 'wettest week in two years'
News.content:
The UK could see as many as 10 consecutive days without rain after an unsettled end to October that featured back-to-back storms.

It comes after the Environment Agency said England experienced its wettest week in two years thanks to Storms Austen and Boelo.

Following this recent unsettled weather, the return of high pressure will bring a prolonged spell of largely dry and calm conditions, with very little rain in sight.

Mist and fog will remain a persistent feature, with some slow-clearing dense patches expected during the mornings.

News.title: UK has 'no authority' over case of woman killed by father in US
News.content:
The mother of a British woman who was shot and killed by her father in Texas has been told that police in the UK have "no lawful authority to intervene" as the family tries to find answers.

Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington was shot in the chest on 10 January 2025 in Prosper, Dallas - found by a UK coroner to be an unlawful killing.

However, no criminal case was brought against her father Kris Harrison, after a grand jury in Collin County declined to indict him.

Lucy's mother Jane Coates wrote to Cheshire Police urging them to "gather evidence" here locally, and then "liaise" with US authorities - but the force has responded and said it was "constrained" by law and jurisdiction.

In a letter to Coates, Deputy Chief Constable Mike Evans said: "Whilst we may share the family's concerns and understand their desire for further scrutiny, we have no lawful authority to intervene in decisions taken by those agencies."

Last month, Coates flew to Texas in a bid to meet the district attorney in Collin County and to call on him to reinstate the investigation but was told he would not speak to her.

News.title: Motorcyclist dies after falling into sea in cliffside beauty spot crash
News.content:
A man has died after falling into the sea following a crash involving his motorbike, police have said.

Officers from North Wales Police were called to reports of a crash involving a black motorcycle on Marine Drive on the Great Orme in Llandudno, Conwy county, at about 22:31 GMT on Thursday.

A multi-agency response including police, the RNLI and HM Coastguard was launched and the man was recovered from the water and airlifted to Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor, where he was pronounced dead.

Police are looking to speak to the driver of a black vehicle - possibly a Ford Fiesta - that they believe was in the area at the time.

The incident happened about one mile (1.6km) from the Toll House towards the direction of the Great Orme summit.

The Great Orme is a headland which rises up to 207m (679 feet) above sea level and has sheer cliffs.

The man's kin have been informed and the coroner has been notified, police said.

Sgt Alun Jones said the force's thoughts were "with the man's family and friends at this very difficult time".

News.title: Man guilty of rape after woman's phone recording
News.content:
Al-Shammari, a Kuwaiti national living in Taunton, was remanded in custody to be sentenced on 27 November.

Al-Shammari denied rape but was found guilty by a majority verdict.

The jury heard Al-Shammari had known the woman for a few weeks, having met her on a night out, and they had slept together once.

On the night of the incident, he tried to persuade her to come out for the evening and when she said no, he convinced her to let him come to her home.

After a few drinks he asked to stay the night and she agreed to let him sleep on the sofa, telling him they were just friends.

The court was told Al-Shammari went to the woman's room and they did start to have consensual sex, but the woman later told police she was feeling "more and more uncomfortable". She said she asked him to stop but he did not.

The jury heard the recording in which the woman said "no" and "I don't like it".

In his police interview, Al-Shammari denied rape and told officers the woman had wanted sex but the positions they tried hurt her so he stopped.

A spokesperson for Avon and Somerset Police said: "Rape is a crime which often happens behind closed doors, leaving a jury to decide which of the two people is telling the truth.

"This is an unusual case as the survivor provided key evidence by recording the attack.

"Avon and Somerset Police remain committed to thoroughly investigating reports of sexual offences, supporting victims and pursuing offenders through the criminal justice system.

"The circumstances of this case highlight the importance of consent in sexual relationships.

"No means no, whether you've had consensual sex before or not. If you have any doubt about their consent, stop."

News.title: 'Greedy' solicitor used fake will-writing invoices to defraud cancer charity out of thousands
News.content:
A solicitor defrauded a cancer charity out of thousands of pounds after submitting fake invoices for work he had not carried out, a court heard.

Michael Fogg, 47, of Cyncoed, Cardiff, offered his services to Cancer Research UK's free will writing scheme, but when the charity contacted people he claimed to represent, they said they had not used the solicitor.

The hearing was told the money it lost as a result of Fogg's actions could have paid for 48 biopsies.

He was sentenced to 10 months' imprisonment, suspended for two years in a hearing at Newport Crown Court on Friday.

An investigation was launched by Cancer Research UK after emails and addresses for Fogg's clients were found to be non-existent.

Judge Carl Harrison said: "You had a position in the legal profession which allowed you to fund your greed."

News.title: Call for lottery gambling controls after dad's death
News.content:
A coroner has called for the National Lottery to be included in a self-exclusion gambling scheme after a man with a gambling addiction took his own life.

Stephen Goff, 54, died from asphyxiation at his flat in Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire, on 18 August 2025, an inquest heard.

Emma Whitting, senior coroner for Bedfordshire and Luton, said there was a risk of further deaths unless the National Lottery draw was covered by GAMSTOP.

The system prevents people who register with it from accessing gambling websites and apps licensed in Great Britain.

The coroner has sent the Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report, external to the Gambling Commission and GAMSTOP.

A spokesperson for the commission said that following the inquest, they had "been working with Gamstop and Allwyn, the National Lottery operator, to consider whether further protections are needed in this area".

News.title: How man's Halloween house display has become bittersweet tradition
News.content:
As people up and down the country look forward to celebrating Halloween this evening, one Greater Manchester man takes the festivities further than most.

Dave Barron, 61, from Bramhall, in Greater Manchester, has been decorating his home for Halloween every year since 2011, and has been preparing this year's Back to the Future-themed display since May.

Dave's efforts are all a tribute to his late wife, Catherine. Accepting donations from Halloween visitors, he has raised more than Â£55,000 for the Macmillan cancer charity, which cared for Catherine before she died in 2020.

"Halloween is emotional for me," Dave said. "I miss Catherine tremendously. She'd think I'm an absolute lunatic, but she was always a big part of it and I think she'd be really proud."

"I have been working on this year's Halloween display since May," he said. "And it does cost me a bit.

"But It's a small price to pay if it helps people who are suffering with cancer."

News.title: Will El Nino and the polar vortex mean more snow for UK this winter?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Freezing temperatures could sweep as early as November as El Niño continues to wreak havoc on global weather.

Forecasters warned the weather phenomenon, which has already smashed global benchmarks to become the strongest weather event in history, could disrupt a large, high-altitude ring of swirling cold winds spinning above the Arctic known as the stratospheric polar vortex.

While a strong polar vortex helps to contain very cold winds and conditions within the North Pole, disruptions can weaken the jet stream, sending severe, freezing Arctic air plunging southward into North America and Europe.

Experts are now predicting the polar vortex will become weaker as early as November rather than in January 2027 as orginally thought.

Forecasts from Nasa show the wind circulation weakening, with wind strength falling to 12.04 m/s (26.9 mph) on October 31, 9.15 m/s (20.5 mph) on November 1, and 4.15 m/s (9.3 mph) on November 3.

open image in gallery Waves crash over the promenade in Largs, Scotland ( Getty )

The polar vortex can grow weaker and spread south towards the UK if there is a sudden stratospheric warming, which according to the Met Office can make the winds in the vortex reverse direction.

“The stratospheric sudden warming can sometimes cause the jet stream to ‘snake’ more, and this tends to create a large area of blocking high pressure,” the forecaster said.

Experts explain that this usually forms over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia. That means northern Europe, including the UK, is likely to get a long spell of dry, cold weather, whereas southern Europe will tend to be more mild, wet and windy.

On the boundary of these areas, cold easterly winds develop and in some cases the drop in temperatures leads to snow, which is what happened in early 2018.

open image in gallery The science behind the polar vortex ( NOAA )

However, forecasters can only reliably predict individual sudden stratospheric warmings about a week in advance.

They can watch how these changes develop and may impact our future weather. The sudden stratospheric warming usually takes a few weeks to influence UK weather.

But it’s not just the polar vortex that could make the UK wetter and colder this winter. The Met Office warns the El Niño “is associated with increased risk of cold snaps.”

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It takes place when sea-surface temperatures across the central and eastern Pacific become significantly warmer than average, altering atmospheric circulation patterns and influencing weather around the globe.

The weather phenomenon has already helped push temperatures to reach the hottest summer on record, and will continue to have “far-reaching” implications for weather conditions across the world, according to the Met Office.

News.title: Man United latest: Michael Carrick on brink again as team fall apart at Chelsea after Lisandro Martinez red card
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Manchester United capitulated at Chelsea after Morgan Rogers’ stunning goal and Lisandro Martinez’s sending off as a third consecutive defeat piled the pressure on Michael Carrick.

United arrived at Stamford Bridge having backed Carrick this week despite a eight-game winless run. Bruno Fernandes was restored as captain and returned to the starting line-up, with the visitors dominating the first half.

But they were unable to take their chances as Fernandes blazed over on the volley and Amad Diallo missed a glaring opportunity to punish a slip from Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana.

Rogers then danced through the United defence to score a wonderful individual goal after half-time, and Carrick’s team collapsed after Martinez conceded a penalty and picked up his second yellow card in the space of two minutes for jumping into Fofana and leading with his forearm while defending a corner.

Cole Palmer converted the penalty to double Chelsea’s lead while the impressive Estevao thought he had added a third for Xabi Alonso’s team, only for it to be disallowed for a narrow offside.

United will now be faced with the same question of whether to continue with Carrick after another dismal defeat, as the club continue to sound out possible replacements that include Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann.

Follow live reaction from Chelsea v Manchester United, below:

News.title: Michael Carrick responds to Lisandro Martinez’s ‘unfathomable’ red card in Man United defeat
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Michael Carrick denied he had been let down by Lisandro Martinez after Manchester United unravelled following the defender’s red card at Chelsea.

The centre-back was booked twice in two minutes and conceded a second-half penalty for his challenge on Wesley Fofana in the box.

After pulling down Morgan Rogers, Martinez led with his forearm and he made contact with Fofana’s throat as he attempted to defend a corner.

Martinez had criticised the United hierarchy in an explosive interview following defeat at Atletico Madrid earlier this month, later apologising for his comments.

But the Argentine’s sending off cost United as Cole Palmer doubled Chelsea’s lead from the spot following Rogers’ excellent opener.

Carrick did not look towards Martinez and appeared to ignore him as he made his way down the tunnel.

But the under-fire United manager replied “no” when asked by TNT Sports if he felt let down by Martinez.

“It has a major importance on the game,” Carrick also told Match of the Day. “A huge moment. I think that is pretty obvious really."

Former Chelsea forward Joe Cole described Martinez’s red card as “unfathomable” during his commentary on TNT Sports.

“He has let [Carrick] down,” Cole said. “He’s made a huge error. I don’t know the lad, but he’s let his team-mates down 100 per cent. It’s a crucial moment.”

open image in gallery Martinez led with his forearm as he challenged Fofana while defending a corner ( AP )

Carrick had restored captain Bruno Fernandes to his team after criticism of his tactics following the Champions League defeat at Como.

It led to an improved performance from United in the first half and Carrick’s side could have taken the lead if Fernandes or Amad Diallo had taken chances.

Martinez is out of contract next summer and Cole added that it may suit both him and United to part ways in January.

“I think they might cut their losses,” Cole said. “He’s clearly a great player but if your head is not at the club then you’ve got to find a solution.”

News.title: Celebrity Race Across the World locations: Where is the new series filmed?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

One of Britain’s favourite adventure travel shows is back, and this time it's the celebrities’ turn to take on Race Across the World.

Celebrity Race Across the World sees four new pairings take part in the adventure as they race to the finish line in Melbourne, Australia.

We met the teams in the Malaysian city of Kuching before they embark on a 4,660-mile race across three countries and two continents, relying only on local transport, a map, and a budget of just £26 a day.

This year’s race includes Brit award-winning singer-songwriter Ella Eyre and childhood friend Nana, as well as former Soccer Saturday presenter Jeff Stelling and his son Matt.

open image in gallery From left to right, Princess Andre, Junior Andre, Nana, Ella Eyre, Sam Ryder, Kaz, Jeff Stelling and Matt. This year's contenstants on Celebrity Race Across the World ( BBC/Studio Lambert/Getty/Cody Burridge/Matt Burlem )

Singer-songwriter and West End star Sam Ryder will also compete with his best friend and tour manager, Kaz, while Katie Price and Peter Andre’s children, influencer Princess Andre and her musician brother Junior, complete the line-up.

As each episode airs, we'll dive deeper into the destinations the teams visit on series four of Celebrity Race Across the World.

To look back at where the teams visited in series six of Race Across the World, which aired earlier this year, check out our page on the race destinations.

The start

Kuching, Malaysian Borneo

open image in gallery Kuching has many statues of cats around the city ( Getty Images )

The teams set off from the city of Kuching, not in mainland Malaysia, but in the Malaysian state of Sarawak on the island of Borneo. Borneo is the third largest island in the world, with its land shared by Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei.

Kuching, also known as “cat city”, is home to some architectural marvels, such as the famous S-shaped Darurl Hana Bridge over the Sarawak River and the Masjid India Kuching mosque, which was designed to look as if it were floating on water. The Kuching Waterfront is the city’s main promenade and a focal point of the city’s historical, cultural, and social offerings, lined with stalls, cafes and museums.

Visitors often try and spot the different cat motifs, statues and sculptures that are found all over the city, paying homage to its name Kuching, which is the Malay word for cat. The city is also home to many ethnic communities, including Iban, Bidayuh, Malay, Chinese, and Melanau, all of which influence festivals, art, and cuisine. Some of the most popular dishes in Kuching are Sarawak Laksa soup and Kolo Mee noodles. Kuching often serves as a gateway to some of Borneo’s most famous national parks, such as Bako, known for its unique rock formations, rainforests and proboscis monkeys.



Checkpoint one

Pangkalan Bun, Indonesian Borneo

open image in gallery Tanjung Puting is one of the best places to see orangutans ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The first leg of the race saw the teams travel 1,000km from Kuching to Pangkalan Bun. The southern Borneo city straddles the bustling Arut River edged with stilted homes, while the city itself is made up of an agglomeration of villages, meaning the city has no real centre. Most visitors to Pangkalan Bun stay in the city to make a trip to the nearby Tanjung Puting National Park, one of the best places in the world to spot orangutans. The park has many destinations that can be reached on guided boat tours, such as Camp Leakey, the famous orangutan research centre founded in the 1970s. The park is also home to an Orangutan Care Centre that rehabilitates wounded primates and cares for babies. Borneo is one of only two islands where orangutans are now found, making it a special place for nature enthusiasts to visit.

Before the teams reached the checkpoint, they had a choice of travelling south via the western coastal fringe or choosing a more direct route through Borneo’s interior, home to traditional communities and dense jungle terrain. Some of the spots that the pairs passed through included the coastal town of Sematan near Mount Kuwai, popular with hikers and Nek Bidang, home to one community of Indigenous Dayak people, who live in dwellings called longhouses and live off small-scale subsistence farming such as rice collecting. Other highlights included Tae Village, where another Dayak community lives in the foothills of Tiong Kandang and the coastal transport hub of Pontianak, which lies directly on the equator and is home to busy ports.



The end

Melbourne, Australia

open image in gallery Melbourne is known for its pedestrianised laneways ( Getty Images )

The teams will race to the finish line in Melbourne, Australia, 4,660 miles away from where they started their epic intrepid journey. Known as the country’s cultural capital, Melbourne is where you can find some of Australia's best galleries, sporting events and world-class coffee scene.

Street art, trendy cafes and boutique shops are tucked away in its famous pedestrianised laneways. Melbourne’s galleries also feature more art, including the Australian Centre for Contemporary Art and the National Gallery of Victoria, the country's oldest gallery. For the city’s sporty side, many visitors will plan a trip around some of the major sport events that are hosted in Melbourne, such as the Australian Open, Formula 1 Australian Grand Prix and Australian Rules Football, the national sport.

Melbourne is home to a close-knit Aboriginal community, whose culture and history can be learned about across many attractions such as the Bunjilaka Aboriginal Cultural Centre inside the Melbourne Museum and the Ian Potter Centre showcasing Aboriginal art.

Celebrity Race Across The World airs on iPlayer and BBC One on Wednesdays at 8pm

News.title: When global diplomacy is done, it's time for American football
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Order of operations: foreign policy, then football.

Fresh from chairing a meeting of top diplomats from the Group of 20 wealthiest nations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio planned to host his foreign minister counterparts on Saturday afternoon at a quintessential American sporting event.

Rubio and a number of his colleagues were expected to attend Saturday’s college football game between Southeastern Conference rivals Florida and Georgia, which shifted to Atlanta from the usual neutral venue in Jacksonville, Florida, due to stadium renovations.

It was not clear which ministers might attend what has been called the “World’s Largest Outdoor Cocktail Party” due the large, boisterous crowds that the matchup attracts. U.S. officials say plenty of them have expressed interest in accompanying Rubio.

Georgia is ranked No. 3 in the country and heavily favored. Florida, where Rubio’s son, Anthony, plays, is No. 17.

News.title: Shabana Mahmood ‘to dilute immigration plans’ after Labour backlash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood is reportedly preparing to dilute proposals to overhaul legal migration rules following pushback across the Labour Party and the cabinet.

Ms Mahmood is expected to announce her final decisions to parliament next week, with ministers poised to scale back plans that would have forced tens of thousands of social care staff already working in the UK to wait up to 15 years for permanent settlement, the BBC reports.

Under the Home Office’s original blueprints, the baseline qualification period for indefinite leave to remain was set to double from five years to 10, with lower-paid foreign workers facing a wait of up to 15 years before securing permanent residency.

But now, following a public consultation that generated more than 200,000 responses, the government is expected to exempt existing social care workers from the lengthened timetable.

open image in gallery Shabana Mahmood is expected to present revised immigration rules to parliament next week ( AFP/Getty )

Most other foreign workers are still expected to face an extended 10-year residency requirement before becoming eligible to settle, though the duration could be reduced for individuals who earn higher incomes or demonstrate sustained contributions to their local communities.

Ms Mahmood had pressed for the stricter regime amid growing alarm in Whitehall over the number of legal arrivals approaching eligibility for settlement, following record net migration figures under the previous Conservative administration.

Amid anti-migrant protests and with political pressure mounting from the Conservatives and Reform UK, ministers have faced growing demands to curb long-term population growth and reduce pressure on public services.

But the prospect of applying the restrictions retrospectively – moving the goalposts for overseas staff who arrived in Britain on the understanding they could settle after five years – has triggered internal conflict within the government.

open image in gallery The measures come amid heightening political pressure to curb migration figures ( Getty )

Before rejoining the cabinet as housing secretary, Angela Rayner delivered a pointed critique of the draft policy, branding retrospective changes “un-British” for penalising migrants who had moved to the UK in good faith.

The Tories framed the reported retreat as a major climbdown.

A Conservative Party spokesperson claimed the home secretary had “caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open-borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain”.

The spokesperson added: “This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low-wage migrants.”

Permanent residence – formally designated as indefinite leave to remain – grants foreign nationals the right to live, work, and study in the UK indefinitely, while opening access to public funds and state benefits.

The Home Office has been contacted for comment.

News.title: FBI visits Dan J. Sullivan donor in candidate's home town as Alaska Senate probe widens
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Federal investigators have begun contacting people who gave money to Dan J. Sullivan, the Alaska U.S. Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, over questions about possible deception.

The FBI reached out to donors on Friday as its investigation into the candidate intensified.

An agent based in Anchorage travelled to Petersburg, a small fishing community reachable only by air or water where the candidate lives, and visited a boat dealership there.

The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician.

Flint gave $500 over the summer to what he regarded as a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for “throwing his hat in the ring.” Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been “misled” about which candidate he was supporting.

open image in gallery Dan J. Sullivan, left, is challenging Senator Dan Sullivan, Republican of Alaska, for his seat ( Sullivan for Senate/Getty )

“I don’t feel like I’ve been misled at all,” Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would “let him waste his time trying to track me down.”

“I don’t think there’s any confusion,” he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.”

The FBI's visit followed confirmation from federal officials that a criminal probe into the candidate exists.

The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed for a court order on Friday to isolate certain Alaska ballots so potential voter confusion can be investigated.

open image in gallery Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola addressed the controversy during a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday ( Getty )

Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”

The developments come just days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied any involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator.

She said she was “deeply offended” by the allegations, which she called “garbage” and part of a “smear campaign” to suppress turnout on the eve of the election.

“I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race,” she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum.

News.title: Judge blasts Trump team for threatening election workers in latest rebuke to midterm plans
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A federal judge has blocked Donald Trump’s administration from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for processing ballots — thwarting the government’s last-ditch attempts to toss out votes before Election Day.

The temporary restraining order prevents the Department of Justice and Homeland Security from demanding state and local election officials stop processing or setting aside ballots in the president’s crusade against alleged noncitizen voters.

“One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear or intimidation,” California District Judge Trina Thompson wrote Friday night.

“Free exercise of the right to vote is a core tenet of our democracy,” she added. “Election Day is around the corner. Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots. Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”

The ruling follows a lawsuit from unions representing election workers and civil rights groups who accused the administration of trying to illegally “intimidate” them with threats of criminal prosecution in the weeks before high-stakes midterm elections, with the balance of power in Congress at stake.

open image in gallery A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from a ‘campaign’ of intimidation aimed at election workers in the president’s crusade against noncitizen voters ( Reuters )

According to Judge Thompson, “high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.”

“Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” she wrote.

Friday night’s order arrived hours after a federal appeals court in the state blocked the administration’s efforts to sequester 20,000 ballots, which another judge warned would “wreak havoc” on elections in the state.

That legal battle could soon head to the Supreme Court next if the administration wants to keep fighting, with just days left before Election Day on Tuesday.

Appellate court judges said the administration’s attempts to set aside ballots while voting is already underway could “jeopardize” midterm elections and disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.

open image in gallery The administration has faced a series of losses in a last-ditch efforts to allegedly target noncitizen voters in California with just days left before Election Day ( Getty )

That 2-1 decision marks the third straight loss for the administration in its efforts to block ballots from alleged noncitizen voters in the state.

“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the court’s majority wrote on Friday.

The court has “major concerns” that the administration’s attempts to seize control of the state’s election process will risk “disenfranchisement of eligible voters” and could put the “entire tabulation process in jeopardy,” judges wrote.

Federal law mandates a “quiet period” 90 days before an election to ensure voters aren’t wrongly disenfranchised without enough time to make corrections.

But the Justice Department launched an unprecedented effort to seize ballots and prevent states from certifying votes with just days left before midterm campaigns come to an end.

The Justice Department is also trying to press officials in Washington state to sequester ballots from at least 400 people the administration has accused of being noncitizens.

The Trump administration is also embroiled in an increasingly volatile attempt to block the certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate results if Trump’s preferred candidate loses.

Election experts and voting rights groups said a court’s intervention in the election workers’ case is a relief for the small army of people who run the nation’s elections.

“This decision is a resounding win for the election workers who make our democracy happen and for all Americans’ freedom to vote,” said Patrick Moran, president of the American Federation Of State County And Municipal Employees, among the unions suing the Trump administration.

Election workers can now “continue to do their jobs, and our elections can continue to proceed freely and fairly,” he added.

News.title: Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick
News.content:
So where do Manchester United go from here? The Chelsea fans seemed to have arrived at their own conclusion, taunting Michael Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and “you’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis-torn for very different reasons.

That was moments after seeing their team go 2-0 up following United’s latest act of self-sabotage on an afternoon that had initially offered their fans fleeting hope of a little respite from the storm, but ultimately gave way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick was given a stay of execution in midweek but United’s hierarchy must now decide whether to keep faith with their manager for Tuesday’s visit of Roma in the Champions League and possibly Aston Villa at Old Trafford five days later or bite the bullet now.

Either way, it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long, whether they currently have a plan for who comes next or not. And that the international break could be a very busy one at Old Trafford.

Depending on how results go elsewhere, United – who were reduced to 10 men after Lisandro Martinez’s second half red card – could feasibly be in the bottom three by the end of the day.

News.title: Red Roses cruise to dominant victory over United States in final WXV game
News.content:
English rugby chiefs have been on a charm offensive in the United States this week, but the players on the pitch opted for more of a brute-force approach.

The Red Roses were in the unfamiliar position of coming off the back of successive defeats and Meg Jones had called on her team to respond. They certainly did that, looking far more like world champions than they have over the past fortnight with a convincing nine-try win – four of them scored by Claudia Moloney-MacDonald – albeit there is still room for them to “grow”, as Jones put it after the game.

That is what the Rugby Football Union (RFU) have been trying to do off the field. Bill Sweeney, the RFU chief executive, and his colleagues used this fixture in New Jersey as an opportunity to tap into the US market by “creating connections” with business leaders and potential investors.

It is little wonder English rugby is trying to get a piece of the American pie. There are an ever-growing number of US owners in British football and with the US hosting the men’s and women’s Rugby World Cups in 2031 and 2033 interest in the oval-ball game is sure to grow too, although the sparse crowd in New Jersey would suggest there is work to do on that front.

News.title: Embarrassing England on brink of historic World Cup exit
News.content:
It is, because they showed their quality and offered themselves a sniff with their Gallic heroics. They had to maintain that pace on Friday to put the pressure on Samoa, but after the ideal beginning they contracted a nasty case of white-line fever from which they could not recover. “It looks like we’re going out of the tournament,” McDermott said. “That second half got scrappy and we should have handled that a lot better.”

McDermott is not blameless. The directives were clearly to offload when they could, and perhaps when they should not have, and the call to start Jez Litten over Brad O’Neill at hooker was, on reflection, a mistake. Litten has so much more impact off the bench and the Hull KR livewire could have been the spark England required when it proceeded to fall flat. It was also strange to see Lewis coming on in the No 9 role.

Yet it must be noted that this was just McDermott’s third match in charge and that Tonga was his first. With no warm-up game and with his English-based players at a disadvantage because of travel and the jet lag, that all-important opener was appallingly timed. Yet having been a member of the exclusive top three for so long, England must now concede they are merely in the top five. This tournament proved as much.

Referee Gerard Sutton (Australia).

News.title: Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot
News.content:
David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

News.title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
News.content:
The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States.

The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating.

A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry.

While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, “flockdowns” (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as “reassortment”, when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain.

News.title: Britain faces unprecedented squeeze on incomes, IFS says
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has ruled out making “crude cuts” to welfare after he failed to tackle the rising benefits bill in Wednesday’s Budget.

The Chancellor acknowledged last night that the current benefits system is “unsustainable” but said he will only look to make cuts “in a Labour way”.

Speaking to the BBC in the wake of Wednesday’s Budget, Mr Healey promised that “there will be a reduction in the benefits bill” before the next election.

However, he said this will not include “crude cuts” to payments.

He said: “We will do that in a Labour way, and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain, or progressive, to have a bigger and bigger benefits bills.

“This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The Prime Minister’s been clear about that. It’s what you do about it.”

He added: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures.”

His comments on welfare come after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused Labour of presiding over a Government that had left Britain “overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system”.

She said: “Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history and our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this Government has put welfare first.”

The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility released on Wednesday revealed that benefits spending is expected to jump by almost 30pc to £431bn by 2032.

Almost half the total is pensions and disability benefits for pensioners, despite the planned abolition of the triple lock. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey launches tax raid on savers as welfare bill spirals | Chancellor to pull in £4.3bn from landlords and savers as Badenoch calls for ‘tough love’ on benefits

What happened overnight

The Chancellor will have woken up to jittery markets after Google-owner Alphabet revealed higher spending on AI.

Alphabet dropped 10pc in after-hours trading, wiping nearly $400 billion off its market value. Microsoft, by contrast, beat forecasts with better-than-expected cash flows that lifted its shares by 3pc.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped 0.7pc, while Japan’s Nikkei fluctuated between gains and losses and was last ⁠up 1pc.

Oil prices retreated as investors latched onto hopes that peace talks to resolve the Middle East conflict could be back on the table.

European stocks were on track to edge higher at the open after the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as widely expected on Wednesday. The European Central Bank announces its next interest rate decision on Thursday.

News.title: Risk of Ebola spread in UK is low, experts stress
News.content:
Infectious disease experts have stressed the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the UK is low after the head of Africa’s health agency warned that the haemorrhagic fever could reach Britain.

The Democratic Republic of Congo is struggling to contain an outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the deadly virus that began in the volatile eastern region of the country. There have been 10,000 cases, including nearly 5,000 deaths, since the outbreak was first reported in May and it has now become the second largest Ebola epidemic in history.

In recent weeks the virus has spread to Kenya, where there have been nine cases including two deaths, and Nigeria. The case in Nigeria is concerning because the patient, the wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, the country’s capital, had no history of travel to the affected region of DRC. She has now been evacuated to Switzerland.

In comments reported by the Guardian Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, described the outbreak as “unprecedented” as it was the first time that the disease had spread to three geographic regions of the continent. He warned that there was scope for further spread.

“We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

On Wednesday the United States announced that travellers arriving by air would have to sign a statement affirming that they had not been in the DRC within the previous 21 days. Anyone found to provide false or misleading information would face imprisonment or a fine.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) stressed that the risk to the UK is low. Dr Sam Collins, head of guidance, clinical and public health response at the agency, said the Ebola outbreak in DRC is serious but “the UK is well prepared to respond safely and effectively to the risk of imported cases arising here”.

UKHSA is monitoring travel routes from the affected countries and is providing information on symptoms.

The UKHSA said it is rare for Ebola to occur in returning travellers and the NHS has “well established procedures in place” for such a situation.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick future LIVE: Man Utd boss facing sack as Julian Nagelsmann 'contacted'
Sports.content:
After Manchester United were beaten by Chelsea in west London, Michael Carrick's position as manager appears to be under immense threat again

Michael Carrick is on the brink, yet again, after Manchester United imploded against Chelsea. Carrick looked to have got a reaction out of the Reds after they were the better team at Stamford Bridge in the first half.

They would have gone into half-time with a 1-0 lead had Matheus Cunha not been fractionally offside when he tapped in from close range. However, the Reds fell asleep after the break and allowed Morgan Rogers to prance through their back line and scoop the opening goal over Senne Lammens.

United looked to still be in the contest, until Lisandro Martinez brainlessly pushed Wesley Fofana over while marking him, resulting in a penalty and a second yellow card being awarded. After Cole Palmer squeezed his penalty through Lammens, Chelsea eased their way to a 2-0 win.

With Carrick enduring a ninth consecutive match in all competitions without a victory, he appears to be on the brink of the sack after last week's 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth. Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann have been heavily linked with the job, though reports on Saturday claimed the latter has been 'contacted' and sounded out over potentially taking over at Juventus, presenting a possible problem for United chiefs.

As updates continue to pour in, Mirror Football will be over all of the latest news and updates regarding Carrick's future.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick past the point of no return as Man Utd stars let him down again vs Chelsea
Sports.content:
Manchester United fell to a 2-0 defeat against Chelsea to pile even more pressure on doomed Michael Carrick.

United started brightly but Amad's failure to convert two clear opportunities and Matheus Cunha's disallowed header meant the game remained 0-0 at the break. However, it took just five minutes after the restart for Xabi Alonso's side to get off the mark.

Morgan Rogers' powerful run in United's half saw him glide past Harry Maguire and lift the ball past Senne Lammens to put his side 1-0 up. The Blues' dominance grew as the game went on and was helped by Lisandro Martinez earning a second yellow card for jumping into Wesley Fofana and giving away a penalty.

The spot-kick was successfully converted by Cole Palmer, despite Lammens getting a hand on it. The 2-0 win not only marked Chelsea's return to winning ways after their defeat to Spurs last week, but could play a major role in the future of Carrick at Old Trafford.

‌
