World.title: Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks
World.content:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi tells Al Jazeera Tehran doesn’t rule out attack, is ‘prepared for all scenarios’.

Share Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks on social media

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a United States effort to open dialogue with Tehran is “a positive step”, but that there are currently no plans for meetings with US officials.

Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had studied a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance in high-level meetings, and set out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which he said would pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.

He added that an Iranian delegation has travelled to Doha, a day after Qatari mediators were in Tehran in an apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the US-Iran ceasefire. Araghchi said one of his aides is in Qatar to continue consultations.

“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” the foreign minister told Al Jazeera.

However, he warned: “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”

‘No need to meet with the Americans’

Araghchi played down talk of upcoming meetings between the two sides.

“What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation,” he said.

“We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” he added.

He said whether Iran would hold direct or indirect talks with the US depended on Tehran’s conditions being met.

“Mediators have presented proposals concerning the nuclear dossier, which we are currently reviewing as part of the second phase,” he said.



“Qatari and Pakistani mediators are continuing consultations regarding our conditions,” Araghchi said.

Conditions for Hormuz

Araghchi said talks with Qatari mediators had shortened the time needed to implement Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days,” he said.

“Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region,” he said, adding, “We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar.”

Iran is also demanding recognition of shipping routes through the strait that it had discussed with Oman, and the closure of other routes, he said.

‘Prepared for all scenarios’

Araghchi also said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.

“We are prepared for all scenarios,” he said.

“We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”

World.title: Syria considering entry into Mecca defence pact, says foreign minister
World.content:
Damascus ‘evaluating’ whether to join the alliance that binds Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Share Syria considering entry into Mecca defence pact, says foreign minister on social media

Syria’s government is weighing whether to enter into a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, the country’s top diplomat says.

“Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain on Saturday.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in the Saudi city of Mecca in August. It states that an attack on one country is to be considered an attack on all three, and has been compared to the NATO security alliance that binds the United States, Canada and 30 European countries.

Saudi Arabia, under heavy fire from Yemen’s Houthis, is a key backer of Syria’s government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, which came to power after the fall of former strongman Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

Under the Mecca pact, Pakistan and Turkiye have pledged military support to Riyadh as it faces escalating attacks from the Iran-backed group. However, neither Islamabad nor Ankara has yet announced any attacks on the Houthis.

Government officials in Turkiye, where the pact’s ratification process is ongoing, have said any future military support for Riyadh would not include deploying Turkish troops to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.

Speaking at the conference in Bahrain, al-Shaibani said Damascus was an “integral” part of regional security and would support any framework aimed at protecting regional stability.

The minister stressed that the region was “in greater need than ever” of developing joint deterrence and defence systems.



He said Syria backs the efforts of Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government to restore “sovereignty and stability across its entire territory” as it battles the Houthis, Syrian state media reported.

He also urged all parties to support the unity and sovereignty of states.

Separately, the minister said Israel has carried out more than 1,000 attacks on Syria in less than two years, killing dozens of people.

“How can calls for border control and placing weapons exclusively under state control be justified while Syrian sovereignty is violated and targeted on a daily basis?” he asked.

World.title: Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot
World.content:
Israel’s parliament remains in deadlock.

After one of the highest voter turnouts in decades, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority in the October 27 polls.

Netanyahu’s camp came first, with 53 seats, five more than the main opposition bloc. The Arab parties surged to a record 19 seats but have been relegated to merely observing coalition negotiations.

Viewed from a distance, the results could appear startling.

The judicial reforms ushered in at the start of Netanyahu’s government term in 2022 provoked the largest street protests in Israel’s history, while the prime minister himself is still embroiled in a corruption trial dating back to 2019. Alleged failures ahead of the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip have still to be reckoned with, despite overwhelming public pressure to do so. Moreover, the genocide has led to growing international isolation, while also providing the pretext for multiple attacks on countries across the region – the latest of which, undertaken with the United States on Iran in February, continues to roil energy markets around the world.

Nevertheless, roughly 2.38 million Israelis on Tuesday made the journey to the polls to back Netanyahu’s coalition, led by his Likud party, while some 2.21 million cast their ballots for the opposition alliance.

Between the two, little space was given to examine the multiple war crimes Israel stands accused of having carried out in Gaza, where Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,500 people and left much of it in ruins, or government complicity in the surging violence and pogroms in the occupied West Bank, where a United Nations commission of inquiry said on Monday that Israel had been committing crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture and rape.



Gaza did not make the ballot

Analysts said the fact that neither Gaza nor the West Bank were a deciding factor in how Israelis voted on Tuesday was largely because they already represented an area of broad agreement across both alliances.

Instead, the election was fought on largely internal issues: the power of Israel’s courts, whether members of the ultra-Orthodox minority should be exempted from military service, and whether the government’s alleged culpability in missing the warnings of the October 2023 attack should be examined.

Leading Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani said the issues were pitched to the Israeli public along broadly similar lines to those used by the politicians enacting the policies.

“I don’t think the problem is simply that people are uninformed or disengaged,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Many Israelis know that Gaza has been devastated, even though they are exposed to a very selective representation of that devastation. But knowing something and recognising its moral and political implications are different things,” Shenhav-Shahrabani added, providing one explanation for the absence of empathy displayed by many Israelis in the face of the widely reported suffering of Palestinians in Gaza.

“Ordinary people, who love their families, care for their friends, and consider themselves decent human beings, can participate in or acquiesce to a political order that produces immense suffering for others,” he said.

For Shenhav-Shahrabani, there has been “a powerful mechanism of denial” at work. “Not necessarily denial of the facts, but denial of their meaning,” he said.

Security on the agenda

For Netanyahu’s supporters, however, this denial could be traced to something more personal.

“The Likud is a tribe, or perhaps a cult and, as far as they are concerned, Dear Leader is always right,” Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman said of the prime minister’s base, which has sustained his rule for a cumulative 19 years – roughly a quarter of Israel’s entire existence.

“For them, the enemy, straight after the Arabs, is the left, and they would vote for Netanyahu regardless of his faults,” added Bregman, a senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.

For much of this electorate, the vote was less a judgement on the government’s conduct than a choice between competing claims to political legitimacy – or as Israeli academic Roi Zur put it, a contest over “the heart and soul of democracy” and the future of Jewish and Israeli identity.



“The most important thing, I think, for turnout among Netanyahu’s supporters is the understanding, or the belief, that the alternative coalition would be weaker on security,” said Zur, an expert on voter behaviour who teaches at Essex University.

What Netanyahu had been particularly successful in doing, he continued, was creating “this campaign of fear and the belief that he is the only one who can deal with this situation, that he is the only strong enough prime minister”.

“The idea that Netanyahu is the only and the strongest leader that can lead Israel through these recent times and the post-October 7 war.”

War and occupation, according to Shenhav-Shahrabani, were not choices to be made on the ballot paper.

Instead, they had become the prism through which, over decades, Israelis had come to view “security, citizenship, and the very meaning of democracy”.

“That is why replacing Netanyahu, important as it may be, would not by itself resolve the deeper problem.”

World.title: Burnham opens door to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
World.content:
The prime minister has ruled out financial reparations despite longstanding Caribbean demands ahead of Commonwealth leaders’ summit.

Britain’s prime minister has opened the door to a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, while ruling out financial reparations.

Andy Burnham set out his position in a Guardian article on Friday, ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Sunday.

The Commonwealth comprises 56 countries, mostly former British colonies, whose Caribbean members have long pressed Britain to acknowledge slavery’s legacy and offer redress.

Burnham offered structured talks with countries and campaign groups affected by slavery, including discussions on whether Britain should issue an official state apology.

“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them,” Burnham wrote.

He expressed “sorrow and regret” for the suffering of millions of enslaved people, but rejected calls for financial compensation.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” he said.

The stance maintains the position of previous British governments, despite his willingness to discuss an apology.

Instead, he proposed an international effort to ease the debt burden on poorer nations by extending repayment periods and cutting interest rates.

Burnham also said that former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown will assist with the initiative, adding that more than 40 percent of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable countries spend more on debt interest than on healthcare.



Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley welcomed the opening for talks but reiterated her government’s position on reparations.

In a statement reported by the Guardian on Saturday, she said cooperation could also cover healthcare, education, development and fairer borrowing terms.

Antigua’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who is hosting the summit, welcomed the debt initiative and promises of cooperation on renewable energy.

CARICOM, the regional bloc of Caribbean countries, has drawn up a 10-point plan for reparations.

Its demands go beyond payments to include an apology, support for health and education, as well as measures to address the economic and social damage left by slavery.

The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations, despite opposition from then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

King Charles III will also attend the summit. However, Buckingham Palace has said he will not issue a formal apology for slavery during his trip, despite calls from countries in the region.

World.title: On the Norway-Russia border, the Sámi people face a growing divide
World.content:
Along the shores of the Neiden Fjord, in Norway’s northernmost county Finnmark, Nils Boine* gazes out across the water. On the horizon, the Neiden River splits around the craggy island of Skogerøya, but lurking beneath its surface is a fisherman’s bounty: hundreds of king crabs.

His grandmother was Sea Sámi, from an Indigenous coastal people whose homeland, Sápmi, stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s heavily militarised Kola Peninsula. In Finnmark’s fjords, Sea Sámi families have fished for generations. But these waters are dissected by more than currents and shoals. Since Norway and Russia fixed their border in 1826, Sámi communities in the region have been divided by a national boundary.

Two hundred years later, this Arctic community is a combination of Sámi, Norwegians, Finns, Ukrainians, Russians, and international seasonal workers. Most of the Sámi population lives in Norway, with roughly 2 percent residing in Russia.

The Sámi have established a cross-border lifestyle, supported by flexible policies, including a Norwegian-Russian agreement allowing visa-free travel for those living within 30km (18.5 miles) of the border.

Security, however, has begun to tighten since the onset of Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine. The West sees Finnmark as part of NATO’s exposed northern flank, as it is directly opposite Russia’s heavily armed Kola Peninsula. The Norwegian border town of Kirkenes has been caught in a spy war with Russia, with multiple Russian operatives having been caught posing as tourists and fishermen while trying to engage in espionage.

Now, border bureaucracy is a daily reality, and reindeer herding, language revitalisation and hunting traditions are increasingly being navigated through permits and regulations, making the wider Arctic infrastructure feel fractured.

“I have friends in Russia,” Boine says. “We used to go shopping in Russia, and go there for weekends.”

Since Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, those crossings have stopped — partly as a display of solidarity with Ukraine, and partly due to safety concerns.

“A local person was just arrested in Russia, so people are afraid to cross the border,” Boine explains. “The rumours say that he had some illegal things in his car, but he was arrested, and the [Ministry of] Foreign Affairs in Norway tried to do something, but it’s very difficult, of course, because we don’t have any diplomats in Russia.”

He is referring to the reported June arrest of a Kirkenes businessman. Lawyer John Christian Elden told the daily newspaper Verdens Gang (VG) that the man was in custody for two months under alleged “possession of weapons or ammunition". Some Kirkenes residents were left shaken by the news, as recreational hunting is common in the region. They fear accidentally crossing the Russian border with forgotten hunting ammunition that might be left in their cars.

The number of Russian tourists visiting Norway has also declined, from 250,000 in 2019 to 52,000 last year.

“Before, we had Russian guests, but not now,” Boine says. Fortunately for his family, who run a tourism company, 80 percent of customers come from Asia or Finland. Their business has emerged relatively unscathed, but other companies have not been as lucky.

“Shops in the area have lost a lot of income without Russian [tourists],” says Boine. “Several shops have had to close.”

In a landscape traditionally connected for centuries, the fragmentation of communities is deeply concerning for both the regional economy and Sámi culture. Cross-border connections are deeply rooted in the regional psyche.

For Boine, the war in Ukraine has put his friendships with people in Russia on hold.

“They are afraid to do something wrong or write something wrong,” he says quietly. “You never know what might happen if they have too close contact,” he says.

“I want to be careful.”

World.title: West Indies thrash Bangladesh by eight wickets in first Test in Mirpur
World.content:
West Indies extend their encouraging run in red-ball cricket with an emphatic eight-wicket victory ⁠over Bangladesh ⁠in the first Test in Mirpur.

Share West Indies thrash Bangladesh by eight wickets in first Test in Mirpur on social media

Brandon King struck a career-best 81 not out as West Indies cruised to an eight-wicket win over Bangladesh in the first Test on Saturday to take a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.

King hit 10 fours and a six in his 115-ball knock to help the visitors chase down the target of 170 in 35.1 overs on the fourth day in Mirpur after Bangladesh were bowled out for 142 in their second innings.

Jomel Warrican, named player of the match, claimed 4-63 to follow up his five-wicket haul in Bangladesh’s first innings as the hosts were bowled out in 48.4 overs.

West Indies captain Roston Chase took 5-36 in the second innings, his fifth five-wicket haul in Test cricket.

Chase said the team was determined to win the series and go up in the rankings.

“The guys were determined, even though we didn’t have a good start in the first innings,” Chase said.

“We lost the lead, but we were still determined to fight back and try to win the game, and that’s what we did.”

Bangladesh had resumed the fourth day at 79-6, holding a lead of 106, but their hopes of setting a challenging target suffered an early blow when Jaker Ali edged Warrican to slip, where Chase took the catch.

Jaker, who scored 22 off 34 balls, was the second-highest scorer for Bangladesh in the innings.

Nayeem Hasan survived two dropped catches off Chase, on 21 and 29, to keep Bangladesh going.

‘Intention was good’

Nayeem added 26 runs with Hasan Mahmud before Warrican trapped the latter lbw for eight.



Taijul Islam contributed eight in a 17-run partnership with Nayeem before Chase dismissed him to leave Bangladesh at 127-9.

Nayeem then reached his maiden Test half-century off 87 balls, with four boundaries, but his resistance ended when he attempted to hit Chase over long-on and was caught by Joshua Bishop.

He made 52 off 91 balls, while Shoriful Islam remained unbeaten on seven as Bangladesh were dismissed cheaply.

Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto said his team failed to execute their plans.

“All three departments didn’t do well, especially in the field. These things can happen sometimes, but I believe the intention and preparation were quite good,” he said.

“Going forward, we need to look at those areas and work out how we can do better in these conditions.”

West Indies started confidently, with openers King and John Campbell continuing their aggressive approach to take the visitors to 64 without loss in 14.1 overs before rain interrupted play.

After a delay of about an hour, they added another 23 runs before bad light and lightning forced a further stoppage of 45 minutes.

King was dropped on 70 by substitute fielder Ebadot Hossain off Taijul after the break, but the opener made Bangladesh pay with his fine, unbeaten knock.

Campbell fell just short of a half-century, bowled by Shoriful for 49 off 55 balls, with six fours and a six.

The victory continued a positive period for West Indies, who recently pushed India in a one-day series and shared a 2-2 draw ‌in ‌a T20 series against the world champions earlier this month.

The second Test will be played in Sylhet from November 5.

World.title: Studios destroyed, traditions saved: Artists fight to save Sudan’s culture
World.content:
Artists in Sudan are working to save culture and traditions amid the country’s war.

Port Sudan, Sudan – Awad Haroun, 45, a visual artist and theatre director, fled his home in Al-Halfaya, Khartoum North, after war destroyed a life he had worked hard to build in the capital.

He moved to Port Sudan with his wife and son, leaving behind his home, artistic workspace and the tools he needed to work, shortly after fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023.

When he fled, he carried little: Two shirts, two pairs of trousers, two books and a few torn drawing papers, expecting to return soon. Instead, he has been forced to rebuild his life far from home.

He lost not only his home but also the tools and materials he relied on to work and make a living.

In Port Sudan, he looked to use his skills in sculpture, design and decoration for some money. He has since participated in theatrical performances at Wasel Festival, organised by Ahalina Cultural Group in partnership with UNESCO, and led traditional arts workshops with cultural groups.

Awad founded Ahalina cultural group in 2013 with a group of young people, using theatre, visual arts, music and puppetry to engage with young people and promote peace and social cohesion.

Drawing, storytelling, music and play have also given children opportunities to express themselves and connect with others.

“Losing my tools does not mean I have lost my skills, and losing my workspace does not mean I have lost my ability to create,” Awad told Al Jazeera.



Awad and other displaced artists found shelter at an old school in Port Sudan, where they helped clean and prepare the building for families forced from their homes.

“Now, concerns about the possibility of eviction have left us uncertain about where we will go next,” he said.

While art cannot replace a lost home or end the war, Awad believes it can preserve memories, bring communities together and offer children space to play and express themselves.

“From the ashes, we will rise” is the motto of Ahalina cultural group. This is more than a slogan for Awad; it is a reminder to keep creating, despite everything the war has taken from him.

The war has taken a heavy toll on Sudan’s cultural life, damaging heritage sites and disrupting the livelihoods of artists across the country.

In June 2026, UNESCO estimated that Sudan’s cultural sector faced a $30m funding gap. But behind this figure are deeply personal losses: Artists killed by the war or forced to leave behind studios, galleries, artworks and the tools they need to create.

In April 2024, UNESCO reported that the Artists and Writers Union in Port Sudan had provided shelter to more than 112 displaced artists and other cultural professionals.

The challenges remain significant, but cultural initiatives have continued. In April 2026, UNESCO said its initiatives in Port Sudan had benefitted more than 350 artists, women, girls and internally displaced cultural professionals, supporting efforts to sustain Sudan’s cultural life amid the conflict.

Asim Abdelaziz, 31, a musician and filmmaker, left El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, amid escalating fighting and repeated drone attacks. He arrived in Port Sudan in November 2023, hoping to find safety and work.

Separated from his family, who are scattered between Omdurman and El Obeid, Asim lives alone in a shelter for displaced artists. The war has uprooted his life and disrupted his career, but he continues to use music to preserve Sudan’s cultural heritage and bring communities together.

In Port Sudan, he has worked with the local Artists and Writers Union, UNESCO and community organisations. He has also collaborated with the Ministry of Culture and Information and other artists on music programmes to address social issues, including hate speech and racism.

Asim said the war has spurred hate speech and deepened divisions between Sudan’s different communities. He believes art can counter these differences by promoting diversity, mutual acceptance and peaceful coexistence.



“I have seen firsthand how hate speech affects people’s lives,” Asim told Al Jazeera. “Through music, I try to remind Sudanese people that we are all brothers and sisters, and that war does not represent who we are.”

Mokhalaya, a project he founded to document and archive traditional music and rhythms from across the country a year ago, is one avenue for this.

“I hope to take the project to international festivals, introducing audiences abroad to [showcase] Sudan’s rich musical traditions and cultural diversity,” he said.

Preserving heritage is not just about safeguarding the past, but also about keeping Sudan’s cultural identity alive during a war that has displaced communities and disrupted lives, he said.

Abdelqader Hashem, secretary of the Red Sea State Writers and Artists Union, told Al Jazeera the union has supported artists and their families who fled fighting in other parts of Sudan since the war began on April 15, 2023.

“We worked to establish a shelter for displaced artists in a school in Port Sudan and sought support from local and international organisations to provide for their basic needs,” he said.

Beyond providing shelter, the union has helped displaced artists take part in the city’s cultural activities, contributing to community awareness programmes that address important societal issues such as the dangers of drug use, a growing concern in Sudan.

“We have also implemented projects in partnership with UNESCO to train children in displacement camps in handicrafts, including concrete crafts,” Hashem said.

“Most of the displaced artists have since returned to their homes in Khartoum following the Sudanese army’s recapture of the capital.”

World.title: Alaska’s two ‘Dan Sullivans’: How common is ballot stacking, does it work?
World.content:
Same names on Alaska ballot triggered political firestorm in US, prompting a Justice Department investigation.

Share Alaska’s two ‘Dan Sullivans’: How common is ballot stacking, does it work? on social media

The Alaska Senate ballot in the next week’s midterm elections in the United States features two candidates with the name Dan Sullivan – one the incumbent Republican senator and another a retired teacher with no prior political experience.

Last week, The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democrat challenging Republican Senator Sullivan for a crucial seat, helped recruit candidates bearing names similar to Sullivan’s in an apparent bid to manipulate the ballot and siphon votes from the incumbent.

The controversy has triggered a political firestorm in the US, and prompted President Donald Trump to order a Justice Department investigation into alleged voter fraud.

“It was a scheme. It was election fraud. Total election fraud,” Trump said. Peltola has rejected the accusations, saying the dispute is distracting from voters’ concerns.

On Friday, US Attorney Michael Heyman said Democrats had “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”, adding that “we are taking that extremely seriously”.

So, how common is this electoral tactic – and does it work? We look at history to find out.

What’s happened in Alaska?

Daniel J Sullivan Jr, the second Dan Sullivan, announced his US Senate candidacy on May 29, just three days before Alaska’s June 1 filing deadline. The Republican nominee on the ballot is also called Dan Sullivan. The second Sullivan has repeatedly denied any Democratic push behind his candidacy.



However, the Times’s reporting earlier this week triggered a political storm over allegations that Democratic operatives had sought to manipulate Alaska’s crucial US Senate race by recruiting candidates to split votes for Republican incumbent Sullivan.

The report alleged that people aligned with Peltola, her campaign’s lawyers and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) had coordinated an initiative to recruit candidates who could dilute Sullivan’s support – internally called the “ballot composition project”.

According to the Times, a Peltola campaign staffer was tasked with identifying Alaskans named Dan Sullivan.

The strategy, commonly called “ballot stacking”, involves recruiting or encouraging candidates to enter a race not necessarily to win, but to influence the distribution of votes and improve another candidate’s chances.

Alaska has four candidates on the ballot – and the presence of two candidates named Sullivan could potentially confuse voters.

The report prompted Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy to order a criminal investigation.

“I just want to clear the air,” Peltola said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital, on Friday. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

The race is considered key to control of the US Senate.

Does ballot stacking work?

Past instances show that the strategy can work at times to manipulate voters.

One of the starkest examples emerged in Florida’s 2020 state Senate race, when Republican political operative and former state senator Frank Artiles allegedly orchestrated a scheme to recruit a namesake candidate to undermine Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodriguez.

According to prosecutors, Artiles paid Alex Rodriguez, who shared the incumbent’s surname, to enter the race as an independent candidate to confuse voters and divert ballots from the Democrat to his Republican challenger, Ileana Garcia.

Incumbent senator Jose lost by just 32 votes – while the other Rodriguez garnered more than 6,000 votes without having led a meaningful campaign.

Later, Alex Rodriguez pleaded guilty to campaign finance violations in 2021 and agreed to cooperate with investigators, and Artiles was later convicted in connection with the scheme and fined.



Similarly, in 2024, Washington’s Democratic state Attorney General Bob Ferguson was joined by two namesakes in the primary race, after a Republican activist was alleged to have paid the other two Fergusons to run.

However, Democratic leader Bob Ferguson threatened legal action – and the decoys dropped out. Ferguson was elected governor.

Have there been other cases of ballot stacking?

Though stacking a ballot is a political tactic used in other countries as well, the US has seen a couple of its own instances, in Florida and Washington.

During John F Kennedy’s first congressional campaign, a second candidate named Joseph Russo entered the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’ 11th Congressional District. The first Joseph Russo was a prominent Boston city councillor who opposed Kennedy.

Kennedy’s campaign manager and his father, Joseph P Kennedy Sr, have been implicated in accounts of the alleged scheme, but the extent of JFK’s personal involvement remains disputed.

In the June 1946 primary, Kennedy received 22,183 votes, while the two Russos collectively received 6,460. Kennedy won the nomination.

In India, the world’s most populous country, fielding such namesakes is a common tactic – but not always a successful one.

In the 2019 national election, Congress president Rahul Gandhi, the scion of the Gandhi family, faced three namesakes in Wayanad, Kerala, in southern India. The candidates were named: Rahul Gandhi K E, Raghul Gandhi K, and K M Sivaprasad Gandhi.

Congress’s Rahul Gandhi won Wayanad by a landslide, however, securing 706,367 votes.

In the 2014 national election, Bollywood actor and a candidate of the Bharatiya Janata Party, Hema Malini, faced two namesakes in Mathura, Uttar Pradesh. The actor also won that election decisively.

In the 2014 election, in Mahasamund in Chhattisgarh, Congress candidate Ajit Jogi faced BJP’s Chandu Lal Sahu in a race with seven other candidates named Chandu Lal Sahu. BJP’s Sahu won by a margin of nearly 11,000 votes, whereas his namesakes collectively got 62,934 votes.

But for some, it has proven costly in India. Also in the 2014 election, incumbent Member of Parliament, K Sudhakaran from Congress, was defeated by a margin of 6,566 votes. His two namesakes, K Sudhakaran Sreeshylam and K Sudhakaran Kollon, secured 2,745 and 4,240 votes, respectively.

World.title: Here is the latest.
World.content:
Pinned

Thousands of protesters were on the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, a now-weekly expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police, and kept the country on edge.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which also falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

Early estimates from the French interior ministry suggested that by midafternoon, crowds were smaller than at the same time on the previous two Saturdays. At 2 p.m., the ministry estimated that 15,000 people were taking part in 65 protests. The numbers were expected to grow as the day progressed. The ministry said it had arrested 27 people, compared with 217 by the same time last Saturday.

The huge demonstrations last Saturday did not descend into the lawlessness that erupted the week before, in part because of a heavy security force, which is being marshaled again. In Paris, the authorities moved the route for marchers to the city’s eastern periphery, as they did previously, drawing outrage and fruitless legal challenges from organizers.

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, warned on Thursday that it could be a “day with a very high risk to public order.” He promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There is ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

While tensions could rise during the day, the authorities said they were most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather in spite of the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration in which public order is disrupted.

Here’s what else to know.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people and inciting them to violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often end up in clashes with far-left groups.

Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

World.title: Evacuees from Russia-occupied city where residents ate weeds arrive in Ukraine
World.content:
"As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region," Zelensky said in a post on X.

"All of them will receive the assistance they need. It is important that government agencies and all the regional and local authorities involved work effectively and help our people adapt."

The evacuees were taken via Russia and Belarus before being driven across Ukraine's northern border on Saturday.

The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.

One evacuee, Liubov, told the Reuters news agency: "Until we got on the buses, we were afraid of everything, we were so worried and nervous. Before that, we spent nights without sleeping, wondering how it would go, what would happen. But everything went well."

Another said they had lost 20 kg in the last year, adding: "My strength left me."

Valera, who did not give his last name, told the AFP news agency: "There was no bread. Nothing."

"Lots of people planted vegetable gardens. We ate whatever was available. Well, thank God, we're here now."

A humanitarian ceasefire took effect across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Conditions had become so desperate in Oleshky that not only was getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape was highly dangerous because the routes out had been mined and subject to drone attack.

Bridges across the nearby River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank has been mined and is dangerous.

One resident who fled the city three weeks earlier told the BBC he had walked through 24km (15 miles) of minefields to get to safety.

World.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
World.content:
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.

This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.

Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.

Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.

The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.

World.title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
World.content:
More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.

Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.

The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.

In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.

Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations, and the second largest in history.

The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.

Testing and treatment is under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.

The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is currently no treatment or vaccine for this strain.

Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.

As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.

Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.

Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.

No cases have been reported in Uganda since August, but travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.

In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths. One woman was confirmed to have the disease in Nigeria, but flown to Switzerland for further treatment.

The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

World.title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
World.content:
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.

Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.

Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.

In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.

"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."

The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.

Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.

One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.

World.title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
World.content:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.

Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.

The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.

Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.

It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.

He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.

Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.

The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.

It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.

Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

World.title: Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
World.content:
Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.

The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.

"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.

"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."

So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.

"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."

But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.

"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.

An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails - very different to the latest collision.

But there is a similar impact.

"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."

For Team SÃ¡nchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.

Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.

Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.

Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.

That's when SÃ¡nchez called an early election.

His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.

World.title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
World.content:
In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.

The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.

Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.

"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.

Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.

That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.

They agreed that action was urgent.

The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.

But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.

As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.

"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.

"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.

This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."

But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".

Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland.

Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.

Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.

In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (Â£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.

But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , external

At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.

World.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
World.content:
In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night.

He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day".

The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.

The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.

Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".

It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".

The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".

Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.

The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

World.title: TRENDING: Toyin posts TikTok partnership after Funke’s Facebook deal, sparks rivalry debate
World.content:
Nollywood actress Toyin Abraham has caused buzz on social media after sharing a throwback to her TikTok collaboration on “Oversabi Aunty”, days after her colleague, Funke Akindele, unveiled her partnership with Facebook for her upcoming film, “The Four: No One Fights Alone.”

Akindele announced the partnership on her Instagram page on Thursday, describing it as an opportunity to take the film to a wider audience.

She described the partnership as a significant achievement in her professional journey, thanking her fans for their unwavering encouragement and support over the years.

She added that Facebook would give audiences an inside look at the film, from production activities and promotional campaigns to premiere moments and previously unseen behind-the-scenes footage.

“We’re taking The Four to the world, and Facebook is coming with us. I’m so excited to announce my partnership with Facebook for The Four: No One Fights Alone! The love you’ve shown me and my stories over the years has brought us this far. Now, let’s make this next chapter one to remember.”

Akindele’s announcement drew congratulatory messages from fans and other social media users. However, some used the opportunity to take jabs at actress Abraham, comparing the two filmmakers.

Some social media users argued that Abraham had earlier pioneered collaborations with social media platforms to promote films. In contrast, others suggested that she and other filmmakers would now follow Akindele’s example by partnering with Facebook.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I’ve done the same”

In response to the criticism, Abraham shared a throwback post highlighting her earlier partnership with TikTok, pointing out that she had done something similar before Akindele’s Facebook collaboration.

On Instagram, she shared a throwback post describing her work with TikTok on Oversabi Aunty as a memorable experience.

The film debuted in cinemas on 19 December 2025 before arriving on Netflix and Kava on 2 October. Abraham produced and directed the comedy-drama, which marked her first outing as a film director.

The cast includes Mike Ezuruonye, Jemima Osunde, Enioluwa Adeoluwa, Toyin Afolayan, Efe Irele and Tana Adelana, alongside Abraham.

The film centres on Toun, a church usher whose commitment to church activities takes a back seat to her habit of criticising and correcting those around her.

Abraham also expressed excitement about exploring more exciting partnerships for her forthcoming film, Bestie.

“Throwback to when TikTok collaborated with Oversabi Aunty! It was such a beautiful experience, and I’m looking forward to more amazing collaborations as we gear up for Bestie. More magic, more creativity and bigger moments ahead! Anyway, fam, are you ready?” She wrote.

PREMIUM TIMES findings

PREMIUM TIMES fact-checked the claims by Abraham and Akindele about their respective collaborations with major social media platforms and found differences between the two announcements.

The photograph Abraham shared on Instagram did not originate from a collaboration programme. Instead, it showed her attending TikTok’s #WhatToWatch Cinema Experience, which took place on 17 December 2025.

TikTok organised the event to bring filmmakers, actors and film content creators together to examine the relationship between social media and cinema, particularly how digital platforms can increase film exposure and audience engagement.

Abraham spoke at the gathering about her experience using TikTok to promote films. She also highlighted her work as a creator and praised the platform’s algorithm for organically connecting content with relevant audiences.

A review of the picture shows that TikTok Africa and TikTok Nigeria mentioned the actress in a post identifying her as an attendee at the event, which gives viewers the impression that she was a collaborator.

Abraham also referred to the gathering as the #WhatToWatch Cinema Experience in the caption of her video. She did not identify it as a collaboration initiative.

She wrote: “Thank you a lot, TikTok. Africa. #Oversabiaunty is #whattowatch in all cinemas from today.”

A different situation emerged from Akindele’s announcement. This newspaper found that Meta, Facebook’s parent company, publicly confirmed its partnership with the filmmaker to promote “The Four.”

According to the company, the partnership covers the film’s world premiere in London and its homecoming premiere in Lagos. It also plans to create experiences that connect content creators, celebrities and audiences.

Meta confirmed the arrangement in a post after Akindele tagged Facebook in her announcement.

“This story is too big for one place. Facebook is partnering with Funke Akindele for the London and Lagos premieres of her movie ‘The Four’, and we’re bringing every moment to her community around the world.

“Follow our page and Officialfunke Akindele right here on Facebook for all the behind-the-scenes details and catch-ups. Stay tuned! Stories. Connect. Community.”

PREMIUM TIMES, however, could not independently establish the first filmmaker to partner with Facebook on the global promotion of a feature film as of press time.

“Rivalry that spanned over a decade”

The latest incident once again drew attention to the long-running speculation surrounding the relationship between two of Nollywood’s biggest actresses.

The perceived rivalry dates back to the early 2010s, when both actresses began attracting significant attention in the Yoruba film industry. While Akindele had already established herself as a prominent figure, Abraham was steadily building her reputation and strengthening her position in the industry.

Fan comparisons and persistent industry rumours reportedly fuelled speculation about competition between the actresses.

The tension reportedly intensified in 2021 when their films, Akindele’s “Omo Ghetto: The Saga” and Abraham’s “The Ghost and the Tout Too”, competed at the box office.

The actresses faced another major box-office showdown in 2024 and 2025 when Akindele released “Everybody Loves Jenifa”, while Abraham promoted “Alakada: Bad and Boujee.”

The competition sparked allegations of bias in cinema screening arrangements, along with claims of behind-the-scenes rivalry and attempts to undermine each other. However, the allegations remained unsubstantiated.

Despite the speculation, both actresses appeared to make efforts to mend their relationship between 2024 and 2025. They addressed the issues on their respective social media accounts and later shared warm moments at a movie premiere. Their public interactions raised hopes among fans that they had finally put the reported disagreement behind them.

However, their latest encounter at the premiere of “The Return of Arinzo”, a film directed by Iyabo Ojo, revived questions about their relationship.

A viral video from the event showed Abraham, dressed in a purple gown, moving around the venue and exchanging pleasantries with colleagues before approaching a table where Akindele sat with other industry figures, including Mercy Aigbe, Shaffy Bello and Ojo.

Abraham appeared to approach Akindele warmly, touching her arm and leaning towards her as she attempted to exchange greetings. The interaction lasted for more than five seconds, but Akindele kept her gaze forward and did not visibly acknowledge her colleague.

Abraham subsequently turned to greet other guests seated beside Akindele. During the movement, the extended chest area of her gown accidentally brushed against Akindele’s hair. Akindele turned sideways and adjusted her hair herself without responding to Abraham.

Abraham appeared to make another attempt to greet her, possibly because she thought Akindele had not heard her earlier attempt. However, Akindele still did not visibly respond.

The video quickly circulated across social media platforms, prompting widespread reactions. While some viewers interpreted Akindele’s conduct as a deliberate snub, others argued that the encounter might have been a misunderstanding.

Reactions

The actress’s post attracted mixed reactions, with Akindele’s fans and other netizens criticising Abraham and urging her to take it down.

Some netizens accused her of fuelling the controversy while attempting to avoid responsibility for the fallout.

However, not everyone shared that view. While some faulted Abraham for posting the throwback collaboration, others backed her and defended her decision.

Below are some of the comments.

World.title: Ebola: Nigeria reports two new suspected cases in North-east
World.content:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has reported two new suspected cases of Ebola disease in Nigeria’s North-east region.

The agency disclosed this in an update posted on its official X account on Saturday, noting that both individuals had been isolated while contact identification and listing were ongoing.

“Laboratory testing is being conducted,” the NCDC said, adding that being classified as suspected cases does not mean the individuals have Ebola, as confirmation depends on laboratory results.

The agency urged Nigerians to maintain good hand hygiene, practise enhanced sanitation and follow guidance from public health authorities.

The development comes 11 days after Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus.

More details shortly.

World.title: Why government funding alone won’t fix Nigeria’s education crisis, By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
For Nigeria, this raises a fundamental policy concern, which is my burning question for this edition. Why should Nigerian universities remain so heavily dependent on government allocations and tuition when their research capabilities could also attract corporate investment, generate intellectual property and support new businesses? This requires more than asking companies to fund universities. It requires institutions capable of producing credible research, protecting intellectual property, and negotiating commercial partnerships.

A country’s investment in research and development (R&D) is one of the clearest indicators of how seriously it takes its future. Scientific discoveries do not happen by accident. They require sustained funding, functioning research institutions, skilled people, technological infrastructure and governments willing to invest in knowledge before its economic benefits become visible. The United States spent an estimated $993 billion on R&D in 2024, approximately 3.4 per cent of its GDP. Nigeria’s internationally reported R&D expenditure data, by comparison, remains remarkably outdated. The UNESCO series available through the World Bank records an expenditure of just 0.22 per cent of GDP in 2007, with no sufficiently recent comparable observation. This is not merely a statistical inconvenience. It raises questions about how seriously Nigeria measures and prioritises the scientific capacity required for development.

In March, I visited the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, where my daughter is currently a pre-med student. The university, often described as one of America’s Public Ivies because of its academic reputation and standing among leading public universities, has Professor Omolade Adunbi, a Nigerian, on its faculty as its director of the African Studies Center. I have maintained a relationship with Professor Adunbi for nearly two decades, and he joined my daughter in welcoming me to campus. During our conversation, I asked him about innovative ways that American universities finance their programmes and what Nigeria and other African economies could learn from these. He then introduced me to what I would call the Michigan template.

One of the things he drew my attention to include the commercial value of university research as a source of funding. The University of Michigan has an extensive research-commercialisation ecosystem, connecting faculty research with corporations, foundations, investors and entrepreneurs through its innovation partnerships office.

At Michigan, research output creates opportunities for corporations to sponsor research, enter partnerships with academics, license intellectual property and commercialise discoveries. Professor Adunbi mentioned Google co-founder Larry Page as an illustration of the relationship between university education, research and entrepreneurship. Page graduated from Michigan before proceeding to Stanford, where he and Sergey Brin developed PageRank, the technology that became foundational to Google. The research that produced Google was conducted at Stanford, but the example illustrates the wider value of university education and innovation.

Our conversation moved effortlessly from the political economy of Nigerian academic institutions to the politics of their governing bodies. Professor Adunbi outlined four pathways through which universities can generate value from research: corporate-sponsored research, in which companies finance research addressing technological or commercial challenges; intellectual property licensing, through which universities protect and license commercially valuable discoveries; university spinouts, which allow researchers to establish businesses around campus innovations; and strategic research partnerships, through which corporations support longer-term research programmes relevant to their industries.

As Nigeria continues to approve licences for more universities, the value of these institutions must extend beyond the degrees they award. It should also be measured by their capacities to produce people, ideas and discoveries that create economic value.

In fiscal year 2025, Michigan recorded $2.16 billion in research expenditures, attracted $170.6 million in corporate-sponsored research awards and supported the creation of 31 startups. Its experience demonstrates what becomes possible when academic research, government investment and private-sector participation reinforce one another.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria’s experience reflects this worrying trend. In 2018, some 26 per cent of Nigerians said they trusted science a lot. By 2020, that figure had fallen to 13 per cent. It recovered modestly to 15 per cent in 2025. Although the recovery is welcome, Nigeria remains 11 percentage points below its pre-pandemic level. Overall, 57 per cent of Nigerians reported at least some trust in science.

For Nigeria, this raises a fundamental policy concern, which is my burning question for this edition. Why should Nigerian universities remain so heavily dependent on government allocations and tuition when their research capabilities could also attract corporate investment, generate intellectual property and support new businesses? This requires more than asking companies to fund universities. It requires institutions capable of producing credible research, protecting intellectual property, and negotiating commercial partnerships.

In connection, On 10 October, the London-based global charity, Wellcome, published a report that draws on interviews with more than 140,000 people across 140 countries. Its findings show that public trust in science has declined globally since the COVID-19 pandemic and fallen below its 2018 level.

Nigeria’s experience reflects this worrying trend. In 2018, some 26 per cent of Nigerians said they trusted science a lot. By 2020, that figure had fallen to 13 per cent. It recovered modestly to 15 per cent in 2025. Although the recovery is welcome, Nigeria remains 11 percentage points below its pre-pandemic level. Overall, 57 per cent of Nigerians reported at least some trust in science.

The survey’s findings on vaccination make the challenge more concrete. Asked whether they would take a vaccine recommended by a doctor or nurse, 35 per cent of Nigerian respondents said they would take it immediately. Another 36 per cent preferred time to think about it, while 24 per cent said they did not take vaccines at all. Someone who wants time to consider a vaccine is not necessarily opposed to vaccination. Such concerns should not automatically be dismissed as ignorance. The more important question is whether people can obtain clear, credible answers that allow them to make informed decisions.

The pandemic provides an important context. Scientific recommendations sometimes change because the evidence has changed. That is not a weakness of science; it is how science works. But when authorities communicate uncertainty poorly, subsequent changes can be interpreted as evidence of incompetence or dishonesty.

Nigeria must nevertheless resist the temptation to explain its figures entirely through COVID-19. For many Nigerians, the most immediate encounter with science is not a laboratory or research institution, but a hospital, clinic, pharmacy or conversation with a health professional.

To be fair, the Nigerian government has announced an initiative that could address some of these challenges. Following Federal Executive Council approval, the Federal Government announced in May plans to establish the National Research and Innovation Development Fund (NRIDF), with an annual funding target of up to $500 million – approximately ₦673 billion at the current official exchange rate. The fund is intended to support competitive research grants, strengthen innovation infrastructure, and commercialise research findings.

As it is, the Wellcome report identifies an important relationship between confidence in healthcare institutions and trust in science. Globally, 43 per cent of people expressing a lot of confidence in their country’s hospitals and clinics also reported a lot of trust in science, compared with 26 per cent across the survey population.

Economic insecurity adds another dimension. Globally, 39 per cent of people living comfortably reported a lot of trust in science in 2025, compared with 20 per cent of those finding it difficult to get by financially. Families preoccupied with food, rent, school fees and medical bills may have fewer resources to seek reliable information or act on professional advice. When institutions appear disconnected from those struggles, their pronouncements may carry less weight.

To be fair, the Nigerian government has announced an initiative that could address some of these challenges. Following Federal Executive Council approval, the Federal Government announced in May plans to establish the National Research and Innovation Development Fund (NRIDF), with an annual funding target of up to $500 million – approximately ₦673 billion at the current official exchange rate. The fund is intended to support competitive research grants, strengthen innovation infrastructure, and commercialise research findings.

However, there is a difference between what a government promises and what it commits to funding. The $500 million figure was announced as an estimated annual target. On 8 October, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Kingsley Udeh, clarified that the exact amount could not yet be determined because the proposed funding mechanism would draw on different sources calculated as percentages on a year-by-year basis. He also confirmed that the enabling bill had been forwarded to the National Assembly. In other words, the government has secured executive approval for the initiative, but the legislative and funding arrangements are not yet fully established. An announcement is not an appropriation, and an appropriation is not necessarily a disbursement.

The government must therefore demonstrate that the fund will be backed by a sustainable revenue framework, independently governed, transparently administered and accessible to credible researchers.

I have not found a specific public response from the Nigerian government to the Wellcome report since its 10 October publication. But to turn discoveries into commercially viable solutions, Nigeria needs research that addresses local priorities and stronger university-industry partnerships.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: OPay withdraws planned $304m US IPO over foreign regulatory inquiry
World.content:
OPay, a Nigeria-focused digital financial services company, has withdrawn its planned $304 million US initial public offering on Friday over a regulatory inquiry by a foreign jurisdiction it did not identify.

The SoftBank-backed digital-payments company described the inquiry as relating to a jurisdiction immaterial to its core operations, Reuters reported.

The company had earlier disclosed that it was raising $304 million in its initial public offering (IPO) and aimed to secure a market capitalisation of more than $4 billion.

The company had planned to list on the NYSE under the ticker symbol “OPay.”

OPay withdrew its planned US initial public offering later on Friday, but it did not identify the regulator or the nature of the inquiry.

OPay said it expected the matter to be resolved satisfactorily in the near future and that the probe should not be misconstrued as a reflection of the company’s business performance, financial condition, operational integrity or regulatory standing.

It explained that the inquiry would not affect its operations, regulatory standing or customer service in Nigeria or its other markets.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Founded in 2018, OPay provides digital financial services across emerging markets, including Nigeria and Indonesia.

Its app offers payments, money transfers, savings and loans in economies where limited access to traditional banking can make everyday transactions difficult.

The company had reached a $1 billion revenue run rate in the second quarter of 2026, recording 137 per cent year-on-year growth and a 19 per cent net margin in the first six months of the year.

The fintech company raised $400 million in 2021 at a valuation of $2 billion. It had about 50 million monthly active users as of 31 July, according to its IPO prospectus.

Citigroup, Deutsche ⁠Bank, Standard Bank, and CICC were among the underwriters.

World.title: What Rabiu, Uba Sani, Yari, others said after Umrah with Tinubu
World.content:
BUA chairperson, Abdulsamad Rabiu, and other members of the delegation accompanying President Bola Tinubu on Umrah to Saudi Arabia have offered special supplications for the nation, focusing on lasting peace, national unity, and the peaceful conduct of the general elections in 2027.

​Mr Rabiu expressed gratitude for the opportunity to join Tinubu in the Holy Land, and emphasised the spiritual significance of the visit at a critical juncture in the nation’s political calendar.

“Alhamdulillah, it’s very significant, and we are blessed and honoured, you know, to accompany His Excellency, Mr President, you know, to the Holy Land, and we are here to, in this sacred, you know, in this sacred place, to pray for Nigeria, to pray for peace, long, long-lasting peace for the country, for unity in Nigeria, and as we know, we are preparing for the elections, which will happen soon.

“So again, we have prayed and will continue to pray for you know free, fair, and successful you know elections in the country. And we pray that Allah accepts all our prayers, you know, and worship here, and we hope and pray that peace and unity will prevail in our country”, Mr Rabiu stated.

​Also speaking, Governor Uba Sani of Kaduna State stated that the visit provided an opportunity to pray over insecurity in Kaduna and other states.

​”The number one priority for us is to pray for our country, pray for our states, and pray for our people. Of course, we have some challenges, as you are aware, which we believe require prayers.

​”On the issue of insecurity in our country, particularly in some states, governors are trying, and security agencies are trying. Even our citizens are making concerted efforts to address these challenges.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

​”However, some of us firmly believe that we must pray to Almighty Allah to intervene. Most of these issues persist not necessarily due to a lack of effort by security agencies, governors, or the President.

​”There are individuals within society who need to work more closely with the relevant security agencies to tackle these problems.

“We must pray for Almighty Allah to touch their hearts and change their ways, because reports from security agencies indicate that there is connivance—not necessarily from politicians, but even among ordinary members of the public who fail to give the necessary cooperation.

​”We must pray for everyone to embrace patriotism and be our brothers’ keepers. That is the only way we can effectively overcome these challenges.
