World.title: UPND is a strong reliable party – Vice President
World.content:
Vice-President, Mutale Nalumango, says the United Party for National Development (UPND) is a strong, reliable and disciplined political party capable of competing effectively in a democratic environment.

Mrs Nalumango says the withdrawal of some opposition candidates from by-elections raises questions about their preparedness to compete politically.

She said this in Parliament today, during the Vice-President’s Question Time in response to Choma Central Member of Parliament (MP) Cornelius Mweetwa, who sought advice for the opposition candidates who had withdrawn from participating in the Mandevu parliamentary by-election.

Mrs Nalumango said democracy thrives on competition and political parties should be prepared to compete within the established rules rather than withdraw when faced with challenges.

She said political competition requires strength, discipline, competence and commitment to one’s political convictions.

The Vice-President observed that political parties should not expect their competitors to create room for them, stating that every party must work hard to win the confidence of the electorate.

Mrs Nalumango further urged MPs regardless of their political affiliation, to work together in promoting national development, noting that all elected representatives were servants of the people.

She, however, expressed concern over what she described as a lack of discipline and competence among some political players, urging them to remain committed to their political principles.

UPND candidate, Adrian Banda, has reportedly gone unopposed in the Mandevu parliamentary by-election after three rival candidates withdrew from the race.

The candidates that have withdrawn are Daniel Chisenga who stood on the Forum for Democracy and Development (FDD) ticket, Ntazana Muntungwa of the Leadership Movement as well as Independent candidate, Daniel Daka.

Banda’s unopposed election means no poll will be held in the constituency.

World.title: Kalusha Bwalya drainage system project nears completion
World.content:
Lusaka City Council says works on the 7.2-kilometre Kalusha Bwalya drainage project is nearing completion as part of efforts to improve stormwater management and prevent flooding in the flood-prone areas.

The project is among several drainage clearing activities being undertaken by the council across the city to ensure that drainages are free from blockages and can effectively channel storm water.

LCC Public Relations Officer, Chola Mwamba, said in an interview with ZANIS today, that the council has successfully completed the excavation and lining of the drainage bed along the entire 7.2-kilometre stretch.

She said that the remaining works involve the construction of concrete walls, of which 1.4 kilometers have already been completed.

Ms Mwamba therefore added that the council remains committed to ensuring that the project is fully completed to improve drainage and reduce the risk of flooding in the area.

World.title: Zambia Aquatics Federation calls for increased investments in swimming
World.content:
Zambia Aquatics Federation President, Guy Phiri, has called on the government to increase investment in swimming facilities particularly in public schools, to improve access to the sport and help prevent drowning.

In an exclusive Interview with the media, Phiri said the shortage of accessible swimming pools remains one of the major challenges facing the development of swimming in the country.

He stated that investing in swimming facilities will provide young people with opportunities to learn the sport and acquire essential water safety skills.

Phiri highlighted that swimming has brought Zambia international recognition, with local swimmers winning medals at the Region 5 Games and the All-Africa Games.

He added that the country is proud of the achievements of its swimmers, clubs and coaches despite challenges in securing adequate funding.

Phiri said the federation will continue working with stakeholders, including the Sports Council of Zambia, to mobilise additional resources to support swimmers and strengthen the development of swimming.

World.title: Malawi: Police Confirm Egyptian Deputy Ambassador Beaten in Lilongwe Attack
World.content:
A senior Egyptian diplomat has been hospitalised after being attacked and beaten in Lilongwe, sparking a police investigation into the shocking assault.

National Police spokesperson Gladys Chiwaula confirmed that Egypt's Deputy Ambassador to Malawi was admitted to a hospital in the capital after the attack.

"Police are following up on the matter and will give more details later," she said.

Chiwaula gave few details.

She did not say where the attack happened, what led to it, or how serious the diplomat's injuries are. Police have also withheld the deputy ambassador's name.

Officers say they are investigating, but the incident is likely to raise alarm over the safety of foreign envoys in the country.

World.title: South Africa: African Horse Sickness Confirmed in Western Cape's Cederberg
World.content:
The Department of Agriculture has confirmed a case of African horse sickness (AHS) in a single horse on a property in the Cederberg Local Municipality in the Western Cape, prompting movement restrictions and intensified surveillance to contain the disease.

Laboratory tests conducted by the University of Pretoria's Veterinary Genetics Laboratory confirmed the presence of AHS virus serotype 7 on the property, which is located within South Africa's established AHS Protection Zone.

Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp said the case was detected through the country's veterinary surveillance systems, enabling authorities to respond swiftly and implement containment measures.

"The swift detection of this case in the Cederberg Local Municipality is a good example of how South Africa's veterinary surveillance system works. As a result, the authorities were able to move quickly to the affected area and take the required stringent actions as stipulated in the Animal Diseases Act and deploy containment protocols," Aucamp said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In accordance with the Animal Diseases Act, 1984 (Act 35 of 1984), and the Western Cape Department of Agriculture's AHS contingency plan, an outbreak containment area has been established and movement controls implemented.

Horse movements within the controlled area ordinarily require a permit issued by the State Veterinarian: Boland. However, the department has advised that no permits will be issued for moving horses out of the affected area, while investigations and surveillance continue.

Veterinary Services, working with authorised veterinarians and industry partners, have also commenced intensive surveillance, tracing and census activities to determine the extent of the outbreak and identify any additional cases.

The department has urged equine owners in the controlled area to cooperate with Veterinary Services and report any animals showing signs consistent with AHS, including unexplained fever, swelling of the head or neck, breathing difficulties or sudden death.

Horse owners are also encouraged to take precautions against Culicoides midges, which transmit the disease. Recommended measures include stabling horses, where possible, from two hours before sunset until two hours after sunrise, avoiding low-lying and wet areas, and appropriately using registered insect repellents and insecticides.

The department has strongly discouraged AHS vaccination at this time, explaining that the currently registered vaccine is live-attenuated and that vaccination during periods of vector activity could result in the vaccine strain being spread by midges, potentially worsening the situation.

Close 

"While there is no proof of large-scale disease activity outside the said property, the department is focused on total vigilance and calls on all horse owners to refrain from AHS vaccination during this period. Veterinary Services will continue to monitor the situation closely and will provide updates as additional information becomes available," Aucamp said.

The department said international trade partners will be notified of the outbreak, with further information on the implications for international trade to be provided in due course.

Updates on containment measures, movement restrictions and permits will be issued by the Western Cape Department of Agriculture. Further information is available from Veterinary Services and at www.myhorse.org.za

World.title: Kenya: No, Kenyan Pastor Victor Kanyari Was Not Killed in a Road Accident
World.content:
No, Kenyan pastor Victor Kanyari was not killed in a road accident

IN SHORT: A fake Citizen Digital news graphic claims Kenyan pastor Victor Kanyari died in a road accident. But the image is fabricated and uses an old photograph of a separate crash.

Social media posts circulating in Kenya feature what appears to be a Citizen Digital breaking news alert, dated 5 October 2026. It claims that pastor Victor Kanyari has died in a road accident along Kangundo Road in the capital, Nairobi.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The graphic shows Kanyari alongside a badly damaged white vehicle surrounded by onlookers.

Collectively, the posts we sampled received more than 162,000 views and 2,000 likes.

Who is Kanyari?

Kanyari is a Kenyan preacher who heads the Salvation Healing Ministry in Nairobi. He made headlines in 2014 after a KTN investigation exposed staged miracles at his ministry and his controversial KSh310 donation scheme, which he later acknowledged was intended to lift him out of poverty.

Kanyari was previously married to gospel singer Beatrice Wairimu Mbugua, popularly known as Betty Bayo. They had two children. Bayo died of leukaemia on 10 November 2025, prompting a custody dispute between Kanyari and the children's stepfather, Hiram Gitau, popularly known as Tash.

On 26 October 2026, a court awarded Kanyari legal custody but ordered a gradual transition, allowing the children to remain temporarily with Tash.

The dispute, along with his active social media presence, has kept Kanyari in the public eye. He has also announced plans to contest the Kasarani parliamentary seat in Kenya's 2027 general election.

Citizen Digital is the online news platform of Citizen TV, owned by Royal Media Services.

But did the broadcaster report Kanyari's death in a road accident? We checked.

Old accident photo used in fake graphic

We found no credible news reports confirming Kanyari's alleged death or a corresponding report on Citizen Digital or Citizen TV's social media accounts.

In contrast, Kanyari's social media accounts feature recent photos and videos of him going about his usual activities.

A reverse image search revealed that the photo of the wrecked vehicle had been shared on Facebook on 27 June 2024, more than two years before the supposed news alert.

Close 

The earlier post was captioned: "Bad accident on Ngong road joining on to Karen road. Multiple casualties."

The vehicle and onlookers match those in the circulating graphic, confirming the photograph predates the alleged October 2026 crash.

The graphic is fabricated. It uses an old accident photo to support a false claim about Kanyari's death. His recent public activities also contradict the rumour.

World.title: Kenya: 46 Ebola Contacts Set for Discharge From Quarantine On November 3
World.content:
Nairobi — Public Health Principal Secretary May Muthoni says 46 contacts under quarantine are expected to be discharged on November 3 after completing the required monitoring period.

Muthoni has directed health teams to prepare the necessary discharge packages and support for those completing quarantine.

"We must also be able to complete the full 21 days of followup and every person leaving quarantine must receive the agreed discharge package and support... we must also continue to follow up the nine contacts outside Kenya with the countries concerned," she said.



She said every person leaving quarantine must receive the agreed assistance as authorities maintain surveillance to prevent further transmission.

The PS urged response teams to ensure all arrangements are in place ahead of Tuesday's planned discharge.

"Kenya is making progress in containing the Ebola outbreak, with no new cases reported in the last 10 days, following coordinated efforts by the Ministry of Health, County Governments and development partners," Muthoni stated.

So far, the country has recorded nine cases and two deaths;.

Following confirmation of the first Ebola case on 6 October, the health ministry conducted "robust contact tracing of anyone who may have been exposed", the World Health Organization (WHO) says. By 22 October, all contacts had been traced, both in Kenya and internationally, and placed in quarantine, it adds.

The government says that the confirmed cases so far are connected and there is no evidence that the virus has spread to the community.

World.title: Your daily coffee habit may affect your brain and mood in unexpected ways, study finds
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning, a new study has found.

A small study out of University College Cork in Ireland found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were linked to changes in gut microbes and some measures of mood. Both types also appeared to have different effects on cognition.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine — it’s a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism and even our emotional wellbeing," study corresponding author Professor John Cryan said in a statement. Caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee may influence health "in distinct but complementary ways," Cryan added.

YOUR MORNING COFFEE COULD BE MAKING YOU MORE TIRED, EXPERTS WARN: 'LIKE A ROLLER COASTER'

The researchers studied 62 healthy adults, 31 who were regular coffee drinkers and 31 who did not drink coffee. The coffee drinkers, who typically had three to five cups a day, stopped drinking it for two weeks; then they were assigned to resume caffeinated or decaf coffee for three weeks.

Researchers then tracked their mood and cognitive test scores and analyzed stool and urine samples.

After coffee was reintroduced, both groups reported lower stress, depression and impulsivity than at the the start of the study.

The caffeinated group also reported reduced anxiety and showed improvement on an attention test. Those who drank decaf showed improvement on a test of episodic memory, which measures the ability to recall information and experiences.

FORGET YOGURT AND SAUERKRAUT: 5 GUT-FRIENDLY FAVORITES MAY ALREADY BE ON YOUR SHELF

The researchers found that coffee drinkers also had differences in certain gut bacteria and both groups had some microbial changes after starting both types of coffee, though the study could not prove gut microbes caused the reported mood or cognitive changes.

"Public interest in gut health has risen hugely," Cryan said. "The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee’s effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear."

CLICK HERE TO 

The study had some additional limitations, noted Rebecca Steele, Ph.D., a New York-based clinical psychologist who was not involved in the research.

People should be cautious about drawing broad conclusions from a small sample, Steele told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Gains on cognitive tests do not necessarily translate into meaningful or lasting improvements in everyday life, she added. "How I perform with a paper-and-pen test might not be the same way that I perform when I’m out in the real world," she said.

Research has found short-term effects of caffeine on alertness, but evidence about its long-term effects on cognition remains inconclusive, she also said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While Steele said the decaf group’s memory results are interesting, changes in sleep and physical activity, along with the possibility of a "learning effect" from taking the same tests more than once, complicate the findings.

"Changes in self-reported stress and depression scores should not be confused with evidence that coffee treats clinical depression," she also cautioned.

World.title: Christian group touts 'ethical' tech features as concerns over out-of-control AI tools persist
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The leader of a Christian ministry that built its own artificial intelligence application to guide users in their spiritual journey warns companies developing AI systems need to implement "ethical guidelines" to ensure their technology doesn't harm people.

Ligonier Ministries president and CEO Chris Larson says that the true highest intelligence is God, and shared a new tool his group created to help answer questions people my have from a faith-based perspective.

"It's interesting that [President Donald Trump] even referred to artificial intelligence now as 'superintelligence,'" Larson told Fox News Digital. "Of course, Christians — and, really, all of us — have access to the 'superintelligece,' the one who has created the universe."

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

The mission of the Florida-based organization, founded by the late Christian theologian R.C. Sproul, is to proclaim, teach and defend the holiness of God "in all its fullness to as many people as possible."

Part of accomplishing that mission was building an app that the organization calls "Grow."

"It's dedicated to helping Christians to better understand the Bible and theology and to go deeper in their faith, put down roots, if you will," Larson said of the new tool. "And so this app has 50 years of teaching in it from more than 800 different teachers, of course, grounded in Dr. R.C. Sproul's lifetime of teaching."

The app draws from a library of tens of thousands of pieces of content help users in their faith journey looking to obtain answers to critical questions.

Inside Grow is an "intelligent answer assistant" which can answer questions from users from a faith-based perspective.

But building an Grow for Christian users required putting a great deal of thought into the ethics of the model, Larson explained.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

"Now, it's not trying to pretend it's a person or anything like that. It is just trained on our library, and then helping Christians to trust the answers, and [it] will only go so far," he said. "And again, I think that's an important guard as well. Because for us, making sure that we have trusted theological answers and that the intelligent answer assistant is acting with integrity and not going outside of that."

When a user pushes the boundaries of the application, it directs them to real human support — a feature most large language model AI tools refuse to implement.

"And so we've given it a sandbox to work within, and any time that somebody tries to push it beyond the borders, we're going to deflect or defer to a real human. Imagine that," Larson said.

For example, if a user discusses suicidality in Grow, the intelligent answer assistant will direct them to the suicide hotline or other real-world resources.

BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: POPE LEO SEES THE AI AGE CLEARLY — AND WARNS WE MUST SAVE OUR SOULS

Over the past several years, there have been a flurry of suicide deaths that victims' family members say AI chatbots were at least partially responsible. In one case from last year, a teenager named Adam Raine took his own life after months of discussing his suicidal thoughts on ChatGPT. According to a lawsuit from his parents, the chatbot provided him information about methods of suicide, validated aspects of planning the suicide and offered to help him draft a suicide note. OpenAI, ChatGPT's parent company, disputes the characterization and says the chatbot directed him to crisis resources multiple times.

"So, we understood that it's important to provide safety guardrails, but also we did not want this intelligent answer assistant to pretend that it was a person," said Larson. "We don't want it to take the place of a pastor or a local church elder or even a parent."

WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT?

Larson said companies developing AI need to consider guardrails for their technology.

"Anybody developing AI tools today needs to think through ethical guidelines, and that's more of the self-regulation and guardrails that we've been talking about," he said.

"I think there's a real concern today because you have great power that's been entrusted to these different companies and they're not really disclosing their worldview," he continued. "How do they know right from wrong?"

For Ligonier, the absolute truth upon which its AI model is built is the Christian faith.

"How are you determining what is right and wrong? As Christians, we believe we have a true answer — a source that we can turn to."

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

World.title: Former Miss USA contestant made a life-changing decision at 26 after cancer devastated family
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

At age 26, Allyn Rose made a life-changing decision after cancer had devastated her family.

The model, who competed in both the Miss America and Miss USA pageants, underwent a preventive double mastectomy, a decision she said even sparked "hate mail" from critics. Today, the mother of two is the founder of The Previvor, a nonprofit organization that educates women about breast cancer risk and prevention options. Oct. 31 marks the last day of Breast Cancer Awareness Month.

"I know a lot of people think that's a pretty radical choice for someone who hadn't been diagnosed with breast cancer yet," Rose, now 38, told Fox News Digital. "But I lost my mom when I was 16. And by the time I was 16, I had lost my grandmother, my great aunt, almost every woman in my family to this disease. And I said that legacy ends with me."

KAI TRUMP REVEALS HOW FAMILY RALLIED AROUND MOM VANESSA AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE: ‘IT’S A LONG JOURNEY’

"I don't want that to be my story," she said. "I don't want to have to tell my 16-year-old daughter someday that she's going to have to spend the rest of her life without her mom. This sad family legacy was not going to take my life if I had anything to do with it."

Rose's mother, Judy Rose, was first diagnosed with breast cancer at 27 and had her right breast removed. The cancer later developed in her remaining breast, reaching stage 3, according to People magazine. Judy died at 51.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the U.S. after skin cancers, accounting for about 1 in 3 new cancer cases diagnosed in women each year, according to the American Cancer Society. About 1 in 8 U.S. women will develop breast cancer during their lives.

WATCH: ALLYN ROSE CHOSE DOUBLE MASTECTOMY AT 26 SO CANCER LEGACY 'ENDS WITH ME'

The organization estimates that 321,910 new cases of invasive breast cancer will be diagnosed among U.S. women in 2026 and that about 42,140 women will die from the disease.

FOX NEWS MEDIA TEAMS UP WITH BREAST CANCER RESEARCH FOUNDATION

Rose was considered at elevated risk of developing breast cancer because of her extensive family history. In 2012, she was crowned Miss District of Columbia, earning the opportunity to represent the district at the 2013 Miss America pageant. That same year, at 24, Rose announced her decision to undergo a preventive double mastectomy. She had the surgery two years later, at 26.

For women with a strong family history of breast cancer, a bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy can lower the risk of developing the disease by up to 90%, according to the National Cancer Institute. The procedure does not eliminate the risk entirely because it is impossible to remove all breast tissue that could become cancerous.

"So much of my life and my identity was wrapped up in the way that I looked and how I presented myself to the world," Rose said. "I paid my bills and my rent with the way that I looked. I didn't think [my looks] were 100% of my identity, but I would be lying if I didn't consider the repercussions of having a surgery like this. It would very likely end my modeling career, my career in pageantry, my career really in the entertainment industry. There were so few women talking about having a procedure like this and coming out on the other side."

"I wasn't married," she said. "I didn't have any children. These were all conversations I was going to have with a future partner someday. And so, it was a really tough choice, and it's one that I'm glad that I made, but it's very difficult to make the decision to have a surgery to prevent a cancer that didn't exist yet."

With her father's support, Rose underwent a preventive double mastectomy to reduce her risk of developing breast cancer. She ended up having three surgeries, including reconstruction, and went through what she described as "very graphic periods of looking completely different, having no breasts, wondering who is ever going to be happy looking at me like this."

Then she remembered her mother, Judy.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"[Losing my mother] drastically impacted my life, not only because it was my mother, but because I didn't know how to be a woman yet," she said. "[When I lost her] I hadn't even gotten my driver's license. I hadn't graduated from high school. I hadn't sent myself off to college yet. I spent a lot of those real pinnacle years of my life without a mentor, without someone to guide me through that. It was a very challenging time really, having to be my own cheerleader, experience all those crowning achievements in my life by myself."

"But I think I've come out stronger on the other side of it," Rose said.

Rose said she received hate mail over her decision, while her father also faced criticism after people learned he had encouraged his daughter to undergo the double mastectomy.

"To see a young person who walked on the Miss USA stage, who worked full-time as a model, who was really in this beauty industry — choosing to almost end my career to prolong my life seemed like a foreign concept," Rose said.

"And there were a lot of radical responses to my decision. I got hate mail. My father received hate mail. People just couldn't fathom that I would take this preventative step. But I didn't want cancer to be part of my story. I wanted it to end with me."

Rose made her decision before actress Angelina Jolie publicly revealed that she had undergone a preventive double mastectomy after genetic testing showed she carried a harmful BRCA1 gene variant.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

In a May 2013 New York Times op-ed, Jolie explained that her mother had battled cancer for nearly a decade before dying at 56. Jolie said her doctors estimated she had an 87% risk of developing breast cancer and a 50% risk of ovarian cancer. She chose to have both breasts removed, which she said reduced her estimated breast cancer risk to less than 5%.

Jolie, who was 37 at the time, said she shared her experience so other women could better understand their own risks and options.

Rose said she thought her modeling career was over. But in 2019, Sports Illustrated Swimsuit featured her, making her the first woman who had undergone a double mastectomy to appear in the publication.

Today, Rose travels across the country to raise awareness about "the power in prevention."

"The thing I wish someone had told me when I was first navigating this was that there is a light at the end of the tunnel," Rose said. "Everything was a question. It was this fear of the unknown. But I said to myself, 'I'm going to still chase all of those dreams. I'm going to go accomplish all the things that I wanted to.'"

When she looks back on her journey, one person comes to mind: her mother, Judy.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I do think about what my mom would think, and I know she would be incredibly proud of me," Rose said, fighting back tears. "One of the last things she said to me was, 'Don't let my life be in vain.' And I made a promise to her that I would make use of every day that she didn't have. And so, that has been my mission from the day that she passed to ensure that I could help as many women as possible not have to walk their lives without their mom. That's my goal."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I have two children," Rose said. "They don't have the same gene mutation that I have. They no longer have an increased risk of cancer. And that legacy ended with me, and I know my mom would be very proud that I did that."

World.title: Can a woman be friends with a hot guy without being romantic? Expert pinpoints warning signs
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The question of whether men and women can remain "just friends" drew fresh attention when Jenny McCarthy and her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, recently bantered on her podcast about whether having an attractive male friend crosses a line.

Attraction alone doesn’t necessarily threaten a friendship, according to Susan Trombetti, relationship expert and CEO of Exclusive Matchmaking in Maryland.

However, unspoken feelings and growing emotional intimacy can blur boundaries, she told Fox News Digital.

5 MARRIAGE MISTAKES COUPLES MAKE WITHOUT REALIZING IT — AND HOW TO AVOID THEM

"I think we can be friends with hot people … but a lot of times, I believe that friendship started with a sexual interest or romantic interest, and the timing wasn't right or the other person wasn't interested in them."

Some people may maintain friendships while leaving open the possibility of a future romantic relationship, Trombetti said.

"I don't think women and men can ever truly be friends," she told Fox News Digital. "I think it was always a sexual undertone that sparked the friendship and a foot-in-the-door for something more, [even if] it's 20 years from now."

YOUNGER MEN ARE ATTRACTED TO OLDER WOMEN FOR REASONS THAT HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH LOOKS

Trombetti said recognizing that someone is handsome doesn’t necessarily lead to feeling chemistry with that person — and finding a friend attractive does not, on its own, constitute infidelity.

The problem, she said, is when harmless awareness turns into an emotional affair. "The line between attraction with a friend and an emotional affair is a slippery slope, especially if you have a partner," the expert cautioned.

The following red flags could signal that a friendship is crossing into an emotional affair, according to Trombetti.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Prioritizing the friend over a partner: This could mean turning to the friend first to share daily victories, disappointments, personal insecurities or long-term dreams.

This could mean turning to the friend first to share daily victories, disappointments, personal insecurities or long-term dreams. Creating an insular universe: Friends may build private jokes, share secret routines and communicate in channels that deliberately exclude significant others.

Friends may build private jokes, share secret routines and communicate in channels that deliberately exclude significant others. Secrecy and deception: Examples include hiding interactions, deleting text chains or downplaying how much time is spent together.

Examples include hiding interactions, deleting text chains or downplaying how much time is spent together. Unwarranted jealousy: Signs may include frustration when the friend dates someone else or criticism of their romantic partners.

Signs may include frustration when the friend dates someone else or criticism of their romantic partners. Outside suspicion: Friends and family may assume the pair are an undercover couple despite protests to the contrary.

Trombetti pointed back to the movie "When Harry Met Sally" to illustrate how emotional intimacy can sometimes be more important than instant physical chemistry.

"Long before they sleep together, they definitely are having an emotional affair, even though they don't recognize it as such," she said. "They are sharing everything. Emotional intimacy turns into long-term relationships."

For those determined to maintain a platonic relationship with an attractive counterpart, Trombetti recommended setting some guardrails: Refrain from flirtatious banter, avoid physical touch, refuse to stoke sexual chemistry, limit late-night texting and ensure full transparency with an existing romantic partner.

If one person develops romantic feelings that the other doesn’t share, the friendship may continue if both are single and respect clear boundaries, Trombetti said.

For people already in committed partnerships, unreciprocated feelings almost always require stepping away to protect the relationship.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

When an existing partner expresses jealousy, Trombetti advised examining the root cause before issuing blame.

World.title: How Obama appointee and Trump nemesis Boasberg ended up overseeing Ilhan Omar warrant, other key cases
World.content:

Federal Judge James Boasberg, dubbed a "Radical left lunatic" by President Donald Trump, is presiding over several high-profile cases challenging actions made by the Trump administration, raising questions about how judges are assigned to cases.

The scrutiny comes as Boasberg, an Obama-appointed chief judge of the Washington, D.C. district court, oversees a challenge brought by several media outlets seeking to force the Justice Department to unseal the search warrant on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., stemming from two federal investigations.

"Judge James Boasberg is now involved with the Ilhan Omar case," Steve Ferguson, a self-described business owner with more than 250,000 followers on X, wrote in a social media post. "Is everything rigged?"

In the federal court of the District of Columbia, cases are assigned to judges randomly by an electronic system managed by the clerk's office operating under the direction of the Calendar and Case Management Committee, according to the rules of the court. The committee consists of three to five judges appointed by the chief justice.

FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

There are exceptions to the random-assignment process. For example, criminal grand jury matters are assigned to and overseen by the chief judge, currently Boasberg. This means Boasberg’s assignment to oversee the fight over unsealing the search warrant for Omar was "not a surprise" to Eric Wessan, Iowa’s solicitor general.

"But there are a lot of cases that seem to be going to judges maybe based on those cases having similarities which is not what the local rules say," Wessan told Fox News Digital.

When a case needs to be reassigned, the Calendar and Case Management Committee will determine how the reassignment is made.

Wessan suggested that concerns over how case assignments are made is valid, considering some of the high-profile cases against the Trump administration which have appeared in Boasberg's docket.

"If one is just following anecdotally, there does seem to be a lot of high-profile cases in front of judges that seem to be expressing unusual amounts of frustration or disagreement with the administration," Wessan said, urging greater transparency in how case assignments are made.

TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH

The fight over unsealing the release of Omar's search warrant is just one of several cases involving the Trump administration and now on Boasberg's docket. Boasberg is also overseeing California’s lawsuit against the Trump administration over voter-roll disputes. On Friday, he ordered the administration to provide the state with the names and supporting information for roughly 20,000 people whom the DOJ claims are noncitizens on California’s voter rolls by the end of the day.

Boasberg has issued several consequential rulings against the Trump administration, including a high-profile March 2025 order directing the administration to turn around deportation flights carrying alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador. The Trump administration fought against the order, pointing to the Alien Enemies Act as legal justification for the deportations. The dispute over the administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act eventually reached the Supreme Court, which vacated Boasberg's temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, ruling that the case was brought in the wrong jurisdiction.

That same month, Boasberg was assigned a lawsuit seeking to preserve Signal messages after top Trump administration officials discussed plans for a Yemen strike in a group chat that accidentally included Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg. He later ordered the administration to preserve the messages.

The string of cases prompted Reps. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, Darrell Issa, R-Calif., and Chip Roy, R-Texas, to send a letter in May 2025 to the court clerk asking for greater clarity on how judicial assignments are made. The lawmakers questioned whether assignments were truly random, as the court’s rules state.

"The Committee cannot independently verify the randomness of case assignments because the composition of assignment decks is kept secrets," the lawmakers wrote.

"We must understand the nature of the case assignment process in the District Court—which is considering a number of cases challenging the Trump Administration’s policy decisions—to consider and develop appropriate legislation," the lawmakers wrote.

FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE

Meanwhile, Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced legislation in July that would require federal district courts to assign cases randomly, without exceptions, naming it the Boasberg Act. The bill is currently stalled in committee.

"Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system. Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts," Schmitt said in a statement.

Under the rules of D.C. Court, the chief justice does not have the power to reassign a case. The Calendar and Case Management Committee handles case reassignments. The court must notify the judges and attorneys involved, but it does not have to publicly explain why a case was reassigned. Wessan has called for greater transparency.

"The rules shouldn’t say one thing if it’s not true. But if it is true, they could just say so. I think the issue is with the exceptions—what happens in those exceptional cases and how often do they occur?" Wessan said.

"Given the frequency of the concerning episodes in the district court, erring on the side of transparency is probably prudent to the extent that there are exceptions to the normal random-assignment system," Wessan said.

World.title: Democrats in key battlegrounds throw Joe Biden under the bus on the border
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue.

Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country.

“I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan.

He’s not alone.

In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

“I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.”

Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired their critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year.

Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024.

Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings.

Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38%, polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term.

“The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night.

Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.”

In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.”

Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border.

In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.”

She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.”

Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement.

“I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad. “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.”

Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.”

Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz.

Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum, he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people.

“We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.”

“So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.”

World.title: Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed clash over Israel ad ahead of planned rally together
World.content:
Days before they were set to headline a rally in Detroit, Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., traded critical messages in statements released Friday, escalating tensions between the two in the final stretch of El-Sayed’s campaign for the Senate.

Stevens said that she expected El-Sayed, the progressive candidate who defeated her in a bitter Democratic primary in August, to formally condemn an ad from an outside progressive group that she called antisemitic, adding that it’s why she agreed to join El-Sayed on the campaign trail for the first time on Sunday.

“This ad tells Michigan families they cannot afford groceries because their money has to be set aside for ‘killing Palestinians,’ and it blames our close ally Israel for everything Michiganders cannot afford,” Stevens said in a statement.

She sought to tie the ad — which is set in a grocery store and suggests Israel and the war in Gaza are squeezing American taxpayers — to comments El-Sayed has made in his own campaign.

“I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well,” Stevens said. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”

El-Sayed is not affiliated with the group that produced the ad, Rebellion PAC, and his campaign distanced itself from the ad in statements to The New York Times earlier this week.

Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down one of his own ads that featured right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson “out of the same respect for Michigan’s Black community.”

El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel, shot back Friday, saying in a statement that Stevens, a strong supporter of Israel, “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago” and that his campaign’s focus was on affordability and healthcare.

“That focus is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70M in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens,” El-Sayed said, referencing Stevens’ support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying group, during the primary.

The exchange comes after the former primary opponents had seemingly reached a reconciliation, agreeing to appear at an event in Detroit alongside Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., a senior Democratic leader, on Sunday. The escalation is also playing out four days before voters will choose between El-Sayed and Republican candidate Mike Rogers to be the next Michigan senator in a race the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as a toss-up.

On Saturday morning, it appeared that Stevens no longer planned to attend Sunday church event in Detroit.

An advisory for the gathering that the El-Sayed campaign sent Saturday did not list Stevens as a participant, only El-Sayed and Clyburn.

Stevens is being asked not to attend El-Sayed campaign events in the closing days because the campaign is concerned about distractions around her, a person familiar with the decision told NBC News. Politico was first to report that Stevens was no longer welcome at El-Sayed’s events.

Stevens did not immediately respond to a phone call and text message seeking comment. She told The New York Times on Friday that she still planned to vote for El-Sayed despite his criticism.

On Saturday morning, Stevens’ fiance, Jason Turkish, told “Fox & Friends,” he wasn’t sure whether the congresswoman still planned to campaign alongside El-Sayed on Sunday.

“I’m not sure. I don’t know where that stands as of Saturday morning,” he said.

Turkish added, “Haley has made it clear to anyone who will listen that she remains on Team Dem. That her only ask, small ask, was to say that we not blame all of society’s high costs on one group of people.”

On Wednesday, Stevens sat for an interview on CNN in which she signaled she would vote for El-Sayed while also calling on him to denounce the ad from Rebellion PAC. That interview came shortly after Turkish, told The Detroit News that he was voting for Rogers.

“Of course I’m voting for our Democratic nominee for Senate,” Stevens said. “I’m voting for the Democratic ticket. But I want to encourage this campaign to shut out the hate and to call it out and to make people who are in my coalition, make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.”

The tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens have drawn in other Michigan Democrats as the party hopes to secure a critical Senate seat in the race to control Congress.

“First of all, I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow said Friday on CNN. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes.”

Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell, a senior member of Michigan’s delegation, sought to downplay the conflict on NBC News’ “Meet the Press NOW,” saying Friday that she helped broker the event Sunday with Clyburn, who is close with Stevens.

“I think that, quite frankly, a lot of people are trying to create more controversy here, when I think the real discussion should be about what’s been happening in Washington and how we’ve got to stand up to what we’ve seen in the last two years,” Dingell said.

World.title: U.S. set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban
World.content:
The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.

The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.

Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa, in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum-seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.

Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.

Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days, at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.

He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.

If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.

They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition, as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.

VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.

“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.

Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.

That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.

VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.

Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.

Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.

‘We just sat there and cried’

Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.

Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.

“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”

Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.

“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.

Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.

“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”

But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”

With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.

“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”

Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.

“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.

“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

The preparations for the deportation flight come nearly a year after a shooting in Washington that killed one National Guard member and seriously injured another. The suspect, an Afghan national who served alongside U.S. troops in Afghanistan and was evacuated to the U.S. in 2021, had been granted asylum by the Trump administration. Immigration restrictions were tightened after the shooting.

VanDiver said the Trump administration may also be using the Pakistan flight as a test case for Camp As Sayliyah, a U.S.-run camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans who had been slated for resettlement in the U.S. have been stranded since Trump returned to office last year.

Asked about VanDiver’s claim, the White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson again said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.”

According to AfghanEvac, the camp was housing 287 men, 319 women and 433 children as of July. Most of them have been approved for U.S. resettlement after extensive vetting, and many of the adults worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan.

The group at Camp As Sayliyah also includes 150 relatives of U.S. military service members, AfghanEvac said.

00:39 Afghan refugees in Qatar protest over travel suspension 00:00 00:00

The State Department said earlier this year that everyone would be removed from the camp by March 31, a deadline that was later extended to Sept. 30. In September, the Trump administration delayed its closure by another nine months, The Associated Press reported.

Earlier this year, the administration considered sending the Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is experiencing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

In a statement on Friday, AfghanEvac accused the Trump administration of planning the Afghan deportation flight as the country is distracted by next week’s midterm election, “hoping no one is watching.”

“The government won’t say where these flights land, because it knows what happens to the people on them when they do,” the group said. “A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it.”

World.title: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
World.content:
American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.

Last week’s global release of “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” came days before the Oct. 29 anniversary of the disaster in the South Korean capital’s nightlife district of Itaewon, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged beyond control in a narrow alley, causing nearly 160 deaths.

The game, which takes place amid a fictional North Korean invasion of the South, features about 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, though it does not refer to the Itaewon crowd crush directly.

Groups representing families of the crowd crush victims had demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was appalling that the game had directly reproduced actual scenes of people performing CPR “while victims lay on the cold streets amid chaos and desperation.”

“If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and empathy for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it should promptly take corrective action,” the Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee said in a joint statement Friday.

The California-based game publisher, Activision, apologized in a statement and said the footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release Nov. 12.

“This game is a fictional work created to provide a realistic and immersive experience,” the company said, according to the South Korean public broadcaster MBC. “In using actual news footage in the game, we never intended to evoke any tragic incident, including the Itaewon disaster, or to trivialize the suffering associated with such tragedies.”

The controversy came as grieving families are still waiting for answers about authorities’ failure to prevent the disaster four years ago. Nearly two dozen officials have been charged in the investigation, which is still underway, while three former police officers have been jailed.

On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed that his government would “uncover the truth.”

World.title: Many on ACA plans face a new crisis in 2027: Insurers fleeing the market
World.content:
Courtney Mroch was already paying a high price for health insurance when she learned her insurer, Cigna, was pulling out of Tennessee’s Affordable Care Act marketplace.

The 56-year-old Nashville resident has diabetes and asthma and is a cancer survivor. She pays $1,250 a month for a silver plan this year, up from $850 a month in 2025 — more than her family’s mortgage. To keep costs down, her husband is enrolled in a separate, non-ACA plan that’s less expensive.

“Who knows who will cover me in 2027 or how much more it’ll cost,” Mroch said.

Many Americans are heading into ACA open enrollment with the likelihood of higher premiums and fewer insurance companies to choose from. In most states, the enrollment period begins Sunday, giving people who buy their own coverage about two months to compare plans for next year.

Insurers that offer ACA plans are proposing a premium increase of about 15%, on average, for 2027 — the second straight year of double-digit increases, according to an analysis from KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group, that looked at public filings from insurers across all 50 states and Washington, D.C.

At the same time, 11 insurers have announced plans to leave the ACA marketplaces in 2027 in at least some states where they currently offer coverage, according to KFF. Among them is Cigna, which will exit all 11 states where it offers ACA plans and has more than 350,000 ACA enrollees. Six insurers have announced plans to enter new marketplaces.

“The main takeaway is that more insurance companies are leaving the marketplace than coming in,” said Cynthia Cox, director of the program on the ACA at KFF.

For people shopping for coverage, that could mean fewer insurers to choose from and more people having to switch plans.

“This is going to create a lot of discontinuities in care and coverage for people,” said Miranda Yaver, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh. “If you have a doctor who doesn’t accept the fewer number of options that are available to you, that can be very disruptive, especially if you’re someone who has a chronic illness.”

“And if the fewer available price points don’t work for you, are you going to remain covered?” she added.

Why are insurers leaving?

The departures come after the enhanced tax credits expired at the end of 2025, leading ACA enrollment to fall by roughly 3 million.

Some healthier people moved to cheaper but worse coverage or dropped insurance altogether. Those who remained on their plans tended to have greater health needs and higher medical costs.

Overall, that can make the marketplace less profitable for insurers as healthcare costs rise, said Jennifer Chumbley Hogue, an insurance broker in Texas.

From the consumer perspective, that means “constant upheaval, whether it’s the plan pulling out or the subsidies have changed or the doctor network has changed,” Hogue said.

In an email, a Cigna spokesperson pointed to April comments from CEO Brian Evanko, who said that leaving the ACA marketplace aligns with goals to position the company’s “core healthcare businesses for sustainable growth.”

For some families, rising premiums alone had already forced difficult financial decisions.

Denise O’Connor and her husband saw their monthly premiums in Colorado more than double this year, from just over $900 to about $2,300, forcing them to dip into their retirement savings.

The O’Connors are also covered by Cigna. She plans to work with a broker to find another plan, but her husband is also considering going uninsured for about six weeks until he qualifies for Medicare.

“It’s a worry,” she said. “He’s healthy, but anything can happen at any time.”

Mark Lathrop, who lives in Idaho and owns a winery just across the state line in Washington, said he and his wife are also looking for new coverage after their insurer, PacificSource, decided to leave the ACA marketplace.

The couple is already facing higher costs. They don’t qualify for the standard ACA subsidies, and Lathrop said a comparable plan for 2027 would cost about $17,600, up from about $16,000 last year. He needs an annual MRI to monitor a spinal cord injury, which costs $2,400, making a plan with a lower deductible important. “We don’t know what we are going to do yet,” he said.

In a statement, a PacificSource spokesperson said that the decision to exit the ACA marketplace was not “made lightly” and that it was made to ensure it can “continue fulfilling our mission and serving members for the long term amid growing pressures across the healthcare industry.”

Yaver said the changes could undermine public support for the ACA. As fewer people enroll and those who remain face higher costs and fewer options, the marketplace could become less attractive to consumers — weakening the law without the Trump administration and Republicans ever having to repeal it.

A recent KFF poll found overall public favorability toward the ACA dropped to 58% from 64%. “We don’t see the repeal and replace of 2017, but we’re making it much harder for patients to remain on these plans,” Yaver said.

Hogue urged enrollees to review their options when open enrollment begins, rather than rely solely on the notices they receive in the mail. The premium and subsidies available to them, she said, may be different from the amounts listed in those letters.

“It’s worth the five minutes to take a look,” she said.

World.title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
World.content:
Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange.

“It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia.

Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions.

Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade.

00:36 Wildfire smoke covers Indonesia skies in orange haze 00:00 00:00

The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution.

On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster.

“We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.”

The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces.

The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning.

“We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.

Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem.

In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea.

World.title: El-Sayed asks fellow Democrat Stevens not to attend final campaign events
World.content:
Washington — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has asked his Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, to stay away from all remaining campaign events in the final days before Tuesday's election, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The pair clashed Friday ahead of what had been a planned Sunday campaign event where they were expected to make a rare appearance together. Politico was first to report El-Sayed had asked Stevens to stay away.

The public rift between the two Democrats comes just days before one of the country's most hotly contested Senate races, as Republican nominee Mike Rogers seeks to peel off centrist Democratic voters. El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens offered starkly differing visions for the future of the party during the primary, and although Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after he won the nomination, the two largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.

In a statement Friday evening, El-Sayed said Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."

The dig came hours after Stevens demanded that El-Sayed — a vehement critic of U.S. aid to Israel — apologize for suggesting during the campaign that "Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care."

"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens said in the statement. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

She also urged El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. The video ad features a couple in a grocery store talking about needing to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf because "we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." The man and woman in the ad then complain about the billions in military support that the U.S. has provided Israel.

El-Sayed's campaign said earlier this week it was not affiliated "in any way" with the ad, which was created by the political action committee Rebellion PAC.

"No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign," his campaign said in a statement.

In her Friday statement, Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down his own ad featuring the far-right podcaster and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson.

Stevens had said she planned to appear with El-Sayed at a Detroit church on Sunday, alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Even before asking her to stay away, an announcement from El-Sayed's campaign about his appearance with Clyburn did not mention Stevens.

Earlier this week, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News he would vote for Rogers. Later that day, Stevens said in a CNN interview that she would vote for El-Sayed, saying, "We're a household divided," but she called on his campaign "to shut out the hate and to call it out."

This Sunday's "60 Minutes" will feature Ross Douthat's exclusive interviews with Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers.
