World.title: Lufthansa to Drop Costa Rica Route in 2027 as Sister Airline Adds More Flights
World.content:
German airline Lufthansa will stop operating its flights to Costa Rica in December 2027, but travelers will not lose the connection to Europe. Instead, sister airline Discover Airlines will take over the Frankfurt–San José route and increase service from five to six flights per week. The change, announced on October 29, will take effect on December 14, 2027, with Discover Airlines operating flights to Juan Santamaría International Airport using Airbus A350-900 aircraft.

The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) confirmed that Lufthansa will continue operating the route through December 13, 2027, before handing it over to Discover, which belongs to the same airline group. For anyone flying here, the important point is that the route is not disappearing. Lufthansa Group will continue to fly to Costa Rica from Germany, although the airline operating the flights will change.

However, there is one important difference in the new schedule. Of the six weekly flights, four will operate nonstop between Frankfurt and San José. The other two will follow a route that takes passengers from Frankfurt to San José, continues to Belize City and then returns to Germany. That means passengers leaving Costa Rica for Frankfurt will need to pay attention when booking. Although the total number of weekly flights will increase, two of the return services will include a stop in Belize.

The change follows negotiations between the ICT and Lufthansa Group that began more than a year ago. Tourism officials said the goal was to move the route to an airline more focused on vacation travelers, which better matches Costa Rica’s tourism market. Discover Airlines specializes in leisure travel and operates from Frankfurt and Munich, serving destinations popular with tourists. It is part of Lufthansa Group, allowing passengers to continue using Frankfurt as a connection point for other destinations in Europe and beyond.

Another significant change will be the aircraft itself. Discover plans to introduce the Airbus A350-900 on the Costa Rica route, replacing the aircraft currently used by Lufthansa. The A350 is a modern long-distance aircraft designed to carry passengers across continents with improved fuel efficiency. Discover expects to receive its first A350 in June 2027 and a second aircraft in December, when the Costa Rica service is scheduled to begin.

The airline is gradually expanding its long-distance fleet, with additional A350 aircraft expected in 2028. The announcement comes as Lufthansa is already increasing its presence in Costa Rica. For the current European winter season, which began October 25, the airline expanded its Frankfurt service from three to five weekly flights and introduced Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft with its newer Allegris cabin design.

Germany remains Costa Rica’s largest source of European tourists. According to ICT figures, 54,794 German visitors arrived in Costa Rica between January and September 2026, an increase of 8.1% compared with the same period in 2025. The Frankfurt connection is particularly important because it serves both German vacationers and travelers connecting through one of Europe’s busiest international airports.

For Costa Rica’s tourism industry, the planned increase in weekly service provides another opportunity to attract European visitors, especially during the busy winter travel season. Passengers planning trips for late 2027 should keep an eye on the new schedules as Discover Airlines updates its booking system. The airline has confirmed the planned route changes, but final operating details and aircraft assignments may still be adjusted before the service begins.

World.title: High Tides Flood Homes in Costa Rica’s Puntarenas
World.content:
High tides flooded homes in Puntarenas on Thursday, October 29, with authorities warning that elevated tides could continue along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast through Saturday, October 31. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) reported flooding in Barrio El Carmen and the community of 20 de Noviembre in Chacarita.

Seawater entered homes, and photographs from the affected areas showed flooded patios and corridors, with furniture and household belongings standing in water. Members of the Puntarenas Municipal Emergency Committee visited the communities to assess damage, identify families’ needs and coordinate assistance. Initial reports did not specify the number of homes affected or provide an estimate of financial losses.

Thursday’s flooding followed repeated high tides earlier in the week. Residents of El Carmen described moving appliances and other belongings off the floor and staying awake to monitor water entering their homes. Flooding was also reported earlier in the week at Playa Zancudo in Golfito and Playa Preciosa in Puerto Jiménez, extending the effects beyond the city of Puntarenas.

The University of Costa Rica’s Oceanographic Information Module, known as MIO-Cimar, warned that the period of unusually high tides could last through Saturday. The CNE urged residents of coastal communities with a history of tidal flooding to watch local conditions and take steps to protect their belongings.

The conditions are associated with spring tides, the higher tides that occur around the new and full moon when the gravitational effects of the Sun and Moon reinforce one another. These events occur regularly and are unrelated to the spring season. MIO-Cimar coordinator Rodney Mora said warmer Pacific waters associated with El Niño were also contributing to higher sea levels, worsening the effects in vulnerable coastal communities. Water expands as it warms, allowing high tides to reach farther into low-lying areas.

El Niño does not cause spring tides, but the combination can increase the risk of flooding along the coast. Mora also warned that similar conditions could recur in November and December, urging coastal residents to prepare for further episodes.

World.title: Costa Rica Gas Prices Jump Sharply as Regular Fuel Becomes More Expensive Than Premium
World.content:
Drivers in Costa Rica will soon be paying considerably more at the pump after the public services regulator approved yet another round of fuel price increases, including a 12.38% jump in regular gasoline that will make it more expensive than premium fuel. The Public Services Regulatory Authority (ARESEP) approved the adjustment a couple of days ago, with the new prices announced yesterday. Regular gasoline will increase by ₡89 per liter, climbing from ₡719 to ₡808, while premium gasoline will rise by ₡42, from ₡764 to ₡806.

That creates an unusual situation at Costa Rica’s gas stations. Regular gasoline, traditionally the cheaper option, will cost ₡2 more per liter than premium, while diesel will also reach ₡808 following an increase of ₡23. The higher prices have been approved but will not take effect until the regulatory resolution is published in the official government newspaper, La Gaceta. Under the resolution, the new rates begin the following day. An exact implementation date had not been confirmed as of Friday morning.

At the new price, filling a 40-liter (10.6-gallon) tank with regular gasoline will cost ₡32,320 (about $71), up from ₡28,760 (about $64) today, an increase of ₡3,560 (about $8) per fill-up and with regular. Drivers filling a larger 60-liter (15.9-gallon) tank will pay ₡5,340 more than before.

For those who commute daily, operate delivery vehicles or regularly travel between Costa Rica’s major cities, the additional expense could quickly add up. The increases are not limited to gasoline and diesel. Households that use propane gas for cooking will also face higher costs, with the price of a standard 25-pound cylinder rising by ₡549, from ₡7,172 to ₡7,721.

ARESEP estimates that approximately 53% of Costa Rican households use this type of cooking gas. Restaurants, small food businesses and other commercial establishments that depend on propane will also be affected. The regulator says the adjustments reflect rising international fuel costs, which have been influenced by instability in global energy markets.

Costa Rica imports all of its finished petroleum fuels, making domestic prices especially sensitive to changes in international supply, shipping costs and the exchange rate between the colón and the U.S. dollar. Energy officials pointed to disruptions involving oil shipments from the Middle East, declining global inventories and higher refining and transportation costs. Diesel supplies have faced particular pressure as demand and supply conditions fluctuate internationally.

The latest adjustment was calculated using fuel purchases made by the Costa Rican Petroleum Refinery (RECOPE) between September 11 and October 8. The exchange rate also played a role. ARESEP used an average rate of ₡456.66 per dollar for the new calculation, compared with ₡450.41 in the previous adjustment. Because fuel purchases are made in dollars, that difference increases the amount paid in colones even when the international price of a product remains unchanged.

For Costa Rican businesses, higher fuel prices can create expenses that extend well beyond the cost of filling a vehicle. Transportation companies, agricultural producers, delivery services and businesses that distribute goods throughout Costa Rica depend heavily on diesel and gasoline. When those costs rise, companies may face pressure to adjust their operating budgets or eventually pass some of the increases on to customers.

Tourism operators could also feel the effects. Rental car companies, shuttle services and tour providers frequently travel long distances between Juan Santamaría International Airport, the Central Valley and popular destinations such as La Fortuna, Manuel Antonio, Tamarindo and the southern Pacific coast.

Tourists coming here and are renting cars will find the same regulated fuel prices as Costa Rican motorists. However, any increase in tour prices, transportation fares or rental rates would depend on decisions by individual businesses and where applicable, additional regulatory approvals.

The latest adjustment comes after earlier fuel increases in October, adding to transportation expenses as Costa Rica approaches the busy end-of-year holiday and tourism season. The approved changes also highlight how fuel prices can move differently depending on the type of petroleum product. Although regular gasoline is typically cheaper than premium, international market conditions and the formulas used to calculate domestic prices can occasionally reverse that relationship.

For those who don’t have a diesel car, once the new rates become effective, premium gasoline will actually be slightly cheaper than regular gasoline, but you should still follow the fuel specifications recommended by your vehicle manufacturer. The regulator’s decision covers nearly two million vehicles circulating in Costa Rica, including private cars, motorcycles, buses, trucks and other commercial transportation.

While our government regulates retail fuel prices, those prices are reviewed periodically and can increase or decrease depending on the cost of imported petroleum products and other factors included in the pricing formula. For now, drivers have a short period before the latest adjustment takes effect. Once the new prices are officially published and implemented, a liter of regular gasoline and diesel will both cost ₡808, marking another increase in the cost of getting around Costa Rica.

World.title: Heading Out for Halloween in Costa Rica? Expect More Police on Patrol
World.content:
Heading to a costume party, a beach bash or a masquerade parade this Saturday? Expect to see more police than usual. Costa Rica’s national police are stepping up patrols across our country for Halloween and they will concentrate on the places where crowds gather. The Public Security Ministry said officers will focus on cemeteries, churches, shopping centers and the streets around bars hosting costume parties.

The goal is to prevent vandalism, spot unauthorized parties and head off trouble at large gatherings. When the national police first outlined the plan, it said it would deploy 1,500 officers from today through Sunday. The ministry’s latest statement, issued yesterday, did not give a number of officers.

Because halloween falls on a Saturday, many parties start Friday night, and that three-day window is meant to cover them. Why cemeteries and churches? Police said incidents in past years, including vandalism and rituals at cemeteries, are the reason officers will patrol them through the weekend. César Anchía, deputy director general of the national police, outlined the weekend operations.

If you’re going out, expect police at the party too. Themed Halloween events and other mass gatherings will see preventive checks and patrols at venues and meeting points. Part of the aim is to catch parties held without permits. Shopping centers, which draw families in costume on Halloween, are also on the patrol list.

If you’re driving, watch for the Caravana del Payaso, or Clown Caravan, a Halloween ride that draws hundreds of motorcyclists. Police will watch the route and the gathering points, and the ministry said highway patrols are meant to prevent crashes. Give riders room and allow extra time where the caravan passes.

Taking kids trick-or-treating? Police are asking parents to stay with their children and keep them in sight the whole time they go door to door. Before you head home, make sure the car you get into is the ride you actually booked. Lat night, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) said it had detained four men suspected of drugging and robbing people outside bars and nightclubs in San José.

According to the OIJ, one of the suspects allegedly posed as the ride-hailing driver victims had requested, then offered them drinks laced with a sedative. Investigators said other members of the group then withdrew cash and moved money out of victims’ accounts and spent it on goods and services, including fuel.

Saturday is also Costa Rica’s National Masquerade Day, when towns celebrate with giant-headed mascareros, cimarrona bands and dancing in the streets. Police said those community events fall under the same security operation. In beach towns, Halloween runs all weekend. Tamarindo has costume surfing, parades and beach parties on the calendar. Big crowds also draw thieves, so keep valuables with you and out of parked cars, where a rental can be emptied in minutes. In an emergency, call 911.

Halloween has grown steadily in Costa Rica alongside our own masquerade tradition, blending a centuries-old holiday with local customs. Authorities are betting that a visible police presence will keep this year’s celebrations safe for everyone who takes part.

World.title: Belize advances Biodiversity conservation efforts at COP17 in Armenia
World.content:
Belize advances Biodiversity conservation efforts at COP17 in Armenia

By Zoila Palma: Belize joined international representatives at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17), held from October 19 to 30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, to participate in global discussions on protecting biodiversity and strengthening conservation efforts.

Belize’s participation provided an opportunity to promote its natural heritage, build international partnerships and exchange knowledge on strategies to address biodiversity loss.

Minister of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, Orlando Habet, led Belize’s delegation during the High-Level Segment on October 27 and 28, accompanied by the technical team from the Belize National Biodiversity Office (NBIO). Belize’s participation comes as countries work to implement the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and strengthen national commitments to protecting nature.

The Corozal Sustainable Future Initiative (CSFI) also participated in COP17, with team members engaging in discussions at the Meridian Exhibition Center’s Blue and Green Zones. In the Blue Zone, discussions focused on implementing global biodiversity targets, including addressing human-wildlife conflict, improving ecological connectivity and exploring the use of technology and artificial intelligence in conservation. In the Green Zone, the team explored innovative initiatives presented by academic institutions and local businesses while exchanging experiences with organizations pursuing similar conservation goals.

Belize’s participation comes as more countries submit updated National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs), which outline national commitments to addressing nature loss.

These international engagements offer Belize opportunities to strengthen its biodiversity protection efforts and safeguard its natural resources for future generations.

World.title: Dia de los Muertos Street Fest comes alive in Benque Viejo this Sunday
World.content:
Dia de los Muertos Street Fest comes alive in Benque Viejo this Sunday

By Zoila Palma: Benque Viejo del Carmen is preparing to celebrate culture, tradition and community at the third annual Día de los Muertos Street Fest on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

The event, organized by Blazeful Vibes in collaboration with the Benque Viejo Town Council, will take place in front of Cancha Marshalleck from 4:00 p.m. until midnight.

The street fest is expected to feature more than 35 vendors offering food, drinks and local products, along with music, performances and competitions with prizes.

Entertainment will include music by DJ IconicSound Chavez, while community members can participate in competitions for Best Dressed Catrín and Catrina, Best Made Ixpasha and Best Decorated Booth for vendors.

Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a vibrant cultural tradition that honors the memory of loved ones who have passed away through remembrance, offerings, flowers and candles.

See you there!

World.title: Belize City Council marks 9th anniversary Super Sale with discounts and live entertainment today
World.content:
Belize City Council marks 9th anniversary Super Sale with discounts and live entertainment today

By Zoila Palma: The Belize City Council is celebrating its ninth anniversary Super Sale today, Saturday, October 31, 2026, inviting residents to shop, save and support local businesses in downtown Belize City.

The event runs from 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., featuring a wide variety of affordable products from local vendors, including crafts, accessories, household goods, food, drinks and more.

The 2026 Anniversary Edition Super Sale will offer shoppers special deals and discounts while giving businesses and vendors an opportunity to showcase their products and connect with customers.

One of the highlights is a 20 percent discount on outstanding property tax arrears, along with a Traffic One-Stop Service at City Hall for residents seeking traffic-related services.

Shoppers will also receive a raffle ticket for every $20 spent, while families can enjoy a Halloween costume competition and a kids’ zone offering free goodies.

The day will feature live entertainment from Tapric, Cocono Bwai, Kenny Gladden and the New Creation Band, Nello Player and other performers.

See you there!

World.title: Belize City Mayor meets Guyana’s President ahead of Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting
World.content:
Belize City Mayor meets Guyana’s President ahead of Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting

By Zoila Palma: On October 30, 2026, Mayor of Belize City Bernard Wagner, Chair of the Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF), met with Guyana’s President, Dr. Mohamed Irfaan Ali, at a cocktail reception hosted at State House in Georgetown on the occasion of the Global Biodiversity Alliance Conference 2026.

The engagement comes as Mayor Wagner continues to play a leading role in high-level Commonwealth discussions on sustainable urbanisation, local governance, and development ahead of CHOGM 2026.

Mayor Wagner described Georgetown’s remarkable transformation as an inspiring demonstration of visionary leadership and strategic investment, offering valuable lessons for cities across the Commonwealth.

In addition, Mayor Wagner expressed sincere appreciation to President Ali for his warm hospitality and Guyana’s growing leadership on the international stage.

World.title: National Institute of Culture and History provides $10,000 to support preservation of Garifuna culture
World.content:
National Institute of Culture and History provides $10,000 to support preservation of Garifuna culture

By Zoila Palma: On October 30, 2026, on behalf of Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture, Albert Vaughan, President of the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) presented a donation of BZ $10,000 to Darius Avila, President of Battle of the Drums.

The donation is in support of the continued celebration and preservation of Belize’s rich Garifuna culture and heritage.

“This contribution reflects our commitment to supporting cultural organisations, strengthening community-led initiatives, and ensuring that Belize’s diverse cultural traditions continue to thrive,” NICH noted.

NICH said that through continued investment and partnerships, it celebrates and preserve the cultural expressions that shape our national identity.

World.title: Belize exploring possibility of railway linking Mexico to Belize City
World.content:
Belize exploring possibility of railway linking Mexico to Belize City

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceño said recently that the Government of Belize is exploring plans to extend Mexico’s Tren Maya railway into Belize, with a proposed 160-kilometer route linking the Mexican border to Belize City and potentially continuing to Guatemala.

Briceño said a feasibility study being conducted with support from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) is expected to be completed in approximately two weeks.

The study is expected to assess the infrastructure requirements, financial resources and potential funding options for the project.

The PM acknowledged that constructing a railway of this scale would require a significant investment, with private investors also being considered as possible partners.

Briceño said the proposed railway could create opportunities for tourism, regional travel and trade, particularly if connected to plans for a modern port in Belize.

“There are a lot of opportunities with the connection of Tren Maya,” the PM said.

“If we can get Tren Maya to come into Belize and then connect Belize City and then connect onto Guatemala, it opens up not only from the tourism industry but also using the port facilities,” he added.

World.title: Government wants lie detector tests for National Security Council personnel
World.content:
Government wants lie detector tests for National Security Council personnel

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Those with access to Belize’s most sensitive security information could soon be required to sit polygraph tests and undergo vetting.

The proposal is part of an amendment to the National Security Council Act, which was taken up in the Senate on Thursday.

Making the case for the change, Leader for Government Business Anthony Sylvestre pointed to the classified material that passes through the council and its secretariat. He argued that anyone with that level of access should face periodic testing and close scrutiny.

“It behooves everyone that the personnel who are engaged, employed in this body, which has such sensitive and classified information within the access of the personnel within the secretariat of the National Security Council, it is important that those persons would be at different points in time, be subject to polygraph tests and a level of rigid scrutiny,” Sylvestre told the Senate.

The council plays a central role in shaping Belize’s security decisions. In recent weeks, it has dealt with the Guatemalan military aircraft incursion into Belizean airspace and preliminary talks with the United States on security cooperation.

The opposition supported the idea of screening but raised questions about how the results would be handled.

World.title: Belize to enjoy several long weekends in 2027
World.content:
Belize to enjoy several long weekends in 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans planning trips, family time or business schedules for next year will be glad to see plenty of long weekends on the 2027 holiday calendar.

Of the 14 public and bank holidays announced by government, most fall on a Friday or Monday.

The year opens with back to back long weekends, with New Year’s Day and George Price Day both on Fridays in January.

National Heroes and Benefactors Day, Labour Day, Emancipation Day and Indigenous People’s Resistance Day will all be observed on Mondays in lieu of their actual dates, creating three day weekends in March, May, August and October.

Easter comes early in 2027, with Good Friday on March 26, Holy Saturday on March 27 and Easter Monday on March 29, giving Belizeans a four day break.

The September celebrations will see St. George’s Caye Day on Friday, September 10, followed by Independence Day on Tuesday, September 21.

Garifuna Settlement Day falls on Friday, November 19.

The year closes with Christmas Day on Saturday, December 25, and Boxing Day on Monday, December 27.

For businesses in tourism and hospitality, the long weekends offer a good opportunity to plan local promotions and staycation packages well in advance.

World.title: Udinese striker Davis still eyeing Reggae Boyz spot
World.content:
Udinese's British forward #09 Keinan Davis celebrates after scoring a penalty kick during the Italian Serie A football match between Inter Milan and Udinese at San Siro stadium in Milan on August 31, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

Udinese striker Keinan Davis says discussions have taken place about representing Jamaica, but the England-born forward is still awaiting the completion of his Jamaican passport application before making the next step towards international football.

Davis, who has been enjoying an encouraging spell with Italian Serie A club Udinese, provided an update on his international future during an interview with CBS Sports Golazo, revealing that conversations have already taken place about the possibility of wearing the Reggae Boyz colours.

“I’ve had some conversations,” Davis said, while explaining that sorting out his Jamaican passport remains a major priority.

The 28-year-old 6ft 3 inches striker, born in England of Jamaican descent, said the administrative process was taking some time but expressed hope that the matter would be resolved.

“The procedure takes a little time, but we’ll see what happens in the future. I’m sorting out the passport,” he explained.

He also admitted that his injury history had previously influenced discussions about committing to international football, particularly given the demands of travelling between Europe and the Caribbean.

Davis, who represented England at the Under 20 level, said that when he spoke with Udinese last year, consideration was given to whether the additional travelling associated with international duty would be the best option for him as he sought to establish himself and remain available for club football.

However, the striker indicated that his current physical condition has improved and that he is determined to maintain his fitness.

“But now I’m well and I want to continue to be well,” he said.

The latest comments will provide encouragement for Jamaica, which has been keen to strengthen its attacking options.

His potential involvement would be a significant addition to the Reggae Boyz’ attacking department, given his physical presence, pace and experience in European football.

– Howard Walker

World.title: FAO equips Jamaican farmers with adapted greenhouse technologies
World.content:
Digital tools are now being used as part of adapted greenhouse technologies to advance precise vegetable production in Jamaica.

SEVERAL vegetable farmers across Jamaica are now combining adapted greenhouse covering materials and digital sensors to improve growing conditions and support more efficient crop production.

These efforts are supported by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) project “Digital Solutions to Improve Horticultural Crop Management in the Caribbean”, which is nearing completion.

In a media release on Friday the FAO said, the project was implemented in collaboration with Jamaica’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, the project has provided beneficiary farmers with adapted greenhouse covering materials and environmental, soil and water sensors, together with technical guidance on their installation, use and application in crop management under protected cultivation systems.

The adapted covering materials were introduced to help farmers manage high temperatures that can affect crop production under protected structures, a common challenge for vegetable production across the Caribbean.

Farmers using the materials have reported noticeably cooler growing conditions and improvements in crop performance.

“The anti-thermic plastic has made a huge difference.

It keeps the greenhouse cooler and takes some of the harsh heat off the plants.

The sweet peppers are doing much better, and you can really see the difference in the plants,” said Conroy Cole, farmer in St Ann.

In Manchester, farmer Diandra Rowe reported a reduction in greenhouse temperatures of at least 2 degrees Celsius (°C) following the installation of the adapted covering materials.

“Even though this has been one of the hottest and driest summers I’ve experienced in 12 years of farming, my yields have been significantly better than in previous years.

It has also made working in the greenhouse much more comfortable,” said Rowe.

The introduction of adapted greenhouse covering materials has also opened up new business opportunities in Jamaica, with some farmers independently importing and distributing these materials to other growers, helping to expand access to the technology beyond the project beneficiaries.

Digital sensors are also 0providing farmers with site-specific information on environmental, soil and water conditions to guide irrigation, nutrient management and other crop management decisions.

Across beneficiary sites, these technologies have been applied in diverse horticultural systems, alongside practical guidance on ventilation, shading, irrigation and fertigation management.

Rowe added, “The digital sensors have given us much-needed insight into exactly what is happening inside our growing spaces in real time.

Being able to access the data remotely means we can make better-informed decisions and adjust our practices where needed.” The project also provided technical guidance and refresher training to help farmers and extension personnel interpret data generated by the environmental, soil and water sensors.

This included practical guidance on monitoring growing conditions and using sensor readings to support adjustments to irrigation, nutrient management and other day-to-day crop management practices.

“The real value of these technologies comes from using them together.

The adapted greenhouse covering helps create better growing conditions, while digital sensors provide farmers with the information to adjust irrigation, nutrient management and other practices based on actual growing conditions.

Together, they can support more efficient and productive protected agriculture,” said Anne Desrochers, FAO plant production and protection specialist and lead technical officer for the project.

Several beneficiary farmers were also affected by Hurricane Melissa, with damage to protected structures and temporary disruptions to production.

Many are now rebuilding and working to resume production, with project- supported technologies being reinstalled or incorporated into rehabilitated greenhouse systems.

The FAO team says it is now consolidating lessons from beneficiary sites and documenting farmer experiences and production results.

These findings will help inform future efforts to scale up digital and climate-responsive technologies for horticultural production in Jamaica.

World.title: Relief in sight
World.content:
Garfield Granston, who broke his spine in May, is seen at Black River Hospital.

KINGSTON Public Hospital (KPH) has pledged an urgent consultation with doctors at Black River Hospital (BRH) to determine Garfield Granston’s next steps to recovery, months after the 57-year-old was referred for specialist care and surgery following serious spinal injury.

In a press release on Friday, KPH’s management said that it had seriously reviewed Granston’s medical history and acknowledged that his surgery was delayed after its C-arm machine, required to carry out the procedure, went out of service.

Granston was referred to the Orthopaedics Outpatient Clinic at KPH in May 2026, after he had fallen from a tree and sustained fractures in two places along his spine. He was initially rushed to BRH, in St Elizabeth, where he was subsequently told that the hospital lacked the facilities to perform the procedure.

In Friday’s press release KPH outlined that after clinical assessment and diagnostic imaging, an orthopaedic consultant recommended that Granston receive supportive care and secure the necessary spinal implants for possible surgery.

The required medical equipment included 10 pedicle screws, 10 set screws, and two rods, at a total cost of $854,000.

The release said that the spinal implants were not made readily available by Granston during follow-up visits, and after the payment was made, the hospital’s equipment became unavailable. While it did not clarify whether the C-arm machine is once more operational, KPH said it remains committed to delivering medical solutions for its patients and maintains that it would move to promptly execute referral and transfer procedures.

“Urgent coordination between the orthopaedics teams at Black River Public Hospital and Kingston Public Hospital will be undertaken to review the patient’s current clinical condition and determine the appropriate next steps. Established referral and transfer procedures will be followed.

“KPH remains committed to collaborating with public health facilities to support continuity of care, facilitate appropriate clinical decision-making, and promote positive patient outcomes while safeguarding patient confidentiality and dignity,” the hospital said.

The update comes in response to a Jamaica Observer story on October 27 in which Elexso Smith disclosed her stepfather’s plight as he endured five months awaiting a surgery date from KPH.

She explained that after receiving the nearly-million-dollar bill for surgical devices, her family sought assistance from the Ministry of Health and Wellness, which provided $554,000, while the family covered the remaining $300,000.

Smith said she was shocked that her stepfather’s surgery was still delayed, even after payment was made.

“Before we pay the money at KPH, and before we got help from the health ministry, the doctor was very harsh because he was arguing, saying that we have to pay the money before we can do surgery. When we get the receipt and gave it to the doctor he said: ‘One more problem. The machine broke down,’ ” Smith told the Observer on Tuesday this week.

“Every time he is to go up there [KPH], they’re always putting him off; or if he’s sent up there, they send him back down [to BRH]. From the last time he went up there [KPH] on the 30th [of June] he has not been back there. And then when they [BRH] call up there they say he mustn’t come, or there is no bed space,” she claimed.

She added that KPH did not state a clear timeline for Granston’s surgery, leaving him to endure severe discomfort while only receiving treatment for his pain at Black River Hospital where he was initially admitted.

Smith, who acknowledged that her stepfather’s care regimen was no easy feat, had called on KPH to provide a clear timeline for the alleviation of his pain.

“I just want to find out what’s really happening with this surgery situation. It’s been months and nothing. We’re not hearing nothing at all. So we just want KPH to state what their position is with this surgery as soon as possible,” Smith said on Tuesday.

World.title: NOON Brunch goes Pink at Devon House
World.content:
Looking delightful in blush pink in support of Jamaica’s breast cancer awareness movement, Tamelia Jones (left) and Yvonne Finlayson spend their Sunday afternoon brunching on the lawns of Devon House at NOON Pink, the brunch party series.

After making its debut in April of this year, the NOON Brunch series returned on Sunday, October 25 with a pink theme and an even bigger turnout.

Held at the iconic Devon House, the event’s patrons enjoyed not only the available delicacies, but also the pulsating musical delights that kept flowing.

Tasked with getting attendees in a dancing mood were DJ Junior Pang, who got things rolling with a number of sing-a-long tunes, Shukkle Bus, and DJ Fastcar, who kept the momentum going.

Fyahman, Steelie Bashment, and Quality International also represented themselves well.

“The first staging of NOON was really an introduction to the atmosphere and overall experience we envisioned for our patrons. It gave people a taste of what we wanted the brand to represent. So, for the second staging, we built on that foundation… We expanded the variety of food options, secured the iconic Devon House as our venue, and adjusted the event time to better accommodate our patrons.

“We also maintained our commitment to delivering a diverse and experienced entertainment line-up. Ultimately, our objective was to elevate the overall experience while preserving the energy and atmosphere that made the first staging memorable,” Dane Wilson, director of brand & marketing for NOON Brunch, told the Jamaica Observer post-event.

He added that the series’ growth speaks to the brand’s potential.

“In just six months we’ve seen the brand gain significant recognition, and that’s incredibly encouraging. When I speak with people I’m often surprised by how many have already heard about NOON or have some familiarity with the experience we’re creating… Our focus now is on converting that recognition into sustained patron loyalty,” he shared.

Wilson shared that one of the most memorable moments was when the rain started to pour and Shukkle Bus kept the energy going. Instead of allowing the weather to dampen the atmosphere, patrons embraced the moment.

“At one point, there was even a conga line making its way through the crowd in the rain! It was spontaneous, energetic and genuinely unforgettable. Those are the kinds of experiences that make an event special,” he said.

Commenting on the food on offer, Wilson noted that the objective was to provide variety and quality while ensuring the food complemented the overall brunch experience.

“Food is a major part of the NOON experience, and for this staging, we wanted to ensure that patrons had a wide selection of breakfast and lunch favourites. The menu featured traditional Jamaican breakfast staples such as ackee and saltfish, callaloo, brown stew chicken, fried dumplings and festival. For lunch we had fried chicken, jerk chicken, soup, rice and peas, and, of course, curry goat. We also introduced a made-to-order omelette station, allowing guests to customise their omelettes with their preferred vegetables and proteins. Waffles, pancakes, pastries and fresh fruits completed the selection,” Wilson explained.

The event, which primarily targets young professionals between the ages of 25 and 45 who appreciate good music and great food.

The next staging will be in March 2027.

“We don’t want NOON to be defined strictly by age. Our vision is to create an inclusive, sophisticated yet relaxed environment where different generations can come together and feel equally comfortable. We want grandmothers, mothers, and daughters to be able to attend the same event, enjoy the atmosphere and create memories together. At its core, NOON is about bringing people together through food, music and a shared appreciation for a great experience,” Wilson reasoned.

World.title: Prosecution rests
World.content:
Kevin Smith, the late pastor of Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James, who is alleged to have instructed murder accused Andre Ruddock to cut the throat of a fellow worshiper on October 17, 2021.

AFTER calling 10 individuals to give evidence since September 17, the prosecution in the Andre Ruddock murder trial closed its case on Friday, opening the way for the defence to call witnesses of its own, if it so desires, next Monday.

A pathologist was the last witness to be called by the prosecution on Friday in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston before it ended its case. The pathologist confirmed that 39-year-old Taneka Gardner was in fact dead and died from having her throat slashed.

If the defence, led by attorney Anthony Williams, decides to call witnesses of its own, it would be to try and prove that Ruddock is not guilty of murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice-type killing of Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James.

It is alleged that Ruddock was acting on instructions from his now-deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Gardner died after her throat was cut, allegedly by Ruddock.

It is a possibility that on Monday, Ruddock could decide to take the witness stand himself. In the meantime, Williams and Venice Brown, who comprise his legal team, await further instructions from him on whether or not he will testify.

The seven members of the jury appeared happy on Friday to learn that the prosecution had ended its case and that the matter, which has taken them away from their private avocations, will be behind them soon.

Williams and Brown defended Ruddock vigorously throughout the trial, although their client confessed to killing Gardner one day after the woman’s throat was cut. He had confessed to detectives in the presence of two justices of the peace that he was responsible for cutting Gardner’s throat. The confession, which Ruddock gave in a caution statement, was recorded in writing by detectives and was also video-recorded.

Following the taking of the caution statement, detectives went on to ask 42-year-old Ruddock questions to get clarity on how the gruesome events, which led to Gardner’s demise, unfolded. That question-and-answer session was also video-recorded.

The videos of both the caution statement and a question-and-answer session with detectives were played in court for the jurors to review. Ruddock did not appear to be under any threat to confess to killing Gardner, although Williams sought to convince the jurors that his client was threatened and intimidated prior to him being taken to Freeport Police Station in Montego Bay.

The main witness in the case — who said he was an adjutant to the pastor of the church, often shaving his head, carrying his Bible and helping him to get dressed — told the court that Ruddock took a knife from another member of the church and cut Gardner’s throat, after that member hesitated to carry out the pastor’s order.

The witness said Gardner did not resist, after she allegedly told the pastor that she believed he could bring her back to life if she was to have her throat cut.

World.title: ‘WE’RE PROUD!’
World.content:
Portmore United players and staff celebrate qualifying for the Concacaf Champions Cup after defeating Violette 4-3 on aggregate in the two-legged semi-final of the Caribbean Cup. Portmore won the first leg 3-1 but lost the second match 1-2 at Sabina Park in Kingston, Jamaica, on October 28, 2026. (Photo: Concacaf)

PORTMORE United Chairman Garwin Tulloch believes the club have made significant strides and are preparing to test themselves against the region’s best in next year’s Concacaf Champions Cup.

The reigning Jamaica Premier League champions will vie for the Concacaf Caribbean Cup title in December, after beating Haiti’s Violette 4-3 on aggregate, despite a 1-2 loss in their second- leg semi-final at Sabina Park on Wednesday.

Portmore’s 3-1 first-leg win was enough to secure a spot in the first-ever all-Jamaican Caribbean Cup final, joining defending champions Mount Pleasant Football Academy who beat Trinidad and Tobago’s Club Sando in their semi-final matchup.

It’s another achievement for the club since the arrival of its new leadership group in 2024, led by Tulloch’s United Sports Group.

“The technical team has learnt a lot along the way and administratively, we have improved and we’re just seeing the results on the pitch from the work of the technical team and the management of the club,” Tulloch told the Jamaica Observer.

“So it may seem like a short space of time in terms of the results on the pitch but the work went in before that.

It’s a great achievement and we’re proud.” Despite winning the now-defunct CFU Club Championship in 2005 and 2019, Portmore had not competed in regional competition for more than five years before this year’s tournament.

However, Tulloch says the team understood the importance of the Caribbean Cup — and their performances reflected that.

“To be honest, I’m very impressed, because it’s easy to motivate the youngsters and the lads at this level because the opportunity to be on the international platforms is what every aspiring young footballer tries to get,” he said.

“In fact, it’s actually harder to motivate them to play in the local competition right now because they’re focused primarily on playing Concacaf, so motivating the technical team and the players is really very difficult.

But, I have to give credit also to our coaching staff who have levelled and made responsible decisions; rotation of the squad is also very important at this time — ‘man management’ is really the word and they’ve done a very good job in doing that.” Regardless of the two-legged final against Mount Pleasant on December 1 and 5 in Kingston, Portmore will compete in the Champions Cup where they could face top clubs from the likes of USA, Mexico, Canada and Central America.

Tulloch says the club will need to take another step if they are to be competitive in the competition.

“The more you advance in the competition, logically, it’s a wider platform and it’s a harder challenge.

And at this point it takes more mettle because, traditionally, we in our region — as in the Caribbean— don’t normally fare well at that level so we’re preparing ourselves to compete at that level,” he said.

“First, we have to win the championship against Mount Pleasant — which is important for us because it gives us a bye into the round of one.

So, it’s important; it’s a wider platform and we’re looking forward to the challenge.” Portmore join Mount Pleasant and Cavalier FC as the only Jamaican clubs to qualify for the revamped Champions Cup.

Portmore return to local competition on Sunday when they visit Montego Bay United in the Legend Jamaica Premier League.

World.title: NSWMA takes aim at more than 50 derelict vehicles in Norwood, St James
World.content:
NSWMA’s Executive Director Audley Gordon speaks with the media while workmen remove one of the derelict vehicles on the streets in Norwood, St James. (Photo: JIS)

THE National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA) deployed four crane trucks to Norwood, St James, on Thursday to remove derelict vehicles and bulky waste as part of a clean-up initiative aimed at improving public safety, enhancing accessibility and restoring order within the community.

NSWMA’s Executive Director Audley Gordon told journalists that more than 50 derelict vehicles had been identified for removal under the operation, which forms part of ongoing efforts to address obstructions on roadways and improve conditions for residents.

He added that crane trucks were mobilised from other regions to support the operation, enabling crews to access and remove abandoned vehicles located in confined and hard-to-reach areas.

Gordon said derelict vehicles are a common feature in densely populated communities across Jamaica.

He noted that while some owners are unable to afford the necessary repairs, others abandon vehicles after acquiring replacements or retain them for spare parts.

According to Gordon, abandoned vehicles often obstruct narrow roadways, making it more difficult for emergency responders, including the police, fire services and ambulances, to access communities in a timely manner.

“Public order must be restored in Jamaica, and we are starting one car at a time to play our part,” declared Gordon.

The work in Norwood also included the removal of bulky waste and the relocation of a large skip from an intersection.

Gordon is encouraging residents to report derelict vehicles in their communities.

He pointed out that once a vehicle is reported, it can be tagged in accordance with the law and removed after the stipulated notice period has expired.

— JIS

World.title: USF restores Wi-Fi hotspots in St Mary
World.content:
Universal Service Fund (USF) Chief Executive Officer Charlton McFarlane (right) demonstrates to St Mary Central Member of Parliament Omar Newell, and Councillor Corrine Dillon McDonald (People’s National Party, Port Maria Division), the functionality of a free public Wi-Fi hotspot in Port Maria, St Mary, following its restoration by the fund on October 29, 2026. The hotspot is among 23 restored across the parish by the USF. Photo: JIS

The Universal Service Fund (USF) has restored 23 free public Wi-Fi hotspots across St Mary, an investment of $50 million, as part of the State’s effort to improve digital access and strengthen connectivity in communities across northern Jamaica.

The restoration follows the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, when more than 95 per cent of the USF’s Wi-Fi sites across the parish were damaged, disrupting access to an important resource for residents, students and small-business operators.

Communities benefiting from the restored service include Broadgate, Castleton, Robin’s Bay, Annotto Bay, Hamilton Mountain, Albion Mountain, Windsor Castle, Friendship Gap, Wood Park, Woodside, Bonny Gate, Mango Valley, Gayle, Islington, Richmond, Epsom, Hampstead, Luna, and Highgate.

Chief executive officer of the USF, Charlton McFarlane, said the restoration represents a significant step towards reconnecting communities and ensuring residents can benefit from reliable internet access.

McFarlane was speaking at the opening leg of the USF Connec’ Di North Coast Tour at Giant Family Mart in Port Maria, St Mary, on October 29, which officially launched the restored Wi-Fi locations and brought Government agencies, utility providers, and other partners together to engage residents and provide access to various services.

He noted that Internet connectivity has become increasingly important to everyday activities, extending beyond communication and entertainment to education, business and family connections.

“In 2026, Wi-Fi is more than connectivity,” McFarlane said. “Many persons here in the parish of St Mary, maybe in the town of Port Maria, are content creators. Some persons rely on the Wi-Fi to do their assignments [while] some persons rely on the Wi-Fi to connect with their families.”

The initiative forms part of the USF’s wider programme to establish 61 community Wi-Fi and 28 public Wi-Fi sites across northern Jamaica, with approximately 47,000 residents expected to benefit from improved Internet access.

In St Mary, an estimated 4,000 people are expected to benefit from the restored facilities. Port Maria is among the locations benefiting from the initiative, with eight access points capable of accommodating more than 500 users simultaneously.

McFarlane said the USF has also introduced several improvements to strengthen the resilience of the Wi-Fi network and reduce the risk of service disruptions during future hurricanes.

Previously dependent largely on fibre-optic cables, the network now incorporates satellite Internet technology, including Starlink, alongside solar-powered systems.

McFarlane pointed out that the fund continues to cover the monthly costs associated with maintaining the service, while encouraging residents to report any outages to its help desk to facilitate timely intervention.

“This is the USF’s gift to the people of St Mary,” he noted.

— JIS

World.title: Merz ‘surprised’ by Asian pushback to ‘Made in Europe’ plan for car industry
World.content:
“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning from his five-day tour of East Asian countries on Friday evening.

Merz admitted the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”

The chancellor vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and to raise them at the next EU leaders' summit. The bloc's leaders are set to meet in Dublin on Nov. 13 for an informal gathering.

Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade” between so-called middle powers in speeches in Seoul and Tokyo. The EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged the international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted" — a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals or the tariff threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.

But the pushback from South Korea and Japan are a sharp reminder of how industry-specific frictions can hamper the implementation of the larger alliance proposed by Merz.

World.title: Burnham ‘open’ to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
World.content:
However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay financial reparations for the slave trade, saying that they would be the wrong solution.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” the prime minister argued.

Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced in June a manifesto by Caribbean leaders setting out the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations from former colonial powers.

Burnham will attend the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, which runs through Wednesday. It will be his first foreign trip with King Charles.

It will be a crucial test for the prime minister, who will try to avoid a fight over slavery reparations that marred his predecessor Keir Starmer’s visit at the last summit in 2024.

World.title: Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries
World.content:
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.

Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.

In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

“Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said.

The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months.

However, the White House said that it won't pay for the Patriot interceptors. "The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies," a statement from the State Department said.

World.title: Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle
World.content:
Inside, Nawrocki told Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges that were recently elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority: “You are not judges [of the Tribunal].”

The confrontation marked a dramatic escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the court’s president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański — both named by PiS and seen as loyalists — claiming authority to take over the court’s management. Święczkowski rejected the move.

In a statement issued around 5 a.m., Nawrocki accused the government of “forcibly seizing a constitutional institution”, demanded that police leave the court grounds and summoned emergency consultations with parliamentary parties for Saturday, citing a “threat to Poland’s internal security.”

Police remain deployed outside the tribunal, where PiS supporters had staged an anti-government protest camp for weeks.

The broader dispute stems from Tusk’s efforts to reverse controversial moves by former PiS governments to fill the court with judges aligned with the nationalist party. These efforts have met stiff resistance from PiS and Nawrocki, who refused to swear in some judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority.

The judges subsequently took oaths in parliament, in a ceremony Nawrocki considers null and void, while Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

World.title: Funding deadlock derails global effort to save nature
World.content:
But behind that grand gesture, governments are still struggling to unlock the hundreds of billions needed to meet global biodiversity protection targets. The reason? A profound and unresolved disagreement over where that money should come from.

“If we’re mutually unhappy that’s probably the closest we can get to on these very delicate compromises,” said a member of the Swiss delegation just before the text was adopted.

After two weeks of negotiations over how to speed up efforts to protect ecosystems, nearly 200 countries secured a hard-fought agreement to "accelerate the implementation" of the global biodiversity framework "including by increased ambition in addressing the gaps, challenges and barriers related to implementation," according to a draft of the text, the final version of which was not immediately available.

Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan, who presided over the summit, said negotiators had "achieved more than we could have expected."

But in the end, governments could not agree on how to increase the number of countries currently contributing to biodiversity finance, instead only stating the obvious: that more funds would be better.

The summit exposed a growing chasm between nations over who should be held financially responsible for funding conservation measures worldwide: historically wealthy countries whose economies have caused immense damage to the environment, or newly rich states whose economies have grown exponentially in the last three decades.

World.title: 8 things we learned at the EU-Canada summit
World.content:
Those challenges have pushed the EU and Canada into a rapidly developing partnership that eclipses anything attempted by Brussels with a non-member country since the bloc was formed.

Here are all the key things POLITICO learned during the EU-Canada meetings.

Carney finally embraced ‘associate membership’

Initially reluctant, the Canadian prime minister came around by the end of the summit to endorse von der Leyen’s controversial label for the global alliance the EU and Canada are building.

Carney set a six-month deadline to firm up the ground rules of what “associate membership” is, trialing an induction process that could be a model for other non-European countries.

“With Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member, in the coming months we will determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership,” he said Friday.

Carney added he will meet periodically with von der Leyen to track progress, including a return trip for the College of European Commissioners to meet with their Canadian counterparts in March.

World.title: 'A lot of lies': Kaja Kallas criticises Russian FM Lavrov following G20 meetings
World.content:
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov of telling "a lot of lies" on topics such as the Ukraine war during talks with G20 ministers in Atlanta on Friday.

 

"We were talking about the big geopolitical crisis, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head on with this," she told the AFP news agency.

"Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives" that Europeans challenged, Kallas added.

European officials also reportedly used the opportunity to put further pressure on Moscow as they sought to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea - prompting pushback from Lavrov, a diplomatic source told AFP.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said he had also told Lavrov in the plenary that "he should have the courage to tell Putin that Russia will not win this war."

The UK minister is also said to have confronted Lavrov over a recent attack on a Dnipro railway that killed 15 people as he stressed Moscow was the "aggressor" in the conflict, which began in February 2022 when Russian forces launched their full-scale invasion.

In a press conference on Friday, Lavrov "welcomed" the US' willingness to engage in dialogue with Moscow while hitting out at what he called Europe's "arrogant boycott."

"This is a good lesson for our European colleagues," he said of Washington's approach.

Several officials at the meetings also reportedly refused to stand for a "family photo" with Lavrov, leading US organisers to cancel the picture.

The G20 meetings come just days before the US' key midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in office.

US approves Patriots package for Ukraine

On Friday, the US State Department announced that Washington had green-lit a package of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has continued to plead with US and European allies for more interceptors for its forces as Ukraine continues to weather Russian missile and drone attacks.

And while he welcomed the new package and thanked the US for its "strong decision," he warned that delivery could take years.

"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.

"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he added. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 in Atlanta.

World.title: 'Northern women and esotericism': Life after death explored at Finnish National Gallery
World.content:
The Latin words arcana and borealis mean "hidden knowledge" and "the north", two elements at the heart of the Finnish National Gallery's latest exhibition.

 

"Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" is the first large-scale museum show to examine how female artists from across the Nordic region and Sápmi have engaged with esotericism, spirituality and alternative systems of knowledge from the 19th century to the present day.

The exhibition brings together more than 200 works by 50 artists and features both well-known and overlooked artists, including Hilma af Klint, Tyra Kleen and Tove Jansson.

Tyra Kleen, Forbidden Fruit, 1909, gouache on paper, Riddarhuset, Tyra Kleen Collection. Photo: © Bobo Lindblad, Lindblad Studio

Previously the connection between modern art and esotericism, occultism and magic has been explored mainly through famous male artists, according to Dr Marja Lahelma, Chief Curator at Ateneum Art Museum and co-curator of the exhibition.

"For quite a long time art history has been dominated by narratives focusing on male artists and on this notion of the individual genius. Our focus is on women and we also draw attention to this idea of communality and working together," Dr Lahelma explained to Euronews Culture.

Tove Jansson, Mysterious Landscape (c.1930–1939). Finnish National Gallery. Collection / Ateneum Art Museum. Photo: Finnish National Gallery / Hannu Pakarinen

Art, spirituality and handicraft

"Arcana Borealis shows how the boundaries between art and spirituality, fine art and craft, object and process, individual authorship and collective making begin to blur when viewed through the lens of artist women and esotericism" added Dr Nina Kokkinen from University of Turku, co-curator of "Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" .

Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism. Installation view, Ateneum Art Museum, 2026. Photo: Finnish National Gallery / Aleks Talve

The range of materials featured in the exhibition is exceptionally wide, including textiles, ceramics, metal engravings, and traditional media from sacral art, such as stained glass and mosaics.

Handicraft involves matrilineal transmission of tradition, that is, passing down knowledge and skills from one woman to the next. Sámi duodji, the traditional Sámi craft tradition, brings together spirituality, the tacit knowledge passed on from one generation to another, and values related to nature.

Hilma af Klint, The Dove no 1, Group IX, Series UW, 1915, oil on canvas, By Courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation. Photo: Moderna Museet

Some of the artists gathered on the exhibition were saying that they were guided by some kind of non human agency whether it was angels or guiding spirits, or in some cases a source of nature.

Halloween or Kekri

"This is a perfect exhibition to visit for Halloween, or Kekri as we say in Finnish. Esotericism is about light and darkness. We can explore themes such as death in art through this esoteric theme and sometimes the hidden knowledge, the secret knowledge that esotericism is all about, can be found through exploring darkness rather than light," explained Dr Marja Lahelm.

Anna Cassel, Untitled II, No. 33, 1915, oil and metallic paint on canvas, Private collection. Photo: By Courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation / Anders Fredriksén

Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism at Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery is on open until 28 February 2027.

World.title: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine amid localised truce between Kyiv and Moscow
World.content:
Evacuees from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region arrived in Ukraine on Saturday after travelling through Belarus amid a humanitarian truce between Kyiv and Moscow.

 

Video footage shared on social media by Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, showed some of the evacuated residents stepping off a bus draped in Ukrainian flags and embracing loved ones after crossing the border.

"The moment we had all been waiting for: residents of Oleshky have crossed the border — the humanitarian mission has been successfully completed!" Lubinets wrote alongside the clip, while also thanking US First Lady Melania Trump for her help brokering the deal.

"This entire mission was successfully carried out thanks to her involvement," he said.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the evacuees had crossed into Ukraine in the Chernihiv region in the north of the country and that they would now "receive the assistance they need."

They had earlier touched down in Gomel in southeastern Belarus before continuing their journey.

Melania, who helped broker the localised ceasefire, said on Friday that a convoy was ready to evacuate more than 750 people "who voluntarily choose to leave Oleshky."

"It includes 25 buses, 50 medical professionals, and ambulances," she said.

The ceasefire is due to last until Sunday evening.

Russian strikes on Ukraine

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said around 280,000 Ukrainian households had been left without power after Russian strikes overnight.

"Russian strikes have created a difficult situation with electricity supplies across our regions," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.

He said around 200,000 households in Dnipro and the wider region were without electricity while a further 80,000 or more in the Kyiv region were also without power.

"Repair crews are working to deal with the aftermath of the strikes and doing everything they can to restore electricity supplies," he said, adding that Russian forces had hit a "combined heat and power plant" in Kyiv on Friday night as well as four electrical substations in the eastern Dnipro region, among other targets.

World.title: Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal crisis explained: a decade-long dispute over legitimacy of the justice
World.content:
After taking office in 2023, Donald Tusk’s coalition moved to reverse judicial reforms introduced by PiS.

 

The dispute entered a new phase in 2026, when President Karol Nawrocki refused to accept the oaths of several judges elected by parliament.

The standoff reached boiling point on Friday outside of the Constitutional Tribunal’s headquarters, with both sides disputing the other’s legitimacy.

Euronews explains the conflict in five key stages.

1. 2015: Five judges, two rival appointments

The crisis began in June 2015, when the outgoing PO-PSL coalition changed the law to allow parliament to elect five Constitutional Tribunal judges before the October elections.

On 8 October, the outgoing Sejm elected Roman Hauser, Andrzej Jakubecki, Krzysztof Ślebzak, Bronisław Sitek and Andrzej Sokala. President Andrzej Duda refused to accept their oaths.

After PiS won the election, the new Sejm declared the previous appointments invalid and elected five alternative candidates on 2 December. Duda accepted their oaths.

A day later, however, the Tribunal ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were constitutional, while two were not. It also said the president must accept the oaths of properly elected judges without delay.

This meant three seats had already been lawfully filled. PiS’s subsequent appointments to those seats were therefore challenged. The three disputed appointees — Mariusz Muszyński, Henryk Cioch and Lech Morawski — became known as the Tribunal’s 'stand-in judges'.

While PO-PSL had overstepped its powers by filling two seats prematurely, PiS also challenged three appointments that the Tribunal had deemed valid.

2. 2016–2023: Changes to the Tribunal and questions over independence

After taking power, PiS changed the rules governing the Tribunal, including how cases were heard, the number of judges required and voting thresholds.

In March 2016, the Tribunal ruled that the first set of changes was unconstitutional. Prime Minister Beata Szydło’s government refused to publish the judgment, arguing that it had been issued under the wrong procedures.

The dispute deepened after Julia Przyłębska became Tribunal president in December 2016. The three disputed PiS appointees were also allowed to take part in its work.

Critics said the changes undermined judicial independence and brought the Tribunal under political control. PiS argued that it was restoring the institution and reforming the justice system.

The conflict also reached European courts. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the Tribunal's composition, including Mariusz Muszyński, did not meet the requirement of a tribunal established by law.

That year, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal also issued rulings challenging the primacy of certain EU law provisions concerning the judiciary.

By 2022–2023, divisions had emerged within the Tribunal itself. Several judges questioned Przyłębska’s continued leadership, arguing that her six-year term as president had expired. She maintained that she could remain in office until the end of her nine-year judicial term.

3. 2024–2025: Tusk’s coalition attempts to reverse the reforms

After the October 2023 election, Donald Tusk’s coalition made restoring the rule of law a central priority.

In March 2024, the Sejm adopted a resolution questioning the status of the three disputed PiS appointees and Przyłębska’s authority to lead the Tribunal.

Two reform bills followed in September. They proposed changes to the appointment of judges and the institution’s functioning. President Andrzej Duda referred both to the Constitutional Tribunal for review, preventing them from taking effect.

In December 2024, Duda appointed Bogdan Święczkowski, a former national prosecutor and close associate of Zbigniew Ziobro, as Tribunal president.

Meanwhile, the government restricted the publication of Tribunal rulings in the Journal of Laws, citing concerns over the institution’s composition. Its leadership said the move was unlawful and that its judgments remained binding.

The result was a deepening institutional standoff: the government questioned the Tribunal’s legitimacy, while the Tribunal challenged the legality of the government’s actions.

4. 2026: Nawrocki refuses to accept four judges’ oaths

The crisis escalated in March 2026, when the Sejm elected six new judges to replace those whose terms were ending: Krystian Markiewicz, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, Maciej Taborowski, Magdalena Bentkowska, Marcin Dziurda and Dariusz Szostek.

President Karol Nawrocki accepted the oaths of Bentkowska and Szostek but refused the remaining four.

His office cited concerns over the appointment procedure, including deadlines and the requirement for individual votes. It also argued that the president was not obliged to accept appointments automatically.

The government maintained that the Sejm had the constitutional authority to elect judges and that the president could not block their appointments.

On 9 April, the four judges took their oaths before a notary in parliament and sent the documents to the presidential office. Nawrocki’s office and Tribunal president Święczkowski rejected the move, arguing that the oath had to be taken in the president’s presence.

The Tribunal added to the dispute on 12 May, ruling in case K 3/26 that the president was not obliged to accept every appointment and had to be physically present for the oath.

The government challenged the ruling, pointing to the disputed status of judges sitting on the panel.

In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure requiring Polish authorities not to obstruct the four judges from taking up their duties. The Venice Commission also said the president’s role in the oath should be ceremonial and that a refusal or delay should not prevent a judge from taking office.

5. October 2026: The dispute reaches the Tribunal’s headquarters

The conflict escalated again in October, when Maciej Berek also took his oath in parliament after receiving no invitation from the president.

Święczkowski refused to recognise oaths taken without the president’s presence and prevented some newly elected judges from sitting on cases.

On 30 October, judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska ordered a one-month suspension of duties for Tribunal president Święczkowski and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański, citing provisions on the temporary suspension of judges. She then took over the management of the institution.

She said the move was necessary to restore the Tribunal’s functioning and allow all judges elected by the Sejm to perform their duties.

The existing leadership rejected the decision as unlawful, arguing that there was no legal basis for suspending the president and that judges sworn in outside the presidential procedure were not full members of the Tribunal.

The confrontation then moved inside the building. After seven judges entered the headquarters accompanied by State Protection Service officers, scuffles broke out. President Nawrocki arrived during the night and described the events as an attempted takeover of a constitutional institution. He called for urgent consultations with political leaders.

On Saturday, Święczkowski said he and the remaining judges would seek to regain control of the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska, meanwhile, announced that she would convene a General Assembly of judges on 3 November.

What is at stake?

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal crisis is no longer simply about appointments or who runs the institution. It raises fundamental questions about the separation of powers, judicial independence and the authority of constitutional rulings.

The consequences extend beyond the political institutions. When judgments are not published and state bodies disagree over their legal force, uncertainty spreads to laws affecting citizens, businesses, taxation and public services.

More than a decade after the crisis began, successive governments and presidents have failed to agree on a common solution. Instead, each change of power has brought new legal interpretations and further disputes over who has the authority to decide.

World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day.
