World.title: Poland political crisis: Constitutional court in chaos as Nawrocki accuses government of staging power grab
World.content:
On Friday evening, protesters and riot police faced off outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal after the court's president was suspended, the latest episode in an intensifying stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.

 

Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who cut short a trip to Senegal and headed back to Warsaw as the crisis unfolded, has since called for emergency talks with political leaders and has accused the government of attempting to forcibly take control of one of the country's key constitutional institutions.

The dramatic overnight events have escalated a long-running crisis surrounding Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, from which the Polish government has been trying for weeks to remove judges - who were appointed under the previous PiS government.

What had largely been a political and legal dispute over judicial appointments and the Tribunal's leadership has now spilled over into a direct confrontation at its headquarters.

The latest episode began when seven people chosen by the Sejm to serve as Constitutional Tribunal judges entered the building on Friday.

According to Tribunal spokesperson Weronika Ścibor, security guards at the Tribunal had been ordered to pack up their belongings and leave the building.

At the same time Bogdan Święczkowski, the Tribunal's incumbent president, and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański, were reportedly denied entry.

Ścibor suggested that the timing of the operation was deliberate and that it took advantage of the fact that some staff members were absent.

Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska subsequently announced that she was taking over the leadership of the Tribunal and suspending Święczkowski from his duties.

The current Tribunal leadership has challenged the legality of these moves.

Nawrocki returns

In response to the unfolding situation, Nawrocki cut short a visit to Senegal and returned to Poland.

At the presidential palace, he met First President of the Supreme Court Zbigniew Kapiński before heading on to the Constitutional Tribunal's headquarters with Kapiński and a group of aides.

Footage posted on X showed scuffles break out with a group of judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, as Nawrocki attempted to gain entry.

Nawrocki accuses government of power grab

Early on Saturday morning, Nawrocki's chief of staff, Paweł Szefernaker, read out a statement from the president in front of the Tribunal, in which he described the night's events as a breach of Poland's constitutional order and a forcible takeover of a constitutional institution.

"Tonight, there has been a breach of the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional organ of the state," Szefernaker said.

"I call for the restoration of the legal order and for the forces of coercion sent there by the government to leave the Tribunal's grounds," he added.

Nawrocki said he had consulted with Kapiński and that neither of them recognised the actions of those who, in his view, are unlawfully claiming authority in the Tribunal.

He said he planned to hold emergency talks with representatives of parliamentary political groups on Saturday, saying the move was necessary due to what he described as a threat to the state's internal security and the need to stabilise the political situation.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has also weighed in on the incident, expressing concerns about the president's behaviour.

"The president's behaviour alarmed me enormously," he said, adding that he hoped the prosecution service would take action and that it was unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way.

He argued that footage showed the president "forcing his way in and attacking the judges."

Żurek also acknowledged that talks had been held about the situation at the Tribunal, including with Bartłomiej Sochański, but that no compromise had been reached.

He stressed that the Tribunal should resume normal work and deal with citizens' outstanding cases.

Protest outside Tribunal

Protests were held around the Tribunal building, involving politicians from PiS and Confederation and right-wing supporters.

Among those present were party leader Jarosław Kaczyński, Mateusz Morawiecki, former Tribunal president Julia Przyłębska and Bogdan Święczkowski.

The PiS leader said the events were an assault on the Constitutional Tribunal. He called for protests to continue, warning that Poland risked turning into a police state.

PiS MEP Patryk Jaki, for his part, said that images from the Tribunal had already gone around the world and could damage the image of Donald Tusk's government.

World.title: The seven days I thought I might have breast cancer
World.content:
Nine o'clock on an ordinary Monday morning. The designated day of an appointment I'd put off for a year, maybe two — too long.

 

I get undressed and enter the room. It's all just routine — isn't it?

"Madame, don’t move. I have to move you into the right position. Turn slightly. Not like that. Let me do it. Stay still. You're too stiff; relax.” The woman is touching me, moving, flattening and squeezing one of my breasts into the machine. It ends up looking as flat as a slice of the Italian sliced cheese 'Sottilette'.

And then the other one. “Turn around. Let me move it.” The process starts again with my breasts being squeezed sideways, which is unpleasantly painful, something many women are familiar with.

When it's over, I'm left alone in a tiny room — half naked, waiting. In that small barren space, my mind races, hitting highs and lows, thinking of the glimpse I got of the X-ray images of my breasts, of the shapes and shadows, looking like the branches in a stylised painting of a giant oak tree.

Is there cancer hidden in those pictures that I can’t interpret? Don't we all think that after looking at those black-and-white encrypted images?

I’m not even sure how long I've been surrounded by those four claustrophobic walls when the door finally opens and I'm moved to another dark room to wait for a doctor and the next examination. But first the smiling doctor says: “Your mammogram is absolutely fine.” And the frown you didn’t even realise was carved into your forehead disappears. You breathe in deeply and then exhale for a long time.

It's time for the echography. You start talking as the lubricating gel is smeared on one breast and then on the other. The scanner's moving probe sends sound waves bouncing off the tissues in your breast, revealing shadows, white and black stains, waves, darker patches.

Suspicious area detected during breast ultrasound. Lyon, October 2026. Monica Pinna

There's a whole world in our breasts we totally ignore and that is just impossible for us to read. I'm explaining to the radiologist how much I hate all this, how almost every woman in my family has had breast cancer and how anxious this all makes me, when she starts focusing the probe on the one particular area and stops talking. She pushes the probe down, then moves it and presses down again. There is silence.

“I think you need a little biopsy." All my fears materialise in that one moment and a single sentence. “There is a darker patch there that doesn’t disappear as I move the probe. It’s best to check it.”

Two days later I returned, wanting the follow-up to happen fast and to quickly know the outcome. In other countries, beyond France, my adopted home, I could have had to wait days between a mammography and an echography and for weeks before the biopsy was done.

First a local anaesthetic, then a small cut which I don’t feel; the doctor smiles reassuringly, but I remain tense and at the same time already off somewhere else in my mind. A long cannula goes deeply into my flesh five times. Some bloody flecks of whitish flesh emerge and are placed in tiny glass containers.

Insertion of a biopsy cannula into a suspicious area of the breast. Lyon, October 2026. Monica Pinna

That was the beginning of a week I will never forget.

I would wait seven days before finally learning if I had cancer. I entered a sort of parallel world, where everything came through a filter and seemed far away. My body and my life were on hold. Plans suspended. A work trip and meetings with friends were postponed. I had started the process of acceptance, with that taboo word – cancer – becoming a possible option. It was possible that I would enter that same room days later to be told that I had to be operated on and then would need chemo.

Everything every cancer patient goes through. Fear, waiting, uncertainty. A time when friends you wouldn’t have thought of show up and when some of those you would have expected to stick with you might disappear. Deep fears resurface and people around you react differently. I was definitely floating, preparing myself. Bracing. The same feeling you'd have about a flight you're due to take when a storm is hitting.

"I have it, I don’t have it. I don’t know. I must wait."

Spiralling thoughts take you into the depths of your mind and your fears, sometimes a long way down. You recall your mother’s experience, as she went through the same fears, was operated on, had radiotherapy and made it through. You recall your auntie who didn’t. Your cousin who is now a beautiful and bright survivor. You think of her sister, who had to have her stomach removed, but who is always smiling and serene despite the medical checks she will have to endure for the rest of her life.

While you recall the faces and the stories of those who made it and those who didn’t, you float, detached from the world. The student protests, the riots and looting in French cities that I would have run to cover as a journalist are just a faraway noise.

The morning of the results, it's like I'm in a different dimension.

I'm trying to prepare myself for the worst, like bracing for an emergency landing. My appointment is at midday and I start wandering the streets of Lyon at 9.00 am. I walk like a lost soul for kilometre after kilometre. The hilarious part is that all this is happening to me during Pink October, the annual breast cancer awareness month. Launched in the United States in 1985, it's become one of the world’s most recognisable public-health campaigns. So, during my “week off”, I would regularly be seeing pink ribbons and breast symbols all over the place.

Worldwide, millions of euros are raised every year, yet organised breast screening participation in France remains below 50%. And look at me: I’m a journalist. I know the statistics; I’ve seen serious illness in my family. And yet I delayed making an appointment. Pure fear. How could I, or anyone, be ready to be told you have cancer? Still, it happens. And early detection can save your life.

Early detection: not only a question of fear, but of access to care

When breast cancer is detected before it spreads, five-year survival approaches 100%, compared with 38% for women diagnosed at an advanced stage. Despite its importance and the European Commission pouring around €80 million to strengthen screening across the bloc under its ‘Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan’ access to screening remains uneven across Europe, meaning that the chances of an early diagnosis can still depend on where a woman lives, not only on her fears. That’s due to screening organisation, access to appointments, out-of-pocket costs and awareness of the benefits of screening, as well as social inequalities, reveal latest research by the EU and the OECD..

As Luis Seijo, Co-chair of the European Cancer Organisation’s Prevention, Early Detection and Screening Network, has said, “Inequalities in cancer screening are costing lives.”

But disparities in Europe exist not only regarding early screening but how long it takes from screening to getting the diagnosis, ranging from a median of eight days in Denmark to 32 days in Romania.

While in my case it took just over a week, for Maria Assunta who lives in the Italian region of Sardinia, it took seven times longer.

She has been having annual breast checks since the age of 40, around ten years before the age generally recommended for routine screening in the European Union. Four years ago, when she was 46, a routine ultrasound revealed a 4-centimeter lump in one breast. She underwent a biopsy one month later and received her breast cancer diagnosis three weeks after that.

Maria Assunta is now in the follow up phase, with checks every 6 months. She describes the care she received “excellent both from a human and medical point of view” and calls her doctors her “angels”. Since going through this experience, she has become a passionate advocate for prevention and early detection.

Maria Assunta taking part in the walk in support of research into women’s cancers. Cagliari, Italy, 18 October 2026. Monica Pinna

Timeline from diagnosis to start of the treatment also differs across countries. In Maria Assunta’s case, there was almost no interval between the diagnosis and the start of the treatment. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) identifies long waits for specialist consultations, imaging and diagnostic tests as a concern in several countries, including Ireland, Greece, Romania and Spain.

Walk in support of research into women’s cancers. Cagliari, Italy, 18 October 2026. Monica Pinna

Stalled process of screening participation

While early detection has improved over the long term and mortality has declined, according to the OECD and European Commission’s “Health at a Glance: Europe 2020”, progress has stalled in many countries and screening participation continues to vary sharply across Europe.

Compared with 2019, breast cancer screening rates rose in nine EU countries with available data, with the largest increases observed in Slovakia by over 12%, followed by Croatia and Estonia.

Preventive breast cancer screenings 2019-2024 Eurostat

Breast cancer on the rise in the EU

As for my own story, the time finally came. I went in and waited for another half an hour till my name was called.

“I can reassure you, there is nothing, but it was best to check,” the doctor said with a smile. All my tension eased; I thanked her and shook her hand like a perfectly polite Italian. But even so, I remain disoriented by everything that has happened.

I was lucky, but every year around 360,000 women in the European Union receive a breast cancer diagnosis, 61,000 in France. Breast cancer is on the rise in Europe due to demographic changes, reproductive patterns — with later and fewer pregnancies — lifestyle habits and metabolic and hormonal factors, with research ongoing on environmental chemicals, pollution and diet impacts too. Statistics show that one in eleven women will develop breast cancer at some point in their life. It doesn’t mean they will die from it, but it doesn’t mean they will have an easy path through it either.

What happens for those who receive a breast cancer diagnosis?

I was lucky enough to walk out of that room with the same life I had before. But for many who receive a different diagnosis, the fear, uncertainty and sense of suspension I experienced for just seven days can become a lasting part of their lives.

So, is the mind cared for as much as the body, whether the journey leads to recovery or, ultimately, the end of life?

OECD’s 2026 European Cancer Inequalities Report found that only sixteen EU countries out of 27, plus Norway and Iceland, include psychological support in the cancer care pathway, and provision remains uneven.

In France, psychological care is part of the official package of supportive cancer care, alongside pain management, nutritional support and social assistance. In Italy access remains limited despite legal requirements and guidelines. A 2024 study of around 3,000 people with cancer found that only 20% reported receiving psychological support, while just 16% said a therapist had helped them throughout their cancer treatment. Much of this support still depends on private initiatives.

Eleonora is now 52 and lives in the Italian city of Genoa: She underwent a mastectomy at the age of 39, after a four-centimetre lump was discovered in her breast during the first ultrasound she had ever had.

In the thirteen years since her diagnosis, she has become a volunteer with the non-profit association Braccialetti Bianchi and a Qigong instructor. Rooted in traditional Chinese medicine, Qigong is one of the complementary practices the association offers to hospitalised patients and those undergoing rehabilitation. Other activities include circle dancing, yoga, empathic support, biodanza* and shiatsu. Eleonora says these therapies “can make the entire cancer journey just more bearable”.

Eleonora participating to a circle dance session in Genova. Braccialetti Bianchi association, 2026

This free support programme was launched around thirty years ago by a group of doctors working at the San Martino Hospital of Genoa. Maria Giuseppina Vidili is one of the oncologists who helped establish the initiative. She specialises in cancer rehabilitation, and she explains doctors and associations do what they can facing limited national budgets and healthcare cuts. She said she has worked tirelessly for years to build friendly spaces for patients at any stage of their cancer pathway.

She retired four years ago and never stopped offering complementary activities, saying that doctors and associations are on the frontline to fill in the gaps of the national healthcare system, at least in terms of psychological support.

According to the Italian Federation of Voluntary Associations in Oncology (FAVO), only around 20% of hospitals provide specialised psycho-oncology support. Such support becomes even less available once cancer treatment has ended. Doctor Vidili says a standardised psycho-oncology service should be available throughout the country. Initiatives like the one she launched are still limited to a reduced number of people. Some Italian hospitals, she says, don’t even have rehabilitation units.

Oncologist Maria Giuseppina Vidili during a Qigong session with cancer patients. Genoa, September 2026. Maria Giuseppina Vidili

Pink October, every month

The day after I received my all-clear, and I’m supposed to go back to work, answer emails, make calls to set up interviews, plan my next reporting trip. To pick up where I left off, as if nothing had happened.

But something did happen and has left a mark.

I wrote most of this article that morning, between 5 am and 9 am. I just had to get it off my chest – literally – hoping that sharing my experience would help even one single woman face her fears and go for regular screenings. But writing this was also a way to delve into a subject that people still prefer to look away from, including myself. I struggled to research and discuss cancer as if it were any other journalistic topic. It comes with a burden.

Today, my thoughts are with those fighting to live and those working to find new cures. Awareness campaigns matter, but awareness alone is not enough. Women need access to screening, prompt diagnosis and appropriate care. They also need to be encouraged to put their health first, even when fear makes it tempting to look away.

Psychological support and complementary therapies should be accessible to everyone, everywhere, not just to the limited number of people who can currently benefit from them across the EU.

And one thing is for sure: my next screening appointment will be on time.

World.title: Travelling beyond the borders of Baku through fiction
World.content:
From the poetry of medieval Azerbaijan to contemporary novels reaching readers from across different continents, Baku's relationship with the written word is rooted in centuries of cultural exchange.

 

Today, that literary heritage is finding new expression as authors, publishers and readers from Europe, Asia and beyond came together in the Azerbaijani capital for the twelfth year running.

The 12th Baku International Book Fair saw 32 countries taking part in an event which was not simply about discovering the latest books.

It was an opportunity to explore how literature connects hearts and minds across languages, generations, and geographical barriers by blending and sharing ideas and stories.

At a time when technology is transforming how tales are told, published, and consumed, the fair also questioned how books will remain an intrinsic and vital part of our futures.

12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Where history meets the modern word

Azerbaijan's literary traditions stretch back centuries and have been shaped by its position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia.

The 12th-century poet Nizami Ganjavi features heavily.

He was born in what is now Azerbaijan and became one of the most influential literary figures of the Persian-speaking world, with his works travelling the globe. He continues to be celebrated today.

Centuries later, writers and poets include Muhammad Fuzuli, who contributed to a rich literary tradition that developed across different languages and cultural influences.

This heritage provides a historical and rich backdrop to the country's modern relationship with international literature, where translation, publishing partnerships and literary festivals help stories reach audiences far beyond local borders and countries of origin.

For Iranian novelist Parinoush Saniee, literature offers a way of exploring the relationships between individuals and the societies in which they live.

Parinoush Saniee signing her book during 12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Her internationally recognised novel The Book of Fate follows the life of an Iranian woman through decades of personal and political change, examining themes of identity, family, education and the expectations placed upon women.

Saniee explained that she initially assumed her work would only resonate regionally, but she was quickly surprised by the global reaction.

"The first translation of my book was into Italian," Saniee recalled.

"When I saw all that reception and various journalists came from different places, I asked them what was interesting about the book for you. They said it was close to us. We also had such experiences. It was very relatable."

Although rooted in Iranian society, the questions raised in her writing resonate far beyond its borders. The works have been translated into numerous languages and demonstrate how literature can offer readers an understanding of lives and experiences different from their own.

She observed this same phenomenon when the novel became a bestseller in Norway, proving that universal themes of suffering and endurance translate seamlessly.

"Human suffering, lifestyles, issues, and problems are overall very impactful for humanity, and we all understand it," Saniee stated. "Therefore, it doesn't matter where it is from."

Darren Simpson during 12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Reaching younger minds

British author Darren Simpson, meanwhile, approaches storytelling through the imagination of younger readers.

He is known for novels such as Scavengers and The Memory Thieves, where he creates unusual worlds and characters exploring friendships, belonging, identity and the challenges of growing up.

Simpson echoed the sentiment that human emotion makes storytelling cross borders effortlessly, noting that children across the globe seek the exact same things from a narrative.

"When I see children from all around different countries connect to my stories in the same way, it speaks to me about the universal nature of a lot of feelings about people's needs and their desire to connect," Simpson explained.

His works reflect the importance of children's literature at a time when arguably young people have an unprecedented choice of digital entertainment and books are not necessarily the most popular choice. Yet, he highlighted that the local reception at the fair had been incredibly inspiring.

"I have been struck in Azerbaijan by how much passion there is here in the young readers," he added.

12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Championing local voices

Alongside its international offerings, the fair is also celebrating the locals who have helped to shape Azerbaijan's contemporary literary identity.

One of those is Reyhan Yusifgizi, a prominent voice in Azerbaijani children's science fiction who brings a unique academic background in computer science to her writing.

When discussing how to cultivate reading habits in a digital age, Yusifgizi explained that increasing a child's interest requires a two-step approach.

"First, this depends on the author," Yusifgizi noted. "They must write well, write in a modern way. With simple language, they must interest the child."

However, she stressed that the second factor is often the most fundamental.

"The parent directly influences the child. The parent stands between the author, the book, and the child," she said.

"First of all, the parent must demonstrate it through their own experience, their own example. They need to read."

Azerbaijani writer and publicist Elmira Akhundova reflected on the profound emotional weight that physical books carry compared to fleeting digital news. For her, literature's ultimate purpose is to promote peace and multiculturalism.

"What is at the end of the most difficult, the saddest book? It is light," Akhundova said.

"It is a call towards tolerance. We must hear these humanistic calls and instill them in our young generation," she told Euronews.

She challenged the next generation to seek out complex, philosophical narratives rather than settling for easy entertainment, noting that every story should ultimately lead the reader towards hope.

"A book must absolutely be geared toward humanism," she added, asserting that no matter what, a book "must be on the sunny side of the street."

The future of the written word

It is recognised that the relationship between books and their readers is changing.

Digital publishing, audiobooks and new forms of storytelling are reshaping the literary landscape, but rather than replacing traditional physical books entirely, there is an advantage to the technological advancements.

Books can now travel at lightning speed. A touch of a button can transport us to another universe, and perhaps that is what makes an international literary gathering even more relevant today.

Beyond the book stands, authors are choosing to move from the desktop to have those important physical discussions, drawn together by that love of narrative.

And what better place to have those conversations than the gateway between East and West?

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

Editor’s note: This story was updated at 13:25 on 30 October 2026 to include a statement from lawyers for Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron, sent to us by counsel for Macron's legal team. It responds to the court’s ruling on Candace Owens’ motion to dismiss the case against her.

In the statement, lawyers for the Macrons said: “We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods. As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”

***

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Germany news: Merkel calls for first female president
World.content:
Skip next section Merkel calls for Germany's first female president

10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Merkel calls for Germany's first female president

These are some of the women under discussion for Germany's next president Image: Theo Klein/epd/IMAGO I Boris Roessler/dpa/picture alliance I Andreas Gora/IMAGO I Manfred Behrens/Future Image/IMAGO I teutopress/IMAGO I Harry Nakos/AP Photo/picture alliance

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, pointing out that no woman has held the office in the country's 77-year history.

Everyone should ask "whether it might finally be time," Merkel told MagentaTV.

She said she knew women capable of doing the job but declined to name anyone.

The Federal Convention elects Germany's next head of state on January 30. Steinmeier cannot seek a third consecutive term. The presidency is mostly a ceremonial role.

Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner has the backing of Markus Soder, leader of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).

Other names being discussed include Bundestag president Julia Klockner, Education Minister Karin Prien and former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, all from Merkel's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Merkel described the debate as "strange" and criticized its "unpleasant undertone."

She also challenged her party's direction, saying the CDU's identity went beyond economic policy. "The CDU was always about building bridges to all parts of society — and that must be brought back to the forefront."

World.title: Massive Gen Z protests set to sweep cities across Germany
World.content:
Skip next section What are the rules governing protests in Germany?

Germany guarantees its citizens the right to protest, as here in Berlin on August 8 against the far-right AfD Image: Michael Kuenne/PRESSCOV/ZUMA/picture alliance

People in Germany have the fundamental right, enshrined in the constitution or Basic Law, to assemble in public provided they remains peaceful and are unarmed.

However, several states have adopted their own assembly acts, which means some of them have additional restrictions, such as a ban on protesting on highways in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Notification generally necessary

Federal law itself imposes the obligation on organizers of protests to notify the local authority entrusted with approving public assemblies at least 48 hours before they invite people publicly to take part.

This aims to allow authorities to put in place security measures and to lessen the impact of any assembly on others by, for example, instigating traffic control measures.

Spontaneous assemblies are, however, also allowed in cases where a topical issue of urgent importance is at stake, and there is no notification requirement for indoor assemblies.

Protests or other assemblies can be banned beforehand or dispersed while they are underway, but this is considered a means of last resort.

Some locations are also subject to restrictions on protests, such as the area around the Reichstag building in Berlin where the German parliament sits, and around the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Demonstrations around the Reichstag are, for example, permitted only when the parliament is not in session.

Germany no stranger to big protests

Post-war Germany has seen several massive demonstrations, including one in 1983, when 250,000 people — according to police estimates — gathered in the then West German capital, Bonn, to protest against the decision by NATO to station American nuclear missiles on German territory.

That was, however, surpassed in size by a protest in Berlin in 2003 against the invasion of Iraq by US-led forces, which drew a crowd of around half a million people.

There is some more detail on the law regarding the right of assembly in this DW article.

World.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
World.content:
A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s.

"In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."

This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.

The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.

The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".

Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).

The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.

For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.

When the underworld ruled Bollywood

In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.

"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.

Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.

During his era, Dawood Ibrahim has been one of the most wanted men in India Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.

When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.

Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.

D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.

Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.

"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.

By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.

A gang run from a prison cell

The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.

Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."

"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.

Lawrence Bishnoi was a student politician in the northern city of Chandigarh before gaining notoriety as a gangster Image: Sameer Sehgal/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.

Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.

His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.

While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.

"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."

Why target film stars?

For Bishnoi, it seems personal.

In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.

Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."

Salman Khan was granted bail in 2018 as he appealed a conviction for killing two rare antelopes Image: AFP

But money and intimidation matter too.

"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.

"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."

Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."

"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."

Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."

But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.

Is Bollywood under siege?

Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.

"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.

The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.

India's banned film 'Satluj' finds new audiences To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."

At any case, the fear remains real.

And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.

"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.

"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.

With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.

Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
World.content:
What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection, as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

How names influence first impressions

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness.



For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.



What do Nigerians think of bullying? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why some names attract negative judgments

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

How humor helps people cope with embarrassing names

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

How an embarrassing name can also offer a sense of belonging

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

Superpower laughter — how humor makes us strong , To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."



Edited by: Richard Connor

World.title: India news: Amit Shah challenges Rahul Gandhi to debate vote theft in parliament
World.content:
10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Vote theft row: Shah challenges opposition as INDIA bloc prepares major protest

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday challenged opposition leaders Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav to discuss allegations of electoral irregularities in parliament, even as the opposition geared for a major rally against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar , according to media reports.

"I am ready to call a special session of Parliament to discuss vote theft allegations," Shah said, accusing the opposition of making baseless allegations against the Election Commission and staging protests while skirting parliamentary debate.

His remarks came as the opposition INDIA bloc prepared to hold a symbolic "public impeachment" of Kumar on Saturday, followed by a major rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on November 1.

Around 30 speakers from 21 opposition parties are expected to participate.

The opposition is demanding Kumar's resignation over his role in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the scrapping of the SIR, alleging that the exercise could disenfranchise voters and benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In a call for the November 1 rally, Rahul Gandhi said "anyone who cares about democracy must come."

"The vote is yours. The fight is also yours," the Congress leader wrote on X.

Earlier, the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) also threw their weight behind the rally saying the movement would lend its support to any organization fighting for free and fair elections in India, including the opposition alliance.

World.title: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
World.content:
The mandate of the UN peacekeeping force in Western Sahara will expire on October 31. The UN Security Council could not agree on a resolution to extend the mission.

The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires.

The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century.

Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory,

The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.

US and Russia wield vetoes

On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component.

Last year, the UNSC backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.

Friday's failed US draft resolution would have gone further and rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination.

The US proposal was vetoed by Russia, which slammed it as a "unilateral approach." A total of 11 of the 15 UNSC members voted in its favor and three abstained.

"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said.

"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of ⁠the draft," ​he added.

The US, with its own veto, then blocked a Russian draft that proposed renewing the mission's mandate for another year while preserving the same terms as before.

"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," the US representative to the United Nations, Michael Waltz, said after the vote.

Western Sahara: Caught between sovereignty and struggle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How did Morocco and the Polisario Front react?

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the peacekeeping mission and said that this "should mark the end of the Security Council's involvement and the removal of this issue from its agenda."

The Polisario Front's UN representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing the US resolution that he said "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."

World.title: European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
World.content:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov declined to comment on Russia's participation in the G20 summit in December, telling DW that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should travel to Russia if he wanted talks with Vladimir Putin.

A Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta got off to a rocky start on Friday after top diplomats from European nations refused to take a "family photo" along with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, decided to scrap the photo before the meeting got underway because Washington didn't want it to become a spectacle or distraction.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters before the first session on Friday that there wouldn't "be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia."

The two-day gathering of the G20 grouping, which includes the EU, Russia, Germany, India, China, Brazil and other major countries, is meant to be a precursor to a G20 leaders summit later this December.

That G20 leaders meeting in December is set to be hosted by US President Donald Trump at his golf club in Miami.

Rubio stresses unity despite fractures

Rubio still opened the talks by stressing unity on major issues, telling his counterparts that they were in a "critical moment."

"We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he said.

He pointed to disruptions to global energy and trade and said many were posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."

But several countries, including the United States and Russia, are involved in separate wars. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have resulted in a spike in food prices for people around the world .

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged to "call on Russia to finally accept Ukraine's offer of a ceasefire, starting in the Black Sea" Image: Megan Varner/REUTERS

While the message is about unity and finding solutions to problems like freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz during the G20 meeting, the reality is that finding common ground will likely be much tougher.

Given a renewed momentum to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine, there was also interest in getting Lavrov to talk about Russia's stance on future talks with Kyiv.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio appealed for unity between members of the G20, despite the US not inviting all of them to the ministers' meeting Image: Erik S. Lesser/AFP

Russia willing to meet Zelenskyy in Moscow, Lavrov tells DW

The US has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in Miami, but it's unclear whether Russia has accepted the invitation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said that he would be open to traveling to Miami to hold talks with Putin if he were also there.

The Kremlin has so far declined direct meetings with Zelenskyy, with Russia's Sergey Lavrov telling DW on the sidelines of the meeting that Putin is willing to meet with the Ukrainian leader if he travels to Moscow.

"President Putin said if he [Zelenskyy] is willing to meet, let him come to Moscow," Lavrov said. "We will guarantee his safety."

Lavrov declined to say whether Putin will attend the G20 summit this December.

Putin has not attended a G20 leaders meeting since 2019 and only attended a session virtually in 2023.

Russia has also continued with its attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, stepping up drone strikes on water and energy infrastructure.

A Russian drone strike on a railway station in Dnipro on October 29 killed at least 14 people Image: Telegram channel on president ou Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyj

EU top diplomat calls out Lavrov's 'lies'

The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said ministers at the G20 meeting were able to call out Lavrov for his "lies" at the table.

"We were talking about the big geopolitical crises, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head-on with this," Kallas said on the sidelines of the meeting.

"Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke," she said.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also called out Lavrov, saying, "If we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine."

Lavrov says no easing of ties with US, 'no illusions' about diesel deal

Lavrov, who is under international sanctions for Russia's war in Ukraine, was invited to the US at a time when the two countries have appeared to have fostered warmer ties.

Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and also waived new sanctions on Russia's energy. The US announced the move just weeks away from the midterm elections on November 3.

Lavrov said on Friday that despite those efforts, "in practice, no real progress in relations with the US has so far been seen."

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

South Africa, a founding member of G20, excluded from US meeting

The Trump administration has been embroiled in disputes with South Africa, having imposed visa restrictions on South Africanswho it said were complicit in discriminating against white people.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year because US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.

But US officials didn't extend that invite to South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.

"We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.

With this many issues on the table, it appeared less likely that there would be a joint consensus at the end of the talks.

Instead of a final declaration, the AFP news agency reported, the meeting is expected to end on Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the US.
