World.title: Haunted, but hardly explored: India's untapped ghost-tourism economy
World.content:
India's ghosts have a customer service problem.

There is almost an abundance of local places which have a reputation of being haunted in each and every state.There are ghost villages where nobody is quite sure why everyone left.

Forts with stories of spirits walking through them at night. Abandoned cemeteries as old as the world wars, forgotten âhavelisâ and stretches of forest that have acquired a mythology of their own.

Out of all these only a few have become tourist attractions; others survive largely through word of mouth, local lore and the occasional paranormal investigation.

India's haunted places do have an audience but it somehow lacks a concrete machinery that could make âdarkâ tourism and âspectralâ cities central factions of an ever growing tourist economy.

The business of the macabre

The tourism industry has a name for this particular appetite for the unsettling: dark tourism. The term broadly describes travel to places associated with death, tragedy, violence and suffering.

Ghost tours, haunted heritage walks and visits to places associated with paranormal folklore occupy a more specialised corner of this spectrum, where history, local legend and the promise of an eerie experience often intersect.





It is an appetite that the tourism industry has increasingly tried to package. Turning a city's darker history into something you can book online. And its most ideal form, the ticket buys you a completely immersive tour full of storytelling with a slight hope of encountering your first paranormal spirit.

The commercial potential of dark tourism is reflected in the market estimates. Grand View Research valued the global dark tourism market at $31.8 billion in 2023 and projects it to reach $34.2 billion in 2026 and $38.6 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 2.9%.

MR puts the market at $32 billion in 2025, forecasting it to reach $46.8 billion by 2036.

The market for ghost tourism as a separate entity is estimated to be worth $2.9 billion in 2025 and projects it to grow to $5.7 billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 7.8%, by Dataintelo. Its estimate includes guided ghost walks, cemetery and underground tours, paranormal investigations, haunted stays and virtual experiences.

For India, the more immediate question may be less about capturing a share of a global market and more about whether these scattered attractions can be turned into viable profitable local experiences.

With a history as rich as ours, the ghosts are not in short supply. The challenge is to turn them into profitable experiences that people can discover, book and pay for, while ensuring that the tragedy is respected and the communities living alongside these places have a stake in the business.

From a haunted reputation to a tourism product

Kuldhara, a site that Rajasthan Tourism itself promotes as a âghost village shrouded in mysteryâ, is a good starting point. The official government site describes its history as a prosperous settlement abandoned in the early 19th century.

The account recounts the popular legend involving the village headman's daughter and the powerful minister Salim Singh, while also identifying the ruins as a protected monument under the state archaeology department.

The village, around 17km from Jaisalmer, already has the ingredients of a tourism attraction, but having a story and having a well-managed visitor experience are two different things.

There are multiple accounts of litter around the site, including discarded plastic and food packaging. How can an atmosphere feel haunted when the landscape is strewn with chips and tobacco packets?

And cleanliness isnât the only issue. Talking to two people who visited the site, the common experience has been mismanaged and under researched tour which leaves most customers underwhelmed at the end of the day.

Bhangarh, in Alwar district, is often described as one of India's most haunted places. Rajasthan Tourism itself recounts the two popular legends attached to the site: one involving the ascetic Baba Balu Nath, whose warning about the shadow of the fort was allegedly ignored, and another about a sorcerer whose failed attempt to enchant Princess Ratnavati supposedly led him to curse the town.

The legends have become part of the destination's appeal, drawing visitors to its ruined temples, palaces and deserted marketplace.

The restriction on entry before sunrise and after sunset, imposed at the site, has only added to its mystique. But tourists who visit the site have also called it unorganised, speaking to TOI they noted that the guide also was not entirely accurate about the historical aspects of the site and the site itself needed to have better management.

The business of making a place come alive

There are already attempts to package India's haunted heritage into guided experiences.

Delhi Tourism lists Haunted Heritage Walks at Malcha Mahal and Feroz Shah Kotla Monument, each lasting around 90 minutes and available on weekends on group demand. The official booking page lists a minimum group size of six and a tariff of Rs 800 plus GST per person.

The Ministry of Tourism's Utsav portal has also listed a Haunted Walk at Bhuli Bhatiyari, organised by Delhi-based Enroute Indian History. The listing describes a guided heritage walk through the old hunting lodge, combining its history with the legends associated with the site.

Enroute Indian History, which has been conducting the experience for around two to three years, says the walks attract a good number of bookings and are designed for adventure seekers as much as for history enthusiasts. The operator says it takes care to keep the historical information accurate, while folklore and supernatural accounts are presented as stories rather than fact-checked historical claims. This distinction is central to the format: visitors are offered a combination of documented history, local legends and the possibility of an unsettling experience.

These initiatives complicate the idea that haunted tourism in India is entirely informal or absent. There are government-backed products and private operators working in the space. The question is whether they have developed the consistency, visibility and scale needed to make haunted experiences a dependable part of a destination's tourism economy.

Ghost is only part of the experience

Detailing her experience to TOI, Kriti notes that she remembers the underground setting of the haunted heritage walk she took in Edinburgh as much as the stories themselves.

The interactive displays and historical details provided by the guide gave the experience a sense of depth that a conventional ghost walk might not have offered.

A ghost tour can take several forms, the attraction lies as much in how visitors encounter the story as in the story itself.

A 2020 study published in Cornell Hospitality Quarterly, titled Paranormal Tourism: Market Study of a Novel and Interactive Approach to Space Activation and Monetization, makes this case through examples from the United States and elsewhere.

It describes how destinations such as New Orleans combine ghost stories with local histories and cultural associations, while Salem packages its reputation around witches and ghosts.

These places do not necessarily sell a standalone encounter with the paranormal; they draw on identities and histories that visitors may already associate with them.

The study talks in detail about Eastern State Penitentiary in Philadelphia, a former prison that closed in 1971 and subsequently fell into disuse.

Limited group tours began in 1988 as part of efforts to preserve the site. A Halloween fundraiser followed in 1991, eventually developing into the annual attraction Terror Behind the Walls. By 1994, the former prison was also offering daily historical tours to generate income for preservation, followed by museum exhibits and a broader marketing campaign.

The study also points to the role of participation in making these experiences engaging.

The experience can continue beyond the visit itself, with reviews, photographs and word of mouth helping to draw in new audiences.

Research into British ghost walks suggests that the appeal is not necessarily dependent on visitors believing in ghosts. An ethnographic study of 14 tours across Edinburgh, York, London and Brighton found that guides use a combination of storytelling, performance and the physical environment to make history tangible.

For India, that distinction could be important. A haunted experience need not rely on sensational claims. It can be built around the history of a place, the folklore that has accumulated around it and the atmosphere of encountering that story on location.

Local community cannot remain part of the backdrop

The opportunity, however, is not simply to make India's haunted sites more theatrical or commercially attractive. It is also to ensure that the people and places behind the stories are not left out of the value chain.

A 2023 qualitative study of local perceptions in Kuldhara, based on 25 interviews with residents and people working in the area, found that respondents saw several economic opportunities in developing mystery and paranormal tourism. Some respondents also pointed to existing livelihood opportunities linked to visitors, including guiding, transport and the sale of local crafts.

The study also recorded expectations around the restoration and preservation of the village, alongside concerns about the role of government and private bodies in developing the destination.

While it offers a glimpse of how residents view the possibilities of mystery tourism, it does not quantify how much income currently reaches the community or how widely those benefits are distributed.

The concerns are not unique to haunted destinations. A 2026 study of tourism in Uttarakhand, while not focused specifically on ghost tourism, raises wider questions about the state's tourism economy. It argues for stronger community participation, local supply chains, training and livelihood diversification.

These concerns are relevant when considering how niche tourism experiences might develop in the hills. A haunted walk could create work for local storytellers, drivers, homestays, food vendors and artisans. But those benefits are not automatic. If an outside operator controls the bookings, supplies the guides and takes most of the revenue, the local community may remain little more than a feature of the landscape.

The challenge is to move beyond treating local legends as raw material that can be packaged elsewhere. Residents may be the custodians of oral histories, but they should also have a stake in how those histories are interpreted and monetised.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

India does not need to manufacture a haunted history. What it needs is a way to bring those stories to visitors without reducing them to cheap thrills or leaving the people who have preserved them out of the business.

The real test of India's haunted tourism economy will not be how many people it can convince that a place is haunted, but how many people it can persuade to stay, listen, and explore.

The ghosts, after all, have been doing their bit for the tourism industry for years. It is time someone took care of the guests.

World.title: The great Indian railway upgrade: How much has really changed for passengers?
World.content:
NEW DELHI: New trains, redeveloped stations and upgraded infrastructure are changing the face of Indian Railways. But has the passenger experience changed at the same pace?

For millions of people who depend on the network every day, the real test of modernisation begins well beyond a station's new facade or a train's sleek exterior.

It lies in whether platforms are manageable, toilets are clean, drinking water is safe, coaches are well maintained and trains arrive on time.

While the Railways has invested heavily in modernisation, government audits continue to flag gaps in basic passenger amenities, onboard cleanliness and maintenance. The contrast raises a larger question: Is Indian Railways building a more modern network without doing enough to improve the everyday journey?

The challenge now is to ensure that the transformation is felt not just in the infrastructure passengers see, but in the quality of service they experience.

A makeover on a massive scale

The Amrit Bharat Station Scheme is among the most visible parts of the railway modernisation drive. Under the scheme, 1,337 stations had been identified for redevelopment by December 2025, with work completed at 155 stations at that point, according to the ministry of railways. The programme envisages improvements to station buildings, waiting halls, toilets, seating, drinking-water facilities, platforms, foot overbridges, lifts, escalators and passenger information systems.





From station facelifts to faster trains: Inside Indian Railways' makeover

The plan also seeks to improve access to stations, connect them better with the surrounding city and integrate different modes of transport. Facilities for passengers with disabilities and spaces for local products under the One Station One Product initiative are part of the wider approach. The idea is to make stations more accessible and useful, rather than treat redevelopment as a cosmetic exercise alone.

The scale of the programme matters in a network where stations serve very different kinds of traffic.

A major city terminal may need to handle large crowds, multiple platforms and complex interchange movements. A smaller station may need reliable drinking water, sufficient seating, accessible toilets and a safe way to cross between platforms. A uniform-looking makeover cannot substitute for facilities suited to the number and needs of passengers using each station.

Redevelopment also has to take place while trains continue to run.

Railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has cited the difficulty of carrying out major construction without shutting down busy stations. Work near operational tracks, shifting utilities, statutory clearances and restrictions imposed to protect passengers and train movements can all affect project schedules.

That is a reminder that infrastructure transformation takes time. It also raises a separate question: While construction continues, how effectively are existing facilities being maintained?

New trains, new expectations

The train itself is another important part of the modernisation story.

Vande Bharat has become the most recognisable symbol of a more contemporary railway experience, with modern coaches, improved passenger amenities and a focus on faster intercity travel.

The demand for these services has been substantial. The ministry of railways said nearly 3.98 crore passengers travelled on Vande Bharat Express services in 2025-26, up from 2.97 crore in 2024-25, an increase of about 34%. Since its introduction, the service had carried more than 9.1 crore passengers through approximately one lakh trips, according to a ministry statement issued in April 2026.

The appeal is understandable. Modern coaches, comfortable seating and onboard amenities can make a long journey less tiring. Faster services can also help passengers who travel regularly for work, education, business or family commitments. The introduction of a sleeper version in January 2026 extended the modern-train push to overnight travel. In its first three months, the sleeper service carried 1.21 lakh passengers over 119 trips, with reported occupancy exceeding 100%.

A railway official, speaking to TOI on condition of anonymity, said the introduction of newer trains was part of a broader effort to improve passenger facilities.

âNew trains such as Vande Bharat and Amrit Bharat are being introduced using push-pull technology, offering passengers improved facilities. The work undertaken over the past few years is gradually beginning to show results,â the official said.

These figures indicate that passengers are willing to use newer services when they offer a compelling travel option.

But the success of a premium service should not become the sole measure of progress across a network that serves passengers with widely differing budgets and travel needs.

For a family travelling in a reserved sleeper coach, the condition of the toilets and availability of water may matter as much as the train's design. For an unreserved passenger, access to a platform without dangerous crowding may be the more immediate concern.

For someone travelling with an elderly relative, working lifts and clear signage can make the difference between a manageable journey and a stressful one.

The next phase of modernisation must therefore be about raising the baseline across the network, not just creating pockets of premium travel.

The basic amenities test

A Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit provides a sobering measure of the gap between infrastructure ambitions and everyday facilities.

Its Report No. 31 of 2026, tabled in Parliament on August 12, examined passenger amenities and sanitation at non-suburban railway stations. Of the 512 stations covered, 458 had deficiencies in one or more essential passenger amenities.

According to the CAG report, the deficiencies involved basic facilities such as toilets, urinals and drinking water. The audit also found E. coli contamination in water samples collected from coolers at eight locations, raising concerns about the safety of drinking water available to passengers.

Railway modernisation vs ground reality: The widening passenger amenities gap

These findings matter because the usefulness of a facility depends on more than its installation. A water cooler may appear on a station's list of amenities, but it serves little purpose if the water is unsafe or the equipment is not maintained. A newly built toilet is not a meaningful improvement if it is dirty, lacks water or is routinely out of order.

The distinction between providing an amenity and delivering a functioning service is central to the passenger experience.

Construction can be measured through expenditure, project completion and the number of facilities created. Maintenance is less dramatic, but it determines whether passengers can actually use those facilities on a particular day.

The CAG findings do not mean every station performs poorly, nor do they erase the benefits of redevelopment. They point instead to unevenness across the network. The task is to ensure that passengers do not have to depend on a station's size, location or level of visibility to access basic services.

Cleanliness does not end at the platform

The problem extends from stations to the trains themselves. A separate CAG audit on cleanliness and sanitation in long-distance trains, covering the period from 2018-19 to 2022-23, found that more than 40% of surveyed passengers were dissatisfied with toilet cleanliness, while over half expressed dissatisfaction with onboard housekeeping.

The survey covered 2,426 passengers across 96 selected trains. The audit identified issues including dirty lavatories, choked washbasins, waterlogging and unclean vestibules.

It also found that 366 passengers, or about 15% of those surveyed, reported a lack of water in toilets or washbasins. More than one lakh complaints about water shortages in train toilets and washbasins were registered through Rail Madad in 2022-23.

The audit also highlighted shortcomings in the deployment of cleaning staff and equipment, as well as gaps in monitoring and enforcement of contractual obligations. It mentioned that 89% of complaints related to toilet cleanliness were addressed within the stipulated timeframe.

That points to a system capable of responding to complaints, but also to the need to reduce the conditions that generate them in the first place.

The railway official said bio-toilets had played an important role in the effort to improve sanitation, but maintenance and passenger awareness remained challenges.

âIndian Railways has taken extensive measures to improve cleanliness, with bio-toilets playing an important role in this effort.

However, the key challenge lies in their adequate maintenance, due to which problems continue to arise. Lack of awareness among passengers also contributes to sanitation-related issues,â the official said.

âAlthough the Railways is working to spread awareness through s and other means, a change in public attitude towards cleanliness is still needed,â the official added.

A complaint mechanism is essential. Yet a passenger should not have to repeatedly report a choked toilet or an empty water tank for routine services to be delivered.

Onboard housekeeping, water refilling and regular inspections need to work as part of normal railway operations, not only after a problem has been flagged.

Cleanliness is not a minor comfort issue. It affects dignity, health and the willingness of passengers to trust the service. A train can have modern coaches and advanced safety features, but if the washroom becomes unusable halfway through a long journey, the experience quickly falls short of the promise.

Punctuality: Progress, but not the whole picture

Reliability is another test of whether the passenger experience is keeping pace with infrastructure investment. A faster train is useful only if its schedule is dependable, while an upgraded station cannot compensate for a journey that routinely runs late.

The ministry of railways reported that punctuality improved from 73.62% in 2023-24 to 77.12% in 2024-25, reaching 77.24% in 2025-26 up to February 2026. The ministry said the network operates around 25,000 trains a day and attributed delays to a range of factors, including fog, track and route constraints, maintenance, signalling issues, agitations and other unforeseen events.

The improvement is significant, but the latest figure also shows that punctuality remains a work in progress. Railway operations involve a vast network in which a disruption in one section can affect services elsewhere. Track maintenance, signalling upgrades and other work may be necessary to improve long-term reliability, even when they cause short-term inconvenience.

The railway official said the growing demand for passenger trains had put pressure on punctuality, and that infrastructure upgrades were being undertaken to address the issue.

âTo address this, the Railways has started operating dedicated freight corridors or undertaken work on them to provide separate tracks for goods trains. The Delhi-Mumbai Dedicated Freight Corridor is a key example,â the official said.

âMajor stations are also undergoing remodelling and interlocking work to reduce additional halts and delays for trains. Sections with heavy traffic are being converted to automatic signalling systems,â the official added.

The official said fog and mist also affected train operations by reducing visibility. âTo address this, fog signal devices have been installed in locomotives. In addition, the Railways is installing the advanced Kavach system, which not only helps improve punctuality but also plays an important role in ensuring train safety,â the official said.

For passengers, however, the experience is immediate. A late train can mean a missed connection, a longer wait at a station or an uncertain arrival time.

Better information about delays and platform changes can ease some of that burden, but communication cannot replace reliable operations.

More dependable schedules, clear announcements, accurate digital information and prompt assistance during disruptions are as important to many travellers as the design of the coach.

Crowds are an infrastructure problem, too

Crowd management has become another part of the passenger experience that cannot be separated from station design.

Wider foot overbridges, holding areas, better access points and clearer passenger information can help manage movement, but they need to be matched to actual footfall and train capacity.

The New Delhi railway station witnessed a stampede in February 2025 that killed at least 18 people.

In March 2026, the railway ministry announced plans for permanent holding areas at 76 identified stations, alongside measures including access control, wider foot overbridges and technology-assisted monitoring.

The ministry also referred to additional ticketing facilities, drinking-water arrangements and separate toilets at New Delhi Railway Station.

The railway official said satellite stations were being developed in large and industrial cities to reduce pressure on major stations during periods of heavy passenger movement.

âIn large and industrial cities, where passenger footfall rises sharply during holidays and other occasions, the Railways has started developing satellite stations to reduce the pressure on major stations,â the official said.

Vande Bharat sees 34% rise in passengers: Is the network ready for more?

The official also referred to the Train on Demand initiative, particularly services with high-capacity unreserved coaches, to accommodate more passengers through fewer trains.

Such measures recognise that a station is not simply a building through which passengers pass. It is a space where thousands of people may arrive at the same time, often carrying luggage, travelling with children or trying to reach a platform minutes before departure.

But crowd management cannot depend on temporary arrangements alone. It also requires better coordination between train schedules, platform allocation, ticketing, station staff and the movement of people inside and outside the premises. The test is whether a passenger can reach the right platform safely and without confusion, particularly during holiday rushes, festivals and other peak periods.

A station's success should not be judged only by its appearance when relatively empty.

Its real test comes when several trains arrive close together and thousands of passengers have to move through the same spaces.

From construction to service delivery

The larger question facing Indian Railways is how to turn a massive modernisation programme into a consistently better everyday service. The answer lies partly in investment, but also in maintenance, staffing, monitoring and accountability.

The government has committed substantial resources to passenger amenities.

In December 2025, the ministry said an allocation of Rs 12,118 crore had been made under the customer amenities budget head for 2025-26, with Rs 7,253 crore spent up to October that year. Such spending can create the physical conditions for better journeys. Whether it produces lasting improvement depends on how effectively facilities are operated and maintained.

There is no single measure that captures the passenger experience.

Station redevelopment figures tell us how much work has been undertaken. New-train numbers indicate the expansion of services. Punctuality statistics measure one aspect of reliability. Audit findings reveal whether basic facilities meet the expected standard. Together, they offer a more complete picture than any one headline figure.

A meaningful assessment would ask how many station amenities remain functional, whether drinking water is safe, how often toilets are cleaned, whether complaints are resolved promptly, and how consistently trains run to schedule.

It would also compare performance across stations and railway zones, so that strong results in one area do not conceal persistent gaps elsewhere.

Indian Railways has good reason to invest in bigger stations, modern trains and improved infrastructure. For a country of India's size, rail travel remains essential to mobility, livelihoods and social connection. The scale of the network makes the task difficult, but it also makes the quality of everyday service especially important.

The next measure of progress should be visible not just in the station's new facade or the train's sleek exterior, but in the ordinary details of a journey: A clean washroom, safe water, a working lift, a manageable platform and a train that arrives when expected.

World.title: 'Couldn't fulfil daughter's wish': Sharmila shifts wedding venue after brother Jagan's refusal
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Andhra Pradesh Congress president YS Sharmila has shifted her daughter's wedding to another venue after her brother,

, refused to allow his Bengaluru property to be used for the ceremony.

In a social media post on X, Sharmila defended her ownership claim over the Yelahanka property and said it was allotted entirely to her and her children as part of the division of family assets after her brother Jagan Reddy became chief minister.

âWhat is mine is mine, but the greed to covet it is not in my nature. After Jagan Mohan Reddy became chief minister, the Yelahanka property, which until then was a joint family property, came entirely (100 per cent) to my share and that of my children as part of the division of assets.

This is the truth, with God as my witness," Sharmila said.

"Since it is my children's right and the house where my father YSR lived, we wanted to hold my daughter Anjili's wedding there, as she had wished. Ask any household in Telugu society, and they will tell you that getting one's daughter married in one's own house is considered a blessing for every parent," she added.

Sharmila said she had decided to organise her daughter's wedding ceremony elsewhere as it was her responsibility to ensure that the event remained free of controversy.





"However, we are very saddened that we could not fulfil my daughter's wish to have her wedding at the very house where she grew up. My salutations to everyone who felt concerned about my daughter after seeing the developments taking place over the wedding venue," she said.

"My daughter Anjili's marriage is a match arranged by elders. It is our responsibility to conduct the wedding without controversy and without any disputes.

Therefore, we have decided to hold the wedding ceremony of YS Anjili Reddy and Somala Raghuram Reddy at a different venue instead of the Yelahanka house, in the presence of relatives, friends and well-wishers. We wholeheartedly wish that the Telugu people will shower their blessings and good wishes on the couple,â she added.

In the letter, he pointed out that a wedding would bring a large number of guests, caterers, decorators, photographers and other service providers into the residential premises.

"At the end of the day, this is my home and I want to ensure that my family and I are safe here," Jagan wrote.

World.title: 'Keep Rahul Gandhi mock PM for life': BJP's dig at INDIA bloc's 'public impeachment' of CEC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (

) on Saturday took a dig at the

, saying that the party should keep

a "mock prime minister for life".

Holding a press briefing parallel to the proceedings of the INDIA bloc's "public impeachment" of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra said: "The world has already realised that Rahul Gandhi lacks the fuel.

This satellite will never launch. Keep him as your mock Prime Minister for life. We have no objection."

Patra said the programme by the Congress-led bloc was "a mockery of the Parliament itself".

Tearing into the Congress party, Patra defended the law that lends immunity and protection to CEC Gyanesh Kumar, saying the BJP "did not introduce any law that did not already exist. Immunity and protection for the President and the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) are already enshrined in the Constitution".

Patra also cited the August 2023 Telangana lower special court order that directed an FIR to be filed against the Chief Election Commissioner.

"The high court immediately quashed the order, stating that this was not the correct procedure and directed that it be dismissed. But it became evident then that, due to political pressure, anyone could file a case or an FIR against individuals, even those holding high constitutional offices who are protected by the Constitution, without any regard for the law.





Therefore, a procedure was introduced. It was merely a procedure.

The legal provision already existed within the Constitution. The Constitution of India provides this protection," he said.

BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad slammed Rahul Gandhi for making "a mockery of the people of the country" and dared him to resign.

"These individuals do not participate in parliamentary discussions; instead, they are making a mockery of the people of the country...

Nehru ji became Prime Minister by stealing votes... How long will you continue to ridicule constitutional institutions? When a decision goes in your favor, the Election Commission seems 'fine' to you... This is shameful. I challenge Rahul Gandhiâif you have the courage, you should resign," the BJP leader told news agency ANI.

'Mock parliament a drama'

Addressing a press brief, BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra said: "If there was ever a vote theft in India, it was committed by the first member of the Gandhi family, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who stole the votes of prominent Congress leaders.

Those leaders had cast their votes in a ballot box to elect Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel as Prime Minister. By stealing those votes, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru became the Prime Minister of the country, an unelected Prime Minister.

"

Patra, who is MP from Puri Lok Sabha constituency, called the "mock parliament" a "drama", and highlighted that the Speical Intensive Revision (SIR) was ongoing and substantiated the claims around the "13 crore delted voters".

"Across various states, the names of 13 crore people have not yet been included in the final electoral roll. Why is this the case? What is this 'ASDD' formula? 'A' stands for 'Absent'. There is an official known as a BLO (Booth Level Officer). The BLO is responsible for an 'enumeration form' that every individual is required to complete. The BLO visits your home three times with this form. If you are not present on any of these three occasions, you are marked as 'absent', and your name is excluded from the electoral roll.

What about 'S' in 'ASDD'? It stands for 'Shifted'âpermanently shifted," Patra said.

Amit Shah challenges Rahul, Akhilesh

Earlier, Union home minister Amit Shah slammed Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav for raising the issue of voter irregularities ahead of the INDIA bloc's Delhi Chalo march and challenged them to discuss the issue during a special session of Parliament.

While addressing a gathering in Uttar Pradesh's Lucknow, Shah highlighted the BJP's electoral victories in states like Haryana, Maharashtra and Bihar, and said that the opposition had realised that it could not win elections.

"In Haryana, the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government after securing the highest number of seats. In Maharashtra, the NDA formed the government with the largest share of seats. In Bihar, for the first time, a chief minister from the Bharatiya Janata Party took office. In Delhi, the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government after three decades. In Puducherry, the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government once again.

In Assam, we achieved a hat-trick by winning 100 seats, and in Bengal, we completely wiped out Mamata Didi," Shah said.

"After the events in Bengal, they have realised that they simply cannot win elections," he added.

The Union home minister said that "Rahul Baba" and Akhilesh were cut from different cloth and accused them of "blaming the umpire" instead of accepting defeat.

"Naturally, when a team loses a match or a game, they should sit down and practise more - that is what is expected, isn't it? But 'Rahul Baba' is cut from a different cloth.

The same goes for Akhilesh and others in the 'INDIA' alliance who are with him. Instead of accepting defeat, they began accusing the umpire of cheating, claiming that votes were stolen," Shah said.

He further said that the opposition had no intention of raising the issue in Parliament and accused it of refusing to let the House function.

"Rahul Baba, I challenge both you and Akhilesh Yadav right here and now: the Bharatiya Janata Party is fully prepared to discuss this in Parliament.

We have nothing to hide. Let us convene a special session of Parliament - but they have no intention of speaking there. They refuse to let Parliament function; instead, they just create a ruckus," Shah said.

INDIA bloc passes resolution against CEC

The INDIA bloc on Saturday demanded the removal of Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of being part of a "devious and malevolent criminal conspiracy orchestrated by the BJP to steal national and state elections". The opposition alliance also demanded that he be tried for "treason" in a court.

The allegations were outlined in a resolution read out by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge during a symbolic "public impeachment" programme against Kumar. The CEC has faced sustained criticism from opposition parties over alleged electoral irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

The resolution said that Members of Parliament belonging to the INDIA bloc had resolved to seek Kumar's impeachment on the basis of the charges listed in the document.

World.title: 'Guilty of centralising electoral rolls': Mallikarjun Kharge lists 6 charges against CEC Gyanesh Kumar, makes 3 demands
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Leader of the opposition in Rajya Sabha

on Saturday accused Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of facilitating "vote theft" and listed six charges against him at a symbolic "public impeachment" organised by the opposition INDIA bloc.

Kharge alleged that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was initiated to remove voters opposed to the BJP. The proceedings began at his residence on Rajaji Marg, with former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar chairing the event.

Kharge accused the CEC of centralising control over electoral rolls and acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah.

During the proceedings, Kharge listed six allegations against Kumar:

Conspired to steal elections

Deleted 13.3 crore voters

Rewrote Form 6 without parliamentary oversight or knowledge

Seized the electoral rolls through ECINET

Breached his constitutional mandate and shut out the two other election commissioners

Acted at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Amit Shah

Kharge also reiterated the opposition's three demands:

The removal of the CEC

An end to the SIR exercise

Changes to the 2023 law governing the appointment of the chief election commissioner.

Kharge also accused PM Modi government of using various means to retain power since 2014, including defections, splitting parties, misuse of central agencies and alleged electoral irregularities.

"The proposal we are bringing today is to safeguard the dignity of a constitutional institution. We have no personal enmity with the CEC. Our intention is that the Election Commission should function impartially in keeping with the spirit of the Constitution. The trust of the common man in it should remain intact. No one sitting in Delhi should be able to wrongly delete the voting rights of weaker sections, women, and youth using a computer," Kharge posted on X.





He further alleged that the government had repeatedly tried to retain power through various means.

"The Modi government has hatched every conspiracy since 2014 to cling to power: stealing MPs, breaking parties, stealing governments, Electoral Bonds, misuse of ED/CBI. And now Vote Theftâcut opposition votes and rule. There are hundreds of examples of Vote Theft," he said.

Kharge also criticised the 2023 law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), alleging that it provided the election commissioner with legal protection.

"Gyanesh Kumar is able to carry out this theft because of the 2023 CEC Act. In December 2023, this bill was passed by suspending 145 opposition MPs. This law gives the CEC a lifelong protective shield that even the President and CJI do not have," he added.

Questioning the results of the 2024 Maharashtra and Haryana assembly elections, Kharge alleged that the INDIA bloc's strong performance in the Lok Sabha elections was followed by a reversal in the state polls due to electoral irregularities.

"In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, we had an excellent performance in Maharashtra and Haryana, but the results flipped in the assembly elections. Reasonâvotes were illegally added before the elections and then all names were removed. This work is being done together by Modi-Shah and Gyanesh," he alleged.

World.title: India-linked Buddha relics to be enshrined in 108 chortens in Bhutan
World.content:
Buddhist relics of Indian origin will be enshrined in most of the 108 jangchub chortens (stupas of enlightenment) that monks and volunteers are scheduled to build simultaneously along a 12 km stretch of the Mau Chhu River in the Bhutanese town of Gelephu on Sunday (November 1, 2026).

The event will mark the spiritual foundation of the Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC), which Bhutan’s King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuk envisions as a spirituality-driven global economic hub. About 240 km south-southeast of Bhutan’s capital, Thimphu, the city borders Assam’s Chirang district.

The Central Monastic Body of Bhutan, the country’s principal institutional carrier of the Drukpa Kagyu lineage of Tibetan Buddhism, said that Buddhists in Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, and Bhutan had donated hundreds of relics, mostly bones and hair.

Stupas of enlightenment

“Malaysia sent three sets of 108 relics of the Buddha, enlightened saints and revered lamas. We received many from Thailand. Most of the relics were established as having been sourced from India,” Choten Dorji, the Principal Secretary to one of the masters of the monastic body, said on Saturday (October 31, 2026).

The relics form part of the ‘zung’, the living embodiment of the Buddha’s enlightened body, speech and mind. The sacred components of the zung include thangkhas (traditional Tibetan Buddhist paintings on cotton or silk fabric), statues, precious stones, rolled mantra scrolls, or dharanis, and relics of enlightened beings.

The jangchub chorten commemorates the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment and symbolises the triumph of wisdom over ignorance. Once consecrated, a chorten is rendered equivalent to the living Buddha.

‘Test of national character’

On February 26, King Wangchuk announced Project 108 at the GMC as a “test of national character”, not merely an initiative to set a world record.

“It is an ambitious undertaking that demands courage, unity, and deep commitment. We must do it to prove to ourselves that, as we face the challenges ahead, there is no limit to what we can achieve when we stand together,” he said.

Officials said that Project 108, involving 40,000 trained volunteers, was Bhutan’s sacred gesture of peace in a world troubled by conflict.

Each chorten is estimated to cost $200,000, and individuals, families, communities, and institutions worldwide have contributed to the project.

According to the blueprint, each chorten will stand 15 metres tall, positioned 108 metres apart in a line along the Mau Chhu River, which runs through Gelephu.

The significance of ‘108’

Bhutan’s spiritual leaders explained the rationale behind the number 108.

“In astronomy, the distance between the earth and the sun is approximately 108 times the sun’s diameter and the distance between the earth and the moon is about 108 times the moon’s diameter,” a monk said.

“In some Tibetan Buddhist traditions, the Kangyur (principal collection of sacred Buddhist scriptures) is arranged in 108 volumes. Practitioners count 108 beads on a prayer mala, circumambulate sacred sites 108 times, and ring temple bells 108 times. In the Vajrayana Buddhist tradition, 108 symbolises spiritual completeness, cosmic balance, and the purification of karma,” he said.

Project 108 also links to Hinduism. “Hindu tradition often speaks of 108 Upanishads (sacred philosophical texts). Many Hindu deities have 108 names. In yoga, the sun salutation is traditionally performed in cycles of 108,” the monk said.

The date for executing Project 108 is significant, too. Bhutan observes November 1 as Lord Buddha’s Descending Day and Mother’s Day. Sunday also marks the 18th coronation anniversary of King Wangchuk, who reached Gelephu with his royal entourage on Saturday.

World.title: T.N. Nurses Development Association demands regularisation of 6,500 contract nurse
World.content:
The State executive committee of the Tamil Nadu Nurses Development Association met here on Saturday (October 31, 2026) and passed a series of resolutions regarding job regularisation, fair pay, and freedom of expression.

A major point of contention at the meeting was a recent circular issued by the Director of Public Health, which barred government employees from criticising Union and State government policies and actions with regard to social, print, and news media, and public gatherings, and participating in events featuring anti-government speeches and resolutions.

The committee resolved to demand its immediate withdrawal. The association’s primary demands focused on the welfare and job security of healthcare personnel.

The main resolution passed at the meeting was pressing the call to regularise the services of 6,500 contract nurses working on a consolidated pay, granting them full time-scale salaries on a par with permanent staff.

The association also urged recruitment and regularisation of all temporary contract nurses through the Medical Services Recruitment Board, scheduling of transfer counselling for newly created nursing positions, and permanent appointment of nurses and nursing tutors across government hospitals and nursing colleges.

The association said from November 2 to 6, the association members would conduct an outreach campaign across Tamil Nadu to engage with nurses, meet MLAs to press their cause, and wear protest badges while on duty.

This will culminate in district-level demonstrations in headquarters on November 12. Additionally, the executive committee announced that the association’s State representative council meeting would be held in Kanniyakumari on January 7, 2027.

The meeting was presided over by State president K. Sasikala, and State general secretary N. Subin presented the core resolutions.

World.title: Coastal Andhra Pradesh fisherfolk face severe financial crisis amid Cyclones and frequent weather bans
World.content:
A series of low-pressure systems, depressions, and the “severe” cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ have plunged coastal Andhra Pradesh’s marine fishing community into an unprecedented financial crisis. Frequent weather warnings and compulsory fishing bans issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) — following a depression that crossed Kakinada on September 23 and Cyclone Arnab’s landfall near Yanam on October 28 — have paralysed maritime trade and disrupted local supply chains. With another storm brewing over the Bay of Bengal and threatening the coast, likely from November 2, stakeholders are bracing for further impact.

In Visakhapatnam Urban district alone, thousands of families depending on 750 mechanised trawlers and 1,890 motor and fibre boats face mounting distress.

Repeated bans across four major weather alerts since June have caused cumulative losses exceeding ₹36 crore. Fisherfolk leader Ajili Dasu noted that Cyclone Arnab alone caused a direct trade loss of nearly ₹20 crore through a mandatory six-day ban. With adverse weather prevailing for five to seven days every month, over 60% of the fleet remains anchored.

Furthermore, unremunerative prices for commercial varieties like tuna, seer, pomfret, prawns, and crabs have compounded the hardship, crippling livelihoods for vendors, auctioneers, ice suppliers, and transport operators.

Demands for Enhanced Relief

Assessing the structural destruction, Fisheries Department Joint Director L.B.S. Vardhan confirmed initial direct losses of around ₹5 crore at the Visakhapatnam Fishing Harbour due to Cyclone Arnab. Preliminary surveys indicate seven mechanised boats sank and 65 suffered partial structural damage, with reports being forwarded for relief under standard State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) norms.

However, fisherfolk organisations have submitted a formal petition to Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu demanding 100% financial compensation for damaged gear and craft affecting 3.32 lakh active marine fishermen State-wide, alongside a daily subsistence allowance of ₹600 per fisherman for seven days of forced idleness.

Organisations argue that compensation should align with expanded Chief Minister’s Relief Fund (CMRF) provisions under G.O. Ms. No. 1 rather than restrictive SDRF limits, ensuring robust support for the crisis-hit community.

The G.O.Ms.No. 1, issued on January 7, 2025, mandates enhanced disaster relief for all future natural calamities funded via CMRF. It increases ex gratia for deaths to ₹5 lakh, house/auto relief to ₹10,000, livestock aid to ₹50,000, and agriculture compensation up to ₹35,000/hectare.

World.title: Prajaseva special drive facilitates e-Khata for 590 owners
World.content:
The Mysuru City Corporation (MCC) issued e-khata certificates to 590 eligible applicants on Saturday, the concluding day of its three-day Prajaseva e-Aasthi special campaign.

Of 730 applications received on October 28, 590 applications submitted along with necessary documents were found eligible for receiving e-khata.

The MCC has decided to conduct another drive on November 5, 6 and 7 to provide another opportunity for eligible property owners within its limits to secure e-khata certificates. Those who could not take part in the campaign this month or failed to submit essential documents can avail this opportunity, a press release from MCC said.

The MCC limits cover more than 2.10 lakh properties, of which e-khata certificates have been issued to over 78,700 property owners.

Officials have been directed to expedite the issuance of e-khata certificates to the remaining eligible property owners, said Minister in-charge of Mysuru district Yathindra Siddharamaiah, who symbolically distributed e-khata certificates to the property owners at a programme organised by the MCC as part of the Prajaseva campaign.

Expressing happiness over the enthusiastic public participation to e-khata special drive, the Minister urged property owners to utilise the opportunity and submit applications along with the required documents. He directed officials to prioritise verification of eligible applications and issuance of e-katha certificates in accordance with the rules.

MLA Tanveer Sait, Deputy Commissioner G. Lakshmikanth Reddy, Regional Commissioner Nitesh Patil, MCC Commissioner Savitha, Zilla Panchayat CEO Yukesh Kumar, and other officials were present.

World.title: Ensure living wage is paid to staff of HR&CE temples: HC
World.content:
The Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court has directed the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department to ensure that living wage was paid to the staff of temples coming under the purview of the department.

A Division Bench of Justices G.R. Swaminathan and P. Murugan said temple staff were paid out of the income generated by the particular temple. This led to an invidious situation. If a particular temple was bereft of properties and was not able to generate sufficient income, its staff were paid a pittance.

“Our conscience is shocked that thousands of temple staff are paid atrociously poor pay. The amount paid to them would be hardly sufficient to keep the body and soul together. We may remark that the lowest National Floor Level Minimum Wage is ₹176 per day. What is drawn by many temple staff in Tamil Nadu is lower than that,” the court said.

The court said linking the pay of a person with the income drawn by the religious institution breached his/her fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution which was all about life and liberty. The only way to remedy the situation was by suitably remunerating the staff.

On a case-to-case basis, a system had to be evolved. This was the paramount duty of the HR&CE Department. It was unfortunate that till date, they had not bothered to lift their little finger to ameliorate the pitiable conditions of temple staff, the court said.

It said there was something called temple economics. It was time to embrace technology. Social media could be deployed effectively to mobilise support for this noble cause.

The court expected the HR&CE Commissioner to take immediate steps in this regard. “It is he who must bell the cat. When binding judicial direction was there to ensure payment of fair wage to the temple staff, the department and its officials cannot be permitted to keep quiet,” the court said.

The court granted two months’ time to the Commissioner to submit an action taken report. The court issued the direction will hearing a public interest litigation petition filed by Periyanambi Narasimha Gopalan of Ambasamudram in Tirunelveli district, who sought a direction to the authorities to pay salaries to all archakas and other temple employees throughout the State as per the Minimum Wages Act and on a par with government servants, irrespective of the income of individual temples.

World.title: SCoR officials celebrate Rashtriya Ekta Diwas
World.content:
Officials of the South Coast Railway (SCoR), Vijayawada, celebrated Rashtriya Ekta Diwas commemorating the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, here on Saturday.

Divisional Railway Manager (DRM) Mohit Sonakiya administered the Ekta Diwas pledge to the officials and staff. Later, the employees organised a walkathon on the occasion.

The railway officials and staff reaffirmed their commitment to preserve the unity, integrity and security of the nation and upholding the spirit of oneness and solidarity.

Meanwhile, Eluru district Additional Superintendent of Police (ASP) Y. Prasad Rao garlanded the portrait of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and paid tributes, in Eluru on Saturday.

Later, the ASP administered the Ekta Diwas pledge to the police officers.

World.title: Sugarcane growers intensify agitation across Kittur Karnataka; bandh evokes mixed response; Road blockades disrupt transport in Belagavi, Vijayapura, Bagalkot, Dharwad and Haveri
World.content:
The Karnataka bandh called by sugarcane growers demanding a remunerative price for their produce evoked a mixed response across the Kittur Karnataka region on Saturday, with road blockades disrupting transport and normal life in several parts of Belagavi, Vijayapura, Bagalkot, Dharwad and Haveri districts.

The growers are demanding ₹5,500 a tonne for sugarcane, including an incentive of ₹1,000 a tonne from the State government. They have also urged the Union government to increase the minimum selling price (MSP) of sugar from ₹31 to ₹60 a kg.

In Belagavi, the bandh evoked a moderate response in the city but had a wider impact in rural areas. Farmers belonging to the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha and Hasiru Sene staged a protest at the Central Bus Stand from 6 a.m. to 8 a.m., disrupting bus services. Commercial activity returned to normal around 9 a.m.

Road blockades continued in Gokak, Kagwad, Yaragatti, Hukkeri, Nipani, Mudalagi, Athani and other towns. Farmers blocked roads connecting Karnataka and Maharashtra near Nipani and Kagwad. At Gokak, protesters blocked the Gokak-Hidkal Dam road and prepared food on the highway. At Ugaragol in Savadatti taluk, a blockade on the road to the Renuka Yellamma temple forced devotees to return without darshan.

In Dharwad, growers blocked the main road near Jubilee Circle for more than two hours, bringing traffic to a standstill. Chigari and State transport bus services were temporarily suspended. Police Commissioner Bhushan Borase visited the spot and persuaded the protesters to clear the road. The blockade was withdrawn around 1 p.m. Hubballi too witnessed traffic disruptions because of protest by farmers. Several shops and commercial establishments r

Haveri witnessed a mixed response amid tense scenes. Farmers began a round-the-clock sit-in outside Sugar Minister Rudrappa Lamani’s residence, erecting a shamiana on the road. The Minister was in Bengaluru, while police barricaded the approach roads.

Protesters urged traders to close their establishments, leading to heated exchanges near Siddappa Circle and the district bus stand. Transport was also affected after farmers blocked the Ilkal-Shikaripura highway near Chowdayyadanapur. Buses were stranded at Guttal and services at the Haveri bus stand were disrupted.

Vijayapura district witnessed a strong response. Babaleshwar observed a complete bandh, while farmers blocked the Vijayapura-Pandharpur highway at Siddapur. At Sangapur S.H. village, protesters surrounded Industries Minister M.B. Patil and demanded his intervention. An argument followed, prompting the police to use lathis to disperse the crowd. Farmers alleged that police personnel had abused and assaulted them.

In Vijayapura city, farmers blocked the Hitnalli toll plaza for nearly two hours. Muddebihal also observed a complete bandh. The agitation received support in several other taluks.

Bagalkot district witnessed a good response, while Gadag saw only symbolic protests.

No agitation today

Sugarcane growers in Belagavi district who had earlier decided to continue their agitation on Sunday, later withdrew the decision saying they were suspending the agitation on account of Kannada Rajyotsava celebrations on Sunday. They, however, said that the protest would continue at Gurlapur.

Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha general secretary Praveen Chougala said the the proposed jail bharo agitation had been postponed. Sangha honorary president Shashikant Padasalagi Guruji accused Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar of adopting double standards. Sangha president Chunnappa Poojari said after Rajyotsava, the agitation would continue until the State government announced the demanded incentive of ₹1,000 a tonne.

World.title: Naidu calls for high alert as another cyclone threat looms over Andhra Pradesh
World.content:
Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has directed officials to expedite restoration works in the areas affected by Cyclone Arnab and called for a high alert in view of the threat of another cyclone.

With a depression over the southeast Bay of Bengal predicted to intensify into a cyclone by November 1, moderate to heavy rainfall is likely in the south coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema regions on November 2, 3 and 4. Mr. Naidu stressed the need for precautionary measures to minimise the impact.

Reviewing relief and restoration measures in the cyclone-hit districts at the Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) Centre in the Secretariat on Saturday, he directed officials to monitor the movement of the depression every six hours using satellite imagery and Doppler radars and take appropriate measures based on its trajectory.

He also called for efficient utilisation of rainwater, uninterrupted mobile phone connectivity and the maximum possible use of battery energy storage systems.

Officials informed him that power restoration works were progressing at a brisk pace in the affected areas, with 7,000 personnel and 400 machines deployed.

Mr. Naidu directed officials to urgently restore the protection wall at Kakinada, clear silt from canals in the Narsapuram and Katrenikona areas, and strengthen drainage systems in Konaseema and West Godavari districts to ensure the smooth flow of water.

He called for steps to extend insurance coverage to all farmers from the next agricultural season and stressed the need to promote natural farming.

The Chief Minister ordered compensation of ₹54,000 per hectare for damage to 1,293 hectares of coconut plantations and ₹1,500 for each uprooted coconut tree. Officials informed him that about 1.95 lakh coconut trees had been damaged. They also said steps were being taken to pay compensation of ₹35,000 per hectare for banana crop losses across 15,000 hectares.

World.title: ‘Very little, if anything, done for KP’: PM Shehbaz rails against PTI’s governance in province
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday criticised PTI’s governance in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, questioning whether the funds available to the now dysfunctional provincial government had been used transparently for the welfare and betterment of the people of the province.

His remarks came during a meeting of the PML-N’s parliamentary party from KP, held in Islamabad.

The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move had drawn criticism from the opposition, as well as Fazl, who had made efforts to reduce tensions between the federal and the KP governments.

Taking aim at the PTI, Prime Minister Shehbaz said: “They have been in power in KP for 13 years. Over these 13 years, they have raised countless slogans, delivered fiery speeches, held long marches and sit-ins, and made numerous promises.”

Recalling PTI’s promises to build hundreds of dams, generate hundreds of megawatts of solar power, and establish hospitals, universities and schools across the province, the prime minister questioned whether any of these pledges had been fulfilled during the party’s 13 years in power.

“How many universities have been established there? How many new hospitals have been built? How much has the healthcare system improved? What facilities have actually been provided to the people? And how much corruption has taken place in the process?” he asked.

The prime minister also questioned whether public funds had been utilised transparently for the welfare and betterment of the people of KP.

“From Peshawar to Kohistan and Hazara, and across the entire southern region of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the majority of people would tell you that the PTI government has done very little, if anything, to address their basic needs,” he said.

The premier maintained that by 2017-18, terrorist activities in the province had been brought to an end to “a considerable extent”.

“Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was among the provinces that made the greatest sacrifices in the fight against terrorism,” he said.

The prime minister highlighted the heavy toll terrorism had taken on the country, saying around 80,000 people had lost their lives and Pakistan’s economy had suffered losses estimated at Rs15,000 billion.

He also praised former prime minister and PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif for his policies to combat terrorism following the 2014 Army Public School tragedy, in which more than 140 students and teachers were killed.

Turning to the PTI, the prime minister said the party had spent the past two and a half years engaged in long marches and protests.

“In 2014, Chinese President Xi Jinping was scheduled to visit Pakistan. We made repeated efforts to persuade the party to call off its sit-in so that President Xi’s visit could proceed as planned, but it refused. As a result, the visit was postponed,” he said, recalling the 2014 D-Chowk protest.

He also criticised the PTI for allowing “brutal terrorists” from Afghanistan to settle in Swat.

“These were among the most painful and heartrending incidents that allowed terrorism to regain momentum,” he said.

The premier further said that thousands of civilians and security personnel had been martyred during the past two and a half years, adding that the PTI had been offered an opportunity to join hands with the federal government to combat terrorism, as it had done in the past.

He also said that hundreds of billions had been allocated to the KP government under a special National Finance Commission (NFC) arrangement to combat terrorism.

“How many Safe City projects have been initiated in KP? How much money has been spent on strengthening the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD)?” he asked.

The prime minister elaborated that even if the PTI-led KP government had spent Rs80 billion on strengthening the police and other law enforcement agencies, they would have been better equipped to tackle security challenges. “But unfortunately, that did not happen,” he added.

He said the federal government had managed to put the national economy back on its feet, but acknowledged that the recovery process would be a long journey.

The prime minister recalled that the government had formed a committee comprising members of the PPP and PML-N to hold talks with the PTI.

“Both sides held negotiations for 48 hours. I was told that the draft had been finalised and would be signed within minutes, following approval from then-chief minister Sohail Afridi. However, the approval never came, and we are still waiting,” he said.

Prime Minister Shehbaz said the federal government was compelled to impose an emergency and governor’s rule, as it had no other option.

He emphasised that the Centre’s decision had been “timely”, warning that the consequences would have been severe had it been delayed.

The prime minister urged PML-N lawmakers from KP to prioritise the basic needs of the people in their constituencies, while putting long-term projects on hold for the time being.

“Focus on short-term welfare projects so that you can help turn people’s fortunes around within the next six months to a year,” he stressed.

PTI hits back at PM’s criticism

Meanwhile, the PTI hit back at the premier’s criticism, challenging the federal government to account for its own record instead of blaming the party for KP’s security and governance problems.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said the prime minister had no moral authority to lecture the party on democracy and governance, alleging that the present political setup had come into power through electoral manipulation and political arrangements.

Waqas accused the federal government of shifting responsibility for the province’s worsening security situation onto the PTI provincial government. He alleged that the federal government had failed to provide the province with necessary resources and equipment for counterterrorism operations.

He also accused the Centre of focusing on political opposition rather than addressing security and governance issues, alleging that PTI leaders and workers had faced raids, arrests and intimidation.

He also challenged the premier to present a comprehensive account of his government’s four-year performance.

Less than a week after emergency and governor’s rule were imposed in the province, a joint sitting of parliament approved the federal government’s move amid a strong protest from the opposition.

The events of Oct 11 followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI — as well as negotiations to bridge their differences — after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups and asserted that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks .

The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre denied . It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticised the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

Additional input from Ikram Junaidi.

World.title: Syria weighing whether to join Makkah pact: foreign minister
World.content:
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Makkah defence pact that binds Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed on Aug 7, empowers the three members to consider an armed attack on one member an attack on all.

“Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Makkah alliance,” Al Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain.

According to Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), speaking about the ongoing regional conflicts, the foreign minister expressed Damascus’s support for the Gulf states against any aggression and condemned missile and drone attacks.

“Geography is destiny, and integration is a choice. We have chosen to make our territory a bridge for prosperity and the exchange of interests, and we stand as a bulwark against turning Syria into a platform for threatening neighbouring countries,” he was quoted as saying.

Al Shaibani also condemned repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory, affirmed that occupied Golan was Syrian land, and called for a path to an independent Palestinian state.

Saudi Arabia has been rallying support against escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, including a deadly strike that closed Riyadh’s international airport for two weeks this month.

Islamabad has two defence pacts with Riyadh aimed at collective deterrence — the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between the two and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement that also includes Turkiye.

Pakistan is providing “whatever support is needed” to defend Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks, the military’s spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said earlier this month.

However, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) director general also clarified that all members of the Makkah Defence Alliance were “absolutely clear […] that this alliance has no offensive intent; it is purely defensive”.

A day earlier, he said that the wording of the pact did not bar new members after being asked about whether Iran could join the agreement.

“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.

In August, two weeks after the Makkah pact was signed, the Syrian foreign minister visited Pakistan and called on Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir.

They both discussed “regional security environment and avenues for enhanced bilateral defence and security cooperation”, ISPR said.

Amid the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, French President Emmanuel Macron made a surprise visit to Riyadh earlier this month and said France had sent troops to help shield a key Saudi oil terminal from attacks.

Also in October, the United Kingdom’s government announced it would deploy British fighter planes to help Saudi Arabia against the attacks.

World.title: Mansehra assistant commissioner injured as vehicle comes under attack in Nowshera
World.content:
PESHAWAR: Mansehra Assistant Commissioner (AC) Adil Waseem was injured on Saturday when unknown gunmen opened fire at his official vehicle in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Nowshera district, officials said.

Muhammad Asim, the spokesperson of Peshawar’s Lady Reading Hospital, said Waseem was “stable” and was receiving medical treatment.

Waseem came under attack in Nowshera’s Panah Kot area while on his way back from his native village Saleh Khana in the district, police officials in Nowshera said.

He sustained injuries and was immediately taken to the hospital.

According to Nowshera District Police Officer (DPO) Sonia Shamroz, the area was immediately cordoned off and a search operation was launched. She added that a team has been constituted to arrest those behind the attack.

DPO Shamroz further said a case has been registered and investigation into the incident was under way.

KP has been witnessing increased terrorist attacks and security challenges in recent years, including attacks on law enforcement personnel and officials.

According to a recent report by the Centre for Research and Security Studies, Pakistan recor­ded a sharp 83 per cent increase in violence-linked fatalities during the third quarter of 2026, re­­versing a declining trend reported in the first and second quarters.

KP and Balochistan remained the epicentres of violence, jointly accounting for 98pc of all fatalities during the period. Balochistan recorded 829 deaths, nearly 59pc of the national total, while KP reported 556 fatalities, accounting for more than 39pc.

On Thursday night, a cop was martyred after terrorists attacked a police post in Bajaur district’s Barang tehsil.

Last week, four policemen, including a Counter-Terrorism Department official and a station house officer, were martyred while two terrorists were killed during an exchange of fire in the Karak district.

In December 2025, Miranshah AC Shah Wali was among four martyred after the official’s vehicle came under attack in Bannu. In July that year, Nawagai subdivision AC Faisal Ismail and four others lost their lives in an explosion targeting a government vehicle in Bajaur.

World.title: Capt Safdar's remarks about women suffering from illness draw criticism, including from CM Maryam
World.content:
LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s spouse, retired Capt Muhammad Safdar, has come under fire for disparaging remarks about women advocating for bodily autonomy.

Speaking at a Khatm-i-Nabuwwat rally in Chiniot earlier this week, Safdar took aim at the slogan “mera jism, meri marzi” (my body, my choice).

He questioned why women who assert control over their bodies turn to religious scholars for prayers when diagnosed with serious illnesses such as cancer.

“They say, ‘My body, my choice.’ But when they fall ill or develop cancer, they turn to religious scholars, seeking prayers and blessed water for a cure. They should understand that if they claim ownership over their bodies, they should also be able to cure them. In reality, the human body is under God’s control,” he said.

On Friday, Maryam responded to a post on X regarding the speech, which stated: “Maryam Nawaz’s husband, Captain Safdar, also lost his mother-in-law to cancer, yet here he is mocking women who are battling cancer.”

The chief minister’s mother, Kulsoom Nawaz, passed away in 2018 after a months-long battle with cancer.

“Heartbreaking,” the chief minister said, posting an emoji of a broken heart.

“The silent battles a woman, a wife, fights behind closed doors … The strength she must find even when she feels like breaking. Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible,” she said.

Apart from CM Maryam, users on social media also took issue with Safdar’s remarks.

“My [mother] has been a cancer patient, and God knows how we managed to get through those difficult times. Her survival was nothing short of a miracle. Listening to Capt Safdar’s remarks on this matter is utterly shameful and disgraceful!” said TV anchor Ajmal Jami on X.

He also thanked CM Maryam for her “thoughtful and compassionate words for all those brave women”.

Another user, Maheen Ghani, said: “So a woman who says ‘mera jism, meri marzi’, which is essentially about autonomy and consent, loses the right to ask for prayers when she gets cancer? Is that seriously the argument?

“To take a woman’s illness, her fear and her faith and turn them into an opportunity to humiliate her. What an ugly, twisted understanding of both women’s rights and religion.”

On the other hand, some, like journalist Benazir Shah, lauded CM Maryam for speaking out.

“It takes real courage to take a public stand like this. More power to you, Maryam Nawaz Sharif,” she said.

Lawyers’ bodies condemn remarks about Asma Jahangir

Meanwhile, two premier lawyers’ bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018. During the rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer “cursed”.

Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements.

Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action.

“The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation,” the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly “deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect”.

The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance.

“The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition,” he emphasised.

Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar.

“These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community,” the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination.

“Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination.”

The SCBA also strongly condemned derogatory remarks by Safdar against women and an illness that was “being valiantly fought back by hundreds of thousands of women across the world”.

“At a time when women are breaking barriers, such remarks are disgraceful and entirely unacceptable,” the SCBA said.

“What makes this conduct even more shameful is that his own spouse holds the highest office of Punjab chief minister, and he himself is the father of a daughter; he should have been ashamed of making such insensitive and degrading remarks directed against the women,” it said.

These statements may also attract penal consequences, the SCBA reminded and called upon the concerned authorities to take immediate and strict notice and proceed in accordance with the law.

“Such divisive, offensive, and intolerant attitudes must be firmly challenged and nipped in the bud.

“Let it be clear to all and sundry, we will not remain silent when the dignity of our legal fraternity, the legacy of a human rights champion, and the respect owed to women are attacked,” the SCBA statement said.

Nasir Iqbal from Islamabad also contributed to this report.

World.title: Turkiye nominates veteran diplomat Sinirlioglu for role of UN chief
World.content:
Turkiye has nominated Feridun Hadi Sinirlioglu, secretary general of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), to be the next United Nations chief, a diplomatic source confirmed on Saturday.
