World.title: Trump touted a record Venezuela oil deal. Now reality is setting in
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump called it the biggest oil deal in history: 17 Venezuelan oilfields holding some 64 billion barrels of reserves, handed to a single company.

Delivering on it falls to North American Blue Energy Partners, a little-known firm led by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who was until recently a target of U.S. money-laundering investigations involving funds embezzled from the state-owned oil company PDVSA. The company’s deal with Washington grants the U.S. a 35%-stake in its corporate parent and the right to buy 20% of output at production cost.

NABEP says it will lift oil output fourfold to more than 1 million barrels per day (bpd), up from about 224,000 bpd in mid-October.

World.title: Trump administration approves potential Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday green-lit the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, the State Department said, but the Ukrainian president warned deliveries could take years.

The approval, which goes to Congress for review, comes after weeks of complaints by Ukrainian authorities that its supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.

“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the department said in a statement.

The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.

But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Friday in a post on X that “deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS.”

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelenskyy said, using an acronym for the weapons.

The Ukrainian leader suggested that the U.S. and European allies could give his country missiles they have stockpiled now, which would later be replenished by this new purchase.

Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles.

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the State Department said.

U.S.-Ukraine tensions spiked earlier this month after Washington struck a diesel fuel deal with Russia. Ukraine also said that the U.S. was slowing its access to satellite internet services and had stopped some intelligence sharing.

Tensions eased after Zelenskyy held talks with U.S. envoys in Oslo on Oct. 20.

The State Department said the weapons sale would be paid for with by donations from Ukraine’s allies but not with U.S. funds.

World.title: After Louvre heist and string of thefts, Europe’s smaller museums are on guard
World.content:
Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cezanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.

Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million ($10 million), to an accomplice and fled. At the museum’s main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.

“Whatever could go wrong, did,” said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.

World.title: Scam centers relocated from Cambodia operate in Madagascar
World.content:
Raids against online scam centers in Madagascar have exposed ties with a criminal group that ran similar operations in Cambodia, also duping African nationals via alleged human trafficking, authorities said.

Conducting romance, cryptocurrency and investment fraud, the sites were mostly operated by Chinese nationals, 148 of whom have been extradited to China, Madagascar’s justice ministry said.

Thirteen Chinese-run scam compounds were taken down in operations in August and September conducted with the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), it said.

World.title: Doshisha chairman apologizes over fatal boat accident in Okinawa
World.content:
The head of Doshisha, which operates Doshisha International Senior High School, has apologized over a boat accident in Okinawa Prefecture that left one female student dead, at his first news conference since the March 16 accident.

“I offer my deepest condolences for (the victim, Tomoka) Takeishi, and sincerely apologize to everyone concerned,” Eiji Hatta, chairman of Doshisha’s board of trustees, said at the news conference in Kyoto on Friday.

He observed a moment of silence for Takeishi, one of the two victims who died in the accident in which two boats carrying students and crew members capsized off the coast of the Henoko area in the city of Nago during an educational program near the construction site of a U.S. military facility set to take over the functions of the U.S. Marine Corps’ Futenma air station in Ginowan, also Okinawa.

Hatta apologized for the delay in holding the press conference, which took place seven and a half months after the accident. He explained that he decided to hold the briefing to make an interim report on Doshisha’s handling of the issue, because the educational institution found that a full investigation into the accident would take time after setting up a committee to examine the neutrality of the high school’s education Oct. 22.

“I bear a heavy responsibility as chairman” in light of the education ministry’s finding that there were serious problems with the school’s safety management system, Hatta said.

The ministry has said the content of the school’s education on the relocation of the Futenma air station to the Henoko area violated the basic law on education, which stipulates political neutrality in education.

“The problem was that peace education was conducted from only one perspective,” Hatta said. “We need to make corrections.”

Hatta said he will resign after paving the way for improvements in the school operator’s governance system. “I want to steadily implement plans to improve education and fulfill my responsibilities until the end,” he said, indicating his wish to remain as Doshisha’s chancellor and trustee.

After the news conference, Takeishi’s parents released a statement that they feel “an indescribable sense of discomfort.” They criticized the school for failing to hold a news conference on many occasions, including when the education ministry announced its view on the school’s educational content.

“We want them to seriously reconsider what it means to fulfill accountability,” the parents said.

World.title: U.S., South Korea and Japan vow ‘complete’ denuclearization of North Korea
World.content:
The United States, South Korea and Japan reaffirmed their commitment to the “complete denuclearization” of North Korea on Saturday, as Pyongyang continues to reject disarmament ahead of possible talks with Washington.

Speculation is mounting over a potential meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at next month’s APEC summit in China, with Trump making repeated overtures to Pyongyang for nuclear talks.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and his Japanese counterpart Toshimitsu Motegi “reaffirmed their resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization” of North Korea during talks on Friday on the sidelines of a Group of 20 meeting in Atlanta in the U.S. state of Georgia, the U.S. State Department said.

They also pledged “full implementation” of U.N. Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs.

Despite long-running U.N. sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.

Trump has made repeated overtures to Pyongyang for nuclear talks, while scaling back joint military drills with ally South Korea.

The mercurial U.S. leader even bucked long-held U.S. policy last year by conceding that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power,” while reaching out to Pyongyang for talks, saying he was “100%” open to a meeting — a suggestion that went unanswered.

Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency say Kim may have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.

South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung — who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions — suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear program in return for sanctions relief.

Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.

Analysts say China may also be moving toward tacit acceptance, pointing to the omission of North Korean denuclearisation from statements after Kim and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in June.

Pyongyang denounced a joint statement on Saturday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementations against it, vowing that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the U.S. and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state.”

World.title: Binance hack exposes unsolvable crypto risk: disappearing money
World.content:
The theft of at least $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from the world’s marquee digital-asset exchange shows that however sophisticated the fortifications, high-tech criminals are still finding a way in.

Hackers absconded with the biggest single haul in the history of cyberattacks, forcing the exchange, Binance, and its partners to freeze billions of dollars of assets, and shaking confidence in crypto-market infrastructure. While Binance promised to reimburse lost funds from customers, the heist was another blow to the security framework of an industry trying desperately to win the trust of institutional Wall Street.

“This is the largest cyber theft on record, not just the largest in crypto,” said Aneirin Flynn, CEO of cybersecurity technology firm FailSafe. “This will damage confidence in crypto. The industry is courting institutional capital, but institutions will not overlook repeated failures in custody and security.”

World.title: Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defenses after Binance heist
World.content:
Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defenses and urging greater industrywide information-sharing after a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance.

Coinbase said it made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline “solely out of an abundance of caution,” while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defenses.

But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as U.S. President Donald Trump’s regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks.

World.title: Hong Kong man falls from luxury housing complex, striking domestic helper below
World.content:
A Hong Kong man believed to have accidentally fallen from a height struck a domestic helper on the podium of a luxury housing estate in West Kowloon on Saturday, with the pair sent to hospital.

Police said they received a report at 7.43pm that the man had fallen at 1 Austin Road West and landed on the podium, hitting the woman.

A police spokesman said both were conscious at the scene, with the man taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital and the woman sent to Kwong Wah Hospital.

World.title: HKT says US order ‘ceased’ as firm reportedly agrees to exit American market
World.content:
A leading Hong Kong telecommunications carrier has confirmed that an order requiring it to justify its operation in the United States has been ceased, after the company reportedly agreed to wind down its business under pressure from a US regulatory agency over national security concerns.

A spokeswoman for Hong Kong Telecom (HKT) told the South China Morning Post on Saturday that the Order to Show Cause issued by the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in October requiring it to justify why the carrier’s right to provide international and domestic services to and from the country should not be revoked “has been ceased”.

Reuters reported earlier in the day that HKT had agreed to halt its operations in the US under pressure from the FCC.

World.title: Wine and Dine Festival vendors report Halloween boost in sales and footfall
World.content:
Vendors at Hong Kong’s Wine and Dine Festival reported a stronger turnout and signs of improving business on Saturday as the annual event entered the weekend, coinciding with Halloween celebrations and extended opening hours until 1am.

Some exhibitors said visitor numbers had increased noticeably compared with the first two days of the four-day festival, while others expressed cautious optimism about sales amid a challenging retail environment.

Henry Leung, a staff member at food and beverage importer Unicube, said business at his booth was about 20 per cent higher than at the same time last year, with the evening’s peak expected after 8pm.

World.title: Hong Kong’s first ‘Halloween Month’ surges to a finale as revellers pack streets
World.content:
Revellers packed Lan Kwai Fong dressed as golden Buddhas, Lipton tea drink cartons and bottles of ketchup and mustard, with bars expecting a business bump of more than 50 per cent as Hong Kong’s first “Halloween Month” roared to a close on Saturday.

By 7.30pm police were urging revellers to celebrate elsewhere as the area in Central was packed.

Party-goers travelling from mainland China and as far away as London described the celebration as a must-see, despite the long waits to enter certain streets.

Party-goers pack Lan Kwai Fong. Photo: Dickson Lee

The campaign, which began on October 17, involves street celebrations in Central, including Lan Kwai Fong, Kai Tak, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui East on three consecutive Saturdays, culminating on Halloween night.

World.title: Hong Kong may raise GDP forecast as growth could hit 5-year high: Paul Chan
World.content:
Hong Kong’s annual economic growth may hit a five-year high, the finance chief has said, raising the possibility of an upward revision to the current forecast of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent for 2026.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Saturday that coming third-quarter figures indicated sustained momentum, noting the economy grew by 5.1 per cent in the first half of 2026 over a year earlier.

“Although the third-quarter figures have not yet been released, I can share that exports remained very strong in the quarter,” he told a radio programme.

World.title: Appeal for private flight to bring critically ill British baby home from Hong Kong
World.content:
A UK-registered air ambulance and family support charity has issued an urgent appeal for a donated private flight to bring a critically ill baby boy home from Hong Kong.

Lia’s Wings said on Friday that nine-month-old Matthew, from Nottinghamshire, had travelled to Hong Kong with his mother several months ago to visit relatives.

He fell ill with influenza A and suffered three cardiac arrests, leaving him critically ill in hospital. His brain was reportedly deprived of oxygen for 47 minutes.

World.title: Hong Kong has released the full report on Tai Po fire tragedy. Here’s all you need to know
World.content:
Hong Kong has released the full report on Tai Po fire tragedy. Here’s all you need to know

From Winnie Ho’s resignation to a bid-rigging crackdown, here are top stories from SCMP’s coverage on the long-awaited report about the fire

World.title: New renovation body may offer bigger subsidies for older buildings
World.content:
Hong Kong’s planned renovation monitoring body will consider bigger subsidies for homeowners in ageing buildings, older districts and areas with more elderly residents who use its supervision services for major repairs, the finance chief has said.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Saturday that the Building Maintenance Support and Services Council, set up to curb malpractice in the industry after the Tai Po blaze, would be non-profit but would have to recover its costs, since owners bore the main responsibility for maintaining private residential property.

Chan said the service charges would depend on factors such as the scope of the work, with fees estimated at several thousand Hong Kong dollars per household, but authorities would subsidise those in need.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.title: Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.content:
Breast milk from mothers with postpartum depression may negatively impact infants’ brain development, a Chinese study has found.

The study, published Oct. 27 in the top academic journal Cell Metabolism, was led by a team at Nanjing University, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Through a mouse model, it shows, for the first time, how depression-related changes in levels of microRNA, a type of gene-regulating molecule, contained in structures called extracellular vesicles in breast milk can affect offspring brains.

Between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide experience postpartum depression. Children of affected mothers are more likely to face challenges in cognition, language, behavior, and school performance, and are at a higher risk of developing depression themselves.

Past research has implicated genetics and the way mothers with postpartum depression bond with, and care for, their infants as contributing to this phenomenon, but the broad and long-lasting effects of postpartum depression on child development remain unclear, according to the researchers.

Because breast milk is increasingly viewed as a “signaling system orchestrating infant development,” the researchers wrote, they looked at the relationship between milk-based microRNAs and extracellular vesicles, key parts of this signaling. Because babies’ blood-brain barrier is more permeable than adults’, these vesicles can enter the brain during nursing, making its development more sensitive to diet.

The researchers compared the breast milk of 40 human mothers clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression, and 51 without, finding that those with depression had elevated levels of three types of microRNA implicated in psychiatric illness. The same was true of the breast milk of depressed mice.

To test nursing’s role in brain development, swapping mouse pups between healthy and depressed mouse mothers. Pups born to healthy mice but nursed by their depressed counterparts showed worse cognitive and emotional behavior than pups born to depressed mothers but nursed by healthy ones.

They also found that neurons in pups nursed by depressed mothers had shorter dendrites and fewer branches in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, a part of the brain believed to play a role in memory development and depression. The problems arose mainly as the neurons matured, were detectable by day 21 after birth, and persisted into adulthood, suggesting that early nursing-environment effects can last into later development.

Giving milk from depressed mothers to healthy pups was also enough to cause cognitive impairment after weaning, while milk where the vesicles had been removed had no such effect, the researchers found.

When the team inhibited Rab27a, a protein and key factor in vesicle secretion, in the mammary glands of depressed mothers, vesicle secretion fell by 58%, and the cognitive and neurodevelopmental deficits in their pups improved significantly.

The researchers also found that microRNA in milk vesicles from depressed mothers blocks a “brake” receptor called mGluR8 in pups’ brains. Without this brake, brain regions can become overstimulated, impairing the development of neural connections. As a result, new brain cells are more active overall but respond more weakly to memory tasks, helping explain the cognitive problems seen in pups nursed by depressed mothers.

The study offers the key findings of both a new communication pathway and a microRNA-based mechanism of inheritance between mothers and babies, according to the researchers.

Breastfeeding is widely seen as good for babies’ brain development, but this study also suggests that breastfeeding by mothers with postpartum depression may have a “double-edged effect on offspring health,” the researchers wrote.

“Elucidating the molecular mechanisms linking maternal postnatal depression to offspring neurological outcomes therefore holds considerable public health value and underscores the urgent need for targeted maternal mental health interventions during lactation,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.title: 90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.content:
Chinese prosecutors have exposed an invoice-trading network that illegally traded special value-added tax (VAT) invoices totaling more than 7.4 billion yuan ($1.1 billion) over three years.

Under the guise of a Shanghai-based advertising business, the group profited by issuing and charging service fees for fake invoices from shell companies it registered to customers seeking to illegally claim tax deductions — which can be claimed for special tax invoices, but not ordinary tax invoices in China — domestic media reported Tuesday.

The case has exposed major weaknesses in business-registration oversight, tax monitoring, and financial regulators’ ability to detect suspicious fund flows between affiliated company accounts, according to experts.

From June 2025 to June 2026, more than 90 criminal suspects on the case were processed by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Procuratorate, some of whom were ordered to return their illegal gains. Processing of the case is ongoing.

The group’s ringleaders, surnamed Cui and Shen, first had employees register over 70 shell companies in their own names. Invoices were then handled via three steps: a sales team first connected with customers, who transferred money to the group in order to receive invoices; then a team obtained invoices from both the operation’s registered shell companies or legitimate businesses with unused invoicing quotas; before another team returned funds to customers following invoice-fee deductions. Customers were charged a service fee of between 7% and 13% of the invoice value.

Chinese tax law requires contracts, fund transfers, invoices, and movement of goods to align. Falsely issuing invoices can result in fines of up to 500,000 yuan, while tax dodgers may be fined up to five times the underpaid tax. Both carry risks of criminal prosecution.

To circumvent the law, customers transferred the full invoice amount to the group, which then transferred the remaining funds back to the customer through a separate, third account.

The group illegally traded over 7.4 billion yuan in VAT invoices, involving more than 420 million yuan in VAT. It also conducted illegal foreign-exchange transactions totaling 420 million yuan.

“The scale of the crimes, the degree of organization, and the length of time over which they were committed were all relatively unusual,” Li Huaisheng, a professor at the School of Criminal Justice at China University of Political Science and Law, told state media outlet CCTV.

Similar cases involving companies that obtained invoices through intermediaries have made national headlines in recent years. Last year, a group allegedly used 15 shell companies to falsely issue almost 3,500 special VAT invoices totaling 300 million yuan, domestic media reported. The defendant, surnamed Li, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison and fined 500,000 yuan.

According to the State Taxation Administration, such companies often disguise themselves as consulting, advertising, or other business services in industries with low fixed-asset requirements, long industrial chains, and large transaction values, such as recycling, road freight transport, and information technology consulting.

Li Huaisheng recommended that market regulatory authorities establish early-warning models to flag suspicious company registrations, and tax authorities improve big-data checks on invoices, capital, contracts, and goods.

In an interview with CCTV, Zhou Xianbao, a lawyer at BZW Law Firm in Beijing, also recommended establishing a system requiring real-name authorization for invoice issuance and formal tax-compliance commitments.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.title: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.content:
When most Chinese people think of World War I, they think of it as a “European war.” This is not simply an oversight. It is the result of a century of forgetting.

Few people are aware that between 1916 and 1918, Britain and France recruited around 140,000 Chinese laborers from Shandong, Hebei, Guangdong, Hong Kong, and other regions to work on the Western Front. They dug trenches, built defenses, and transported ammunition. After the fighting ended, they stayed on to help with reconstruction, clearing battlefields and filling in shell craters. Some did not return home until 1922.

Sending laborers overseas was not simply a matter of supplying manpower. It was also part of a carefully considered political strategy. Politicians such as Liang Shiyi — an influential adviser to then-President Yuan Shikai — believed that Germany and Austria-Hungary were unlikely to defeat Britain and France, and advocated a “laborers-as-soldiers” strategy that would allow China to participate indirectly in the war and break its diplomatic isolation. Meanwhile, figures associated with the New Culture Movement, an early 20th-century intellectual and cultural reform movement, saw sending laborers overseas as an opportunity to develop China’s working class. They included Li Shizeng, a French-educated anarchist and organizer of the Diligent Work-Frugal Study Movement, and Cai Yuanpei, a leading educator and president of Peking University.

Yet China’s participation in the Allied war effort did not bring the diplomatic gains its leaders had hoped for. At the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, the victorious powers agreed to transfer Germany’s former rights in Shandong province to Japan rather than return them to China, a decision that helped spark the May Fourth Movement, a wave of student-led protests that became a turning point in modern Chinese history.

The contributions of the Chinese laborers themselves also received little recognition. When they returned home in the 1920s, they found a country gripped by political upheaval and were often met with indifference or even suspicion.

The result was a double erasure. The West forgot their contributions, while China forgot their sacrifices.

In July 2019, a delegation from Belgium’s In Flanders Fields Museum visited Shanghai University. The two institutions agreed to jointly investigate, excavate, study, and exhibit the remains of Chinese labor camps on the Western Front during World War I. By then, scholars from the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Germany, Canada, and other countries, led by Professor Nicholas J. Saunders of the University of Bristol, had spent nearly a decade systematically surveying the physical remains and landscapes of the Western Front. Yet the Chinese labor camps remained a missing piece of the puzzle. Although frequently mentioned in historical records, they had never been systematically investigated or excavated by archaeologists.

In May 2023, Shanghai University officially launched the Chinese Labour Corps (CLC) Camp Project, in collaboration with the In Flanders Fields Museum, Ghent University, and Howest University of Applied Sciences. A non-invasive geophysical survey was completed in April 2024, and excavation began in February 2025. The project concluded in March 2026.

Before we began digging, information about the Chinese labor camps could be found in historical documents, but it was fragmented. Official military archives paid little attention to these noncombatants from China, while local records offered a more vivid picture. One example is the diary of Belgian priest Achiel Van Walleghem. In August 1917, he recorded the presence of two Chinese labor camps in the village of Reningelst, near the Belgian town of Ypres, a major battleground during World War I. In January 1918, he noted that some shop owners had begun learning Chinese to attract the laborers. And on the night of April 13, 1918, when one of the camps came under German artillery fire, he recorded 10 deaths and more than 30 injuries. In fact, the threat of shelling had already prompted strikes and protests among Chinese laborers in late 1917. British military records provided another crucial detail: the 75th Company of the Chinese Labour Corps was stationed there from August 1917 to April 1918. Gu Xingqing, an interpreter for the Chinese laborers, also described the night of the bombardment in his memoirs.

Historical records also reveal differences in how the British and French treated Chinese laborers. Those recruited by the French worked alongside locals under relatively loose supervision, making the remains of their camps difficult to identify. By contrast, British-recruited laborers — organized into the Chinese Labour Corps — were subject to military-style discipline and housed in enclosed camps surrounded by barbed wire. The camps followed a military organizational structure. Initially, each battalion consisted of 1,031 men, with 10 to 12 sharing a tent. Each camp had just one iron gate, which was locked at night. To leave, the men had to obtain permission and travel in groups, and they were forbidden from venturing more than 3 miles away.

Documents even record how the laborers died and were commemorated. The leading causes of death were tuberculosis and the 1918 influenza pandemic, rather than artillery fire. However, the death tolls vary considerably: British records put the figure at around 2,000, French records at approximately 1,500, while Chinese figures suggest that at least 20,000 did not come back to China. Chinese laborers recruited by the British were buried in military cemeteries. Their headstones followed the same style as those of British soldiers, but bore inscriptions in both languages, including the laborers’ names and places of origin in Chinese, alongside English epitaphs such as “Though Dead, He Still Liveth” and “A Noble Duty Bravely Done.”

After the war, returning French and Belgian residents sometimes blamed the surviving Chinese laborers for social unrest. Yet the laborers were still bound by their contracts and remained to clear the battlefields. Some stayed in France to work in mines until 1929, while others married and settled there permanently.

In June 1921, the British military issued a total of 93,357 commemorative medals at its Chinese labor base in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao. Some were presented in person, while others were mailed to the laborers’ homes. Even today, these medals can occasionally be found in remote villages across Shandong and Hebei.

If historical records tell us so much, why was archaeological excavation necessary? Because documents can tell us where the camps were and what happened there, but they cannot fully reveal what the camps looked like. Their layouts were never systematically recorded, and the sites had long since been cleared and leveled after the war. This is where archaeology comes in.

The non-invasive geophysical surveys of the site we commenced in spring 2024 used high-resolution electromagnetic induction and magnetic survey techniques. The data revealed numerous anomalies at depths of 1 to 1.5 meters, including fragments of artillery shells of various calibers. This was consistent with local farmers’ accounts of still unearthing shrapnel when plowing their fields.

The two intersecting trenches excavated in February 2025 covered 512 square meters. We uncovered two ash pits with traces of burning at their bases, eight shell craters ranging from 1 to 5 meters in diameter, foundation stones from barracks, tent pole bases, and clusters of communication cables. For the first time, we were able to reconstruct the layout of a camp whose physical arrangement had never been documented, identifying its barracks, tent area, and main road.

We also unearthed more than 520 artifacts that offered glimpses of everyday life: belt buckles, Royal Engineers and Royal Artillery cap badges, surgical forceps from a field hospital, piles of bullet and shell casings, and nearly intact British army-issued rum jars and lemonade bottles. If historical documents help us understand the Chinese labor camps, archaeology brings us closer to the people who lived in them.

The significance of the project extends beyond the discoveries themselves. For a long time, World War I archaeology was mainly the preserve of metal detectorists, while professional archaeologists generally avoided the subject. This began to change with archaeological investigations conducted ahead of construction of Belgium’s A19 highway in 2002, which helped establish the field as a serious area of academic research.

Our excavation of the Chinese labor camp was the first of its kind to be led by a Chinese academic institution.

The project also opened up new avenues for Chinese archaeological research in two fields. The first is conflict archaeology, which looks beyond weapons and battlefields to examine entire societies caught up in war. The second is industrial archaeology, which can shift attention away from industrial achievements alone and toward the people and human efforts behind them. At its heart, this approach is about focusing on people rather than objects.

The Chinese laborers were not merely supporting characters in World War I. They found themselves caught up in a conflict involving Eastern and Western societies, working and dying amid misunderstanding and hostility. Yet even in the face of constant danger, they found ways to express themselves, creating trench art engraved with dragon motifs and landscape scenes.

Even the idyllic scenery of Flanders today was partly shaped by Chinese laborers, who filled in many of the trenches and craters left by the war. The experiences of these 140,000 ordinary Chinese men lie at the intersection of 20th-century Chinese and world history, reflecting the interactions and tensions between different societies.

“In Flanders fields the poppies blow / Between the crosses, row on row,” wrote John McCrae in his poem “In Flanders Fields.” Today, the poppies still bloom every year. But among those fields and crosses, Chinese laborers once lived and worked. Archaeology cannot bring them back to life, but it can give the soil a voice and remind the world that they were here.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A British soldier and a Chinese laborer examine written identification ribbons during a roll call at a Chinese Labour Corps camp in Samer, France, May 26, 1918. From the collection of the Imperial War Museums)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.title: China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.content:
China’s popular chili sauce brand Lao Gan Ma has drawn public scrutiny for adopting AI-driven production, allegedly at the expense of hundreds of jobs.

The controversy began after multiple domestic media outlets reported that Li Xin, Lao Gan Ma’s executive vice general manager and chief quality officer, touted the company’s use of AI at a provincial business conference last month in China’s southwestern Guizhou province, where the sauce originates.

Li reportedly said the number of workers on one production line fell from over 600 to just 48 after the company introduced an AI-powered pepper inspection system last year. He added that the company’s 2025 revenue reached a record 5.4 billion yuan ($810 million), crediting AI with reducing production errors to almost 0%. Li’s full remarks are not publicly available online.

The company’s history of touting its dedication to working people has drawn particular criticism over the potential layoffs, according to a commentary by Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper. Lao Gan Ma’s founder, Tao Huabi, whose portrait adorns the brand’s jars and is known across China, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997.

As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal has garnered more than 120 million views on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users said automation is a standard part of industrial upgrading that can help improve efficiency and ensure consistent product quality. Others argued that the company should consider its responsibilities to workers.

“If everything is done by AI and robots, and people have no jobs or income, they won’t be able to afford to consume. What’s the point of producing so much, then?” one highly upvoted Weibo comment read.

Many also called for a boycott of the brand, reposting one user’s comment: “If you lay off workers, we’ll get your products pulled from the shelves.”

Responding to the controversy, Lao Gan Ma human resources representatives stated in an interview with domestic media on Oct. 26 that Li had not referenced staffing figures in his remarks.

In response to the company’s denial, users scrutinized its social insurance enrollment figures, which often reflect a company’s workforce size. Corporate filings disclosed by business data platforms Tianyancha and Qichacha show that the number of employees insured by the company fell from nearly 3,000 in 2022 to 740 in 2025 — a roughly 75% decline.

However, changes in social insurance enrollment do not prove AI use drove the layoffs, as other factors such as retirement and employee turnover also affect employment figures.

The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative impacts on employment. On Oct. 23, the State Council issued guidelines calling for “maximizing AI’s potential to create jobs, empower workers in traditional occupations, improve job quality, and stimulate innovation” while “slowing down the impact of AI-related job replacement.”

The guidelines also urge companies to deploy AI with caution in labor-intensive industries. They encourage employers to provide transition periods for displaced workers, give advance notice before large-scale AI rollouts, and offer retraining and support for locating new jobs.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019174/Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.title: Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019174/Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.content:
When glimpsing the Terracotta Army for the first time, almost everyone is awestruck by its sheer scale: thousands of armored clay figures standing in perfect formation, their gray earthen bodies stretching rank upon rank. At first glance, the ghostly 2,000-year-old soldiers look as if they were cast from a single mold.

But look closer, and the impression of uniformity begins to dissolve. No two faces are exactly alike: brows thick or faint, eyes wide open or slightly narrowed, cheekbones high or low, jawlines rounded or square. When viewed individually, each warrior is far more than a figure: it is a work of art as intricate as many Renaissance statues.

Zhao Hui (Steve Zhao) has spent much of the past 25 years trying to capture this hidden artistry. A veteran photographer who trained under cinematographer Peter Levy in the 1980s, Zhao became well known for his portraiture. His 1996 project “China Story” has toured more than 30 countries.

Since 2001, he has applied his talent for portrait photography to the Terracotta Army, amassing images of more than 2,000 figures. The works offer a striking new perspective on the warriors, often zooming in close enough to highlight the carved stroke of an eyebrow, the turn of a cheekbone, or even faint fingerprints left in the clay by a Qin dynasty artisan.

For Zhao, the project is also about more than changing perceptions of the Terracotta Army; it’s part of a wider effort to document, classify, and analyze it. The vast photo archive helps researchers understand the production processes, craftsmanship, and organization behind the relics — and, most importantly for Zhao, the anonymous master sculptors who carved them.

In this interview, Sixth Tone sat down with Zhao to discuss how his project began and how it has shaped our understanding of the Terracotta Warriors. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: The Terracotta Army has long been a research focus for archaeologists and historians, but what led you to study them through high-definition photography?

Zhao: At first, it was just a routine assignment. In 2001, the China National Tourism Administration approached me to photograph the Terracotta Warriors. It was a rare opportunity, of course.

My task was to capture the warriors in the finest possible detail. That is far harder than most people imagine: heritage photography is not simply pointing a lens at an object. Every click of the shutter is a repeated negotiation with light, angle, material, and patience. The warriors are massive and their preservation conditions special, so every shoot requires meticulous preparation and on-site coordination.

After taking enough high-definition images, I began to notice striking details — the rise and fall of a brow ridge, the hooked line at the corner of an eye, the marks left by the sculptors’ hands. Perhaps it’s because I’m a portrait photographer, trained to observe people.

Looking at all those warrior faces, I noticed not only the differences between them but couldn’t stop wondering how those differences came about. Behind them lie the techniques and aesthetics of their makers. That is how I began studying the craftsmanship of the Terracotta Warriors — 25 years ago now.

Sixth Tone: You have said the creation of the Terracotta Army was not just a feat of manufacturing, but an artistic process. Why do you believe that?

Zhao: You have to distinguish between three separate steps in the production process. First, the rough cores of the heads, hands, and torsos were made separately; then a layer of fine clay was applied over the cores, and the details refined; finally, the parts were assembled and joined, air-dried, fired in kilns, and painted.

The key point is that the heads and torsos were made separately and joined only at the end. The torsos were mainly the work of craftsmen. They coiled strips of clay round and round to build up the body, tapering gradually from the legs to the waist, then carved the robes, armor, armor studs, and knotted cords. I’ve taken close-ups of torsos; magnified, you can see the traces of clay coils stacking and tightening upward.

As for the heads: a rough core was made first, then ears, topknots, braids, and caps or headcloths attached, followed by the fine carving of the facial features. This was the heart of the entire production — and the people responsible were probably not ordinary craftsmen, but a group of highly skilled sculptors and their assistants.

Sixth Tone: What evidence led you to that conclusion?

Zhao: Look carefully at the faces, and you’d reach the same conclusion. Those vivid, highly individualized faces are works of art: brows range from thick to sword-shaped; eyes are wide open, slightly narrowed, or upturned; the fullness of the cheeks, the height of the cheekbones, the roundness or squareness of the chins — all of them are different. These details embody each figure’s appearance, character, and psychology.

By carefully comparing different images, I can even recognize the signature techniques and styles of individual sculptors. Now, whenever I see a certain technique, I feel I’ve run into an old friend, and I want to say to that nameless sculptor: “Hi, it’s you again.”

In my view, these face-makers who left no names behind can rightly be called China’s Michelangelos.

Sixth Tone: But there’s a problem here. Even a sculptor as industrious as Michelangelo only produced a few dozen sculptures in his lifetime, while the Terracotta Army contains an estimated 8,000 figures. It’s hard to imagine so many high-level sculptors were available at that time.

Zhao: Good point. These sculptors made only faces — far less work than carving an entire figure — but 8,000 is still a staggering number. So I expect there was a “master-and-apprentice” model being used during production.

I’ve found some supporting clues: comparing groups of figures similar in style and technique, I often find that within a group there is one figure of finer modeling and more accurate proportions, while the others are relatively rough and unpolished. The former likely came from a master’s hand, the latter from apprentices.

Even so, the scale of the project still astounds me. In just over three years, they produced some 8,000 life-size figures with varied faces — a feat that pushed the limits of stamina and craft, and a testament to the Qin Empire’s extraordinary organizational capacity.

Sixth Tone: Back to your methodology. Your findings are largely based on observing the warriors up close through high-definition photographs. Now that 3D digitization technology is maturing, do you think it could provide further research breakthroughs?

Zhao: Digitization shouldn’t be oversimplified. If you can’t even take a good flat photograph, then creating a 3D model will be even harder. The workload and cost of 3D data acquisition are far higher than in 2D, and the processing difficulty grows exponentially.

Of course, photographing the warriors does “distort.” Turning three dimensions into two — how could it not? A single photograph is never a complete replica of “reality”; it is constrained by angle, lighting, and timing, and it carries the photographer’s choices and judgments. It is essentially a limited rendering of the objective world under specific conditions.

But don’t forget: my photography is a long process. When one photograph becomes 1,000, then 10,000; when images of different times, angles, and individuals converge into a system that can be cross-verified — photography becomes a cognitive tool for observing, comparing, and deducing. It prompts people to see cultural relics anew and provides material for further historical interpretation. That’s why I now call my work the “Visual Art of Archaeology.”

(Header image: Terracotta Warriors. Photo by Zhao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019171/Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.title: Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019171/Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.content:
A new study has found that women and adolescents, not only men, helped build China’s 2,000-year-old Terracotta Army.

The study used fingerprints found on a portion of the 8,000 statues of soldiers and horses in the tomb of China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, to assess their makers’ ages and sexes for the first time, domestic media reported this week. The research was conducted by the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum in Xi’an, capital of the northwestern Shaanxi province, and Shandong University’s School of Archaeology, in the eastern city of Jinan, and will be published in Volume 82 of the Journal of Cultural Heritage at the end of the year.

Past studies of labor forces during the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) relied primarily on legal texts and largely treated men as the default workers, with 15 reportedly the minimum age for service. Prior research has also neglected to examine the genders and ages of the workers behind the Terracotta Army.

Previous analysis of the identities behind ancient fingerprints has also failed to account for factors such as similarities in fingerprint size and ridge distribution between women and teenage boys, differences between ancient and modern fingerprint size, and clay shrinkage after firing, the researchers said.

In contrast, the new study used a Bayesian mixture model to account for these factors and estimate fingerprint-related parameters at both the individual and population levels through probabilities. The model assigned the fingerprints possible ages and sexes, analyzed their mean ridge breadth (MRB) or thickness, and compared these to growth curve-projected values.

The team analyzed 79 well-preserved fingerprints from 36 figures in Pit 1 of the Qinshihuang mausoleum. The results showed that 45% belonged to males, 32.7% to females, and 22.3% to juveniles under 15.

The research provided quantitative biological evidence challenging previous assumptions that large-scale craft production in the Qin dynasty relied only on adult male labor. It also offers a better understanding of the Qin dynasty’s labor systems and institutionalization of apprenticeships.

While textual records and artifact-based inscriptions had previously challenged the theory that the project relied exclusively on male labor, the team’s findings offer a new framework for quantitatively studying ancient craft production and the ages and sexes of the laborers involved.

“This biological evidence highly corroborates numerous historical records, vividly reconstructing the production scene in the Qin dynasty’s state-run workshops where men and women served together, and adult artisans worked alongside juveniles, who may have been helpers or apprentices,” the study’s authors wrote.

However, they also identified several limitations of the study. For one, the percentages attributed to adult and juvenile, and male and female fingerprints may not equal the percentages of actual workers with those traits, they said, as multiple fingerprints may have come from the same person.

They also wrote that more experienced workers may have left fewer fingerprints, which may have increased the proportion of juvenile prints, while the reference database was both based on modern Czech-Caucasian fingerprints, not East-Asian prints, and contained more female samples, potentially skewing the results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Types of fingerprints on the terracotta figures. From Journal of Cultural Heritage and Xinhua)

World.title: Reel to Real: The ‘Voy Boys’ and the Movie That Never Was
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019166/Reel to Real: The ‘Voy Boys’ and the Movie That Never Was
World.content:
It’s late 2024, and Bilali Yasen barrels toward goal, the football skipping at his feet as he narrowly passes his opposition. In the pitch darkness, he hears only the sound of his heartbeat and the faint calls of his teammates.

He shoots and hits the back of the net, capping a 5-1 rout.

Having lost their first four games at China’s 2024 National Blind Football Championship, the win marks a major milestone for the 16-year-old striker and the rest of the “Voy Boys,” a newly formed team of visually impaired players from China’s northwestern Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

Born with glaucoma and cataracts, Bilali had never expected to play football again after his sight began fading at age 7. But at the final whistle, he is brimming with confidence and even envisioning a call-up to the national squad.

China has had a national men’s blind football team since 2006, winning eight Asian titles as well as silver at the 2008 Beijing Paralympic Games.

Yet the sport remains largely unknown in the country. For this young Xinjiang team, the struggle to secure sufficient long-term funding, along with professional coaching and management, is just beginning.

Even more improbably, the Voy Boys wouldn’t exist if not for a movie that was never made.

Cameras, action!

Su Yiyan, a dancer turned movie producer in Beijing, had been toying with a story about blind football for a while before starting production in 2021. The idea centered on a disillusioned big-city football coach who takes over a small-town team of visually impaired children, with both sides finding healing in each other.

Initially, she planned to base the movie in the southwestern Yunnan province, which already had a relatively strong tradition in the sport, but was encouraged instead to head north by Shanghai’s Xinjiang aid office, part of a national paired-assistance program in which wealthier cities coordinate economic, educational, and infrastructure projects in underdeveloped areas.

In the spring of 2021, Su and her crew arrived in Xinjiang to find local boys who could appear in the movie. The only real criteria were that they needed to be visually impaired and in good physical condition.

After visiting schools in several towns and cities, they traveled to Shache County, on the southern rim of the Taklimakan Desert in Xinjiang’s Kashgar prefecture, where they invited 13 students aged 13 to 14 from its Special Education School to take part in a basic running test.

“I was stunned. Every one of them had the bravery to run,” recalled Su, highlighting the fact that it takes immense courage to do that when you can’t see clearly.

The following summer, two physical education teachers from Kashgar were drafted in to begin training the children in skills and tactics at the school.

Blind football uses a modified ball with bells inside, allowing players to locate it by sound, and is played on an enclosed 40-by-20-meter pitch. Each team fields four visually impaired outfield players, all in blackout eye masks, and one sighted or partially sighted goalkeeper. Teams can also use a sighted off-field guide to call and direct players toward the goal.

Much of the initial training focuses on building the players’ courage to run and prepare for the inevitable collisions.

Abudumijiti Memet, a 19-year-old defender with congenital cataracts, said he was frightened at first, and would always lean backward when moving at pace. “The coach told me that the more afraid you are, the more likely you are to get hurt when someone runs into you,” he said. “Players who keep moving forward are less likely to be injured.”

Zhang Jian, head coach for the Shanghai Blind Football Team, provided remote support in 2021 and briefly led on-site training in 2023. He was surprised by how quickly the team took shape and impressed by their boldness, coordination, stamina, and general enthusiasm. Zhang took special note of Bilali, whose performances were “beyond everyone’s expectations.”

“It’s rare for someone of his height to perform as well as he does,” he said, referring to Bilali, who stands at a relatively short 1.65 meters. “He wasn’t good at dribbling at first, and his coordination could be poor … but he was certainly the bravest and the most determined in matches.”

For Bilali, it was a joy to be playing the “beautiful game” again. “Once I started running, I felt I’d rediscovered a familiar feeling,” he said, explaining that football was his favorite pastime before his eyesight faded. “The wind was blowing past my ears — it made me happy. Only on the pitch can we run without fear.”

Missing the target

Although things looked good on the field, by 2022 the movie project was stalling. The pandemic had caused scheduling issues, and some promised production financing never materialized. The money the crew did have — mainly from Su’s friends and connections — was vanishing fast.

Attempts to drum up further investment had all failed.

“To film my original idea required tens of millions of yuan, but we had no backers,” said Su, explaining that she had initially hoped to cast a big-name actor in the coach role. “One director suggested I change the focus of the movie to the children, which would only cost about 5 million yuan ($740,000). But we still couldn’t raise the money.”

With the project still in its early stages, she decided to shut it down. That summer, she flew to Xinjiang to break the news to the cast and their coaches.

Without a movie, there was no one to organize coaching or matches. “We’d just discovered blind football, and with it found hope,” said Bilali. “We all feared that the opportunity would disappear and we’d feel lost again.”

After returning to Beijing, Su couldn’t stop thinking about the children. “You can’t give people something and then take it away, especially a group of visually impaired kids so eager to play football,” she recalled thinking.

A year later, Su quit her job and teamed up with filmmaker Li Zhiwei to continue the project as a documentary about Xinjiang’s first blind football team. They used their own money, a bank loan, and about 260,000 yuan borrowed from friends to rent recording equipment and buy supplies including balls, goals, eye masks, and pitchside barriers.

“To save money, we sometimes took three connecting flights in a single day, getting up at 3 a.m. to reach the airport and arriving in Shache at nearly 11 p.m.,” Su once told domestic media. “Our crew spent no more than 100 yuan a night on accommodation. When we ran out of money, we went back out to raise more funds.”

In the summer of 2023, Zhang invited four boys from the Xinjiang team, including Bilali, to his annual training camp at the Shanghai School for the Blind, where they could learn from veteran players.

In addition to football practice, the trip included visits to the Shanghai Zoo, Shanghai Tower, and a café staffed by visually impaired workers. For Bilali, it was a glimpse into another world.

His elder sister, Maierwanimu Yasen, said her brother was different upon his return. After losing his sight, he’d become withdrawn and less talkative, and physically weaker, “but now he told us much more. He’d realized that visually impaired people could do all kinds of things — not just massage, but run cafés and pursue other careers,” referring to the default vocation for blind people in China.

He also now felt that if the team trained hard enough, it could play in more major cities, taking on China’s 10 or so provincial teams.

Taking another shot

In October 2023, Su’s crew arranged an exhibition match between the Xinjiang youth squad and the Shanghai Blind Football Team. The game was played on the pitch at Shache’s special education school, with relatives and local officials watching on.

“That’s when I first saw them play,” said Maierwanimu. “I felt then that they could really do it. I realized this wasn’t just a game they were playing for fun.”

The Xinjiang team won 2-0.

Almost a year later, the Xinjiang Disabled Persons’ Federation announced the official establishment of the region’s first men’s blind football team, comprising 11 members, and the opening of a dedicated arena and training facility in Korla, almost 1,ooo kilometers by road from Shache.

The team — nicknamed the Voy Boys for the players’ shout of “voy” (Spanish for “I go”) to warn others they are moving — immediately began preparing for the 2024 National Blind Football Championship in Fuzhou, capital of the eastern Fujian province.

Bilali’s five-goal display in the team’s final match of the tournament provided the climax to Su’s documentary, “Voy Boys,” which went on limited release nationwide in July 2026. So far, it has grossed just over 340,000 yuan, far less than the 3 million yuan it cost to make.

Final whistle?

When the cameras stopped rolling in 2024, life carried on for the team.

Xinjiang finished in ninth place in Fuzhou. However, to encourage them and other newly formed squads to keep competing, all participating teams received automatic qualification for the combined National Games for Persons with Disabilities and the National Special Olympic Games, co-hosted in December 2025 by the southern Guangdong province along with the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions.

The team went on to finish seventh in that competition and then fourth at the 2026 national championship, held in Korla.

Luo Chengmian, a 28-year-old former blind football player from the eastern Zhejiang province, took over as head coach in 2024. He was assisted by Mahemuti Rozi, vice principal of the Shache’s special education school, who’d followed the team’s progress from the beginning.

“At first, I thought playing football was unnecessary, so I didn’t pay much attention,” said Mahemuti. “But in every match I saw how they gave everything they had. They fought with everything, always pushing to play out the entire match. It really moved me.”

However, the team has struggled to recruit for certain positions, including goalkeepers and off-field guides. Often, candidates are found just a day or two before a match and lack experience.

The players being separated by large distances is another challenge. Because the Shache school launched its high school program only in 2025, Bilali, Abudumijiti, and five other players had earlier transferred to a special education school in the Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, about 1,700 kilometers away, to continue their studies.

After Luo quit in late 2025 over disputes related to his salary and the players’ subsidies, it was up to Mahemuti to keep the team going. He juggled the job alongside his responsibilities overseeing the school’s logistics and cafeteria, and connected with coaches in Yunnan for remote guidance and training plans. This December, he aims to help the players in Changji arrange internships in Shache so they can restart training with the rest of the team.

Without a regular coach, those in Changji had to organize their own training sessions before morning reading and in the hour between classes and evening study.

“If we get the chance, we just want time to train, a better pitch, medicine, and a coach,” Abudumijiti said. “At least we chose this path ourselves. We want to keep walking it until we can’t go any farther.”

By contrast, Luo now coaches the Sichuan Blind Football Team’s women’s squad, based in Chengdu, capital of the southwestern Sichuan province, where players train six hours a day, receive daily allowances, and enjoy full medical insurance and access to traditional Chinese medicine massage services.

Su told Sixth Tone that the Xinjiang players receive a few hundred yuan a month in food subsidies, and hope for further support, including for medical supplies. The Xinjiang Disabled Persons’ Federation did not respond to Sixth Tone’s request for comment.

At least four of the Voy Boys are expected to graduate high school next June, creating a dilemma over what to do next.

For visually impaired people in China, massage therapy remains one of the most accessible careers. Bilali and Abudumijiti both chose massage courses after transferring to Changji, yet the school didn’t even have textbooks for visually impaired students. They had to take photographs of the materials with their phones and use text-to-speech apps to understand the content.

“And I feel this kind of work often means staying indoors. You can’t feel the sunshine,” Abudumijiti said. “That made me reluctant to pursue it, even though many people told me it was the most suitable profession for someone like me.”

Without that option, though, he’s unsure about the future. The son of a police officer and gas station worker, he’s now thinking about working with his older brother, who plans to open an auto repair shop.

“If we have to rely on our families’ money to continue training outside school, honestly, that’d be too much of a burden,” Abudumijiti added. “A dream is a dream, but we also need to plan. What happens when we get too old to play and haven’t earned enough money? We can’t live on dreams.”

Su, now 51, has quit show business and is paying off her debts working as a bungee fitness instructor in Beijing. She argued that, like anyone, disabled people need opportunities: “It’s us, as able-bodied people, who imagine that they can’t do this or that. We assume they don’t need to create social value, and that as long as they are safe, that’s enough. But they don’t want to live that way. They still want to find their own worth.”

After an accident during training earlier this year involving a Xinjiang player, Su proposed the China Blind Football Players’ Sports Injury Protection Fund, aiming to provide medical insurance coverage to registered players. The idea is still awaiting approval from authorities.

In March 2025, Bilali was selected for the national team’s reserve squad, based in Fuzhou. For the first time, he encountered professional gym equipment, a dedicated medical team, and an individualized training plan. “The intensity was high. I’d never experienced such demanding training in Xinjiang,” he said.

Later, he joined a national team training camp ahead of the recent 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, but wasn’t selected. China took gold on Oct. 23 after defeating the hosts 1-0 in the final.

“I’m looking forward to eventually going back to Xinjiang to see my family and teammates, but I’m also afraid that I won’t be able to train anymore,” he said. “I worry that my skills will fall behind.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A poster for “Voy Boys.” Courtesy of Su)

World.title: Rack and Ruin: How China’s Trillion-Yuan Womenswear Market Lost Its Color
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019172/Rack and Ruin: How China’s Trillion-Yuan Womenswear Market Lost Its Color
World.content:
Editor’s note: According to Syntu Data, e-commerce platforms made a combined 1.6 trillion yuan ($239 billion) in sales last year during “Double Eleven,” China’s annual online shopping event in November. Clothing accounted for 14%, driven largely by womenswear.

Zhou Keke used to get excited when she ordered clothes online. Not anymore. Now she returns about 70% of what she buys, either because of poor quality or because the dimensions don’t match what was listed.

Browsing the Chinese e-commerce platform Taobao recently, she stumbled across a store clearing out unsold stock from a decade ago. She says it was like stepping into another world. Compared with the “simple and vanilla” skirts, scarves, and tops on sale today, she found designs that were bold, irregular, thoughtful, even avant-garde and ingenious.

“So this is what fashion looked like when the economy was booming?” thought Zhou, who lives in China’s eastern Zhejiang province. She bought seven pieces for less than 1,000 yuan ($150) and posted a review on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, receiving nearly 10,000 likes and 1,000 comments.

The womenswear market in the Chinese mainland exceeded 1.23 trillion yuan in 2025, up from 619.7 billion yuan in 2011, according to iiMedia Research. Still, social media is today awash with complaints from female consumers over the blandness of modern clothing. As one netizen put it, “Beauty used to come in 100 forms; now even ugliness is mass-produced.”

However, industry insiders argue that this isn’t a one-sided problem but rather a feedback loop. They say that, as China’s economy slows, most online shoppers are tightening their belts and are less willing to spend on distinctive or niche designs, so brands have no option but to follow what’s selling.

Meanwhile, in the physical space, more consumers can only choose between fast-fashion outlets and luxury brands, as mid-range and boutique stores continue to disappear from malls nationwide.

How’s it looking?

Li Li, a 19-year-old university student from Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, recently found a matching top and miniskirt — vivid red with huge black embroidered flower buds — at a vintage clothes market.

“You could tell at a glance it was meant to stand out. A lot of womenswear now comes in muted Morandi colors, or other pale shades,” she says, adding that clothes in the 2000s were “much brighter.”

Li notes that when a piece sells well on Xiaohongshu and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, there’s immediately a rush of near-identical versions.

Zhou says clothes today feel cut-and-paste, with only the logos changing. “If everyone’s designing like that, honestly, what am I supposed to choose? All I can do is compare the price and the fabric. It’s so boring,” she adds.

Gu Hawen, a fashion designer at Unreal World, a clothing company based in the eastern Jiangsu province, recalls that when she entered the industry in 2019, designs in the domestic womenswear market were flourishing. She began noticing a slide in 2023.

“Whether you look at high-end luxury, affordable luxury, or ordinary brands, it’s the same story now,” she says. “Everything is more alike. Some clothing has been stripped back so far that there isn’t a single decorative detail.”

She explains that an unspoken chain of imitation runs through the Chinese womenswear industry: mass-market and fast-fashion brands follow designer and luxury brands in terms of color, silhouette, and other details, and online shops follow mass-market brands.

“The public is more receptive to designs from big-name brands. If companies want to sell, we have to keep up with international tastes and aesthetics,” says Gu, although she stresses that “we only take inspiration; we don’t copy outright. Online sellers copy brands wholesale. It’s a vicious cycle.”

Chen Chen launched her own online clothing brand this year, selling products that stick closely to the design concepts of major labels. The first item she listed, inspired by the British fashion house Vivienne Westwood, sold more than 100 pieces — no easy feat. Within six months, several items promoted on her page had become modest hits on Xiaohongshu, approaching 1,000 sales.

Chen feels modern Chinese consumers tend to follow the crowd, and tastes are becoming increasingly uniform as e-commerce platforms grow.

“Instead of discovering things for yourself, you end up in an algorithm bubble,” she says. “Maybe the first time you see an item of clothing, you don’t even like the style. But the platform keeps pushing it, and then it’s all you see. Eventually, everyone gets conditioned into the same very narrow idea of what looks good.”

She argues that not all consumers recognize or value original design. “You can be selling in exactly the same category, but someone else slaps ‘same style as Chanel’ on their listing and wipes the floor with you.”

In Chen’s view, online womenswear brands that invest in developing unique designs are being squeezed out. Spending six months refining a collection no longer works, as everyone is chasing the next viral hit, and keeping up is the only way to make money.

“Trends change way too fast now,” she adds. “A brand might plan its collection for months, but by the time it hits the rails, everything looks dated. Then a new bestseller suddenly appears, and they have no choice but to follow. … Copying a bestseller means lower costs, less risk, and higher profit margins.”

Imitation game

Zhou feels China’s womenswear market is not only becoming more conservative and homogeneous but also that brands are cutting corners on materials compared with a decade ago, creating a false economy. “Brands are becoming less responsible, so more shoppers are sending items back more often. But returns cost the sellers money. It’s a vicious cycle.”

Industry insiders argue the root of the issue lies in an underlying shift in consumer psychology, as younger consumers place greater emphasis on value for money.

“It’s become harder for people to earn money these past few years,” says Chen. “They’re expecting more from every penny.”

With consumers more price-sensitive, brands have grown cautious about what they charge, applying pressure further down the supply chain.

“Sewing workers are putting in more effort, but their pay hasn’t gone up, so the quality keeps getting worse,” Chen explains. “The pressure on workers at the bottom of the industry is intense. They have to get orders out by a fixed deadline. Companies keep squeezing them and demanding more pieces per day.”

Gu also sees the domestic market’s homogenization as a symptom of the broader economic chill. “Staying alive matters far more than being original,” she says. “After all, beyond the designer, there’s a sales team, logistics, and 50 or 60 other mouths to feed. No business owner is going to bankrupt themselves simply to underwrite a designer’s personal aesthetic.”

For clothing companies, a design’s main job is to keep the business alive, so giving the market what’s familiar is the safest survival strategy, Gu explains.

“Designers have the least say in whether a garment gets made,” with the final decision usually in the hands of marketing and store managers, she adds. This group’s preference is for more “universal garments” that match a wide range of body shapes and personal tastes. “Designed pieces are selective — they can depend on a person’s height, figure, looks, their whole bearing.”

Even when an inventive design survives internal vetting, an unusual cut or trim can increase the retail price, potentially sending consumers elsewhere. Gu recently incorporated neo-Chinese style elements including knot buttons, mandarin collars, and wide cuffs into her garments, but they sold poorly. The feedback was that shoppers deemed the items too expensive.

Copycats are also astonishingly fast. Gu says imitations of her designs have appeared for sale online within as little as 24 hours, at a fraction of the price. “It gets to the point where it feels original designs are a bit of a joke,” she says with a resigned sigh.

Market gap

According to the domestic retail industry tracker Linkshop, at least 40 well-known Chinese online womenswear stores announced they were closing or halting new product releases in 2024, while e-commerce news outlet Ebrun reports that more than a dozen more shuttered in the first half of this year.

Meanwhile, many mid-range sellers have withdrawn from city malls across China, widening the gap between high-end and cut-price clothing stores.

“Expensive clothes are just getting more expensive. In malls, items can cost 5,000 or 6,000 yuan, or even more than 10,000. At the other end, there are fast-fashion brands like Uniqlo and Zara,” says Chen. “Some of the really good mid-range brands, ones pricing items at 1,000 or 2,000 yuan, seem to have gone from the malls. Even where you find them, their designs and quality are far less appealing than they used to be.”

Like Zhou, many shoppers are now turning to secondhand and vintage clothing stores. Others are even learning to sew and making their own clothes, to ensure they get the design, fabric, and cut they want.

“I miss a time when imagination could go anywhere, when people dared to design and weren’t in such a hurry to see results,” laments Li.

Some designers have tried to resist uniformity, like Gu, who makes small adjustments while sticking to her company’s established style. Last year, she took one of its hit jackets and added seams at the collar or cuffs, and extra trim, to achieve something “slightly different.”

She hopes the market turmoil will ease within the next couple of years. “When people are doing a little better financially, and companies have some breathing room — when one bad season no longer means bankrupting the business — things should get much better.”

(For privacy reasons, Zhou Keke, Li Li, and Gu Hawen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Xiaotong.

A version of this article originally appeared in Oh Youth! (36Kr). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.
