“Kaniv, and particularly the Kaniv Hydroelectric Power Plant, has come under fire more than once. But our academic council collectively decided not to evacuate anything outside the country,” says Hanna Manzhara, the museum’s senior collections curator.

She is 80 and cannot imagine her life apart from the museum.

“We resumed work in July 2022 because the number of visitors kept growing. That was such an incentive! We moved the exhibition to the basement, which had been converted into a bomb shelter. At the beginning of this year, we returned to the surface, to the galleries.”

Unlike monuments in Kyiv, Shevchenko’s memorial in Kaniv has not been covered with sandbags. It is not simply a sculpture but a burial mound with a crypt inside, a place where people come to pay their respects.

Yet Russian forces have also struck cemeteries: in Cherkasy in July 2025, in Odesa in October 2024 and in Kramatorsk in April 2023.

Hanna Ivanivna Manzhara, senior collections curator. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow

The conversation naturally turns to Russia. The Moscow and St. Petersburg periods of Shevchenko’s life and work cannot simply be erased from his story.

Hanna Manzhara recalls taking part in Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow in 2003, together with Vita Dzyma, a senior researcher.

“The Ukrainian Center on Arbat Street asked us to take part.

“We brought an exhibition featuring lifetime editions of individual poems, as well as publications from 1911 and 1914, marking the 50th anniversaries of his birth and death. We added woven Ukrainian folk towels made by Marуsia Vasylashchuk, a traditional craftswoman. The response was fantastic! Teachers from Moscow came, along with members of the Ukrainian diaspora. Our fellow museum professionals were particularly remarkable in the attention they gave us.”

“And, of course, there were collectors,” Dzyma continues. “I won’t name them; we lost contact a long time ago. But copies of Moscow newspapers reporting on Taras Shevchenko’s funeral found their way to Kaniv through antique shops on Arbat Street.

“The museum was preparing for reconstruction, and we were trying to build up our collection.”

Manzhara adds: “You see, the life and work of the Kobzar are far broader than anything we ourselves could convey to an audience.”

Dzyma has a similar story. In the family of the St. Petersburg literary scholar Ieremiya Aizenshtok, a self-portrait of 16-year-old Taras was discovered, dating from the time he served as Engelhardt’s personal attendant, or kazachok. Research and evidence suggested it was the earliest portrait of the Kobzar.

“But Aizenshtok’s relatives asked for a very high price. The Kaniv museum simply couldn’t afford it. What happened to the portrait, and who owns it now, is unknown.”

At that moment, the author’s phone begins to vibrate: an air-raid alert has been issued in Kyiv.

On social media, Russian military personnel who have spent nearly five years launching missiles, including at Ukrainian museums, are sarcastically dubbed “Pushkinists.” Among the institutions hit have been the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum in Skovorodynivka, the Kupiansk Museum of Local History and the Odesa Fine Arts Museum.

A Shrine to an Icon: The Museum Under Soviet Rule

“Now the working people of Ukraine and the Soviet Union will be able to become more familiar with the great legacy of the poet-revolutionary, a fighter against the social and national oppression that weighed so heavily on the peoples of the former tsarist Russia,” the republican newspaper Kommunist wrote in 1936.

The newspaper recalled that in 1923, a temporary monument had been erected over Shevchenko’s grave “in place of the cross so hated by the poet and all working people,” and that a temporary exhibition had been set up nearby in 1934. At the same time, construction of a museum was underway on Taras Hill.

Visitors often ask why the Soviet authorities invested so heavily in the project during the Holodomor, the famine that devastated Ukraine. It was the first building in Ukraine designed specifically to house a museum. Until then, museums had generally occupied historic aristocratic or manor houses.

Vita Dzyma offers an explanation:

“Look around: every home had a portrait of Shevchenko – embroidered, painted, burned into wood or assembled from straw. Kobzar lay beside the Bible, or took its place when the campaign against religion began.

“The villages at the foot of Taras Hill were being starved to death. People hired themselves out to work on the construction site for a piece of bread. They carried stones by hand, as in ancient Egypt. Yet they were proud of their work. The Shevchenko Museum was no less than a temple.

“Arguing with Ukrainians about this is a losing battle. Taras is both a father and a prophet!”

Vita Dzyma, senior researcher at the museum. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

A sculptural composition of Lenin and Stalin was installed in the entrance hall, while Shevchenko’s bust was moved to the second floor so that it would not compete with them. According to Dzyma, whose account is supported by research, Soviet propagandists in the 1930s seriously pursued the idea of finding a physical resemblance between Lenin and Shevchenko.

The burial mound was given an upgrade, too. Behind a granite balustrade at the base of the monument, a platform was built resembling the speaker’s tribune at Lenin’s Mausoleum, intended for members of the Ukrainian Communist Party’s Politburo.

In 1939, marking the 125th anniversary of the Kobzar’s birth, Nikita Khrushchev, the first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, spoke at the opening of the museum and the unveiling of the new monument.

“The tradition of placing microphones beside Shevchenko and addressing the community as if speaking on his behalf, from his elevated position, has survived to this day,” Hanna Manzhara explains.

The museum under nazi occupation: Director Dmytro Lebedko

In mid-August 1941, the last train carrying mobilized troops left Kaniv across the bridge over the Dnipro. The bridge was bombed, and its ruins can still be seen from Taras Hill.

There was no time to evacuate the museum before the Nazi occupation. Its staff scattered. The women I spoke to avoid going into detail about what happened next. “It would be disrespectful to the local residents,” they say.

Dmytro Lebedko, a former librarian at the reserve who had been mobilized into the Red Army and survived the bombing of his train, found himself in two roles at once: collaborator, having agreed to work with the occupying forces, and preserver of the museum’s collection.

The Nazis did not close the museum. Instead, they ordered it to be put in order and kept open. Visitors, mostly German soldiers, were brought through in formation. For the first time, not a single entry appeared in the visitors’ book.

The local population was afraid to visit Taras Hill, even though in the nearby district center of Horodyshche, the Nazis had toppled a statue of Karl Marx and replaced it with one of Shevchenko.

Archival documents preserve Lebedko’s testimony: “In 1941, I managed to recover from the village of Pekari 15 chairs, about 2,000 books, two carpets embroidered with portraits of Shevchenko, six silk curtains and a number of other valuables.”

After becoming director, he carried out a full inventory of the museum’s collection, cataloguing 4,000 items. He was not afraid to compile a list of paintings and drawings that the local Nazi district commissioner had supposedly taken for “temporary use.” He also recorded every vase and carpet appropriated by yet another official with an interest in “Slavic exoticism.” Then he took a risk that could have cost him his life: he moved the most valuable objects into a hiding place, sealed it behind a wall and went into hiding himself.

After Soviet troops arrived, Lebedko still managed to help restore the museum, which the Nazis had ransacked shortly before retreating. He voluntarily admitted in court to having been involved in a “Ukrainian nationalist Bandera organization.”

The authorities demanded that he strengthen his self-incriminating statement. “I thought Soviet rule would no longer exist in Ukraine and that Ukraine would become independent. I now understand the serious political error in my views,” he was made to say.

He was convicted of treason and sentenced to the maximum term. Three years later, he died in the Norilsk labor camps from a perforated stomach ulcer.

Dmytro Lebedko was 47, the same age as Taras Shevchenko. His name was erased from the history of the reserve for decades. Museum staff emphasize that only 10 exhibits from the prewar collection have survived to this day.

Yanukovych’s makeover

Toward the end of Leonid Kuchma’s presidency, plans emerged for a major restoration project in Kaniv. A nationwide fund was established specifically to restore historical and architectural heritage sites, and UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya, a Ukrainian research and design institute specializing in restoration, was selected to develop the project. Its specialists proposed returning the building to its original appearance, based on the drawings of architect Vasyl Krychevsky.

In the 1930s, Krychevsky had been unable to realize his full vision. His design was deemed “too Ukrainian,” and both he and his closest student, Petro Kostyrko, were removed from the project. The construction was completed by more compliant hands. As a result, museum staff, whose building had received no major restoration since World War II, were afraid even to express their hopes aloud.

The project stalled, then resumed under President Viktor Yanukovych. According to those involved, the massive, even pompous building made a strong impression on him. If the museum was to host the annual Shevchenko National Prize ceremony, Ukraine’s highest state award for achievements in culture and the arts, it had to meet the president’s aesthetic standards.

Few understood Yanukovych’s tastes better than Hanna Herman, one of his closest allies, a member of parliament from the Party of Regions and head of its humanitarian policy team, and her protégé, architect Larysa Skoryk.

“History repeated itself,” Vita Dzyma says. “At the final stage, UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya was removed from the project, and the national character of the design was discarded. ‘No painted decoration on the exterior – this isn’t some village hut!’ they said. But the preparatory work for the majolica facade had already been completed. The same was true of the alfresco work – the decorative painting in relief.

“The Ministry of Culture’s scientific and methodological council convened and decided: whitewash it!”

Hanna Manzhara adds: “Even the surviving fragments of Krychevsky’s original work, which had miraculously survived the previous war and were rediscovered during the restoration, were covered up again.”

Skoryk developed a stripped-down design concept. The polychrome landscape inspired by the poem Haidamaky was replaced with a monochrome version.

The original coffered ceiling was concealed behind a stretch ceiling. Red lines of Shevchenko’s poetry ran across the gray fabric like information scrolling through a subway station. Glass replaced the wooden mosaic partitions in the entrance hall, while granite slabs took the place of parquet flooring.

“We wanted at least to restore the unique botanical and floral patterns on the columns.

“Both museum staff and Krychevsky’s relatives wrote to Yanukovych. It made no difference. What we got was a gray-and-white renovation,” Dzyma concludes.

She asks whether the author noticed the granite boulder at the entrance, in the center of the lobby. The author is puzzled. Surely this is not a geological museum.

▇ “Shevchenko is the cornerstone of the national idea. It’s a metaphor!”

Photographs From 1944 and a Forced-Labor Camp in the Museum

The author’s attention was drawn to two framed photographs on the wall, dated the last day of January 1944. Yakov Davidzon, a frontline correspondent, arrived at Taras Hill immediately after Kaniv was liberated. He found the museum surrounded by barbed wire, with burned books, torn paintings and shattered sculptures. Sixteen shrapnel wounds had been counted on the pedestal of Shevchenko’s monument.

“We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section.

She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup.

Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death.

Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner?

The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region:

“We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!”

Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka

In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling.

The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum.

The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar.

“There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged.

“In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.”

More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission.

Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced.

“We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls.

The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran.

In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world.

The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda

“Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.

“The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’

“They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’

“To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.”

“The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues.

Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.”

The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve.

Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian.

Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity.

But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance.

World.title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
World.content:
TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies

Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation.

The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies.

Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed.

Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service.

According to the list published by Transparency International Georgia, the officials named include:

Merab Bekaia – deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +.

Solomon Gorashvili – head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani.

– head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani. Roland Abuladze – head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative.

– head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative. Bidzina Mekvevrishvili – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Akhmeta Municipal Council and head of the Magraani agricultural cooperative.

What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Council of Europe chief: Ban on opposition parties in Georgia could be challenged in Strasbourg court
World.content:
Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset has said that legal issues surrounding the initiative to ban opposition parties in Georgia could come before the European Court of Human Rights.

On 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearing a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. The lawsuit alleges that these parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits parties whose aim is to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. All five parties deny the allegations. Hearings are scheduled to continue until 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

Berset made the statement at a meeting of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg on 27 October.

He described the deterioration of democratic processes in Georgia as alarming and urged the authorities to protect political pluralism.

Berset commented on Georgia’s political situation after Nadine Pittfield, a British politician and head of Derby City Council, asked about developments in the country and the Constitutional Court case seeking to ban five pro-Western opposition parties.

Berset said the deterioration of democratic processes in Georgia, new laws restricting civic space and pressure on the opposition were causes for serious concern.

“All of this undermines political pluralism and the country’s commitments as a member of the Council of Europe,” Berset said.

He noted that Council of Europe member states must respect the European Convention on Human Rights and the case law of the European Court of Human Rights.

Berset stressed that any decision to ban a political party must have a strong legal basis and strictly comply with the principles of necessity and proportionality.

He said he would refrain from predicting the outcome of the ongoing constitutional dispute in Georgia, but did not rule out the possibility that important legal aspects of the case could eventually come before the Strasbourg court.

He urged Georgia’s ruling majority to protect political pluralism and stressed that his statement was not intended to influence the Constitutional Court’s decision.

The Secretary General noted that he had always sought to take an active role in the work of the Council of Europe delegation in Georgia and maintain close contact with the authorities.

“In September, during a meeting with Prime Minister Kobakhidze in New York, I discussed the decline of democratic processes in Georgia and stressed the importance of honouring the country’s commitments. I would also like to mention the Venice Commission’s recent recommendations on restrictive legislation in Georgia.

“The situation is quite difficult at the moment. Membership of the Council of Europe means more than joining a club of countries. It entails accepting high-level commitments based on the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as an obligation to comply with court rulings,” Alain Berset said.

He noted that he regularly meets representatives of the Georgian government because Georgia is one of the Council of Europe’s 46 member states.

World.title: Azerbaijani MFA welcomes Feridun Sinirlioğlu’s UN Secretary-General candidacy
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) welcomes the initiative to nominate Ambassador Feridun Sinirlioğlu, who currently serves as the Secretary General of the OSCE, for the position of Secretary-General of the United Nations (UN), spokesperson for the MFA, Aykhan Hajizada, said today.

He made the remark in response to the media’s question regarding the candidacy of Türkiye’s nominee, Feridun Sinirlioğlu, for the post of UN Secretary-General.

"We reiterate the importance of a selection process guided by the principles and objectives of the UN Charter, one based on the candidates' professional qualifications, international and diplomatic experience, impartiality, and ability to build consensus among member states.

We believe that, as a result of ongoing consultations and constructive dialogue among member states, a decision will be reached that strengthens the UN's capacity to respond more effectively to contemporary global challenges," Hajizada noted.

World.title: Baku Boulevard to host concert on Victory Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. A celebratory concert will be held in connection with Victory Day on November 8.

Organized jointly by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and the Baku City Executive Power, the concert will take place at the Seaside National Park in Baku, near the Clock Tower.

Dedicated to the sixth anniversary of the victory achieved by the Azerbaijani Army over the enemy during the 44-day Patriotic War, under the leadership of the President and Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev, the concert will feature renowned Azerbaijani artists, including singers and dance ensembles.

The evening will conclude with a fireworks display.

World.title: Fishing boats attacked in southern Iran – Hormozgan's deputy governor
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Two fishing boats were attacked by the U.S. near the coast of Qeshm Island, in Iran's southern Hormozgan Province, Deputy Governor of Hormozgan Province, Ahmad Nafisi, said.

This was reported by the Governorate of Iran’s Hormozgan Province.

"Around 11:00 local time, two fishing boats were attacked 18 miles from Mesen village in the Qeshm County. There were two people on board each boat," Nafisi noted.

He remarked that two of the individuals were injured in the incident and have been taken to a hospital for treatment. Two others are missing, and a rescue operation is currently underway to locate them.

Tensions between the United States and Iran escalated again on July 8. On that day, U.S. forces launched several waves of strikes on Iranian territory, reportedly in response to an attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. The strikes marked the first such U.S. action since a memorandum was signed between Washington and Tehran.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced the termination of the ceasefire with Iran later that day. In response, Tehran began striking U.S. facilities in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Oman.

The conflict has brought maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz to a standstill.

World.title: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine amid ceasefire
World.content:
Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have reached Ukraine under the most significant truce since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, which the White House says was brokered with help from US first lady Melania Trump, began at 3am local time on Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.

It was a rare joint Russia-Ukraine humanitarian effort, a brief respite in the grim war.

Civilians from Oleshky, on the Dnipro River, began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday.

Evacuation begins from Oleshky Starving residents of Oleshky in southern Ukraine begin evacuating as part of a joint relief operation by the opposing sides.

The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said those who chose to travel from Oleshky to Ukrainian-held territory were taken to the Russian city of Anapa and flown to the Belarusian city of Homel.

They were accompanied by Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, it said.

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the US first lady posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

Reunions after some families separated for over two years

Civilians from Oleshky began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.

Volunteers from organisations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.

Liza Paliy, who last saw her father over two years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.

"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.

He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.

"We realised that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.

She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

AP

World.title: Iranian military ordered to counter any attack swiftly and without restraint
World.content:
Iran's Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has issued new strategic orders to his military chiefs that they should respond to any military or terrorist attack on Iran with an "immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response".

The orders suggest Iran is prepared to widen the war across the region — and possibly further — if the US and Israel launch a new attack on Iran, further alarming Gulf countries which came under attacks from Iran earlier in the year and which have been urging the United States not to restart conflict with Iran.

The message outlining the orders, which appeared on Khamenei's X account also "expressed his appreciation for the intelligent steadfastness of the Resistance Front in various countries".

A big, expensive, global excursion into hell What so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions.

The Resistance Front is an Islamist militant organisation and proxy group operating in Jammu and Kashmir.

Mr Khamenei described the "unity of fronts" as a decisive factor with a strategic impact on shaping the new political and security order in West Asia.

Iran's military chiefs have also been ordered to update the "Targets Bank" so that all kinds of tangible and intangible assets of the US and Israel would be within the reach of the armed forces, his statement said.

The orders indicate that Iran would broaden the targets it strikes from predominantly military ones, and that it would instruct its satellite organisations — Hezbollah and Hamas — to also engage.

The orders were issued as reports from Washington suggested US gulf allies had been warned to expect a new assault on Iran as early as Wednesday, November 4, immediately after the US mid-term elections.

Mjotaba Khamenei has ordered his military chiefs to meet any attack on Iran with an immediate and unrestrained response. (Reuters: ISNA/WANA/Hamed Jafarnejad)

The New York Times reported last week that the US and Israel have drawn up joint plans to attack Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections.

Qatar has been attempting to broker negotiations between Iran and the United States, first in meetings in Tehran and now in Doha.

Despite suggestions that representatives from Iran and the US would come to Doha for direct talks, it subsequently emerged that there were no US representatives in Doha for the meetings.

Both the US and Iran have been ramping up their rhetoric in the days leading up to the US midterm elections, due to be held on Monday.

And Mr Khamenei's threats came after it was reported that that the head of United States Central Command (CENTCOM) Admiral Brad Cooper had briefed Mr Trump on options for renewed attacks on attacking Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal.

At the same time,The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance had offered to meet Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, in person to negotiate an end to the war.

Saudi Arabia and Türkiye's leaders have urged Trump to give diplomacy with Iran more time, while Netanyahu is lobbying for a joint US-Israeli military operation against Iran immediately after the US midterm elections.

Efforts to open dialogue with Iran 'a positive step'

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that a US effort to open dialogue with Iran is "a positive step", and that talks with Qatari mediators have resulted in reducing the period required to implement Iran's proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz.

"The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days," said Mr Araghchi.

Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28. (AP: Razieh Poudat/ISNA)

"Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region. We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar," Mr Araghchi added.

He said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.

"We do not rule out any possibility regarding the outbreak of war, and we are prepared for all scenarios," Mr Araghchi said.

"We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms; our forces are at the highest level of readiness."

'Supertanker' strikes mine in Hormuz

Loading...

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says four oil tankers, including a "supertanker" carrying more than two million barrels of oil, hit mines and caught fire while travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.

The IRGC said the tankers suffered explosions on Friday after attempting to use unauthorised routes through the strait.

The Guard's navy claimed the vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings. Iran's report did not identify the vessels or provide details about the crews.

Oman said it had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked in the strait, 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, catching fire. It is unclear whether that incident is related to the fires described by Iran.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre also reported on Friday that a vessel was struck by an "unknown projectile" south of Lavan, an island just off mainland Iran near Shidvar.

The British military organisation, which monitors maritime safety, said the crew was safe.

An Iranian official said two fishermen were missing and two others injured in an attack on two other boats in the strait, blaming the US.

Iran has repeatedly warned that vessels passing through the strait without Tehran's permission would face "destruction."

Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28.

World.title: Canada hoping to become EU’s first 'associate member' in deal
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is hoping to wrap up an unprecedented deal with the European Union by June to make Canada the bloc's first "associate member".

Mr Carney and EU leaders launched what they called an "Alliance for the Future" at the end of a two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal where they agreed to several initiatives centred on digital trade, critical minerals and artificial intelligence among others.

"Today we move toward associate membership for Canada, and we launch a new alliance for the future," Mr Carney said.

US President Donald Trump's trade war and persistent threats have accelerated efforts by Canada and Europe to reduce their dependence on Washington and strengthen their economic and security ties.

"What brings us together goes far beyond geography. We see the world through the same eyes," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"These headwinds won't stop blowing. This change is permanent."

European Council President Antonio Costa, Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen were upbeat about future Canada-EU relations. (Reuters: Roger Lemoyne)

Mr Carney said the alliance would help Canada and Europe withstand economic pressure and make their own decisions rather than be dictated to by more powerful countries.

Mr Trump has threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered the proposed arrangement unfriendly.

Alliance aims to reinforce sovereignty

Mr Carney did not directly say whether the US could eventually be invited to join the alliance, but insisted the arrangement was not retaliatory.

"It is about reinforcing sovereignty. Why? So we can live our lives as we choose, our people can live their lives as they choose and have the full freedoms that people enjoy in the European Union and in Canada," Mr Carney said.

"It's not against anything, it's for," he said.

Mr Carney said Canadian Cabinet ministers and European commissioners would meet in March before he attends European Council meetings in June, where he intends to conclude negotiations on the proposed relationship.

European Council President António Costa confirmed the invitation and said more details would be announced then.

Ms Von der Leyen said on Friday there was broad support for bringing Canada closer to the EU.

"On one thing I'm absolutely sure, having spoken about it in the last weeks, is the broad support of having Canada much, much closer to the European Union," she said.

Both sides have expedited efforts to strengthen their economic and security ties. (Reuters: Christopher Katsarov)

A new economic partnership

Friday's negotiations in Montreal produced a new digital trade agreement between Canada and the EU to make it easier for businesses to sell across the Atlantic.

Canada also signed an agreement allowing the European Investment Bank to finance Canadian critical minerals projects, potentially opening a new source of investment for the country's mining industry.

Canada will also join a European supercomputing initiative which Mr Carney said could transform research. Europe's JUPITER supercomputer can complete in one day calculations that would take Canada's most powerful research computer six months, he said.

The two sides also concluded negotiations on an agreement intended to curb anti-competitive practices and lower prices for consumers.

Alliance could broaden

The Alliance for the Future could eventually broaden to include other like-minded countries, with Canada and the EU at its core.

The US-Canada 'divorce' and the $1.2 trillion fallout The US and Canada are often referred to as North American cousins, but the family feud has turned bitter as their trading relationship falls apart.

Mr Costa said the two sides wanted to create a relationship unlike any seen previously with a country outside the bloc.

"Our relationship is so special that we want to create something new: to go beyond a simple association, everything short of full EU membership," he said.

The leaders also agreed to study the feasibility of exporting Canadian liquefied natural gas to Europe and explore new undersea cables connecting Canada, Europe and Asia.

Canada and the EU will begin talks on expanding Canadian participation in Europe's student exchange program.

The two sides also agreed on a new border security arrangement and pledged closer cooperation on defence, cybersecurity, Arctic security and countering foreign interference.

The US accounted for 71.7 per cent of Canada's merchandise exports in 2025. Mr Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade.

AP

World.title: Bodycam video shows ICE agent's car swerving toward man in Texas
World.content:
An ICE agent has been indicted by a grand jury in Texas after hitting a Mexican construction worker with his car last month.

The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was charged on Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, accused of intentionally ramming the car at the man, prosecutors said.

The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV in Houston on October 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Sean Teare announced the indictment at a news conference. (AP: Melissa Phillip/ Houston Chronicle)

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remained in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, said District Attorney Sean Teare, who announced the indictment at a news conference that included body camera video of the encounter and a recording of Morales calling 911.

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Mr Teare said was contradicted by video.

"The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated," he said.

Morales's attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client did not commit a crime.

Texans turn against Trump over ICE's 'terrible' actions In south Texas, the aggressive enforcement of immigration laws has hollowed out restaurants, building sites and even churches — and the backlash is threatening to turn the traditional red state blue.

He and ICE both said Morales did not intentionally strike Parra Hernandez and accused the Democratic district attorney of indicting Morales for political reasons.

"Mr Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement," Mr Lindenmuth told The Associated Press.

"To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident, the DA's office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air."

Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Mr Lindenmuth said.

Morales, charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody on Friday and a warrant would be issued for his arrest, according to Mr Teare.

Body camera footage shows ICE car's sharp movements

Sean Teare and Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez announce the indictment. (AP: Melissa Phillip/ Houston Chronicle)

Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County, Texas, for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Mr Teare.

He was in a vehicle that ICE tried to stop.

He jumped out and was followed by Morales, who was in a Jeep Cherokee.

Previously released surveillance video shows the Jeep speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

Morales's body camera footage that Mr Teare played on Friday shows the officer making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes.

Loading...

In the video, Morales stops the vehicle then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away.

Parra Hernandez is on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain.

Morales is heard saying, "He got hit with a car, bro." It is not clear to whom he is talking.

"I was coming in and I hit him with the car," Morales says after another ICE officer arrives.

In a 911 audio recording in which Morales requests an ambulance, Parra Hernandez can be heard yelling.

Morales tells the operator, "He's fine. He's just complaining of pain."

Parra Hernandez told deputies that he believed a police officer was stopping the vehicle he was in but got scared and fled when the man started putting on a mask.

ICE tactics could impact midterms The Trump administration's immigration crackdown was a vote winner in the 2024 presidential election, but is proving more divisive ahead of the midterms.

He repeatedly told deputies that Morales "threw the car at me", according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP.

Morales told deputies he did not intentionally hit Parra Hernandez.

He acknowledged that he did not brake before hitting Parra Hernandez and said he was trying to avoid another truck in the parking lot.

Body camera video indicated that Morales had two other suspects in custody in his back seat, according to the report.

But the deputy wrote that Morales told them there was no-one else inside.

"From the beginning, the video told a different story than what was offered by the agency," Parra Hernandez's attorney, Kim Bruno, said on Friday.

She said her client has suffered not just fractures in his leg, but nerve damage and chronic pain.

Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation

FIEL said Mendoza-Cervantes's daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. (AP: Melissa Phillip/ Houston Chronicle)

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day.

ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.

Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him.

FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes's daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017.

Mr Teare's office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years

Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a separate fatal shooting by an ICE officer in Texas.

AP

World.title: Locals protest against proposed AI data centre in Adelaide Hills
World.content:
Residents in and around the Adelaide Hills have said they will fight an AI data centre proposed for a block just outside of Mount Torrens.

Quantum DC is proposing a 1,200-megawatt hyperscale data centre along with energy infrastructure on Collins Road in Tungkillo, about 41 kilometres directly east of the Adelaide CBD. The first stage would commence in 2028.

It had scheduled two community consultation sessions this week but postponed them to late November amid safety concerns.

In their absence, locals instead convened their own protest meetings, one in Tungkillo on Thursday, followed by a public rally in the nearby town of Mannum today.

Local organiser Magdalene Lippett said she had communicated with Quantum DC officials in email, but they had declined to attend Saturday's community event.

She said residents were opposed to the construction, having raised concerns about the use of land, water supplies and the impact of noise and light pollution.

"We're not going away," Ms Lippett said.

" We don't want the data centre, we will fight it using every legal means possible. "

Magdalene Lippett says the community will pursue all "legal means" to prevent the construction of the data centre. (Supplied)

She said the community was not opposed to development, citing the Tungkillo Battery Energy Storage System being constructed at the nearby existing substation.

"There just has to be a point where we slow down a little bit and start to question what trade-offs we're giving up to have this AI data centre there and what are the risks for … primary production, the agriculture and the lifestyles of everyone around that area."

Application on hold

No formal application to construct the Tungkillo AI facility has been lodged with state planning authorities by Quantum DC.

Its chief executive Alby Tomassi said about 80 per cent of the project's electricity needs would be met by two on-site substations connecting to existing ElectraNet power lines, with supply via solar and wind contracts.

It would also construct an on-site gas-fired power station to provide firming capacity, with captured and recirculated rainwater used to meet the facility's water needs.

Mr Tomassi said the facility would not utilise water from the nearby River Murray or existing groundwater reserves.

Quantum DC has rescheduled its consultations to November 20 and 21.

"We respect the community's views, and that is why our engagement is taking place before anything is lodged, so that we hear and consider those views first," Mr Tomassi said.

" What we hear will help inform and shape the proposal we lodge, and a summary of what we heard and how we responded will accompany our application. "

At 120 hectares the infrastructure build would cover an area about a third of the size of Adelaide's CBD and would be larger than the current "Colossus" campus operated by Elon Musk's SpaceXSI, which is less than 100 hectares in size.

Crossbench calls for halt to project

Planning Minister Nick Champion said that any application to build a data centre would need to pass through a "rigorous planning system", including meeting power and water requirements.

Mr Champion said an application's assessment would be determined by the government, and could be handed to the State Commission Assessment Panel or to the minister for evaluation.

"Whatever the pathway, the process is rigorous," Mr Champion said.

Government members did not attend Saturday's meeting in Mannum, however representatives from the opposition and crossbench did address protesters.

Members of the local community attended the protest in Mannum. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Though the Liberal Party, Greens and One Nation support the local push against the project, they differ on how to approach the question of data centres in South Australia.

"We're not against data centres but at the end of the day you've got to take community sentiment into consideration," said Liberal upper house leader Nicola Centofanti.

"This community is saying right from day dot: 'We don't want it here.'"

Greens leader Robert Simms called on the state government "to put a moratorium on any new data centres and to include data centres within their royal commission", while One Nation MLC Carlos Quaremba pointed to the recent move by the three parties to support a Greens motion to block gas fracking in the state's south-east.

Mr Quaremba said his party took "the principled position" of looking "at everything as risk-versus-reward" and suggested a similar tri-party alliance could be forged on the data centre issue.
