Jockey: James McDonald

Trainer: Joseph O'Brien Trustyourinstinct is among the leading chances for the international raiders. (PA Images via Getty Images: Niall Carson) Trustyourinstinct is a winner of two races this year in his native Ireland, including the Curragh Cup (2,816m) where he defeated one-time 2025 Cup favourite Al Riffa. His final run before heading Down Under was a well-held fourth when no match for star stayer Scandinavia in the Irish St Leger (2,816m) in September. Trustyourinstinct seems to produce his best when he's held up for a final sprint, and he'll have no better jockey than James McDonald to present him at the right time on Tuesday. McDonald, a winner aboard Verry Elleegant in 2020, will be sporting the famous green and yellow silks of JP McManus, whose major victories include the Cheltenham Gold Cup and Grand National. 3. Knight's Choice $34 | Barrier 2 | 56.5kg Read more Read more 7yo gelding (Australia)

Jockey: Robbie Dolan

Trainer: John Symons & Sheila Laxon Knight's Choice is out to repeat his narrow victory in 2024. (AAP: James Ross) Knight's Choice and his singing jockey Robbie Dolan landed a shock victory at $91 in 2024 and they're back for an encore; note that only the great Peter Pan (1932, 1934) has won non-consecutive Cups. The now seven-year-old had been sidelined by injury after his famous Cup triumph, but he looked to be getting back into form with a close third behind the well-rated Pinhole in the Herbert Power Stakes (2,400m) on October 10. However he was never a factor in an incident-packed Caulfield Cup (2,400m) a week later, finishing 14th behind Kingswood beaten 10 lengths. Improvement is expected back to Flemington but once again Knight's Choice will be an outsider — anyone else sensing some déjà vu? 4. Middle Earth $13 | Barrier 1 | 56.5kg Read more Read more 7yo gelding (Great Britain)

Jockey: Mark Zahra

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Middle Earth ridden by Mark Zahra wins the Australian Cup Prelude at Flemington racecourse on March 8, 2025. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Scott Barbour) Middle Earth (insert Tolkien reference here) finished third for Ciaron Maher last year and has been building towards a second Cup tilt with five unplaced runs this campaign. The seven-year-old made ground from well back in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m) to finish ninth, beaten 5.4 lengths behind Kingswood, Saint George and Enfjaar. A week later he had his final Cup lead-up with a seven-length eight behind Cosmic Crusader in the Cox Plate (2,040m). Middle Earth wasn't suited by the race shape on that occasion and is much better preferred back to a 3,200-metre handicap in the hands of two-time Cup winner Mark Zahra (Gold Trip 2022, Without A Fight 2023). 5. Vauban $51 | Barrier 22 | 56.5kg Read more Read more 9yo gelding (France)

Jockey: Jordan Childs

Trainer: Gai Waterhouse & Adrian Bott Tim Clark riding Vauban wins the Sky High Stakes at Rosehill Gardens on March 15, 2025. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng) Punters know this former Irish-trained galloper well, as he's helped them part with their money in the past three Melbourne Cups (14th 2023, 11th 2024, sixth 2025). Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott have given Vauban a more European preparation for this year's race, having just the one run since his third in the Doomben Cup (2,000m) in May. Just under a fortnight ago Vauban was only fair when ninth, beaten 6.2 lengths, behind Point Of Law in the Geelong Cup (2,400m). He'll derive extra fitness from that run and appreciate any give in the surface on Tuesday as he attempts to become the first nine-year-old to win the Cup. 6. Enfjaar $21 | Barrier 8 | 56kg Read more Read more 7yo gelding (Ireland)

Jockey: Ray Dawson

Trainer: Roger Varian Enfjaar's biggest success to date came in the Glorious Stakes at Goodwood. (PA Images via Getty Images: Andrew Matthews) The winner of five from 17 starts, the English-trained Enfjaar only had his first test over a staying trip in August, reaching a career peak when leading all the way in the Glorious Stakes (2,412m) at Goodwood. One runner behind him that day, Opportunity, has formlines through Cup contender Hopewell Rock, who has form tied to Small Fry, who ran a strong second to Cup favourite Point Of Law in the Geelong Cup (2,400m) — still with me? At his first Australian appearance Enfjaar took up a handy position and fought bravely in the straight to finish third behind Kingswood in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m) and ahead of eventual Cox Plate winner Cosmic Crusader. Provided he can see out the extra distance on Tuesday, Enfjaar should give a good showing for trainer Roger Varian, whose previous Cup runner My Ambivalent finished 17th in 2014. 7. Royal Supremacy $51 | Barrier 21 | 56kg Read more Read more 6yo gelding (Ireland)

Jockey: Ben Allen

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Royal Supremacy is out to make amends for a below-par effort last start. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng) Royal Supremacy will certainly appreciate any rain to soften the track in his bid to improve on a 15th-place finish in last year's Cup. The six-year-old ended his last campaign with a dominant all-the-way win in Brisbane's rich Q22 (2,200m) ahead of Melbourne Cup winners Half Yours and Knight's Choice. The signs were good when he again led from start to finish in the JRA Cup (2,000m) in September, but he blotted his copybook using the same tactics in Caulfield Cup (2,400m) when he weakened noticeably to finish 15th, beaten 17 lengths by Kingswood. Punters rate Royal Supremacy the outsider of trainer Ciaron Maher's seven runners, and he'll be a second Melbourne Cup ride for Ben Allen, who finished sixth aboard Thomas Hobson in 2017. 8. Wine Dark Sea $61 | Barrier 23 | 56kg Read more Read more 5yo gelding (Great Britain)

Jockey: Damian Lane

Trainer: Harry Charlton Wine Dark Sea will be hard to miss on Tuesday. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: George Sal) The prize for the most eye-catching jockey silks certainly goes to Wine Dark Sea, the design of which is the brainchild of his majority owner, Brisbane roofer Sonny Glebe. Wine Dark Sea won three of four starts in England this year, including the Geoffrey Freer Stakes (2,671m) when he made all from the front and lowered the colours of the highly regarded Dubai Honour, a regular visitor (and winner) Down Under. At his first Australian appearance in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m), Wine Dark Sea was forced to race wide early and hit the front rounding the turn but weakened in the closing stages to finish 11th, beaten 6.6 lengths, behind Kingswood and Cup rival Enfjaar. The lightly raced five-year-old will likely derive a fitness benefit from the outing and has the services of Damian Lane, who is searching for his first Cup win. 9. Asterix $101 | Barrier 6 | 55kg Read more Read more 8yo gelding (New Zealand)

Jockey: Jye McNeil

Trainer: Chris Waller Not many eight-year-olds like Asterix have won the Cup. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng) Asterix's only start over 3,200 metres was a fourth in the 2024 Auckland Cup before he crossed the Tasman to join the stable of 2021 Cup winner Chris Waller. Fast-forward to 2026 and Asterix scored three victories at Group and Listed level last campaign, but so far this spring his best performance was a third behind Cup rival Zahrann in the Naturalism Stakes (2,000m). Asterix was a distant last on a heavy track behind Cosmic Crusader in the Turnbull Stakes (2,000m), and then made minor headway from the back of the field when 12th, beaten 7.1 lengths, behind Kingswood in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m). The punters aren't giving this veteran much of a chance, and history looms against him as only three eight-year-olds (Toryboy 1865, Catalogue 1938 and Twilight Payment 2020) have won the great race. 10. Goodie Two Shoes $31 | Barrier 19 | 55kg Read more Read more 8yo mare (Ireland)

Jockey: Wayne Lordan

Trainer: Joseph O'Brien Goodie Two Shoes is hoping to go one better than last year. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: George Sal) Goodie Two Shoes has only had four runs since her brave second behind Half Yours in last year's Cup when a $41 chance for Irish trainer Joseph O'Brien. Racing in the famous green and yellow silks of JP McManus, she scored a narrow victory in the Lillie Langtry Stakes (2,816m) at Goodwood in August. But the eight-year-old then raced well below her best and trailed the field behind Cup rivals Sons And Lovers and James J Braddock in the Kilternan Stakes (2,414m). Nevertheless she has made the trip Down Under. Goodie Two Shoes is being asked to carry 3.5kg more than last year, and to her credit, of the 50 mares to run in the Cup since 2005, she is one of only three — High Emocean (2022) and Verry Elleegant (2021) being the others — to have finished top three. 11. Juja Kibo $11 | Barrier 14 | 55kg Read more Read more 6yo gelding (Ireland)

Jockey: Sam Clipperton

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Juja Kibo stormed into Cup contention with victory in the Moonee Valley Cup. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Brett Holburt) Juja Kibo is one of the leading hopes for trainer Ciaron Maher who has seven lining up this year to emulate his success with Gold Trip in 2022. The six-year-old comes into Tuesday's race on the back of successive wins, the first of which was a dominant victory in The Metropolitan (2,400m) where he defeated the likes of Cup rival Soul Of Spain. He then finished over the top of Cup rivals Mr Monaco and Strictly Business to claim the Moonee Valley Cup (2,500m) and punch his golden ticket into the Cup. Juja Kibo is being kept safe in the market and will be partnered again by Sam Clipperton, whose only Cup ride to date was eighth aboard Stockman in 2022.

12. Hopewell Rock $9 | Barrier 15 | 54.5kg Read more Read more 5yo gelding (Ireland)

Jockey: Zac Lloyd

Trainer: George Boughey There's been a good amount of betting interest in Hopewell Rock in recent days. (Getty Images: Sam Mellish) This lightly raced five-year-old worked his way through lower-level staying races in England before winning a handicap over 2,816 metres at Goodwood, defeating one-time Cup contender Small Fry. Small Fry would go on to frank that form when runner-up to Cup favourite Point Of Law in the Geelong Cup (2,400m). Hopewell Rock's form also lines up well out of his close second in the time-honoured Ebor Handicap (2,786m) at York; alongside him that day was Opportunity, which finished behind Enfjaar at Goodwood. Enfjaar would later run a strong third in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m). While he is yet to be tested over the 3,200 metres, Hopewell Rock can handle rain-affected ground and there's plenty of money to suggest he'll give a forward showing with young gun Zac Lloyd in the saddle. 13. Onesmoothoperator $101 | Barrier 13 | 54.5kg Read more Read more 9yo gelding (United States)

Jockey: Declan Bates

Trainer: Tim Fitzsimmons Onesmoothoperator is out to recapture the form that saw him win the Geelong Cup in 2024. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Pat Scala) This former English-trained galloper is making his third attempt at the Cup after finishing 12th in 2024 and 16th last year. A previous winner of the Geelong Cup (2024) and Moonee Valley Cup (2025), Onesmoothoperator's jockey could offer no excuses when he finished 11th, 9.4 lengths behind Point Of Law in the Geelong Cup (2,400m) almost a fortnight ago. It didn't appear to be the run of a coming Melbourne Cup winner, and Onesmoothoperator will need to create history as no nine-year-old has won the race in its 166-year history. But win, lose or draw, it'll be a memorable first Cup runner for Bendigo-based trainer Tim Fitzsimmons, who took over the training of Onesmoothoperator less than a year ago. 14. Soul Of Spain $41 | Barrier 5 | 54.5kg Read more Read more 6yo gelding (Ireland)

Jockey: Tommy Berry

Trainer: Chris Waller Soul Of Spain is one of two runners for champion trainer Chris Waller. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri) This Chris Waller-trained galloper finished second in the Sydney Cup in the autumn at his only attempt at 3,200 metres, but his form this campaign doesn't seem to be quite at the same level. Soul Of Spain finished seventh, beaten 6.5 lengths, behind Juja Kibo in The Metropolitan (2,400m) in Sydney before running eighth in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m). He settled well back in a slowly run race that day, and made a bold mid-race move to sit outside the leaders before tiring in the straight to finish 4.7 lengths behind Kingswood. Soul Of Spain's connections will be hoping the likelihood of a wet track will help his chances, but he remains an outsider as top Sydney jockey Tommy Berry continues to search for his first Cup victory. 15. Zahrann $23 | Barrier 11 | 54.5kg Read more Read more 5yo stallion (Ireland)

Jockey: Ben Melham

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Zahrann has drifted in Cup betting following his past two starts. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Reg Ryan) Zahrann was highly rated in Ireland when purchased by Australian interests and shipped to the Ciaron Maher stable as a potential Cups horse. The five-year-old looked on track to justify that aim when scoring a dominant win over one-time Cup contender Saint George in the Naturalism Stakes (2,000m). And despite a well-beaten 11th on a bog track behind Cosmic Crusader in the Turnbull Stakes (2,000m), Zahrann was sent out as second favourite in the Caulfield Cup (2,400m) and settled well back before making steady ground without threatening to finish 3.9 lengths behind Kingswood in fourth. Ben Melham takes the ride, hoping to go one better than his second aboard Johannes Vermeer in 2017. 16. So You Are $19 | Barrier 7 | 54kg Read more Read more 5yo gelding (Australia)

Jockey: Rachel King

Trainer: Bjorn Baker So You Are made it four in a row in the Bendigo Cup. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Brett Holburt) There will be few fitter horses on Tuesday than this grinding stayer, who comes into the Cup after four wins on the bounce. So You Are's winning streak began in the Tatts Cup (2,400m) at Randwick and was followed by victory in the Colin Stephen Quality (2,400m) at Rosehill. Then the step up to 2,600 metres of the ATC St Leger proved no issue, before a perfect ride from Rachel King helped him salute in the Bendigo Cup (2,400m) last Wednesday. While So You Are hasn't been racing against the elite level, expect King to have him positioned up near the lead where he won't go down without a fight — and he won't be afraid of a wet track either. 17. Future History $71 | Barrier 12 | 53.5kg Read more Read more 9yo gelding (Great Britain)

Jockey: Jamie Melham

Trainer: Gregory Hickman Future History makes a second Cup appearance as a veteran nine-year-old. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri) Future History squeaked into the field after other runners were forced to withdraw due to fitness concerns; their loss is Jamie Melham's gain as she now has a chance to emulate her victory last year aboard Half Yours. Future History has been running OK without winning since joining the Greg Hickman stable at the start of the year, with his best result a second to Cup rival Royal Supremacy in the JRA Plate (2,000m) in September. Since then he's finished fourth behind Pinhole in the Herbert Power Stakes (2,400m) and ninth, beaten 3.6 lengths, behind Cup rivals Juja Kibo and Mr Monaco in the Moonee Valley Cup (2,500m). One of three nine-year-olds in this year's race, Future History finished 15th behind Without A Fight in the 2023 Cup at his only attempt at 3,200 metres. 18. James J Braddock $13 | Barrier 24 | 53.5kg Read more Read more 4yo gelding (Great Britain)

Jockey: Craig Williams

Trainer: Joseph O'Brien James J Braddock runs in the Cup at only his eighth career appearance. (PA Images via Getty Images: Damien Eagers) Named after the world heavyweight boxing champion of the 1930s (and inspiration for the Russell Crowe movie Cinderella Man), plenty of punters feel James J Braddock and jockey Craig Williams can deliver a knockout blow on Tuesday. A third in the English Derby (2,420m) reflected trainer Joseph O'Brien's high opinion of James J Braddock, but he then disappointed when a distanced sixth in the Irish Derby (2,414m). His latest performance showed a glimpse that he might appreciate the 3,200 metres, staying on strongly before not seeing much room in the closing stages of the Kilternan Stakes (2,414m) in Ireland. The formula of bringing well-performed Northern Hemisphere three-year-olds to Australia for the Cup has proven successful, evidenced by the likes of Rekindling (1st, 2017), Cross Counter (1st, 2018), Il Paradiso (3rd, 2019) and Tiger Moth (2nd, 2020). 19. Kizlyar $41 | Barrier 20 | 53.5kg Read more Read more 5yo gelding (Ireland)

Jockey: Beau Mertens

Trainer: Joseph O'Brien Kizlyar scored a thrilling Royal Ascot victory back in June. (Action Images via Reuters: Andrew Boyers) Kizlyar was a late inclusion in the Cup field at the expense of his well-fancied stablemate Defiantly, who failed to pass a vet inspection and was withdrawn by the stewards on Saturday. He actually lowered Defiantly's colours after a stirring battle down the straight at Royal Ascot over 4,013 metres, and then finished second in the Irish St Leger Trial (2,816m) in August. But Kizlyar raced well below expectations at his Australian debut when beaten almost four lengths behind Cup rivals Juja Kibo and Mr Monaco in the Moonee Valley Cup (2,500m) a week ago. His record shows that Tuesday's distance is of no concern, but he'll need to improve sharply to reverse the disappointment of last start. 20. Point Of Law $6 fav | Barrier 9 | 53kg Read more Read more 4yo stallion (Great Britain)

Jockey: Ethan Brown

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Point Of Law showed sustained speed for an impressive win at Geelong. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Pat Scala) The second of two Northern Hemisphere three-year-olds in this year's Cup, Point Of Law surged to the top of betting following a victory in the Geelong Cup (2,400m) that impressed ratings experts. It was his Australian debut for trainer Ciaron Maher after being purchased in August from King Charles who bred and raced him to a fourth at Royal Ascot over 2,846 metres and a victory in the Bahrain Trophy (2,615m) at Newmarket. European three-year-olds on an upward trajectory have featured prominently in the past decade, namely Rekindling (1st, 2017), Cross Counter (1st, 2018), Il Paradiso (3rd, 2019) and Tiger Moth (2nd, 2020). Ethan Brown stays on board, and many people think he's a great chance to at least emulate his third place aboard Middle Earth last year in his only Cup ride to date. 21. Strictly Business $101 | Barrier 4 | 53kg Read more Read more 4yo mare (Australia)

Jockey: Michael Dee

Trainer: Thomas Carberry The career highlight for Strictly Business was her Oaks victory a year ago. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Reg Ryan) Strictly Business has won two races in her career, and none since her famous Victoria Oaks (2,500m) triumph at Flemington almost a year ago. In the autumn she added a second place in the South Australian Derby (2,518m) to her resume, but the mare has struggled racing against open-class horses this spring. The four-year-old struggled to make ground when 12th, beaten 10 lengths, behind Pinhole in the Herbert Power Stakes (2,400m), and then finished last of 16 behind Juja Kibo in the Moonee Valley Cup (2,500m) a week ago. A sharp turnaround in form will be needed for Strictly Business to figure on Tuesday. It's worth noting that of the 50 mares to run in the Cup since 2005, only three — Goodie Two Shoes (2025), High Emocean (2022) and Verry Elleegant (2021) — have finished top three. 22. Mr Monaco $26 | Barrier 16 | 52.5kg Read more Read more 6yo gelding (Great Britain)

Jockey: Jabez Johnstone

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Mr Monaco booked his spot in the field by winning the Bart Cummings in early October. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri) The possibility of a rain-affected track won't bother this former English-trained gelding, who's another of Ciaron Maher's seven-strong attack on the Cup. Mr Monaco won his way into the great race with victory in the Bart Cummings (2,500m) in early October, and then was far from disgraced when a close third to stablemate and Cup rival Juja Kibo in the Moonee Valley Cup (2,500m). He'll get a 2kg weight advantage on Juja Kibo on Tuesday in his bid to improve on his only previous run at 3,200 metres, which was a disappointing 11th behind Changingoftheguard and Soul Of Spain in the Sydney Cup. Mr Monaco will be a first Cup ride for 20-year-old Jabez Johnstone, who's looking to become the first apprentice jockey to win the Cup since 15-year-old Ray Neville saluted aboard Rimfire in 1948. 23. Zakouma $34 | Barrier 10 | 52kg Read more Read more 6yo gelding (Australia)

Jockey: William Pike

Trainer: Grahame Begg The Andrew Ramsden back in May was Zakouma's golden ticket into the Cup. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Scott Barbour) This stoutly bred six-year-old secured his spot in the Cup with victory in the Andrew Ramsden (2,800m) at Flemington in May. Zakouma's spring campaign has therefore been designed for him to peak on Tuesday; he closed off strongly for sixth behind Zahrann in the Naturalism Stakes (2,000m) and was fifth behind Pinhole in the Herbert Power Stakes (2,400m). Ignore his last of 11 behind Surfin' Bird in the Crystal Mile a week ago over 1,600 metres; that's well below his best distance and the run was nothing more than a maintenance gallop to have him primed for his grand final. Trainer Grahame Begg has engaged the services of West Australian wizard William Pike, who is riding high after his Cox Plate victory aboard Cosmic Crusader a week ago. 24. Shockletz $11 | Barrier 17 | 51kg Read more Read more 5yo mare (New Zealand)

Jockey: Harry Coffey

Trainer: Ciaron Maher Shockletz is out to match her sire and win a Melbourne Cup. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: George Sal) Shockletz's dominant victory in the Archer Stakes (2,500m) in September booked her place in the Cup field, one of seven runners for trainer Ciaron Maher. Her two runs since then have been about having her primed to peak on Tuesday; she recorded good closing sectionals when sixth behind Pinhole in the Herbert Power Stakes (2,400m), and then a fast-finishing second to Soverato in the Tesio Stakes (2,040m) cemented her place among the leading contenders. Shockletz will have to buck history to a degree; of the 50 mares to run in the Cup since 2005, only three — Goodie Two Shoes (2025), High Emocean (2022) and Verry Elleegant (2021) — have finished top three. But she will have the benefit of the low weight of 51kg, which her sire Shocking also carried to Cup glory in 2009 in the same colours of owner Laurence Eales.

Odds at 4.20pm AEDT Saturday

Credits

World.title: Roos make AFLW history with three straight minor premierships
World.content:
Jasmine Garner has spearheaded North Melbourne to a third consecutive AFLW minor premiership in a rousing 68-point victory over Richmond.

Knowing a win would make the Kangaroos the first team to top the ladder three straight times, the captain sparkled in her team's 15.11 (101) to 5.3 (33) thumping at Windy Hill on Saturday.

Her 28 disposals and one goal contribution firmed her position for the league's best and fairest award, the star midfielder playing an integral role in helping North finish its campaign 11-1.

The Roos will certainly be the team to beat in the finals series as they've won their games by an average of 43.2 points and thrashed the second-placed Geelong by 73 points earlier in the year.

Richmond did provide a scare when it kicked two of the first three goals, but the visitors found a new gear, booting the next seven majors to put them in the box seat for victory.

Midfielder Ash Riddell (32 disposals) was typically inspirational, along with forward Tahlia Randall (three goals), while Monique Conti (33 disposals) was busy for the Tigers.

St Kilda's horror season ends with 11th loss

St Kilda was left devastated after its wooden spoon finish was virtually cemented in a weather-affected 7.9 (51) to 7.3 (45) loss to Port Adelaide.

The Saints (1-11) end their season having won just one game and will need either Collingwood or Essendon to suffer a massive loss in order for them to avoid last place.

The loss finishes a tumultuous campaign for the team whose coach, Nick Dal Santo, stepped down midway through the campaign, and the club is independently reviewing the program.

But the Power won't celebrate the result too wildly either, as they needed a huge victory to put themselves in finals contention.

Although they are equal on points with the eighth-placed Hawthorn (24), they have a significantly lower percentage, meaning 2022 All Australian Kirsty Lamb and captain Justine Mules-Robinson won't get to end their glittering careers with a finals appearance.

AAP

World.title: Australia slumps to horror defeat as Warner decries 'deplorable' batting
World.content:
David Warner has slammed Australia's "deplorable" batting after the tourists limped to a 176-run defeat following a monumental top-order capitulation in the third Test at Newlands.

South Africa wrapped up a 2-1 series victory just before tea, although the result was not in doubt from the early morning as Australia completely imploded on a turning track in Cape Town.

Kagiso Rabada took 3-39, including two wickets in the first over, while player of the match Simon Harmer befuddled Australia with 6-16 in 21.1 overs.

Australia were 8-62 at lunch, and all out for 111 only thanks to the efforts of Nathan Lyon (33 not out) and Pat Cummins (11) in a chastening defeat.

"Within the first hour, the game was away from us," Pat Cummins said.

"We didn't give ourselves a chance."

Australia started the final day of a fiercely contested series with legitimate aspirations of victory.

Six balls later it became clear that if Australia were going to get anything out of the final day's play it would have to be via a recovery job of epic proportions.

Rabada, off colour in the first bowling innings due to illness, was a man reborn, bowling with pace and accuracy to end Australia's hopes before they even got going.

Kagiso Rabada celebrates the dismissal of Matt Renshaw with the second delivery of the fourth innings. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Matt Renshaw (0) feathered a leg side delivery to Ryan Rickelton may be considered unfortunate.

Marnus Labuschagne's decision to leave a ball that angled in from outside off stump to be given out LBW without playing a shot for just 4 runs, cannot.

The Queenslander's torrid tour ended on the sourest note possible, his immediate future surely to be spent away from the Test team as patience finally runs out with his lack of form.

Rabada was not done yet, finding the edge of Travis Head (14) off the last ball of his fourth over to leave Australia 3-22.

Marco Jansen claimed two catches in the first session. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

But it got no better, as Australia's batters gave up their wickets in increasingly fragile fashion to be 7-60 at lunch.

Josh Inglis was incomprehensibly run out for 4 attempting an insane single, precipitating a collapse of 3-2 as Alex Carey (2) and Cooper Connolly (0) were both bamboozled by Harmer.

Mitch Starc (0) also fell to the veteran off spinner following a baffling 25-ball stay in which he turned down runs.

"It's deplorable. It's un-Australian. There is no fight whatsoever, it's disgraceful," David Warner said on Fox Cricket.

"The batters have let the bowlers down all series … I think the batters have been disgraceful, utterly disgraceful."

He was far from the only one to be disappointed.

Travis Head edged behind to be Kagiso Rabada's third wicket. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

"Words can't describe how disappointing it is for Test cricket today," Phil Jaques said on commentary for ABC Sport.

"I bounced out of bed this morning hoping for a really good day of cricket ... and then Australia just didn't show up.

"They've been found wanting on numerous occasions ... it's just been pretty poor from Australia, to be honest, and really deflating as a cricket fan."

After lunch, if possible, things got even worse, Australia scoring just three runs in an hour, turning down runs regularly in a spell that saw a 78-ball period without a single run scored as right-hander Green was sheltered from Harmer's off breaks.

In that time though, remarkably, Cameron Green still found a way to get out after Harmer switched ends, with Green changing the 37-year-old Essex legend who bowled him expertly through the gate for 27.

Nathan Lyon and Pat Cummins endured for 17 more frustrating overs in a partnership worth 45 runs, showing a resilience that their top order counterparts could do well to learn from.

However, with players crowding the bat, they could not hold out for ever as Harmer trapped Cummins LBW for a 90-ball 11 in the shadows of tea, bowling Josh Hazlewood soon after to claim his first ever Test 10 wicket haul.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Brisbane portrait prize now among Australia’s richest art awards thanks to funding boost
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArts Brisbane portrait prize now among Australia’s richest art awards thanks to funding boost Nick Dent November 1, 2026 — 1:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Lord Mayor’s Prize, the top award in the annual Brisbane Portrait Prize, will increase by 50 per cent from $50,000 to $75,000 from 2027. The funding boost puts the prize among the nation’s richest art awards and brings the overall prize pool to $139,500. Brisbane City Council funds the Lord Mayor’s Prize and acquires the winning portrait each year. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the extra prize money was a way of supporting Brisbane’s talented artists and important stories.



“As our city continues to grow and change, it’s important we celebrate our history, embrace our identity and support the artists who bring Brisbane’s stories to life,” Schrinner said. Brisbane Portrait Prize chair Anna Reynolds said the prize was now of national significance. “As the world’s attention turns to Brisbane over the next six years, a place-based prize like this embodies our city, our arts, our culture and our character,” she said. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner with artist Pat Hoffie, winner of the Lord Mayor’s Prize in the Brisbane Portrait Prize 2026. Brisbane Portrait Prize Brisbane Portrait Prize launched in 2019 and is open to artists with a connection to Brisbane.



In addition to the Lord Mayor’s Prize, smaller cash prizes are given in eight other categories, along with grants. The winner of the Lord Mayor’s Prize in 2026 was Pat Hoffie for her portrait of her elderly father. Hundreds of art prizes are awarded in Australia each year, both government funded and privately funded, and at least seven award $80,000 or more for a single artwork. The most famous is the Archibald Prize, which has been given out most years since 1921 and is worth $100,000. World.title: Aussies humiliated after another batting collapse in Cape Town
World.content:
Australia have fallen to a series defeat in South Africa and lost top spot in the Test rankings after a calamitous morning in Cape Town led to a 176-run flogging.

On a horror final day of the series for Australia on Saturday, Pat Cummins’ side were all out for 111 in pursuit of 288 to lose the three-Test series 2-1.

South African players celebrate their victory over Australia. AP Photo/Halden Krog

Australia lost Matt Renshaw and Marnus Labuschagne in the opening over at Newlands and never really recovered.

And while Pat Cummins’ 90-ball vigil and Nathan Lyon’s unbeaten 33 in the hope of a draw delayed the inevitable, their fate was sealed when Simon Harmer bowled Josh Hazlewood just before tea.

Kagiso Rabada took 3-39 as he became the fastest man to 350 Test wickets, before Harmer’s 6-16 ripped the heart out of the tourists.

The chaos was summed up when Cameron Green defended a ball past Marques Ackerman at silly point, took off and ran Josh Inglis out in the process.

Harmer also took two wickets in one over during the collapse, getting Alex Carey reverse-sweeping before Cooper Connolly was caught behind for a duck.

It reached the point of Australia’s lower-order trying to shield Green from facing Harmer, before the spinner swapped ends and bowled the right-hander immediately to make it 8-62.

Only Travis Head (14) and Green (27) reached double figures out of Australia’s top-eight, with the side at least avoiding being all out for less than 100 in consecutive Tests for the first time since 1936-37.

“The trend of this game was once you got yourself in there, there were runs to be scored and you could face lots of balls,” Cummins said.

Australian captain Pat Cummins batting. AP Photo/Halden Krog

“Within the first hour, the game was away from us. We didn’t really give ourselves a chance.”

Australia’s batting was badly exposed in Gqeberha last week when they were bowled out for 99 on the fourth day, and asked to follow on and lost the match.

But Saturday was been even more disastrous, with the series on the line at Newlands.

Renshaw was out in the first over when he tickled a ball down legside off Rabada and was caught behind before Labuschagne was lbw leaving for four.

The Queenslander reviewed and was out on umpire’s call, before trudging off in what could be his last Test after 49 innings without a century.

Head then edged Rabada to gully while trying to drive outside off, before the Inglis run out headlined Australia’s horror show.

The result leaves Australia with losses in three of their past five Tests, with the shock defeat to Bangladesh in Darwin no longer a one-off.

Australia’s last visit to Cape Town for a Test marked the side’s lowest day, with the ball-tampering scandal in 2018.

Simon Harmers peaks with Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood after South Africa’s victory. AP Photo/Halden Krog

Saturday was not quite as bleak, but as far as an on-field effort it was not much better.

A series loss for Australia looked near impossible when they had South Africa 6-110 on day three of a wet Gqeberha Test after winning the first in Durban.

But the Proteas fought back, rolled through Australia and won comfortably.

And a little over a week on, South Africa had won the series after overcoming a 100-run first-innings deficit in Cape Town.

Beyond their bowling, Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder’s centuries on day four proved decisive, with Australia’s attack unable to get anywhere near the same purchase.

It means the Proteas take first spot off Australia in the ICC Test rankings, while also leapfrogging them into the top two in the race to next year’s World Test Championship final.

“We came here really confident and thought we were good enough to win, but we weren’t,” Cummins said.

World.title: Bethany thought only veterans and first responders got PTSD. Then she gave birth
World.content:
PoliticsFederalMental health Bethany thought only veterans and first responders got PTSD. Then she gave birth Brittany Busch October 31, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Bethany Luna-Riley did everything she could to prepare for the birth of her first child. She attended all the courses, researched online, listened to podcasts and peppered midwives with questions to avoid being blindsided by labour. Bethany Luna-Riley thought PTSD was something experienced by veterans or first responders before her traumatic birth. Wolter Peeters “I think where it unravelled for me was I was not prepared, and no one discussed with me what would happen, if all of the things that I didn’t want to happen happened at once,” she says. Luna-Riley’s trust in the system first ruptured when her preeclampsia symptoms were dismissed. The then-26-year-old first-time mum ultimately had an emergency c-section, despite having dreamed of a vaginal birth, and was then separated from her daughter, who went into intensive care because she was having trouble breathing.



Related Article Opinion

Pregnancy One in three Australian mothers suffers birth trauma. I’m one of them Sophie Walker Writer and podcaster Breastfeeding was supposed to be Luna-Riley’s saving grace, after feeling like she had lost control of her entry into motherhood. But her daughter Sydney had trouble latching, and the hospital’s lactation consultant scolded Luna-Riley for “confusing” the baby with a bottle. The Penrith mother’s confidence was shattered, and she felt like a failure. She says the repeated dismissal by healthcare providers led her down a dark path – even more so than the emergency cesarean itself. She was later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety. “I genuinely thought ... I wasn’t meant to be a mum,” she says. “I thought that my daughter hated me.” Luna-Riley is one of thousands who have made submissions to a Senate inquiry into women’s health, with a focus on postpartum care, ahead of its first hearing on Monday in Sydney.



One in five women develop a mental health condition in the perinatal period – between conception and a year post-birth – every year. Suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in Australia, with social stigma around those struggling with early parenthood exacerbating a lack of access to support. South Australian senator Marielle Smith is shepherding the committee after her own challenges with breastfeeding and postnatal anxiety following the birth of her first child. Senator Marielle Smith announced the inquiry into postpartum health in Canberra in August with Assistant Minister Rebecca White (left) and Emma McBride (right). Dominic Lorrimer The Labor MP says she was fortunate to have secured help from a private lactation consultant after suffering recurrent mastitis, but not every parent was so lucky. “I don’t think good quality postpartum healthcare should ever come down to a matter of luck, and shouldn’t come down to where you live, or certainly not what you can afford,” she says.



Her committee will examine how to improve services while empowering parents to access existing resources. It will also consider women’s pain, and access and affordability of fertility treatments. Related Article Exclusive

Women's health ‘We can’t just sit around and admire the problem’: How experts plan to make birth less traumatic States have held inquiries into birth trauma, but the federal committee will travel around the country to put the issue of postpartum health into a national frame, with support services saying they are overwhelmed by the level of need. Arabella Gibson, the chief executive at Gidget Foundation Australia, says waitlists for the not-for-profit’s 10 free mental health sessions – granted with a GP referral – have grown to up to three months. The foundation, whose namesake is a new mother who died by suicide, has made 32 recommendations to the committee, including boosting funding, establishing nationally consistent care pathways, and broadening mental health referral powers to other healthcare professionals, not just GPs.



“Service investment is critical,” says Gibson, who is also a director for Motherland Australia and the chair of Perinatal Mental Health Australia. “We can’t actually deliver the services unless we have the workforce, and the allied health professionals within the mental health space are few and far between,” she says. “There’s nothing worse than someone being screened, being diagnosed, and having nowhere to go.” Gibson also makes an economic case: the foundation reports perinatal ill health costs Australia $877 million annually, while for every $1 invested in Gidget services, $3.70 is returned to the economy. Luna-Riley, now 28, says getting the mental health support she needed through the Gidget Foundation saved her life.



Meeting other advocates and realising she wasn’t alone also fostered conversations with friends about their own struggles. “People opened up to me a bit more about, oh no, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows,” she says. “I realised, oh, this is actually such a common problem.” “A lot of my trauma could have been avoided if people just spoke to me like I was a human,” Luna-Riley says. Wolter Peeters Luna-Riley wants greater trauma-informed care in hospitals and says a standard six-week check-up for new parents is inadequate. “It might take six weeks for some women to just get out of the haze of shock of what happened to them,” she says. She points to the meticulous tracking of a baby’s development in their first year, which in NSW is recorded in what is known as the “blue book”.



“Where’s the blue book for the mother? Like, are we checking in on her?” she says. “You’re not just done and healed in six weeks.” Perinatal mental health support is available from the PANDA National Helpline on 1300 726 306 and the Gidget Foundation Australia on 1300 851 758. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 131 114 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636.

World.title: Dearden, Walsh thrive as clunky Kangaroos hammer Cook Islands
World.content:
Sam Walker might not get another chance to impress future employers this World Cup after Tom Dearden did more than enough to keep the Australian No.7 jersey on Saturday night.

And coach Kevin Walters will need to somehow find a spot for Ethan Strange on the interchange after he injected plenty of life when brought into the action just after half-time during the 66-6 win against the Cook Islands.

Tom Trbojevic scored a hat-trick for Australia. Getty Images

The Kangaroos dropped too much ball and gifted their rivals too much field position in the first half in Townsville.

Their second half was much better, but they will need to lift again if they are to stop the winner of Tonga or Samoa in Sydney next Sunday.

At least fullback Reece Walsh was firing on all cylinders again and gave the 19,172 fans something to cheer.

If Walsh has a mortgage on the No.1 jersey ahead of James Tedesco, Dearden has done enough to keep Walker on the sidelines.

Walker was in the press all week after his contract was withdrawn by the Sydney Roosters, and the Bondi club then told him he was free to leave early if he could find a new club for 2027.

Walters went with Dearden ahead of Walker and said the dramas in clubland had nothing to do with why he opted for hometown hero Dearden to partner Cam Munster in the halves.

Dearden produced some lovely passes for Tom Trbojevic and Kotoni Staggs to score in the first half, and he was a threat with his running game the longer the game went.

Kotoni Staggs and Tom Dearden celebrate. Getty Images

Munster was forced to take over the goal-kicking duties early in the game when Walsh appeared to hurt his ankle. The wider Munster had to line them up from, the better the Storm playmaker went.

Strange came on to the field for lock forward and skipper Isaah Yeo in the 45th minute and immediately gave Australia extra options around the ruck. He was always going to have a big say on the game when the Kangaroos had so much possession, but he looked solid and connected with those around him.

Trbojevic and Jack Bostock finished with hat-tricks, while Walsh was all class, despite appearing to be troubled by an ankle injury on more than one occasion.

TV commentators noted after the win the Kangaroos will need to get tougher in the middle of the park, with Tonga and Samoa known for their excellent packs.

Rua Ngatikaura celebrates his try for the Cook Islands. Getty Images

The Cook Islands, much like Fiji six days earlier, made plenty of metres the middle early in the game.

A lovely Walsh cutout put Jack Bostock over for the first four-pointer of the night after a few minutes.

But the Cook Islands hit back after 10 minutes when Rua Ngatikaura dummied and then crashed over from dummy-half. Val Holmes slotted the conversion and the ball landed in the middle of the excited Cook Islanders.

With a bit more class, the Cook Islands could have pressed for more points, but still lost no admirers. Brad Takairangi, 37, bowed out of the game with a memorable performance, and reminded fans how he still has one of the best torpedo bombs in the game.

World.title: Common sense prevails over politics on the railway line
World.content:
The problem with common sense is that it’s not all that common. That’s why I was so pleased to see it prevail over winning (or is that losing?) political votes (“None on board: Backdown over train timetable”, October 25). The T4 line between Waterfall and the central city was proposed to take 14 minutes longer due to extra stops, affecting thousands of travellers including myself, who has caught the train from my home station, Engadine, since 1972. Premier Chris Minns had the common sense to reverse his government’s initial decision after the unpopular backlash that followed it. He took the public reaction on the chin and couldn’t be accused of assigning the blame for a decision to others. The premier might have also thought that the light at the end of the tunnel was not a solution to his problem but a train building up a head of steam in his direction, with the front light on high beam. Paul Hunt, Engadine

The proposed new train timetable, on which trips would be longer and more complicated, has been withdrawn. Getty Images

As with most things related to public transport, I believe these changes were designed by people who do not regularly travel by train. When they do the redesign again, I suggest the planners be required to travel at peak and off-peak times, carrying luggage, and with a less-fit companion and/or children and a stroller, and change from bus or light rail to train. And just because I do not live near a station, that does not mean I do not use trains regularly. Helen Howes, Collaroy

Blunderers in Chief

Regarding the article “Reality of life in Chiefs’ bubble” (October 25). Apart from saying very little, what it does say is misleading. There are thousands of Australians with families residing in PNG. I do, as do my son and his family. We live very busy social and sporting lives. You can drink the tap-water, Wi-Fi is as good as it is in Sydney, and my son, his family and mine move through the community daily without security. It seems to me the only group who fixate on security in PNG is the diplomats whose pay is determined, to a large degree, by the security situation of the country they are assigned. Groups of diplomats and their spouses on early morning walks being followed and led by security vehicles (as we pass on our solitary walk) is a strange and perplexing sight. What the majority of Australians living in PNG dislike with a passion, as I do, is the waste of Australian taxpayers’ dollars on a football team. If the Australian government was serious about assisting PNG, these moneys would be spent on education and health, not on making mostly Australian footballers millionaires. Winning the hearts of PNG citizens using the geopolitical assault of the Chiefs is a serious and stupid blunder. It will not work. Peter Lowing, Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea

World.title: Chris Waller and James McDonald dominated Derby Day, but Waller wasn’t even there to enjoy it
World.content:
Master trainer Chris Waller came tantalisingly close to making it a clean sweep of Derby Day’s three group 1 races but, in a sign of the times, was not even at Flemington as star jockey James McDonald dominated the start of the Melbourne Cup carnival.

McDonald had a day out with four winners, including the Victoria Derby and Empire Rose Stakes aboard Waller’s duo Stormy Marco and Lady Shenandoah respectively, but they were nosed out by Ciaron Maher’s glamour colt, The Next Episode, in the Coolmore Stud Stakes.

Loading

Instead of basking in the glory at Flemington, Waller was at Randwick for Sydney’s lucrative Golden Eagle meeting, which, along with The Everest, has reshaped the Australian racing calendar.

Bethany Luna-Riley did everything she could to prepare for the birth of her first child. She attended all the courses, researched online, listened to podcasts and peppered midwives with questions to avoid being blindsided by labour. Bethany Luna-Riley thought PTSD was something experienced by veterans or first responders before her traumatic birth. Wolter Peeters “I think where it unravelled for me was I was not prepared, and no one discussed with me what would happen, if all of the things that I didn’t want to happen happened at once,” she says. Luna-Riley’s trust in the system first ruptured when her preeclampsia symptoms were dismissed. The then-26-year-old first-time mum ultimately had an emergency c-section, despite having dreamed of a vaginal birth, and was then separated from her daughter, who went into intensive care because she was having trouble breathing.



Related Article Opinion

Pregnancy One in three Australian mothers suffers birth trauma. I’m one of them Sophie Walker Writer and podcaster Breastfeeding was supposed to be Luna-Riley’s saving grace, after feeling like she had lost control of her entry into motherhood. But her daughter Sydney had trouble latching, and the hospital’s lactation consultant scolded Luna-Riley for “confusing” the baby with a bottle. The Penrith mother’s confidence was shattered, and she felt like a failure. She says the repeated dismissal by healthcare providers led her down a dark path – even more so than the emergency cesarean itself. She was later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety. “I genuinely thought ... I wasn’t meant to be a mum,” she says. “I thought that my daughter hated me.” Luna-Riley is one of thousands who have made submissions to a Senate inquiry into women’s health, with a focus on postpartum care, ahead of its first hearing on Monday in Sydney.



One in five women develop a mental health condition in the perinatal period – between conception and a year post-birth – every year. Suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in Australia, with social stigma around those struggling with early parenthood exacerbating a lack of access to support. South Australian senator Marielle Smith is shepherding the committee after her own challenges with breastfeeding and postnatal anxiety following the birth of her first child. Senator Marielle Smith announced the inquiry into postpartum health in Canberra in August with Assistant Minister Rebecca White (left) and Emma McBride (right). Dominic Lorrimer The Labor MP says she was fortunate to have secured help from a private lactation consultant after suffering recurrent mastitis, but not every parent was so lucky. “I don’t think good quality postpartum healthcare should ever come down to a matter of luck, and shouldn’t come down to where you live, or certainly not what you can afford,” she says.



Her committee will examine how to improve services while empowering parents to access existing resources. It will also consider women’s pain, and access and affordability of fertility treatments. Related Article Exclusive

Women's health ‘We can’t just sit around and admire the problem’: How experts plan to make birth less traumatic States have held inquiries into birth trauma, but the federal committee will travel around the country to put the issue of postpartum health into a national frame, with support services saying they are overwhelmed by the level of need. Arabella Gibson, the chief executive at Gidget Foundation Australia, says waitlists for the not-for-profit’s 10 free mental health sessions – granted with a GP referral – have grown to up to three months. The foundation, whose namesake is a new mother who died by suicide, has made 32 recommendations to the committee, including boosting funding, establishing nationally consistent care pathways, and broadening mental health referral powers to other healthcare professionals, not just GPs.



“Service investment is critical,” says Gibson, who is also a director for Motherland Australia and the chair of Perinatal Mental Health Australia. “We can’t actually deliver the services unless we have the workforce, and the allied health professionals within the mental health space are few and far between,” she says. “There’s nothing worse than someone being screened, being diagnosed, and having nowhere to go.” Gibson also makes an economic case: the foundation reports perinatal ill health costs Australia $877 million annually, while for every $1 invested in Gidget services, $3.70 is returned to the economy. Luna-Riley, now 28, says getting the mental health support she needed through the Gidget Foundation saved her life.



Meeting other advocates and realising she wasn’t alone also fostered conversations with friends about their own struggles. “People opened up to me a bit more about, oh no, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows,” she says. “I realised, oh, this is actually such a common problem.” “A lot of my trauma could have been avoided if people just spoke to me like I was a human,” Luna-Riley says. Wolter Peeters Luna-Riley wants greater trauma-informed care in hospitals and says a standard six-week check-up for new parents is inadequate. “It might take six weeks for some women to just get out of the haze of shock of what happened to them,” she says. She points to the meticulous tracking of a baby’s development in their first year, which in NSW is recorded in what is known as the “blue book”.



“Where’s the blue book for the mother? Like, are we checking in on her?” she says. “You’re not just done and healed in six weeks.” Perinatal mental health support is available from the PANDA National Helpline on 1300 726 306 and the Gidget Foundation Australia on 1300 851 758. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 131 114 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636.

World.title: Dearden, Walsh thrive as clunky Kangaroos hammer Cook Islands
World.content:
Sam Walker might not get another chance to impress future employers this World Cup after Tom Dearden did more than enough to keep the Australian No.7 jersey on Saturday night.

And coach Kevin Walters will need to somehow find a spot for Ethan Strange on the interchange after he injected plenty of life when brought into the action just after half-time during the 66-6 win against the Cook Islands.

Tom Trbojevic scored a hat-trick for Australia. Getty Images

The Kangaroos dropped too much ball and gifted their rivals too much field position in the first half in Townsville.

Their second half was much better, but they will need to lift again if they are to stop the winner of Tonga or Samoa in Sydney next Sunday.

At least fullback Reece Walsh was firing on all cylinders again and gave the 19,172 fans something to cheer.

If Walsh has a mortgage on the No.1 jersey ahead of James Tedesco, Dearden has done enough to keep Walker on the sidelines.

Walker was in the press all week after his contract was withdrawn by the Sydney Roosters, and the Bondi club then told him he was free to leave early if he could find a new club for 2027.

Walters went with Dearden ahead of Walker and said the dramas in clubland had nothing to do with why he opted for hometown hero Dearden to partner Cam Munster in the halves.

Dearden produced some lovely passes for Tom Trbojevic and Kotoni Staggs to score in the first half, and he was a threat with his running game the longer the game went.

Kotoni Staggs and Tom Dearden celebrate. Getty Images

Munster was forced to take over the goal-kicking duties early in the game when Walsh appeared to hurt his ankle. The wider Munster had to line them up from, the better the Storm playmaker went.

Strange came on to the field for lock forward and skipper Isaah Yeo in the 45th minute and immediately gave Australia extra options around the ruck. He was always going to have a big say on the game when the Kangaroos had so much possession, but he looked solid and connected with those around him.

Trbojevic and Jack Bostock finished with hat-tricks, while Walsh was all class, despite appearing to be troubled by an ankle injury on more than one occasion.

TV commentators noted after the win the Kangaroos will need to get tougher in the middle of the park, with Tonga and Samoa known for their excellent packs.

Rua Ngatikaura celebrates his try for the Cook Islands. Getty Images

The Cook Islands, much like Fiji six days earlier, made plenty of metres the middle early in the game.

A lovely Walsh cutout put Jack Bostock over for the first four-pointer of the night after a few minutes.

But the Cook Islands hit back after 10 minutes when Rua Ngatikaura dummied and then crashed over from dummy-half. Val Holmes slotted the conversion and the ball landed in the middle of the excited Cook Islanders.

With a bit more class, the Cook Islands could have pressed for more points, but still lost no admirers. Brad Takairangi, 37, bowed out of the game with a memorable performance, and reminded fans how he still has one of the best torpedo bombs in the game.

World.title: Chris Waller and James McDonald dominated Derby Day, but Waller wasn’t even there to enjoy it
World.content:
Master trainer Chris Waller came tantalisingly close to making it a clean sweep of Derby Day’s three group 1 races but, in a sign of the times, was not even at Flemington as star jockey James McDonald dominated the start of the Melbourne Cup carnival.

McDonald had a day out with four winners, including the Victoria Derby and Empire Rose Stakes aboard Waller’s duo Stormy Marco and Lady Shenandoah respectively, but they were nosed out by Ciaron Maher’s glamour colt, The Next Episode, in the Coolmore Stud Stakes.

Loading

Instead of basking in the glory at Flemington, Waller was at Randwick for Sydney’s lucrative Golden Eagle meeting, which, along with The Everest, has reshaped the Australian racing calendar.

World.title: Pursuit of power may mean compromise
World.content:
Independents option Peter Hartcher paints a miserable picture of the four main political parties competing for attention and votes. Yet he makes no mention of the fifth contemporary force in Australian politics: the community independents in the House of Representatives and the significant independents in the Senate. For the past few weeks, we have had people and politicians across the spectrum rightly lauding the character, leadership, and work ethic of community independent Helen Haines following the shocking incident in Wangaratta. Members of parliament such as Helen Haines have shown just how valuable and valued independents are in our political landscape. At the next election, undoubtedly Labor and the Coalition will lose several seats, but they might not go to One Nation or the Greens; they may instead go to community independents. This would be a good outcome, as would a minority government requiring negotiations with a large crossbench of high integrity, high-quality independents. Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen

Think compromise Columnist Peter Hartcher identifies significant issues likely to stop any one political party from forming government alone ( Comment , 31/10). Many countries have this problem regularly, including Italy and Israel. They have horse-trading of policies and cabinet positions after elections, with compromises reached. The closest example in recent Australian history involved Julia Gillard’s government. Three pre-teal independents supported Labor on supply and no confidence motions, in return for some policy concessions. On current opinion polling, the Victorian state election might force Ben Carroll or Jess Wilson into similar or wider deals with the Greens or One Nation, whatever the protestations now. In 2028, Anthony Albanese could be forced to promise with the Greens and/or independents more radical carbon emissions cuts, in return for parliamentary support. One Nation might extract concessions from Angus Taylor on migration numbers or a further reduction of climate efforts. Our major parties could avoid the worst of the apocalypse by compromising with close rival parties. John Hughes, Mentone

The forgotten ones

As much as I like Ross Gittins’ explanations of monetary policy, I don’t agree with him about raising the GST (Comment, 28/10). The low wage and welfare benefit recipients are always forgotten when it comes to the GST. Yes, workers would have lower taxes but what if you don’t pay tax or you’re a low-income earner? The price of goods would rise and make life even more difficult for these people. It’d be OK if you earn a decent wage, it’ll all work out but not for people with less money. Even people earning well now have trouble paying their rent. A raised GST would just make it harder to survive every day. Imagine being on the dole and prices rising even more to cover a GST?

Chris Hooper, Castlemaine

The forgotten lesson

Jewish philosopher Hannah Arendt understood something fundamental about political freedom: its greatest enemy is not disagreement, but the abandonment of independent judgment.

Jillian Segal’s latest proposals seem to have forgotten this lesson. In the name of combating antisemitism, she wants greater oversight of public broadcasters, enforceable conditions on arts funding and tighter restrictions on protest. Meanwhile, she identifies progressive social justice advocates as a particularly pervasive source of antisemitism. The irony is extraordinary. People who insist that human rights must apply universally, including to Palestinians, are now being treated as a threat to social cohesion.

Antisemitism is a serious evil. But so is the political habit of turning moral disagreement into grounds for suspicion and institutional punishment. Universities exist to question accepted truths. Journalists exist to scrutinise power. Artists exist, among other things, to disturb our certainties. None should have to demonstrate political conformity to retain public support.

Arendt knew where the suppression of independent judgment could lead.

We should be especially wary when restrictions on freedom arrive dressed in the language of moral responsibility.

Fernanda Trecenti, Fitzroy

An actor’s legacy

The death of Sir Patrick Stewart at 86 is a loss that reaches far beyond the worlds of television and cinema.

While millions will remember him as Captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier of the X-Men, we should not overlook the distinguished Shakespearean actor whose extraordinary voice, presence and command of language brought such depth to both characters.

Yet perhaps his greatest legacy lies in the message of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Gene Roddenberry’s vision of humanity’s future was one worth aspiring to: a united Earth, free from racism and prejudice, with no nations waging wars against one another, and a humanity that had moved beyond greed and division to embrace knowledge, exploration, and co-operation.

Watching today’s world, with its wars, nationalism, racial hatred, and political division, one wonders how far we have travelled in the wrong direction.

Perhaps the greatest tribute we can pay Stewart, and the fictional captain he brought so magnificently to life, is to remember that this vision was never simply science fiction. It was a challenge to humanity.

Make it so.

Darren Grindrod, Glenroy

Lose-lose situation

With US Defence Secretary (aka Secretary of War) Pete Hegseth busily firing all the expert leaders in US defence and downgrading America’s military strength, why are our leaders continuing to align Australia with America and paying billions of our dollars for submarines we will never get and America can’t actually build? We are aligning ourselves with a “superpower” that can’t even win against Iran and is subservient to Russia. It’s a lose-lose disaster for Australia. Pull out now, PM.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights

Childhood’s end

I supervised two VCE exams last week, 50 years after I sat my own finals. It seemed like a blink of an eye since that time, until I read through the General Maths paper and realised I couldn’t answer any of the questions.

Observing these kids, I wondered if their demeanour was a hint of their future: one gazing into nothing; a boy wielding his highlighter like a light-sabre, supremely organised; another, jiggling their leg incessantly as they flipped in a frenzy between exam booklet and calculator.

Many of these students will never again utilise the ″⁣Hungarian algorithm″⁣ (a mystery to me, too), or calculate a seasonal index; but hopefully they’ll retain for a few years some vestige of the sharp analysis required for such a testing time. I feel for these kids. I hope the resilience that got them into this room keeps them strong for what’s outside the door. The world is a scary place, even more so, 50 years on.

Jane Neville, Wattle Flat

Off message

Who in One Nation thinks that cartoons depicting politicians being run over and a colouring book for children, depicting Bluey, obviously scared, being held at knife point, is a legitimate way of getting their message across.

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor

World.title: Black Ferns complete series clean sweep of France
World.content:
The Black Ferns have completed a series clean sweep over France with a 36-7 win at Christchurch.

New Zealand's opening try came from an outrageous no-look overhead pass from No.8 Liana Mikaele-Tu'u in the build-up, finished off by wing Shyrah Tuliau-Tua'a.

Scoring and converting the second try, fullback Braxton Sorenson-McGee became the first Black Ferns player to score 100 points in a calendar year. She had another try disallowed moments later for a forward pass in the build-up.

France were rewarded with a try from close range to hooker Maïlys Mailagi on the stroke of halftime, giving them some hope of a second-half comeback.

After the break, Tuliau-Tua'a doubled the lead with a try in the corner, capitalising on some outstanding passing skills from prop Chryss Viliko.

Replacement prop Maddi Robinson powered over for her first test try, but Tuliau-Tua'a left her team shorthanded, when she was yellow-carded for a high tackle.

Unperturbed, New Zealand extended their advantage with a try to replacement Mererangi Paul, before hooker Vici-Rose Green crossed in the final stages to set the seal on victory.

New Zealand won 10 of their 11 tests this year, including four against France. Their only defeat came at the hands of world champions and world No.1 England.

Afterwards, Black Ferns flanker Elinor-Plum King was named World Rugby XVs Breakthrough Player of the Year, while loose forward Kaipo Olsen-Baker was named Player of the Year.

World.title: Two out of five clients asking for help with peptides, needle exchange, agency says
World.content:
The operators of a needle exchange programme say two out of every five clients is asking for help with peptides.

Health NZ says it has distributed 2300 peptide injecting kits through the programme since mid-September.

A black market for unapproved peptides, mostly for weight loss or performance enhancement, has taken hold in New Zealand as many Kiwis find approved drugs like Wegovy too expensive.

The Aotaroa Drug Information Outreach Trust is one of the organisations contracted to manage the needle exchange programme, and provides the service for most of the upper and central North Island.

Chief executive Dr Lesley McTurk has seen a surge in new users.

"Our more traditional clients, who would be injecting psychoactive drugs, would've comprised 85 to 90 percent of our clients," she said, noting that the remaining 10 percent tended to be steroid users.

"These peptide clients [have become] around 40 percent, so yes there's been a big increase."

Aotaroa Drug Information Outreach Trust chief executive Dr Lesley McTurk. Supplied / University of Auckland

McTurk said it wasn't for her to say whether that was cause for alarm.

"The purpose of the needle exchange programme is to reduce the spread of bloodborne viruses amongst people who inject drugs, our kaupapa is all about harm reduction and we don't judge the people that come to us," she said.

"We take a very strong line on neither condoning nor condemning the use of drugs."

Her focus was on providing clean needles and good advice.

"Making sure the site is clean, how to dispose of the needles, [warning them] not to use tap water, to use sterile water so they're not getting bacteria into the injection, that's the sort of advice we give them," she said.

Peptides were injected subcutaneously, meaning the needles were short and only needed to pierce skin and fat, rather than a vein.

"It's not a particularly difficult injection to give yourself. Diabetics, for example, do this daily. It's a lot more straightforward than doing an intravenous injection, but it still poses some risks, risks of infection, so we want people to know how to do it safely," McTurk said.

A spokesperson for Customs said staff worked closely with Medsafe to identify unapproved peptides crossing the border.

"When goods that are located require a prescription or are classified as a medication, as in the case of several peptides, they will be referred to Medsafe," they said.

World.title: Porirua deputy mayor Kylie Wihapi dies
World.content:
Tributes are pouring in, after the death of Porirua deputy mayor Kylie Wihapi, aged 45.

Mayor Anita Baker said she was numb with shock and disbelief at the sudden loss.

"She was such a vibrant, outgoing and generous person, full of life, warmth and a deep love for all of Porirua," she said.

Baker said Wihapi died on Saturday morning, as the result of a fall.

"There will be more to say about Kylie's extraordinary contribution in the days ahead, but right now, my thoughts and deepest sympathies are with her whānau, especially her husband Adam, son Cooper, step-son Arama, her mum and dad Marlene and Rob, her brothers and wider family. My heart breaks for them.

Baker said Wihapi had made history as Porirua's first elected Māori ward councillor.

"She brought wisdom, courage, compassion and an unmistakable energy to everything she did.

"I have lost a trusted adviser and friend, and her fellow councillors have lost a much-loved colleague."

Kylie Wihapi Supplied/Barbara Edmonds Facebook

"Kylie was Porirua through and through. She loved this city, believed in its people and worked tirelessly to make it a better place.

"We will miss her terribly."

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said she was "so very sad to hear of Kylie's passing".

"She was so passionate about Porirua, every conversation with her was of huge pride for the whole community.

"My deep condolences to her whānau... Moe mai rā e te taonga."

Labour MP Barbara Edmonds said she was "heartbroken" at the loss of "one of our most amazing local wahine".

Barbara Edmonds and Kylie Wihapi. Supplied/Barbara Edmonds Facebook

"Kylie was everywhere and anywhere.

"Whether it was on the netball court as a dedicated referee, hosting her annual Pink Breakfast to raise funds for the Breast Cancer Foundation, co-ordinating her annual Christmas pet food drive, filling in for the mayor Anita Baker, coaching netball teams or following her beloved son Cooper on the rugby field side-lines."

Edmonds described her as "selfless" and "always keen for a dress up".

"Her energy for life was just immeasurable. No matter what it was, Kylie always made time for the community of Porirua that she loved so much.

"Thank you e hoa for all that you've done for us and for Porirua. La manuia lau malaga."

Wellington City Council deputy mayor Ben McNulty said he was devastated.

"Kylie was an incredibly warm and welcoming person, and deeply passionate about Porirua.

"To her family, friends and wider community, I am so sorry for your deep loss."

Pāuatahanui general ward councillor Ross Leggett said Wihapi was "true child of Porirua" and "gone far too soon".

"To say the loss of Kylie Wihapi... is a shock would be an understatement.

"I was elected to the council alongside her in 2016, and we were all the better for her openness, humour, warmth and sheer industriousness. She made a fine deputy mayor and gave so much to the city she loved."

The former mayor of Lower Hutt, Campbell Barry, said Wihapi's passing was not fair.

World.title: Nearly 200 schools 'of concern' or worse - Education Review Office
World.content:
The Education Review Office says 199 schools need help for the sake of their students.

Its 2026 annual report says students at those schools are at risk without timely intervention.

The schools included 172 regarded as "of concern" and 27 regarded as having "significant concerns".

"A school may be identified as being 'of concern' where evidence shows significant improvement is required in student achievement, attendance, underperformance across core areas, like learner success and wellbeing, leadership and governance, curriculum, and teaching and learning," ERO told RNZ.

"'Serious concern' is the higher threshold, where problems are more severe or persistent, risks to learners are greater, or previous support and intervention have not produced sustained improvement."

The review office told RNZ the proportion of schools of concern or serious concern was eight percent, which was about the same as previous years.

"The proportion of schools identified as being of concern has been fairly stable over time at around 7-9 percent, although individual schools move into and out of the category, as their circumstances and performance change. ERO has strengthened how it identifies and monitors schools requiring improvement.

"The more significant issue is that too many schools remain of concern for too long and do not achieve sustained improvement, despite receiving support."

ERO's annual report said the schools were concentrated in the upper half of the North Island.

"While these schools remain a small proportion of the overall system, the distribution of concern is not even across the country," the reports aid. "The highest numbers of these schools were located in Tai Tokerau, Waikato, Bay of Plenty/Waiariki, Tāmaki Herenga Waka and Hawke's Bay/Tairāwhiti.

"Schools identified as having significant concerns were more commonly secondary schools, which accounted for approximately two-thirds of all cases in this category. This suggests that, while concerns arise across all parts of the system, challenges in secondary settings are often more complex, and may require more intensive monitoring and intervention."

The annual report said the office reviewed 628 schools and 542 early childhood services this year. It found eight percent of the schools required improvement, half of them in "learner success and wellbeing".

Just one percent were told their teaching needed improvement.

"Around four in five schools reviewed this year are embedding or excelling in leadership (80 percent), teaching and learning (79 percent), and curriculum (81 percent), compared with 67 percent of schools in learner success and wellbeing," the report said.

"This suggests that, while schools are increasingly strengthening the conditions that support improvement, it may take longer for these efforts to be reflected in learner outcomes."

The early childhood education reviews found that one percent of English-medium services required improvement, as did seven percent of Māori-medium services.

The report said four percent of the English-medium schools ERO visited in the past year were already meeting the government's 2030 goal of 80 percent of students attending regularly, but 51 percent were behind or significantly behind the target.

Regular attendance was defined as attending more than 90 percent of the time.

The office found 17 percent of the schools it visited were already meeting the government's 2030 target of ensuring 80 percent of Year 8 students were achieving at or above their expected curriculum level for reading, writing and maths.

A further 69 percent were making progress toward the goal and 14 percent were not making sufficient progress.

World.title: Kiwi Ferns overpower Papua New Guinea for World Cup semifinal spot
World.content:
Papua New Guinea made the Kiwi Ferns work, before they eased clear 40-12 on a soggy Gold Coast and make it three wins from three Rugby League World Cup pool games.

New Zealand will be top qualifiers from Group B for next weekend's semi-finals, where they face Samoa in Newcastle.

While the Ferns romped to a 92-0 win over France in Christchurch last week, their two other matches have been decent contests, including their opening 18-12 defeat of group runners-up Fiji, who will face Australia in the other semi.

PNG were particularly difficult to break down in the first half, with a try to Kaiyah Atai on the stroke of the interval inching New Zealand to a 14-12 advantage.

Play opened up in the second half, with the Kiwis adding five more tries to their overall tally of eight, while keeping their tiring opponents scoreless.

Kiwi Ferns perform their pre-game haka against the Orchids. www.photosport.nz

They started the second spell on the best possible note, when front-rower Otesa Pule scored a runaway 70m solo try almost from the restart.

Backs Mackenzie Wiki and the impressive Abigail Roache both completed doubles after the break, as their team unearthed greater cohesion and reduced the error count.

Duel international Stacey Waaka and Wiki bagged tries early in the match, but both were cancelled out by PNG, who responded with converted tries to Tia Molo and Elsie Albert.

Captain and halfback Raecene McGregor said her team would need to be better in the knockout phase.

"Obviously, I'm proud that we were really resilient and got through it in the end," she told Sky Sport.

"There were a couple of errors in that first half and even in the second half - we need to be better, especially coming into the semis."
