World.title: Ruthless Kiwis bury Fiji to reach Rugby League World Cup semis
World.content:
NZ Kiwis have delivered a statement performance at the Rugby League World Cup, crushing Fiji 78-0 on the Gold Coast to power into the semifinals.

Boom centre Casey McLean crossed for four of their 13 tries, while winger Jamayne Isaako landed every conversion attempt, as New Zealand eclipsed the Bati in every department.

The only blot was a red card to wing Ronaldo Mulitalo for a high tackle, which left both teams to play the rest of the game with 12 players, after Fiji halfback Brandon Wakeham was also sent off for retaliation.

Fiji were expected to provide a stern test, after pushing Australia in a 36-22 defeat in Brisbane last weekend, setting up a virtual quarterfinal against New Zealand, with the losers eliminated.

However, there would be no repeat of the infamous 2017 quarterfinal, when Fiji stunned the hosts 4-2 in Wellington in one of the great tournament upsets.

The scene was set in the opening 13 minutes, as the Kiwis powered across for four tries, with half Jahrome Hughes cantering through a gaping hole to score from their very first set.

That 24-0 lead had doubled to 48-0 by halftime, with Fiji's cause not helped by the loss of experienced captain and hooker Api Korisau to a suspected broken jaw.

The opening exchanges of the second half were overshadowed by Mulitalo's tackle, which resulted in a head injury to opposite Ronald Philitoga, forcing him from the field.

Ronaldo Mulitalo checks on opposite Ronald Philitoga, after his red-carded high tackle. photosport

Both teams came together in a tense exchange, with Wakeham also shown red for throwing a punch.

New Zealand's scoring resumed soon afterwards, with McLean - part of a potent left edge - crossing twice in four minutes to add to his first-half double.

Forwards Briton Nikora and Erin Clark also scored, before fullback Keano Kini bagged his second late in the contest.

Centre Dane Gagai, captain James Fisher-Harris, Mulitalo and forward Xavier Willison also scored tries, as the Kiwis showed why they will be a handful for any side in the knockout stage.

The Bati struggled throughout the game to contain New Zealand's forwards, who produced numerous offloads and rapid play-the-balls.

Their frustration boiled over again late, when prop Jordan Miller was sin-binned for a high shot that sparked another scuffle.

Isaako landed 13 from 14 conversions in 82-16 thrashing of Cook Islands in Christchurch last weekend - a NZ test-record 38-point haul - and his record was even better this time, slotting 13 from 13.

The result means the Kiwis will advance from Group A into the semis, alongside hosts and defending champions Australia.

Their opponents will depend on the result of Sunday night's group match between unbeaten Pacific rivals Samoa and Tonga.

The Kiwis hope star fullback Kalyn Ponga will have recovered for the knockout stage of the tournament, after breaking his forearm in the opening 24-22 loss to Australia just two weeks ago.

Recap the live action below:

World.title: Fiji Bulikula into World Cup semis with win over France
World.content:
There were mixed results for Fiji's rugby league teams in Saturday afternoon's third round of matches of the Rugby League World Cup.

Fijian fans who had packed into the Cbus Super Stadium celebrated the Fiji Bulikula, as they created history by securing their semifinal spot after a commanding 54-6 win over France.

But celebration turned to disappointment later, as Fijian fans were left stunned as the Fiji Bati men's side lost their semifinal campaign, going down 78-0 to the New Zealand Kiwis.

The Kiwis led 48-0 at halftime, with eight tries in the first spell of 40 minutes, before running in five more in the second spell.

Tough win for Bulikula

On their way to clinching their first semifinal spot, the Fijian women dominated proceedings against the French outfit, who held their own for about 15 minutes in the first spell and scored one lone try in the second spell of 35 minutes.

The Bulikula had too much power and experience, running in 11 tries, with Tahlia Marshall getting two in the match.

Fiji led 22-0 at halftime, with four tries before they added seven more in the second half.

The Bulikula's win means they will battle Australia in one of the two semifinals next weekend, with fellow Pacific islanders Fetū Samoa taking on New Zealand in the other.

Fullback Cassie Staples told the post-match conference it was a tough battle for them and France had given their all.

"The scoreboard didn't really reflect the intensity of the game," she said.

"It was a tough first half and the scoreboard did not reflect that.

"There were tough challenges and things we will need to work on.

"Proud of the girls, proud of what they did today."

Assistant coach Isaac Michael said the team achieved what they had set out to do and will work on next week once they have rested and recovered.

"We came in today wanting to put in a complete 70-minute performance," he said.

"Errors kind of broke the game for us and we will be looking into that and remedy that during the week."

It took the Fijians just four minutes before they crossed the French line for their first try of the game.

Tahlia Marshall finished off a move on the right after playmaker Losana Lutu had dummied and sent the ball wide, with Marshall in free space to finish off.

Playmaker Losana Lutu said it was a tough first half and said the conditions were a challenge also.

"It is pretty hot but we still need to get the job done," she said as the team walked off for the halftime break.

Luisa Yaranamua and Lutu combined well as the halves combination.

France managed to hold their own and countered with their own attacks after Fiji's first try, forcing a knock-on from Fiji fullback Cassie Staples.

Led by captain Elisa Akpa and supported by Melissa Medina, Perle Ramazeilles, Haoua Kessely, Camille Boudaud and Lisa Diraison, the French attacked hard from the ensuing six-tackle count but Staples got to the ball over the line to save Fiji as France looked dangerous.

Fiji were found struggling to execute under pressure as France stepped up, showing a lot of spirit.

Captain Sereana Naitokatoka led the Fiji attacks with Leilani Ahsam, Elizabeth Naleba, Nanise Vakacavu, and Talei Holmes driving forward.

In the 20th minute, Lutu's high bomb saw winger Maria Paseka outjump the defence of Margot Canal, catch the ball inflight and run in to score behind the posts, giving Fiji a 8-0 lead. Yaranamua's conversion saw them move up to 10-0.

France had one of their best chances to get a try in the 24th minute, but winger Haoua Kessely got her hand over the sideline as she dived over to score in the corner in Staples' tackle. The try was disallowed.

The following minute saw Talei Holmes and Latisha Smythe combining again, setting up middle plays, which resulted in replacement Aliti Namoce crashing her way to the line. Yaranamua's kick saw Fiji lead 16-0, before Namoce broke through a hole and sent the ball to Lutu who ran across to the corner to score, for Fiji to lead 22-0 at halftime.

The Bulikula continued with where they left off at halftime, attacking the French defence again.

Two minutes in Yaranamua reached over the line but fell short, before the ensuing set play saw Naomi Tegu crash over in between the posts.

But a bunker review ruled Tegu had lost the ball in the tackle.

France celebrated their only try through Stecy Bessiere, who finished off a good run through the middle by Fanny Ramos, breaking the Fijian defensive line. Lisa Diraison added two points from her conversion as France trailed 6-22.

The Bulikula then turned the tide on, with livewire fullback Staples crossing over in the corner in the 39th minute, after Yaranamua set her up.

Marshall got her second six minutes later, before Latisha Smythe, Leilani Ahsam, Taina Naividi and Lorren Ieli added one try each, sending the Bulikula to the last four with a big scoreline.

Kiwis dominant against Bati

Keano Kini of the Kiwis celebrate scoring a try against Fiji. photosport

Meanwhile, in the men's clash the Kiwis shut Fiji off and had too much pressure, showing brutality to outscore and outplay the Fijians, who had held the Australian Kangaroos before a close loss last weekend.

The Kiwis scored 13 tries in total by the end of the match, as they dominated both on attack and defence.

It was the worst of three World Cup performances by the Bati, who looked lost and bewildered during the match.

Kiwis Ronaldo Mulitalo and Fiji's Brandon Wakeham were both sent off in the 51st minute as tempers flared, following a Mulitalo high tackle on Ronald Philitonga.

Wakeham hit Mulitalo with a punch on the deck as he retaliated to the high tackle hit on Philitoga.

Fiji's Jordan Miller was also sin-binned late in the second half.

The win means the Kiwis will join Australia as the two teams to qualify for the semifinal from Pool A.

World.title: Kangaroos pile on the points in World Cup thrashing of Cook Islands
World.content:
The Kangaroos finished the group stage of the Rugby League World Cup undefeated, closing out the Pool A action with a 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville.

On a sweaty night up north, the Australian men were below their best to start and briefly trailed the Islanders 6-4 before asserting their dominance with 10 unanswered tries.

Wingers Tom Trbojevic and Jack Bostock both finished with hat-tricks while Tino Fa'saumaleaui grabbed a double.

Fullback Reece Walsh was named player of the match after a try, five assists and a pair of line breaks, but his fitness is somewhat concerning.

Walsh grabbed at his foot after converting Kotoni Staggs's 27th-minute try and, despite looking untroubled while finishing off a spectacular team try on the half-hour mark, handed over goal-kicking duties.

Cameron Munster kicked goals for the rest of the game and Walsh closed out an impressive performance that will likely quiet calls for him to be replaced by James Tedesco.

The Kangaroos will play their semifinal on Sunday, November 8 at the Sydney Football Stadium, but their opponent will not be known until after the clash between Tonga and Samoa tomorrow night.

Look back at all the action as it happened in our live blog below.

World.title: Joanna Wietrzyk wins first HYROX race after incontinence controversy
World.content:
Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has made a triumphant return to HYROX competition in Germany after taking a six-week break following a controversial incident at a race in Beijing last month.

The 24-year-old from Melbourne faced widespread criticism after continuing to compete despite suffering severe diarrhoea during the race.

Videos showing Wietrzyk running with faecal matter streaming down her legs were widely shared on social media.

Although she crossed the finish line first, Wietrzyk subsequently withdrew from the event, forfeited her points and issued a public apology.

The backlash took a heavy emotional toll, with Wietrzyk saying she considered quitting the sport altogether.

Loading Instagram content

But after stepping away from competition and social media, she returned in emphatic fashion, cruising to victory over Lauren Weeks at HYROX Hamburg in Germany.

The event marked the opening round of the 2026-27 HYROX Elite 15 Series and Wietrzyk's first competition since the Beijing controversy.

The women's solo professional HYROX world record holder said she relied heavily on family support during what she described as a mentally and emotionally taxing period.

Joanna Wietrzyk shared an apology online on Thursday, withdrawing and handing back points from the race she won. (Instagram: @joannawietrzyk)

In an earlier interview with the BBC, Wietrzyk acknowledged she had made "the wrong decision" by continuing to race in Beijing but said she was shocked by the scale of the online abuse.

"To personally experience that was very eye-opening to me, seeing the effect of social media for someone who's 24 and out there racing," she said.

" Yes, I did make the wrong decision but I don't believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online. "

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) holds the HYROX Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

"I didn't really think about those around me, which looking back in hindsight, was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry to everyone I did affect in that situation."

Wietrzyk also revealed how close she came to walking away from the sport.

"I've gone through moments and weeks of 'maybe we should just stop' and just go back to doing a normal job and just remove myself from social media entirely," she said.

"I went through a very, very low period mentally and emotionally. It was great that I had my family with me and I could kind of isolate myself from the world but I can't do that forever."

Wietrzyk's next major event is the HYROX Elite Series in London, scheduled for December 3-6.

HYROX is a global fitness race combining 8 kilometres of running with eight functional work-out stations, testing strength and endurance.

World.title: Horses pulled from Derby Day after trainer allegedly has syringes in car
World.content:
Flemington trainer Nick Ryan had two runners withdrawn from today's meeting after Racing Victoria (RV) stewards charged him with alleged possession of a prohibited substance.

Ryan was charged after a stable inspection this morning by RV's Compliance Assurance Team, which resulted in the forced scratchings of Anglaise (Wakeful Stakes) and Doubt Time (Coolmore Stud Stakes).

"Mr Ryan was found to have in his possession, in the glove box of his motor vehicle, two syringes of Darbepoetin Alfa which is a prohibited substance under Prohibited List A of the Australian Rules of Racing," RV stewards reported.

Ryan, a former champion jockey, reserved his plea and the hearing was adjourned until Monday.

Zahra overcomes fall to claim first Group 1 of Melbourne Cup Carnival

Mark Zahra has bounced back from his nasty fall to pilot The Next Episode to a brilliant victory in the stallion-making Coolmore Stud Stakes (1,200m) at Flemington.

Mark Zahra riding The Next Episode wins the Coolmore Stud Stakes. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

The Ciaron Maher-trained colt stamped himself as the nation's premier three-year-old sprinter, finishing a long neck clear of Chris Waller's St Gotthard in the $2 million Group 1 sprint.

Mbube was third, with Under Focus fourth.

Zahra returned to action today just two weeks after a horror Caulfield Cup fall on Half Yours.

His win in the first Group 1 event of this year's Melbourne Cup carnival comes after his dominant showing with four victories on Victoria Derby day 12 months ago.

It was Zahra's third Coolmore Stud Stakes victory and second in as many years after his win aboard Tentyris last year.

"They're very similar horses. He's a real dude now, this horse," Zahra said.

"He's so relaxed, but when you want him he just goes 'bang'. It's great to be on two magnificent colts within two years."

Zahra took a week off under doctors' orders after his Caulfield Cup fall and missed Cox Plate day, but would not be denied another shot at Flemington glory.

Loading...

"Any other time of year I'm probably having a holiday in Byron or Ibiza, but this time of year you just can't do it," Zahra said.

"I just had to suck it up. It's been a tough two weeks, but this time of year is what I live for and ride for.

"Great help by the doctors and with a few Nurofen today we're bang on song."

It was Maher's first Coolmore Stud Stakes victory. The master trainer paid tribute to close friend Zahra.

"He's a super jock, Mark," Maher said.

"He had the fall the other day, and to get up and be riding at the top of his game, they're marvellous, the jocks.

"Mark's a great mate and I'm sure we'll be popping the top off a couple of champagnes tomorrow."

Earlier, Waller had success in the first race of the Melbourne Cup carnival, when Damian Lane steered The Roaring Sun to victory in the Group 3 Carbine Club Stakes.

Waller had the quinella with Unhinged, ridden by James McDonald, finishing second ahead of Conquer The World in third.

It is the sixth time Waller has won the traditional carnival opener, and third in succession after triumphs by Aeliana (2024) and Panova (2025).

Waller also claimed the Group 2 Wakeful Stakes with De Armas, ridden by Blake Shinn.

J-Mac, Waller combine for Victoria Derby win

James "J-Mac" McDonald and Waller combined for another major victory as Stormy Marco surged home to claim the $3 million Victoria Derby (2500m) at Flemington.

The three-year-old colt charged to the lead in the straight and raced away from second-placed Cold Shower for a stunning victory under McDonald in Australia's oldest classic.

Quick Finish was third as the first filly in the race since 1990, with Murshidi fourth.

It was a fourth Derby triumph for Waller and second for McDonald.

AAP

World.title: Two sent off after high shot and punch as Kiwis humiliate Fiji 78-0
World.content:
New Zealand has marched itself into the semifinals of the Rugby League World Cup with a 78-0 thrashing of Fiji, with two players being sent off from the fiery clash on the Gold Coast.

New Zealand was ruthless from the opening whistle, scoring 13 tries in a one-sided contest.

The Kiwis had scored eight tries in the first half and with the result beyond doubt, before the match was thrown into turmoil when each team had a player marched from the field after an ugly episode.

New Zealand winger Ronaldo Mulitalo, who scored one of the Kiwis' eight first-half tries, rushed out of the defensive line and hit Fiji's Ronald Philitoga flush in the head with his shoulder.

That high-shot had the Fiji Bati players seeing red, with halfback Brandon Wakeham hitting Mulitalo with a punch to the head while he was still on the ground.

Referee Grant Atkins sent both players from the field, with each player certain to be on the charge sheet when it is released tomorrow.

Wakeham will play no further part in the World Cup with the Bati failing to make the semifinals, but Mulitalo's hopes of playing in the semifinals appear to be in serious doubt.

One week after giving Australia a huge scare at Lang Park, the Fijian Bati were hoping to pull off a huge upset in Saturday's de facto semifinal.

But the Kiwis were ruthless from the start, scoring four tries in the opening 12 minutes to end any hope of the Bati knocking them out of the competition like they did in 2017.

The Kiwis scored its first try in the second minute through Jahrome Hughes, then crossed again three minutes later when fullback Keano Kini used his speed to slice through the defensive line.

Centre Casey McLean scored the Kiwis' third in the ninth minute, then Bati captain Apisai Koroisau suffered a head knock which ruled him out of the remaining 70 minutes.

When Dane Gagai picked up a loose ball that was dropped by the Bati on their goal-line to score in the 12th minute, the score was 24-0 and the match was all but over.

The Kiwis would score another four tries to round out a spirit-breaking 48-0 first half.

The tension at the Gold Coast did not cool after the two send-offs, with several big shots and a pair of flare-ups between the two sides.

Kiwi lock Joseph Tapine was put on report for a high tackle, while Bati interchange player Jordan Miller was sent to the sin bin late for an alleged headbutt.

The Kiwis would score five more tries in the second half, with McLean ending the day with four.

Jamayne Isaako was perfect off the kicking tee, converting all 13 shots at goal.

The Kiwis will likely face either Tonga or Samoa in the semifinals, while England still has a mathematical chance of qualifying for the knock-out phase.

World.title: Ferrari fastest as Verstappen says Kiwi rival should 'act a little smarter'
World.content:
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fastest in both practice sessions for a Mexico City Grand Prix set to crown 20-year-old Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli as Formula 1's youngest champion.

Antonelli missed Thursday's media day to recover from a viral illness, but the Italian was second on the time sheets in the first session and fourth in the later one at the capital's high-altitude Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title in Mexico The Mexico City Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Kimi Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Antonelli is 123 points clear of teammate George Russell at the top and needs only two more points, a ninth place, to be sure of the title while the Briton has to win on Sunday to stay mathematically in the game with four rounds remaining.

Leclerc, who was also fastest in both Friday sessions in Texas last week before Antonelli won, produced a best effort of 1:17.827 in the second practice, when the times were much closer, after going top in the first by 0.659 with a lap of 1:18.128.

"Overall, our performance looks quite all right, but we still need to work on some of our limiting factors. It was quite tricky on track today, as the surface was slippery," Leclerc said.

McLaren's reigning world champion and last year's winner, Lando Norris, was second fastest in the later session, 0.103 slower, with Russell third.

Leclerc's teammate and seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, a two-time winner in Mexico, stopped on track and triggered a virtual safety car with half an hour remaining. "I lost all power," Hamilton said.

Red flags were shown and the session halted after Red Bull's Max Verstappen, a five-time winner in Mexico, and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, a former teammate, made contact with 47 minutes to go, leaving debris from the Dutch driver's car on the track.

"He literally just drove into me. Every weekend," Lawson said over the radio.

Verstappen hit back at the New Zealander, whose place has yet to be confirmed for next year.

"At the end of the day, it is not going to change my weekend, but if I were him I would act a little smarter. And when you're fighting for your seat, it's not very smart behaviour," he said.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Mexico City Grand Prix on Monday, November 2, from 5:30am AEDT.

Reuters

World.title: Fancied Melbourne Cup horse Defiantly ruled out by vets
World.content:
One of the leading international challengers for the Melbourne Cup, Defiantly, has been ruled out of the race after failing a vet's inspection on Saturday.

The Joseph O'Brien-trained horse, which had been a long-time favourite for the race, had won the Group Two Prix Kergorlay race over 3,000m at Deauville in France.

Defiantly was in quarantine at Werribee after arriving in Australia, and had failed an initial inspection on Thursday.

The horse was re-examined on Saturday morning.

"In the opinion of the veterinarians, Defiantly remains unsuitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup and has been withdrawn from the race by order of the stewards acting on veterinary advice," Racing Victoria said in a statement.

Williams eyes Melbourne Cup success Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Craig Williams hopes racing's version of a blind date will quickly evolve into a successful partnership as he eyes further glory in the race that stops a nation.

Defiantly's absence makes it likely that another Joseph O'Brien-trained horse, Kizlyar, will take its place in the field.

Two other international chances in the race, Enfjaar and Wine Dark Sea, had also failed initial assessments, but they passed inspection on Saturday and are approved to accept their spots in Tuesday's race.

Defiantly is the second international ruled out of this year's Melbourne Cup. Japanese entry Stinger Glass was ruled out after CT and PET scans showed the horse was at heightened risk of injury.

The Ciaron Maher-trained Saint George, who was runner-up in the Caulfield Cup a fortnight ago, before coming fifth in the Cox Plate last weekend, was also removed from the race after CT scans showed he was at heightened risk of injury.

The scans and vet inspections are part of veterinary protocols to ensure each horse is suitable to accept a place in the final field.

The field will be finalised at 4:30pm AEDT, followed by the Melbourne Cup draw an hour later.

ABC

World.title: Triple premiership coach Chris Fagan joins Carlton as director of football
World.content:
Chris Fagan has made the next step in his football career, with the triple premiership coach joining Carlton as director of coaching.

The newly created role will see Fagan, who announced his departure from Brisbane after the team's third consecutive grand final win, join the Blues to provide support to coach Josh Fraser.

The move reunites Fagan with Blues chief executive Graham Wright. The pair worked together at Hawthorn when Fagan was head of coaching and development and then general manager of football operations as the Hawks won three flags in a row between 2013 and 2015.

Fagan steps down from Brisbane Lions AFL premiership-winning coach Chris Fagan has stepped down from the club days after securing a third-straight grand final victory.

In a club statement Fagan said the chance to join the Blues was "an opportunity too good to pass up".

"While I loved my 10 years as a senior coach, this is a role I am passionate about and where I know I can have a real impact in this next phase of my football career," Fagan said.

"Supporting people to get the absolute best out of themselves is what I love most about football, so the chance to now be able to do that on a full-time basis is incredibly exciting.

"I can't wait to connect with each person in the football department, and in particular work closely with Josh to help every coach and player be the best Carlton person they can possibly be."

After four finals in 2023 and 2024 combined, Carlton missed finals in 2025 before coach Michael Voss was sacked after a 1-8 start to 2026.

Interim coach (now permanent) Fraser then led the Blues to 11 wins and a draw from the final 14 games to get Carlton to the finals. The Blues beat Melbourne in a wild card game before an elimination final loss to Geelong.

ABC

World.title: Ruthless Cats crush Bulldogs in AFLW finals statement
World.content:
Geelong star Jacqueline Parry has kicked five goals on return from injury to help the Cats ruthlessly cut down the Western Bulldogs by 68 points and lock in a top-two AFLW finish.

The Cats were simply a class above the Bulldogs on Friday night, piling on seven straight goals across the first half en route to a 13.10 (88) to 3.2 (20) triumph at Kardinia Park.

Geelong (11-1) can finish no lower than second on the ladder, with defending premiers North Melbourne — who boast the better percentage — to take on lowly Richmond on Saturday.

Rejuvenated by flag-winning coach Mick Stinear's arrival at the end of last year, the Cats will end their two-year absence from finals in red-hot form after extending their winning streak to 11 games.

The Bulldogs (8-4) have similarly enjoyed a change in fortunes in their third season under coach Tam Hyett, sitting sixth ahead of the weekend's games to earn their first finals berth since 2022.

But Friday's result will be a crude reminder of where the Bulldogs realistically sit in the premiership race.

The visitors could do little to contain Geelong's star on-ball brigade, with Georgie Prespakis controlling the tempo alongside Amy McDonald and Mikayla Bowen.

Parry's five majors on return from concussion saw her surpass Sydney star Chloe Molloy (24 goals) with a league-high 26 goals this season, while young gun Chantal Mason kicked three.

There was no hero to spark the comeback for the Bulldogs, with experienced midfielder Ellie Blackburn rested ahead of finals.

Co-captain Deanna Berry was playing in her first game since round two, but her lone goal in the third quarter — which was the final score for the Bulldogs — was not enough.

Berry had struggled to break back into the side after being sidelined for a month with a collarbone injury earlier this season.

Cats forward Parry wasted no time in making her return known and drew first blood within the opening minute.

The Bulldogs went coast-to-coast to find an immediate response through a Rylie Wilcox goal, only for the visitors to then lose their way.

Geelong soared to a 20-point lead at the first break after taking 86 disposals to the visitors' 41, and 11 forward entries to just two in the first quarter.

The gulf between the Cats and the Bulldogs became more apparent, with the hosts building to a 44-point lead at half-time en route to victory.

AAP

Tech.title: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
Tech.content:
While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page.

My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions.

Tech.title: Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it’s hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape, which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced single “Down On My Luck”? Maybe you didn’t even realize that Mensa was a rapper. Maybe you know him from his roles on The Chi or Bel-Air. Or perhaps you’re mostly aware of him through his activism, social media presence (peeling oranges and waxing poetic), or his podcast The Vic Mensa Show.

Point is, the man wears many hats. Part of the secret to being so prolific, it turns out, is Voice Memos. Just capture those ideas before they disappear.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Voice Memos. Everything starts there for me. Songs, essay ideas, orange tree thoughts, voice notes to myself at some wild hour, little things my son says that I do not want to lose. My phone is a million distractions in one rectangle, but Voice Memos is one of the few parts of it that still feels honest. Just press record before the thought disappears.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

Instagram, for better or worse. That’s definitely where my voice has really found its legs. I started out peeling an orange and talking through whatever was on my mind, and it turned into this whole conversation with people about politics, history, music, grief, jokes, fatherhood, all of it. That response helped show me there was room for The Vic Mensa Show too. Instagram can be a circus, obviously, but it’s also a very valuable tool for connection.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

Maybe Meta glasses. Them motherfuckers seem like they’re being used for evil.

What creation are you most proud of?

Probably my upcoming album right now. It’s the first album that I’ve really taken myself completely seriously as a producer. The surrounding art, videos, design, clothing, and world I’m building around it is something that really excites me as well.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I either do my Shambhavi Mahamudra meditation that I learned from Sadhguru or the Wim Hof breathing method. Ideally, I’ll do the Wim Hof breathing method in the steam room and then the meditation.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Anything that touches your life every day. A good mattress. Good headphones. Quality food. Clothes you will actually keep for years. Experiences with your child. I have wasted money on plenty of dumb shit, so I am trying to be better about buying things that either last or make a real memory.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Live from the contradiction.

What is the last GIF or meme you used?

Ummm… that is not Vic Mensa. Also, the letter casing here is pure chaos.

Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 150, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy Halloween, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)

This week, I was in the Smoky Mountains in Tennessee on a family vacation. It was delightful (and the reason this week’s Installer is a little short). I’ve also been reading about job hunting and 30 Rock and crypto detectives, testing the DuckDuckGo browser after a bunch of you told me to add it to the list, watching the adorable new Pixar short over and over, getting caught up on VisionQuest, playing with my new Pebble Index 01 now that it finally arrived, listening to music on my rad-looking new CMF Speaker S, and eating a worrying number of pumpkin chocolate chip muffins.

I also have for you some new gear from Apple and Amazon, a better way to read books on your phone, a resurrected note-taking app, an absurdly expensive robovac, and much more. Let’s do it.

(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / listening to / playing / giving to trick-or-treaters this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)

The Drop

The new iPad Mini . With apologies to With apologies to the touchscreen iMac , this is the most intriguing new Apple product of the week. I, too, am annoyed that there’s no ProMotion screen, but I’m excited about thinner and lighter, and I’m very excited about the idea of a functionally water- and dustproof tablet.

Tech.title: Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts
Tech.content:
“Its James Talarico. Can you please please please please pretty pretty please rush in even just $1?”

“Who’s working to elect James Talarico? Marxists.”

“Wow! Wow! Wow! Mark Kelly just made a HUGE announcement!”

“We asked Ben Verlander, MLB analyst and former Tigers prospect, to record a quick video about the election this Tuesday, November 3rd.”

“See which of your friends or family members have voted in the past and remind them to vote this year.”

If any of these messages sound familiar, it’s likely because they’re part of the massive stream of text messages flooding your phone leading up to the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The scale of the issue is not entirely clear, but call-blocking company Robokiller found that 15 billion political texts were sent in 2022, thanks in part to a Supreme Court decision the year prior that made it easier to send some mass calls and texts without consent. Alex Quilici, CEO of spam protection service YouMail, has an even higher estimate of 25 billion to 30 billion political texts this year, but caveats it’s an informal approximation. The volume is about the same to 10 percent higher than in 2024, he says.

There’s some good news and some bad news about these messages, says PIRG consumer watchdog director Teresa Murray. “The bad news is that political calls and political texts are exempt from the do-not-call-list rules,” Murray says. “The good news is that the election is next Tuesday, and hopefully within a few days after that, we’ll know what the results are and there won’t be any need to have any texts, or calls, or emails anymore after that.”

There are still some things consumers can try to stem the flow of these messages blowing up their phones — but it likely won’t significantly reduce it before Tuesday.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts … there are going to be some scams in there”

The simplest thing you can do is send “stop” or block and report the messages as spam, which will notify your service provider of a likely spam number. That probably won’t result in any immediate change, Murray says, but if enough people report the same number in a certain period of time, the provider might begin to block it or label it as spam. You can also file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission or your state attorney general if you believe a number is using an autodialer without your consent — something that even the people behind political texts are not supposed to do. Whatever you do, Murray says, do not click any links you receive from numbers you don’t know.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts that are going out to support this candidate, or vote against that candidate, or vote for this issue, or whatever, there are going to be some scams in there,” Murray says. “If you want to donate money at this point, I would recommend going directly to the website for that political candidate, or for that PAC, and donating it that way.”

How did all of these campaigns get your number in the first place? If you’ve donated to a political candidate or issue group, that might seem obvious. But campaigns are also likely getting your information — including details about whether you might be likely to contribute to or vote for their candidate or issue — through data brokers that have nothing to do with politics. Data brokers collect and sell information from both public and private sources, such as public voter rolls, your online behavior observed by advertising web trackers, and loyalty programs. By collating all of this information, campaigns can try to infer your behavior, though they also might end up with outdated info, like old addresses that lead you to getting texts about a state you no longer live in (or even erroneous info that invites them for states you never lived in).

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do?’”

“Errors in the processing of this information and the identification of individuals are very prevalent,” says Sara Geoghegan, consumer privacy program director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Sometimes multiple people use the same device. Sometimes people have similar names. Sometimes people move. And this is such an unregulated ecosystem that there aren’t really rules in place to make sure that this is being effective and accurate, let alone free from bias, discrimination, and verified for privacy impact before processing this information.

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do, and how many numbers do they need to block, and what are the toggle and privacy settings that they should toggle on?’” Geoghegan says. Meanwhile, “the companies that are trading in our most sensitive information are the ones who should stop harmful surveillance and the use of harmful technologies to have us better engage civically with our society, and not the other way around,” she says.

“I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”

Geoghegan worries that the harm of being bombarded with unwanted political texts isn’t just that people get annoyed, but that they stop engaging civically as a result. “Having this surveillance apparatus that invades people’s privacy and really annoys them actually pushes people away from this,” she says. “I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”

Unfortunately, you might get on some political text lists whether you engage in the civic process or not because of data brokers. Murray says the best long-term solution to minimize these spam messages is to limit how frequently you give out your phone number in general, like in an online shopping portal. If you need to give a number, you might consider using a VoIP number like a free Google Voice number, so at least you can silo those messages into another app you don’t need to frequently check or get notifications from.

Murray says she rarely gives out her personal number and limits where she gives out her Google Voice number, too. But even she has seen an uptick in political texts over the past couple of weeks. That’s likely in part because some groups may try to dial numbers in order in a certain area code, or her number could still be floating around on lists from long ago. “You can’t really do anything about the people or the businesses or the political entities that you have already shared your number with in the past,” Murray says. “But I would encourage people to just draw a line in the sand.”

Murray and Geoghegan encourage consumers to take the actions available to them to help limit the unwanted texts they receive, but they say the real solutions to the broader issue will likely come from Congress or regulators. Geoghegan says greater enforcement of existing laws could limit robocalls and texts, and Murray says concerned voters could contact their representatives about putting more pressure on the FCC to address the problems.

“Don’t get just frustrated with what you can’t change in four days, but you may be able to make a difference for the future,” Murray says. “By all means, reply to a text and say, ‘Stop.’ … But just don’t make it your life’s quest because it’s probably a fool’s errand.”

Tech.title: Apple Intelligence is finally coming to China with iOS 27.3
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple will launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3, the company announced on its Chinese newsroom website, as reported by MacRumors. The Apple Intelligence features will be available first in an iOS 27.3 beta that’s set to launch on November 4th, with a full iOS 27.3 release scheduled for December.

This launch doesn’t bring the new Siri AI to China. Instead, Apple is launching several of its earlier Apple Intelligence features like notification summaries, real-time translation, rewriting and proofreading tools, visual intelligence, and removing objects from photos. Apple also says it has worked with Ailbaba to add support for its Qwen chatbot in some experiences, which sounds similar to iOS’s integration with OpenAI’s ChatGPT that launched in 2024.

Apple Intelligence was approved in China in July, which signalled that the launch of the AI tools was getting near. Apple trained its own LLM specifically for China, Reuters reported in August.

Tech.title: Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set.

While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key.

The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample.

Previous Next



1 / 3

There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment.

Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths.

Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

Tech.title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
Tech.content:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.

But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.

You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”

Tech.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.

The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.

The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”

Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.

While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”

Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

Tech.title: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
Tech.content:
“I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”

I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh!), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.

By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.

Image Credits:Cheddar

When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.

As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases. I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.

As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.

Image Credits:Cheddar

There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.

“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”

As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)

I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.

Image Credits:Cheddar

Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.

Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.

This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)

In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.

Image Credits:Pinterest screenshot

For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.

Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.

I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.

However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.

This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.

Image Credits:Apple

It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.

Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.

There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.

Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID.)

Image Credits:Apple

Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.

Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.

For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.

Below are a few photos shot with the Duo versus others shot with the 17 Pro Max. None of the photos are using any special settings or filters; they are intentionally just average, non-professional point-and-shoot shots. Among my complaints are that the Duo’s image processing can, at times, make fine details, like the leaves on trees, look overprocessed. Meanwhile, distant landscapes can appear flatter or smoothed over — though, to be fair, the Blue Ridge Mountains are naturally hazy, so it’s hard to say how much of that is the camera. (Shots from the mountaintop were in low-light conditions — it was getting dark out.)

DUO PHOTOS:
